text:
September is putting electric transportation in the spotlight, and PECO is using National Drive Electric Month and National Clean Energy Week (Sept. 14-18) to connect southeastern Pennsylvania customers with resources that can help them make the switch to an EV.

Together, the two national campaigns highlight the connection between cleaner energy and smarter transportation.

PECO supports the region’s transition to electric transportation by strengthening the local energy grid to meet customers’ evolving needs, expanding the use of electric vehicles in its own operations, and providing practical resources for customers interested in making the switch.

Customers can use PECO’s EVsmart online toolkit to compare electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles, find public charging stations, and explore the potential costs and environmental benefits of driving electric.

The toolkit also connects customers with information on available tax credits and rebates, including PECO’s $50 EV Driver Rebate. Customers can also explore time-of-use rates, PECO’s Flex & Save program to help lower at-home charging costs, and incentives for installing charging equipment at homes and businesses.

These efforts are part of PECO’s Path to Clean. PECO and its parent company Exelon are on a mission to reduce operations-driven emissions by 50 percent by 2030 and achieve net-zero operations-driven emissions by 2050.

As part of that commitment, PECO currently operates approximately 340 electrified vehicles, including fully electric vehicles, hybrids, and vehicles with plug-in idle-mitigation units.

It just got a little easier to top up your EV’s battery at Red E Charge stations across the United States.

text:
Red E Charge is adding a nice convenience feature at its EV chargers across the United States.

After an initial account setup, drivers will no longer need a physical credit card or the company’s smartphone app to charge.

Red E Charge was one of the fastest-growing DC fast charging networks in the second quarter, ahead of Electrify America, EVgo, and Ionna.

It just got a little easier to top up your EV’s battery at Red E Charge stations across the United States. The Detroit-based company, which was one of the fastest-growing DC charging networks in the country in the second quarter, has enabled Plug & Charge functionality at many of its dispensers.

With Plug & Charge, EV drivers need to complete a one-time setup in the charging network’s smartphone app, adding details about their vehicle and a payment method. After the setup is complete, they can simply plug in and charge at compatible stations, with the payment being handled automatically. No more scanning QR codes, opening an app, or getting out a credit card.

The operator has dubbed this service Red E Go, saying that the feature is available at certain stations. Currently, the network has over 1,000 locations and roughly 4,600 charging ports across 46 American states, according to the Department of Energy’s Alternative Fuels Data Center. Out of the total, 2,159 ports offer fast charging at 579 stations, with 600 of the locations also offering almost 2,500 Level 2 charging ports.

On the DC charging side, Red E was the fourth fastest-growing network in the country in the second quarter of this year, according to a Paren report. With 315 new ports, Red E ranked below Tesla, Walmart, and ChargePoint, but overtook Electrify America, EVgo, and Ionna.

What’s more, Red E’s customers are quite happy with the charging experience. The network ranked fifth in terms of overall satisfaction in JD Power’s latest Electric Vehicle Experience (EVX) Public Charging Study, after Ionna, the Mercedes-Benz Charging Network, the Rivian Adventure Network, and Tesla’s Supercharger network. With 628 points on a 1,000-point scale, Red E was just below the 666-point segment average, but higher than Electrify America, EVgo, and ChargePoint.

The power output of Red E’s stalls ranges from just 10 kilowatts to a rather impressive 640 kilowatts, depending on the location and plug type. The network offers J1772, CCS1, NACS, and CHAdeMO plugs, with prices ranging from $0.40/kilowatt-hour to $1.15/kWh, according to DCFC Tracker.

title: Chinese-Made EVs Surpass 35% Share in South Korea—8% Tariff Wall Proves Inadequate
description:
Chinese-made vehicles have surpassed a 35% share of South Korea's electric vehicle market this year.
Chinese-made vehicles accounted for just 1.1% of South Korea's EV market in 2021.
Tariff Barriers in Major Economies vs. South Korea's Reality Major auto-producing nations are raising defensive barriers against Chinese-made EVs.
Debate on Introducing a Production Tax Credit Japan has already shifted from consumption subsidy-centered policies to supporting domestic production investment.

text:
Chinese-made vehicles have surpassed a 35% share of South Korea's electric vehicle market this year. The share stood at just over 12% only two years ago, and its rapid expansion has prompted warnings that South Korea's finished-vehicle industry could follow the same collapse trajectory as Italy's.

At a seminar on "Measures to Strengthen the Competitiveness of South Korea's EV Industry" held at the National Assembly Members' Office Building in Yeouido, Seoul on the 18th, Park Jung-kyu, visiting professor at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) Graduate School of Technology Management, pointed to Italy as the path South Korea must avoid, stating, "When finished vehicles collapse, the parts ecosystem collapses with them."

Italy was once an automotive powerhouse producing 2 million vehicles annually, but production plummeted to 238,000 units last year, dropping the country out of the world's top 20 producers. The demise of its finished-vehicle industry led to a cascading collapse of the parts ecosystem.

Chinese-Made EVs Now Account for One in Three Sold in South Korea

South Korean EV sales totaled 235,000 units from January through July this year, up 99.3% from the same period a year earlier. Of that total, Chinese-made vehicles surged 148.9% to 83,000 units. Yoon Kyung-sun, managing director at the Korea Automobile & Mobility Association (KAMA), said, "The share of Chinese-made vehicles in South Korea's EV market has expanded from 12.6% in 2023 to 35.3% in the January-July period this year."

BYD, China's largest EV maker, climbed to fourth place in South Korean EV sales on the back of surging domestic demand. Other Chinese automakers including Geely, XPeng, and Chery are also expanding their presence in South Korea, while Chinese parts suppliers that have acquired South Korean component makers are becoming increasingly active.

Chinese-made vehicles accounted for just 1.1% of South Korea's EV market in 2021. The share has expanded more than 30-fold in just over four years.

Tariff Barriers in Major Economies vs. South Korea's Reality

Major auto-producing nations are raising defensive barriers against Chinese-made EVs. According to KAMA, the United States imposes a total of 127.5% on Chinese-made EVs, combining base tariffs with Section 301 and Section 232 tariffs under the Trade Act. The European Union applies a base import tariff of 10% plus manufacturer-specific countervailing duties ranging from 17.0% to 35.3%, for a maximum of 45.3%.

Japan has implemented domestic production tax incentives and restructured its subsidy framework to favor domestic manufacturers. Mexico, Brazil, India, and Thailand are also protecting their industrial bases through high tariffs or local production requirements.

South Korea, by contrast, applies its existing tariff rate of 8% on Chinese-made passenger vehicles, as passenger cars were excluded from tariff elimination under the Korea-China Free Trade Agreement (FTA) that took effect in 2015. This is even lower than the 15% tariff China imposes on South Korean vehicles.

Park said, "Even in Europe, which defends itself with tariffs, Chinese brand share jumped from 4.5% to 11% in a single year. Markets without defensive measures get eroded within one to two years." In Chile, an open market with zero tariffs, Chinese-made vehicles account for 39% of all automobiles, while in Brazil they represent 95% of EVs.

China's "Swarm Strategy" and the Scale of Government Support

Park characterized China's competitive approach as a "swarm strategy." The central government sets the direction, local governments distribute subsidies, and numerous companies enter simultaneously, imitating and competing with one another. "Overcapacity created by subsidies ultimately floods out through exports," he explained.

According to a report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), Chinese government policy support for its domestic EV industry totaled $230.9 billion from 2009 to 2023. That amounts to 18.8% of China's total EV sales revenue over the same period.

Yoon summarized Chinese EVs' competitiveness as "a structural cost advantage combining government support, supply chain internalization, low production costs, and economies of scale." Chinese manufacturing wages are roughly 30% of South Korean levels.

China's export expansion is also steep. From 2020 to 2025, Chinese-brand automobile exports grew 12.1-fold to Russia, 8.1-fold to ASEAN, 6-fold to Latin America, and 5.3-fold to the Middle East. Even as China's domestic demand has been declining by around 20% each month this year, exports have risen to roughly 1 million units per month, keeping total sales on the same trajectory as the previous year. The next destination is the South Korean market, according to Park.

Debate on Introducing a Production Tax Credit

Japan has already shifted from consumption subsidy-centered policies to supporting domestic production investment. According to a report by the Korea Mobility Society, Japan had injected up to ¥671.1 billion (approximately $4.3 billion) in subsidies into finished vehicles and materials and equipment sectors as of March this year.

Discussions on production-linked support have also begun in South Korea. Rep. Yoon Han-hong of the ruling People Power Party introduced a bill last month to amend the Restriction of Special Taxation Act to include EVs in the Domestic Production Tax Credit. Lee Hyung-il, nominee for Minister of Economy and Finance, has also indicated he would gather industry input.

Chung Dae-jin, chairman of KAMA, stressed, "Corporate efforts alone are insufficient to counter the onslaught of Chinese-made EVs. We must support domestic investment through an EV production tax credit, demand expansion, R&D and facility investment support, and strengthening of core supply chains."

Yoon added, "We need to establish production-linked support mechanisms such as a domestic production tax credit, maintain EV purchase subsidies over the medium to long term, and strengthen differentiated support for domestically produced vehicles."

title: TERREPOWER launches EV battery lifecycle brand across EU and NA
description:
TERREPOWER has launched Ontility, a brand dedicated to EV battery lifecycle solutions covering reuse, remanufacturing, repurposing and recycling, across its operations in Europe and North America.
TERREPOWER CEO Duncan Gillis said both regions are entering a stage of EV adoption where extending battery life will matter as much as producing new batteries.
TERREPOWER pointed to EV adoption trends as the basis for entering both markets at this stage.
TERREPOWER's launch also coincides with tightening European regulation governing battery lifecycle management.
The regulation also raises portable battery collection targets and mandates full collection of automotive and industrial batteries for recycling.
text:
TERREPOWER has launched Ontility, a brand dedicated to EV battery lifecycle solutions covering reuse, remanufacturing, repurposing and recycling, across its operations in Europe and North America.

TERREPOWER, formerly known as BBB Industries, describes itself as the world's largest sustainable manufacturer by volume. Founded in 1987, the company operates 19 manufacturing facilities and 14 distribution centres across North America and Europe, selling products under 28 brands in more than 90 countries, with a focus on automotive and industrial aftermarket components.

Under Ontility, the company is offering validated, warranty-backed battery systems for out-of-warranty EVs, installation-ready units intended to reduce service turnaround time, and lower-cost alternatives to full battery replacement.

The brand also covers scalable lifecycle services for OEMs and aftermarket partners, as well as repurposing and recycling pathways once a battery reaches the end of its usable life in a vehicle.

TERREPOWER CEO Duncan Gillis said both regions are entering a stage of EV adoption where extending battery life will matter as much as producing new batteries.

"As millions of EVs age, the industry needs trusted partners capable of restoring, validating and extending battery value at scale," Gillis said.

Michael Boe, TERREPOWER's president for Europe, said the company's approach prioritises restoring batteries to service ahead of treating them as waste.

"By restoring batteries to service, we extend vehicle life, reduce material consumption and help create a more circular approach to electrification," Boe said.

TERREPOWER pointed to EV adoption trends as the basis for entering both markets at this stage.

The company cited North America's EV adoption rate, domestic battery manufacturing investment, and a regulatory environment that it said increasingly favours reuse over the extraction of virgin materials.

In Europe, TERREPOWER cited 38% year-on-year growth in battery EV sales in the first half of 2025, which it said would drive a surge in first-life batteries reaching the end of their automotive service life over the next three to five years.

Diagnostic gaps and tightening regulation are shaping the case for lifecycle management

The launch lands against a backdrop of emerging data showing meaningful variation in how individual EV batteries age, even within the same model.

Austrian diagnostics firm AVILOO found that battery health can differ by as much as 13.5% between individual examples of the same EV model, based on more than 500,000 independent tests, with AVILOO's CEO arguing that a gap of that size represents a real difference in range, resale value and reliability that dashboard readings alone cannot reveal.

A separate study from UK diagnostics firm Generational found that around 1 in 85 used EVs carries a hidden cell-level imbalance not visible through standard State of Health reporting, a fault that can affect range and charging behaviour without triggering any warning light.

Both findings point to a similar conclusion: a single health metric, whether from a model average or a dashboard reading, can obscure problems or variation that only direct testing uncovers, a gap that lifecycle management providers like Ontility are positioning themselves to address before deciding whether a battery should be restored, repurposed or recycled.

TERREPOWER's launch also coincides with tightening European regulation governing battery lifecycle management.

Under the EU's 2023 Batteries Regulation, industrial and electric vehicle batteries with a capacity above 2kWh placed on the market from January 2026 are required to carry a digital battery passport, an electronic record intended to track a battery's composition, condition and history through its life.

The regulation also raises portable battery collection targets and mandates full collection of automotive and industrial batteries for recycling.

text:
China Briefing 17 September 2026: EV five-year plan | BRICS summit | Clean-energy investment drop

Welcome to Carbon Brief’s China Briefing.

China Briefing handpicks and explains the most important climate and energy stories from China over the past fortnight. Subscribe for free here.

Snapshot

EV five-year plan published.

Xi said the global south “must improve global climate governance”.

Carbon-market allocation plan issued.

Carbon Brief examines why cleantech investment has fallen.

New science on link between temperature and crime, and aircraft payload.

Key developments

Xi’s speech at BRICS

SUMMIT STATEMENT: Chinese president Xi Jinping said at the BRICS summit in Delhi that global south countries “must improve global climate governance” and promote “full and effective implementation of the Paris Agreement”, said state news agency Xinhua. [BRICS is a grouping of countries including Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa.] According to the transcript, Xi also proposed greater cooperation on five areas, including “trade and investment”. The joint statement published at the summit recognises the “need to promote just, orderly, equitable and inclusive energy transitions and reduce [greenhouse gas] emissions in line with our climate goals”. But it also notes that “fossil fuels will still play an important role in the world’s energy mix”.

OTHER MEETINGS: Meanwhile, a meeting of APEC energy ministers – representing 21 economies across the Asia-Pacific – in Beijing resulted in a joint statement saying “[both] conventional and zero- and low-emission energy sources” provide “energy security” and “strong and sustainable economic growth”. It added that “each economy will choose an energy system mix consistent with its domestic priorities”. Separately, Chinese environment minister Huang Runqiu said at the Kunming dialogue, which discusses progress on the Kunming-Montreal global biodiversity framework, that countries must “strengthen resolve for action” on biodiversity, reported Earth Negotiations Bulletin.

EV five-year plan

SALES TARGET: China aims for “70% of new cars” to be electric vehicles [EV], plug-in hybrids or hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles by 2030, according to a new five-year plan for smart new-energy vehicles (NEVs), reported Bloomberg. It added that the plan also calls for “40% of new commercial vehicles sales” to be NEVs. A representative of Sinopec Economics and Development Research Institute, a thinktank attached to one of China’s largest oil companies, told Reuters that NEVs could comprise 75-80% of new domestic car sales by 2030, up from 65% currently. [See Captured below.]

MARKET ‘LEAD’: “Policy targets for NEV market share have lagged market developments for several years,” Anders Hove, senior research fellow at the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies, told Carbon Brief. He added that this was a signal of the government’s “desire to allow the market to take the lead” in determining the future trajectory of the industry. The plan also included calls to “curb overinvestment” and encourage “industry consolidation”.

COST CLAMPDOWN: Meanwhile, the government also issued a notice on “low-price disorderly competition” that includes pledges to scrutinise reported costs in sectors such as EVs, said the Hong Kong-based South China Morning Post. Carmakers are also being encouraged to “pay suppliers faster”, as part of ongoing efforts to combat the “price war” in the industry, said Bloomberg. Approvals for planned new battery manufacturing capacity have also been “suspended”, reported Cailianshe.

More sectoral plans

CLEANTECH MANUFACTURING: A new five-year plan covering advanced electronics manufacturing called for consolidating China’s lead in batteries and solar, reported BJX News. The power-news outlet added that the plan also called for developing “next-generation” technologies, such as space-based solar and solid-state batteries.

EMISSIONS ACCOUNTING: A five-year plan on statistics reform and development was also released, reported financial newspaper Securities Times. It said the plan set goals including: improving carbon-emissions accounting; energy and emissions reporting; and links between energy and emissions data.

OTHER PLANS: State broadcaster CCTV News said that an information and communications sector five-year plan set out several targets for the industry’s “green development”. A five-year plan for culture and tourism development also called for “greening” the sector, said state news agency Xinhua. A five-year “implementation plan” for coordinating the “digital and green transition” encouraged computing facilities to meet provincial renewable-energy consumption quotas by 2030, reported BJX News.

More China news

CARBON ALLOWANCES: China has issued new carbon-market allocation plans for the power sector for 2025 and 2026, as well as for steel, cement and aluminium in 2026, according to the People’s Daily.

POWER ‘PUSHBACK’: ClearBlue Markets’ principal analyst Qin Yan wrote on Bluesky that the carbon-market plans only tightened coal-power benchmarks by 0.1%, following “pushback from the power industry”.

FLOODED CITY: Torrential rain from Typhoon Saudel flooded Putian city in Fujian province, breaking daily precipitation records, reported state broadcaster CGTN.

DISRUPTIVE RAINS: Over 42,000 people were evacuated as heavy rains in south China’s Hainan province triggered flooding, said state-run newspaper China Daily. In Jiangxi province, the death toll from rain-fuelled mud- and landslides has risen to 16, said the Associated Press, citing state media.

EXPORT SURGE: China’s electric-vehicle (EV) exports jumped 155% year-on-year, while domestic sales shrunk by 10%, according to Reuters.

‘DANGEROUS DEPENDENCIES’: European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said in her state of the union address that the EU has “dangerous dependencies” on China for materials such as critical minerals. She added that the EU must “double down on our affordable, homegrown, clean energy”.

Captured

Sales of new-energy vehicles (battery EVs and plug-in hybrid EVs) accounted for 65% of the total vehicle sales in China in August 2026, according to data from the China Passenger Car Association, courtesy of Robbie Andrew.

Spotlight

Why China’s clean-energy investment is falling

In this issue, Carbon Brief looks at Rhodium Group findings that China’s investment in clean energy fell in the first half of 2026, driven by changes in the domestic policy landscape.

China invested $294bn in clean energy in the first half of 2026, a 36% decrease year-on-year, according to research firm the Rhodium Group.

Its figures include the manufacturing and deployment of clean-energy technologies, as well as decarbonisation of industry.

Investment fell 49% to $141bn in the first three months of the year, compared to the last quarter of 2025. It then rose slightly to $153bn in the second quarter.

As a result, Rhodium found that China’s share of global cleantech investment also fell from 52% in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 39% in the second quarter this year.

Nevertheless, the country remained the world’s largest investor in the energy transition by far in the first half of the year. It outspent the next-largest investor – the EU – by $100bn.

China’s investment decline comes after several years of expansion. Its investment in clean energy rose from $185bn in 2019 to $725bn in 2023, $844bn in 2024 and $906bn in 2025, according to Rhodium figures.

Sectoral shifts

By sector, investment in electric vehicles (EVs) fell to $136bn in the first half of 2026, roughly 26% below the same period in 2025, according to the data.

This was caused by a decline in purchases of electric cars and vans – so-called light-duty EVs – which make up the vast majority of all EV sales.

By contrast, purchases of medium- and heavy-duty EVs, such as buses and trucks, “moved in the opposite direction”, said the report, rising 64% from the first half of 2025.

Alfredo Rivera, associate director at the Rhodium Group and one of the authors of the report, told Carbon Brief that the divergence reflected “different stages of market development and different demand drivers”.

He explained that the economics of medium- and heavy-duty EVs have been improved by falling battery costs, expanding charging and battery-swapping networks, as well as government support for replacing older commercial vehicles.

Meanwhile, in the clean-electricity generation and storage sector, investment dropped by 43% to $134bn in the first half of 2026.

Solar remained the largest segment, but saw investment fall 66% year-on-year to $54bn, while wind fell 26% to $31bn.

Investment in the manufacturing of clean-energy technologies and the decarbonisation of industry also decreased by 41% year-on-year to $24bn in the first half of 2026, continuing a decline from a 2023 peak.

Policy drivers

Rhodium linked the decline in investment – particularly the 49% drop in the first quarter – to the timing of changes in domestic policy.

For example, a 2025 policy on shifting China’s power markets towards market-based pricing drove a rush of solar installation in the second quarter of last year.

This pushed forward the completion of solar projects that could otherwise have come online in 2026, making this year’s additions look small by comparison. Nevertheless, installations so far this year remain comparable to 2023 levels.

Similarly, EV purchases increased in the final quarter of 2025 ahead of changes to purchase-tax incentives, which came into force in January. This leads to a decline in investments in EVs – particularly light-duty EVs.

Prof Christoph Nedopil at the University of Queensland, who was not involved in the research, told Carbon Brief that quarterly figures can reflect policy and geopolitical factors that bring investment forward or cause it to be delayed.

However, he noted, they “should not be over-interpreted as long-term trends”. He added: “Looking at the annual trends, the numbers suggest continued strong [cleantech] manufacturing investment growth across China and the world.”

Watch, read, listen

YEAR IN REVIEW: An Ember launch event unpacked the findings from its new report on China’s energy transition progress.

HORMUZ RESPONSE: The Energy Policy Now podcast examined how the Hormuz crisis is testing China’s energy security strategy.

MONEY MATTERS: Bloomberg’s Zero podcast discussed how China became a “green-finance superpower”.

FOSSIL TRANSITION: NGO Germanwatch featured China’s starting points and trends in a paper on transitioning away from fossil fuels through renewables-based electrification.

title: EPA eliminates rule that limits planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants
description:
WASHINGTON -- The Environmental Protection Agency said Monday it is repealing rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas and announced it is taking a separate but related step to prevent future administrations from regulating climate pollution from power plants.
Environmental groups also are likely to challenge the separate rule proposed Monday that could prevent future administrations from regulating greenhouse gas emissions from power plants.
The February action eliminated all greenhouse gas emissions standards for cars and trucks.
Coal-fired power plants would have been forced to capture smokestack emissions or shut down under a strict EPA rule issued in 2024.
Greenhouse gas emissions from coal and gas-fired plants "are a small and decreasing part of global emissions,″ the EPA said.
text:
WASHINGTON -- The Environmental Protection Agency said Monday it is repealing rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas and announced it is taking a separate but related step to prevent future administrations from regulating climate pollution from power plants.

The rule change, first proposed last year, represents a fundamental shift from efforts by Democratic Presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama to address climate change and regulate carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases that trap the sun's heat.

Environmental groups decried the change, saying it would come at a cost to Americans' health and further degrade the environment.

Revoking the Biden-era power plant rule would save industry more than $300 billion in costs and help "unleash" American energy, the EPA said. The change will allow utilities to "make the best decision for the ratepayers based on cost and cost savings, instead of being required to shut down facilities," said EPA Assistant Administrator Aaron Szabo.

The power plant rule, to take effect soon after publication in the Federal Register, is expected to face immediate legal challenges.

Environmental groups also are likely to challenge the separate rule proposed Monday that could prevent future administrations from regulating greenhouse gas emissions from power plants. The proposal, expected to be made final next year, follows on EPA's action earlier this year revoking a scientific finding that long has been the central basis for U.S. action to regulate greenhouse gas emissions and fight climate change.

The February action eliminated all greenhouse gas emissions standards for cars and trucks. The new plan would apply similar logic to a broader undoing of climate regulations on stationary sources such as power plants.

ANNOUNCEMENTS COINCIDE WITH GATHERING OF G20 ENERGY OFFICIALS

The announcements came as EPA chief Lee Zeldin, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Energy Secretary Chris Wright host a G20 ministerial meeting on "energy abundance" in Houston. The announcement of the rule, coming on the same day, is both a nod to the important role oil-rich Texas plays in the energy industry and a potential snub of European and other international allies in attendance who have pursued environmentally friendly policies that the Trump administration has moved to undo.

Republican President Donald Trump called climate change "the greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world" at a speech to the United Nations last year, and his administration withdrew the U.S. -- for the second time -- from the 2015 Paris climate accord that sets voluntary goals to curb planet-warming emissions.

Trump has boasted of U.S. energy abundance even as the Iran war continues to disrupt global fuel markets and gas prices top $4.31 a gallon, up more than a dollar from a year ago.

The rollbacks are meant to fulfill Trump's repeated pledge to " unleash American energy " and make it easier for utilities to supply electricity for homes and businesses.

Former Vice President Al Gore said the EPA's action moves the United States "in the exact opposite direction of the rest of the world. With ongoing disruption in global energy markets, the clear answer to rising costs and energy security is clean energy."

Even as the Trump administration "is dragging the U.S. backwards," the transition to clean energy "will continue to take hold ... both in the U.S. and globally," Gore said Monday in a email to The Associated Press. "That's because clean energy is cheaper, creates more jobs and bolsters energy security."

THE ADMINISTRATION HAS BEEN UNDOING DOZENS OF ENVIRONMENTAL REGULATIONS

The power plant rule is among nearly three dozen environmental regulations that Zeldin targeted in early 2025 when he announced what he called the "most consequential day of deregulation in American history."

Zeldin said Monday that the Trump administration "has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on."

Environmental and public health groups called the new rollbacks dangerous and vowed to challenge the rules in court.

"Tearing down our national protections against climate pollution from power plants will have enormous costs for the health, safety and well-being of families across the country," said Vickie Patton, general counsel for the Environmental Defense Fund. "Americans everywhere are already suffering from record-breaking heat, more dangerous floods and storms, and skyrocketing insurance costs."

The EPA has a legal responsibility to protect the public from harmful pollution, Patton said, adding that "clean, affordable and reliable technologies are widely available to power our homes and businesses."

Coal, gas and oil-fired power plants are responsible for about one-quarter of the nation's total climate pollution, second only to the transportation sector. Pollution from power plants is one of the largest sources of climate-changing pollution in the world.

TRUMP PROPOSALS TARGET EPA RULES THAT COULD PREVENT THOUSANDS OF DEATHS, AP ANALYSIS FINDS

The rules targeted by Trump's EPA could prevent an estimated 30,000 deaths and save $275 billion each year they are in effect, according to an Associated Press examination last year that included the agency's own prior assessments and a wide range of other research.

Even a partial dismantling of the rules would mean more pollutants such as smog, mercury and lead -- and especially more tiny airborne particles that can lodge in lungs and cause health problems, the AP analysis found. It would also mean higher emissions of greenhouse gases, driving Earth's warming to deadlier levels.

Biden, a Democrat, had made fighting climate change a hallmark of his presidency. Coal-fired power plants would have been forced to capture smokestack emissions or shut down under a strict EPA rule issued in 2024. Those rules are now being upended.

In its proposal last year, the Trump EPA argued that carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases from fossil fuel-fired power plants "do not contribute significantly to dangerous pollution" or climate change and therefore do not meet a threshold under the Clean Air Act for regulatory action. Greenhouse gas emissions from coal and gas-fired plants "are a small and decreasing part of global emissions,″ the EPA said.

Zeldin, a Republican and former New York congressman, said Biden-era actions were designed to "suffocate our economy in order to protect the environment," with the intent to regulate the coal industry "out of existence" and make it "disappear."

The coal industry and groups representing coal-fired power plants have denounced the Biden rule as "overreach" by the EPA and urged its repeal. Lifting the rule "will protect grid reliability and shield electricity consumers from higher costs at a time of surging demand from data centers, artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing," said Michelle Bloodworth, CEO of America's Power, a trade organization for the U.S. coal fleet.

title: States should make clean-energy lemonade - - Minot Daily News
description:
Western Europe suffered a record heat wave this summer.
New York has imposed a one-year moratorium on new hyperscale data centers.
New data centers have also become an issue in this year’s elections.
Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed has called for state and federal moratoriums on building data centers.
States could also require data centers to reuse cooling water.
text:
In 2026, Americans have been handed two lemons: a warming climate and an artificial intelligence data-center boom straining the nation’s electricity and water systems. Maybe it’s time to squeeze them together and make lemonade.

First lemon: Temperatures are rising around the world. Western Europe suffered a record heat wave this summer. Spain, for example, recorded 61 heat wave days, with Barcelona hitting 105 F, the hottest temperature since measurements began over a century ago. Researchers suspect rapid glacial melting and unusually warm conditions contributed to a catastrophic flood in Nepal.

Record heat is hitting the U.S. as well. In August, the Los Angeles suburb of Woodland Hills reached a record 111 F, while downtown LA itself tied its record of 98 F.

Scientists attribute global warming primarily to greenhouse gases, especially carbon dioxide released by burning fossil fuels like coal, oil and natural gas. And what is the Trump administration doing about all this? Fanning the flames. It has repealed most Biden-era carbon limits on coal- and gas-fired power plants, opened 13.1 million acres of federal land to future coal mining, halted new offshore-wind leasing, and used emergency authority to keep coal-fired generating plants open.

Second lemon: The AI gold rush requires staggering amounts of electricity to operate and grow. At the end of 2025, the U.S. had 580 operational hyperscale data centers, with another 437 in the development pipeline, run by companies like Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Meta and Oracle. A single new gigawatt-scale AI center can consume as much electricity as a sizable city.

Unwilling to wait for more generation capacity, Elon Musk’s xAI has been using 69 temporary mobile natural gas turbines at its site in Mississippi to power its data centers. The mobile turbines are relatively inefficient and can emit 40%-60% more CO2 per megawatt-hour than modern natural gas plants.

All this new demand is arriving as electricity prices are rising. Residential electricity prices nationally were 5% higher in June than they were a year earlier, with increases of more than 10% in some states, including Michigan and Pennsylvania.

On top of that, data centers can affect clean-water availability and cost, especially in arid regions and in communities where drinking water is used for cooling. Even three years ago, the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that generating the electricity used by U.S. data centers consumed roughly 211 billion gallons. Although a newer national water estimate is not yet available from the lab, data-center electricity consumption has continued to climb.

New York has imposed a one-year moratorium on new hyperscale data centers. Legislators in 15 other states are considering similar moves. Unwilling to wait, local governments in states including Michigan, Georgia, North Carolina, Indiana, Missouri and Illinois have imposed their own stoppages.

New data centers have also become an issue in this year’s elections. Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed has called for state and federal moratoriums on building data centers. Wyoming Republican U.S. House nominee Chuck Gray won his primary after campaigning to “stop data centers” and calling for a federal ban.

Lemonade: U.S. companies are racing to build these centers as they innovate and compete for leadership in AI. The projects bring investment and construction jobs, but they also impose substantial new demands on electricity and, in many cases, water.

Why then not require these hyperscale data centers to cover their added electricity demand with low- or zero-carbon generation, such as wind or solar? An AP-NORC/Energy Policy Institute poll conducted in July found 65% of Americans are in favor of requiring data centers to use clean energy.

Washington has imposed no such energy or water requirements. But states don’t have to wait. They can take action now.

With demand from leading American technology companies, accelerated investment and innovation in clean generation and storage has the potential to lower costs for all users. On top of that, state laws could help America become a leader in green energy despite the efforts of the current administration to stifle it.

States could also require data centers to reuse cooling water.

It looks like it’s up to the states to take action.

text:
Geothermal startup Mazama Energy raised $135 million in an oversubscribed Series B, the startup said Thursday.

The fresh funding will help the company develop horizontal wells in super-hot rocks capable of generating 15 megawatts of electricity per well.

Mazama plans to start generating electricity sometime next year and said its first site in Oregon is capable of producing 10 gigawatts of electricity. That’s a sharp upward revision from the company’s estimate last year, when investor Vinod Khosla said the site had the potential to produce 5 gigawatts.

Enhanced geothermal startups are shaping up to be the dark horse in the battle to power AI data centers and other large loads on the grid. While tech companies and data center developers have been throwing their weight behind natural gas, geothermal startups have been quickly advancing their technology.

Unlike previous geothermal projects, enhanced geothermal startups are targeting deeper and hotter rock. Mazama, for example, has drilled past 10,000 feet in 15 days on its way to about 15,000 feet deep. At those depths, the company can access 750˚ F (400˚ C) heat, which at high pressures turns water into a “supercritical” fluid that’s neither fully liquid nor fully gas — a state that lets it absorb far more energy than ordinary steam. Mazama said that will allow each well to produce up to 10 times more power than traditional geothermal technologies.

Given the depths Mazama is targeting, the potential payoff is significant. Tapping just 1% of super-hot rock worldwide could generate more than 63 terawatts of electricity, according to the University of Twente and the Clean Air Task Force.

While work at its Oregon site is still in the early stages, the startup has already secured land for a second development. Mazama aims to complete development of the first site by 2030, at which point it says it should generate 200 megawatts of electricity.

The new round was led by Centaurus Capital and Doerr Capital, with participation from ConocoPhillips and Shell Ventures. Existing investors including Khosla Ventures and Gates Frontier returned, and new investors SiteGround Capital, H. Barton Asset Management, and the Jeffrey and Marieke Rothschild Foundation also joined the round.

Mazama was incubated at Khosla Ventures.

text:
SALT LAKE CITY — The Trump administration is scrapping Biden-era emissions rules for power plants, saying the rollback will save the industry $310 billion.

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin finalized the repeal Sept. 14 — then pushed for more.

He proposed cutting every remaining greenhouse gas standard, projecting an additional $370 billion in savings.

The EPA's press release stated the Biden administration's greenhouse gas regulations "have imposed unnecessary requirements and drained the power sector's resources, while producing virtually no benefit."

The EPA's move strikes most of the 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards — stating the standards surpassed allotted authority by "requiring control technologies that are not adequately demonstrated, effectively forcing plants to retire rather than setting standards they could actually meet," the press release read.

Utah House Public Utilities and Energy Committee Chair Colin W. Jack, R-St. George, said the former administration's regulations are "the greatest threat" to electricity in recent years.

"That rule was a direct threat to modern life," he said. "We had to overrule that, and I'm just so relieved that it has finally happened."

Carbon vs. CO2: What's bad for you?

The true debate lies not in what legally can or cannot be enforced — but what ought to be.

Utah politicians hold different views on the effects CO2 emissions actually produce on the environment and health.

Sen. Nate Blouin, D-Salt Lake City, said he believes the change would cause another 1,000 deaths per year. He said emissions regulations bring "less emissions, less air quality issues, less cancer, less other disease, less asthma attacks."

Though the current repeal focuses only on CO2 emissions, Blouin says regulating solely CO2 doesn't mean other harmful chemicals won't be affected.

Jack — who is also an electrical engineer and former chief operating officer at Dixie Power — said the deregulations deal solely with CO2 emissions, not particulates, sulfur, mercury or nitrogen oxides, saying "none of those standards have changed."

"We're not talking about carbon emissions — we're talking about CO2, which is entirely different," he said. "CO2 is an odorless, colorless harmless gas, and in concentrations that have essentially no effect on the atmosphere, no effect on human well-being. So, it does sound scary, and it was deliberately designed to sound scary."

In the press release, the EPA stated current models show that greenhouse gases from power plants "have no material impact on global climate change.

"In fact, if all carbon dioxides were eliminated tomorrow, there would be no meaningful climate impact."

Not everyone agrees.

Hana Vizcarra, deputy managing attorney at Earthjustice, said his group believes power plants have significant impacts on communities across the nation, possibly leading to more wildfires, public health impacts and more severe weather.

What does it mean for Utah?

Utah's two biggest coal plants — Hunter and Huntington — were supposed to shut down in 2036 and 2042. Last year, as regulations already began to loosen, Rocky Mountain Power announced the plants would continue running until at least 2045.

Now, with repealed regulations on greenhouse gases and more in the possible future, additional changes could be coming.

A third power plant in Delta had its coal units shut off last November. Supposedly, that plant is being replaced with a gas plant that can eventually run on hydrogen — unless emissions rules continue to dip, which could make the plant attractive to a potential buyer.

Jack said he has been working with the state to keep that as a "viable option."

"This rule will certainly give that new owner operator comfort that they'll be able to run that," he said.

text:
Idaho environmental groups said the Environmental Protection Agency’s rollback of regulations on fossil fuel-based power plants could lead utilities to abandon their clean energy commitments.

The agency recently finalized its repeal of limits on greenhouse gas emissions from coal and natural gas plants.

Lisa Young, director of the Idaho chapter of the Sierra Club, said while Idaho does not have coal-fired plants, state utilities still import electricity from coal plants in the region. She added when the Trump administration changes the rules, utilities in Idaho and the U.S. take note.

“It makes it so that actually, they could keep burning coal a little longer,” Young contended. “They could have some other polluting plants like gas plants without as much of a financial cost. That impacts their decision-making, and we could absolutely see utilities like Idaho Power and others changing their plans for the future to keep coal plants running.”

The rule would have required power plants to capture 90% of greenhouse gas emissions by 2032. The EPA said the change will save $310 billion. The agency also wants to rescind all remaining greenhouse gas requirements for U.S. power plants. The Trump administration said the move will supply reliable, affordable power and expects it to “unleash” America’s energy resources.

Young believes climate change impacts will worsen because of the rule change and other environmental rollbacks. She pointed out Idahoans are already seeing heat waves, wildfires and drought, and emphasized it is not too late to push decision-makers toward different energy choices.

“We can say, ‘Hey, let’s look at the science. Let’s make good decisions here.’ Clean energy is still the cheapest, fastest, best way for us to produce our electricity,” Young stressed.

An International Renewable Energy Agency report found 91% of renewable projects are less expensive than fossil fuel options. Young added the Sierra Club and other groups plan to fight the EPA’s power plant rule repeal in court.

NEW YORK, Sept 17 (Reuters) – US electric grid ​operator PJM Interconnection called on large energy consumers across ‌13 states to curb consumption on Thursday, as high temperatures stoked power demand and risked blackouts.

PJM runs the biggest regional electric grid in the US and ​covers the Mid-Atlantic and Midwest. It said its system ​had about 36,000 megawatts of power generation outages, ⁠shrinking the availability of electricity supplies.

The “demand response” program that PJM activated pays ​participating customers to temporarily reduce or cut power when called ​upon, to address rolling blackouts.

Above-average temperatures raise demand from homes and businesses using cooling systems, straining supplies just as transmission and power plant operators are entering ​maintenance season.

Surging demand in PJM, which controls the flow of ​electricity to one in five Americans in its region, has outpaced the addition ‌of ⁠new electricity supplies in recent years and tightened energy margins.

The US Department of Energy also granted PJM’s request to temporarily wave environmental permit restrictions for certain power plants and allow energy-intensive ​data centers ​to switch to ⁠backup generators, which can be more polluting than other electricity sources.

PJM services the world’s biggest ​data center hub in northern Virginia, known as “Data ​Center ⁠Alley,” and burgeoning new hubs in states like Pennsylvania and Ohio.

The operator said it may also curtail exports as part of ⁠its ​emergency measures, noting weather is ever ​hotter for neighboring systems to the south and west.

Britain's electric vehicle battery industry has secured more than £7 billion in investment, with the UK quietly building one of Europe's most diverse and innovative supply chains, according to a report.

The UK's EV Battery Economy: A strategic review of the UK's battery manufacturing sector, was produced by transport research group New AutoMotive and is billed as the most comprehensive audit of the sector to date.

It lists more than 14 major projects, spanning lithium extraction, chemical refining, gigafactories and recycling.

Ben Nelmes, chief executive of New AutoMotive, said: "The UK has built real momentum in the battery supply chain, securing over £7 billion in investment for projects that will drive our industrial future.

"Delaying or diluting the EV transition now would directly undermine investor confidence, putting those billions of pounds, thousands of skilled jobs, and our broader competitive edge at risk.

"Businesses need a stable, long-term policy framework to build these factories and secure Britain's role as a leader in the global clean energy transition."

The UK's battery sector already generates £4.2 billion a year and supports more than 10,000 high-value jobs, the report says.

It highlights Envision AESC's 15.8 GWh gigafactory in Sunderland and Agratas's £4 billion, 40 GWh site in Somerset, saying both are helping revive industrial regions.

The report also points to progress in domestic mineral extraction, including Cornish Lithium projects in the South West and geothermal brine operations in County Durham, which could help build a UK supply of critical minerals.

Chemical refining is also growing, with Tees Valley Lithium and Green Lithium planning UK facilities to process battery-grade materials.

The report says recycling could give the UK a competitive edge.

More than two million electric vehicles are now on UK roads, while EVs make up around 30 per cent of monthly car sales. That means a growing stock of old batteries contains valuable minerals.

The report says the UK has an advantage over mainland Europe because it is an island and uses right-hand-drive vehicles.

The report says these vehicles are rarely exported second-hand, so most retired EV batteries stay in the UK, providing a domestic supply of lithium, nickel and cobalt.

Recycling firms including Altilium, which operates in Plymouth and is expanding to Teesside, and Wolverhampton-based Recyclus Group can recover more than 95 per cent of these minerals using hydrometallurgical processes.

The method produces 50 per cent fewer emissions than traditional mining and could support a circular, low-carbon supply chain for UK gigafactories.

Despite the progress, the report warns that the industry's future depends on continued political support and policy certainty.

The report warns that weakening the Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) Mandate could deter investment and slow growth.

By 2035, the UK is expected to need around 115 GWh of battery cells a year for vehicles and energy storage.

By Meg Flippin, Benzinga

There are several reasons for the shortages. For starters, silver is used in everything from EVs to data centers, with the growth of both driving demand for the metal. At the same time, the number of new silver mines coming online is not very large, with many miners bogged down by long permitting times and dwindling ore grades. It doesn’t help that most silver is mined as a byproduct of copper and zinc, which means production can’t easily be amped up just because prices for silver are soaring.

Bringing More Silver Online With New Pacific Metals

But without a stable supply of silver, the green revolution and tech transformation could face an expensive problem that forces manufacturers to absorb soaring material costs, delay rollouts of new technology or develop cheaper workarounds. It’s something that countries and industries around the world generally don’t want to see happen, and what New Pacific Metals Corp. (TSX.NUAG) (NYSE-A: NEWP), the Vancouver, British Columbia, mining exploration and development company, is working hard to prevent.

The company reports it owns two of the world’s largest undeveloped open-pit silver projects, Silver Sand and Carangas, which have the potential to produce nearly 23 million ounces of silver annually.

Silver Sand, located in Bolivia’s Potosí department, has a mineral resource containing over 200 million ounces of silver. Its pre-feasibility study projects an estimated production of 12 million ounces of silver annually. The project is currently advancing through the permitting stage. Meanwhile, the company reports Carangas has a mineral resource containing over 200 million ounces of silver and an estimated production of 15.5 million ounces of silver annually. The project is advancing through permitting and technical work with New Pacific Metals hoping it becomes an important source of global silver as the world looks for the next generation of production.

Late last month, New Pacific Metals signed the Administrative Mining Contracts for its Carangas Silver-Gold Project, giving it a 30-year fixed term and representing a key milestone in advancing the mine from exploration to production. New Pacific said the signed AMCs will be submitted for ratification and approval, representing the next key step toward formally obtaining the mining tenure. Following legislative approval, the company expects to advance the Carangas project’s remaining permitting and technical work, including the environmental categorization and subsequent Environmental Impact Assessment process.

Drilling To Commence

At the same time, New Pacific Metals said drilling at the site is kicking off in the first half of September, with about 25,000 metres of the 30,000 metres of drilling to upgrade mineral resources in both the silver zone and the gold zone, and the balance focused on step-out drilling for potential extensions and testing new targets. The drill campaign strengthens the path toward development and puts Carangas in a small group of potential future silver producers that have the capability to scale and make a meaningful contribution to the global market, noted the company.

What makes Carangas stand out isn't just its size but how efficient the company says it can be. It’s planned as an open-pit mine, making it generally cheaper and safer to operate. During its first eight years, the company expects it will cost about $12 to produce each ounce of silver after selling off byproduct gold and base metals to cover costs. Meanwhile, prices hit an all-time high early this year, and J.P. Morgan predicts that silver prices will reach $63 per ounce in Q4 2026, averaging $70/oz for the year and $63/oz in 2027. The project is expected to pay back its setup costs in less than two and a half years, with enough resources in the ground to keep operating for nearly two decades.

If the mine meets its targets and can produce more than 15 million ounces of silver a year during the first eight years, New Pacific Metals said it alone would represent about 1.8% of 2025’s global mine production. If production increases to 25 million ounces a year, the company said its contribution on the world stage gets even more impressive, to around 3%. text:
Your browser does not support the audio element.

The Arkansas Public Service Commission has denied Entergy Arkansas’ request to enter into a 20-year power purchase agreement with a Mississippi County solar project.

Big Island Solar, being built by Pattern Energy, will be a 440-megawatt solar facility on 3,200 acres in Mississippi County near Wilson. The project has a operational target date of 2028.

A power purchase agreement is a contract wherein a developer builds a power generator and a buyer, Entergy Arkansas in this case, purchases the electricity. According to Arkansas law, the commission must approve power purchase agreements that are longer than five years and that include costs that customers must cover.

Entergy was seeking to bill customers for the costs of the agreement plus an additional sum in an energy cost recovery rider — a tariff that helps Entergy recover fuel and purchased power costs.

Entergy has not made public how much the 20-year agreement and additional sum would cost.

“As the commission does not find the cost of the PPA reasonable and prudent, does not find that the PPA will provide savings for retail customers as compared to other generation and power supply options over the term of the agreement, does not find that the PPA is required by the public convenience and necessity, does not find that the PPA is necessary to supplement or replace (Entergy Arkansas) existing generation resources, and does not find that approval of the PPA is in the public interest, the commission denies (Entergy Arkansas) application,” the commissioners wrote in the order.

In regulatory filings, Entergy estimated the overall monthly cost for a residential customer could be about 60 cents in year one of the agreement with Pattern Energy and by year five could fall to 35 cents.

The monthly cost would add to a string of recent increases facing Entergy customers.

In January, monthly rates for average use Entergy residential customers rose by $6.08, as part of Entergy’s formula rate plan, which allows utilities to increase rates by 4% annually without filing a formal rate case.

In February, Entergy filed an application for a formal rate case, which could lead to a monthly bill increase of about $1.16 for average residential customers. If approved by the commission, new base rates would take effect in January 2027.

In June, residential customers saw a monthly increase of about $5.77 on their bills — through a separate rider — to help pay for the construction of three power generation projects, as allowed by the Generating Arkansas Jobs Act. That rider can be adjusted annually as long as the projects are under construction.

According to regulatory filings, Entergy signed a proposed power purchase agreement for solar energy resources with Big Island Solar on December 18, 2025. Entergy said the agreement would provide net benefits to customers, will help add diverse generation to its portfolio and support new growth.

Entergy’s application for commission approval of the agreement was submitted on Jan. 29.

At a May public evidence hearing before the commission, Kristin Dalrymple, vice president of business operations and strategy at Entergy, said the Big Island power purchase agreement could help support Entergy’s partnership with Google.

Entergy has entered into a 20-year special rate contract to help power Google’s $4 billion West Memphis data center. Over the course of the agreement Google is expected to pay more than $2.1 billion in total upfront and minimum demand payments which will be amortized.

Google has said it aims to power all of its data centers with carbon free energy by 2030. Dalrymple said at the hearing the Big Island agreement would produce renewable energy credits, that Google could purchase to help it meet that pledge.

Renewable energy credits serve as proof that a company uses electricity from clean energy sources like solar farms, according to the Retail Energy Supply Association. Google can then “retire” the credits to offset its reported greenhouse gas emissions from its data centers to meet corporate clean-energy goals, or it could sell the credits on the open market.

According to the commissions orders, Dalrymple said that Entergy is in active discussions with Google about the renewable energy credits.

“While the Commission acknowledges that the Big Island PPA will produce (renewable energy credits) to help meet Google’s obligation to match its energy consumption at all data centers with carbon-free energy by 2030, the commission notes that alternative arrangements may be possible to accomplish such a goal without the costs of an uneconomic facility being borne on (Entergy Arkansas) ratepayers.” the commissioners said.

The commissioners said they encourage Entergy to explore alternative arrangements if Entergy is committed to acquiring renewable energy credits for Google.

The commission also noted that if Entergy and Google reach an agreement for the renewable energy credits, and that agreement is approved by the commission, then Entergy may refile its application for the power purchase agreement with Big Island.

“The commission encouraged us to work with our customer to determine whether we can address the commission’s concerns regarding the (renewable energy credits),” Lamor Williams, a spokesman for Entergy said. “If we can address those concerns, we plan to ask the commission to reconsider its decision.”

Google has already secured a power purchase agreement for one of America’s largest solar and energy storage projects, also being built in Mississippi County.

The Steel River Energy Center, also near Wilson, is being developed by Cypress Creek Renewables. Google’s power purchase agreement will be for the electricity created by the first two phases of Steel River, designed to deliver a total of 1.6 gigawatts of new solar generation and 1.9 gigawatts of new battery storage to the grid.

title: 30% EV Battery Growth Expands Markets for Lithium & Non-China Nickel Supply
description:
1.2 TWh EV Battery Deployment Expands Lithium Demand Across Chemistries Light-duty vehicles represented more than 85% of EV battery deployment in 2025.
LFP Growth Expands Lithium Demand as Nickel Use Concentrates Outside China Growth in LFP batteries redistributes demand among battery metals rather than eliminating it.
Lithium demand therefore benefits from overall battery deployment, while nickel demand depends more heavily on regional chemistry and vehicle mix.
LFP accounted for just over 10% of European Union EV battery demand, while its US share almost halved from its 2024 level.
Procurement & Financing Advance Hydrometallurgical Nickel Supply Hydrometallurgical processing can expand non-China nickel supply by converting mined feedstock into customer-qualified products without conventional smelting.
text:
Electric vehicle battery deployment rose almost 30% to 1.2 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2025, more than 7 times the 2020 level, expanding the volume base for lithium & nickel demand.

Lithium is used in both lithium iron phosphate and nickel-containing batteries, so changes in cathode chemistry alter lithium use per battery rather than eliminate demand for the metal.

Lithium iron phosphate accounted for more than 55% of global electric vehicle (EV) battery deployment in 2025, but nearly 80% of deployment outside China still used nickel-containing chemistries, preserving a distinct regional market for nickel supply outside China.

China controlled more than 80% of battery manufacturing capacity, while Chinese producers supplied almost 75% of electric-car batteries in 2025, concentrating supply-chain risk and strengthening the commercial case for customer-qualified battery materials produced outside China.

Projects with costs below expected sale prices, binding offtakes, permits, detailed engineering, and demonstrated processing reduce financing risk and improve production prospects.

30% EV Battery Growth Expands Lithium Demand & Regional Nickel Use

Despite weaker EV policy support in parts of the US and Europe, the International Energy Agency (IEA) reported that EV battery deployment reached 1.2 TWh in 2025, almost 30% above 2024 and more than 7 times the 2020 level. EVs accounted for more than 70% of total battery deployment, making vehicle electrification the sector’s largest demand source. The 1.2 TWh deployment base spans multiple regions and vehicle segments, supporting lithium demand broadly and nickel demand where nickel-containing chemistries dominate.

1.2 TWh EV Battery Deployment Expands Lithium Demand Across Chemistries

Light-duty vehicles represented more than 85% of EV battery deployment in 2025. Average battery sizes remained near 70 kilowatt-hours in the European Union and below 60 kilowatt-hours in China, indicating that higher vehicle volumes, not larger packs, drove most of the capacity increase. Lithium is used in both lithium iron phosphate (LFP) and nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) batteries, so rising vehicle volumes support demand across both leading cathode families. A 30% increase in battery deployment does not imply a 30% rise in lithium consumption because chemistry mix, inventories, manufacturing yields, and lithium intensity per kilowatt-hour determine material demand.

Electric-truck battery demand more than doubled in 2025, raising its share of global deployment to approximately 8% from less than 5% in 2024. Because trucks use larger packs, each additional truck adds more battery-metal demand than a light-duty EV. Across all EVs, China accounted for 60% of battery deployment, the European Union almost 15%, the US 10%, and emerging markets outside China 6%, making regional policies and vehicle requirements key determinants of LFP and NMC demand.

LFP Growth Expands Lithium Demand as Nickel Use Concentrates Outside China

Growth in LFP batteries redistributes demand among battery metals rather than eliminating it. LFP excludes nickel and cobalt from the cathode but retains lithium, while NMC and related chemistries use nickel where automakers prioritize energy density, driving range, payload, or cold-weather performance. Lithium demand therefore benefits from overall battery deployment, while nickel demand depends more heavily on regional chemistry and vehicle mix.

55% LFP Share Sustains Lithium Demand Across Leading Battery Chemistries

LFP accounted for more than 55% of EV batteries deployed globally in 2025, up from nearly 50% in 2024. LFP packs were more than 40% cheaper per kilowatt-hour on average than NMC alternatives, helping explain the chemistry’s share gain. Lower pack prices reduce EV and battery energy storage costs, supporting deployment even though lithium intensity varies by product. Lithium therefore remains necessary across the leading lithium-ion chemistries, making its price a direct input into battery-pack costs across both families.

Lithium prices at the beginning of 2026 were more than double year-earlier levels but remained approximately 70% below the 2022 peak. Growth in battery-storage demand, low Chinese inventories, and temporary mine disruptions tightened near-term supply and lifted prices. Higher lithium prices reach battery costs once lower-priced inventories are consumed and existing contracts reset. Sodium-ion batteries offer a potential substitute, but existing manufacturing capacity equaled just over 1% of lithium-ion capacity, limiting near-term substitution.

Nearly 80% Nickel-Containing Battery Share Sustains Demand Outside China

Global chemistry shares conceal a regional split, as nearly 80% of batteries deployed outside China in 2025 used nickel-containing chemistries such as NMC and nickel cobalt aluminum. LFP accounted for just over 10% of European Union EV battery demand, while its US share almost halved from its 2024 level. Nickel demand therefore depends on where batteries are installed and which vehicle requirements manufacturers prioritize. Faster LFP adoption outside China would reduce nickel use per battery, but the 2025 chemistry mix still supports demand for nickel suppliers that meet non-China customer specifications.

Mark Selby, Chief Executive Officer of Canada Nickel, explains why constrained supply supports non-China nickel projects:

“The reality is, with Indonesia basically limiting supply going forward and nickel demand growing at 5% plus a year, which is another almost 200,000 tons of nickel per year, we’re in great shape. People want supply from somewhere other than Chinese-controlled entities.”

Canada Nickel expects to finalize the equipment and fleet-financing arrangements in the first quarter of 2027, strengthening construction readiness and Crawford’s potential as a long-term source of non-China nickel.

China’s Battery Dominance Raises the Value of Diversified Supply

Global lithium-ion battery nameplate capacity, the rated maximum output of manufacturing plants, exceeded 4 TWh at the end of 2025, approximately 30% above 2024. China controlled more than 80% of that capacity and produced more than 80% of global battery output, while the European Union and US each held 6% to 7% of capacity. Chinese manufacturers also supplied almost 75% of batteries deployed in electric cars in 2025. This concentration means jurisdiction, customer qualification, processing access, and trade policy can determine market access and financing alongside grade and operating cost.

Manufacturing Concentration Raises Non-China Costs & Financing Needs

Europe and the US have built cell plants, but cell capacity alone does not create an independent supply chain. Cathode precursors, LFP materials, graphite anodes, machinery, and technical expertise remain concentrated in China, leaving new plants dependent on Chinese inputs. The IEA estimated that battery-production costs in Europe and the US were as much as 50% higher than in China before public support. New facilities can take more than 5 years after opening to approach rated capacity, while profitable operation generally requires production yields above 90%.

Procurement & Financing Advance Hydrometallurgical Nickel Supply

Hydrometallurgical processing can expand non-China nickel supply by converting mined feedstock into customer-qualified products without conventional smelting. Once consistent recovery and product quality establish the processing route, the investment focus moves to construction readiness. Detailed engineering defines the build, while procurement advances the required equipment and services. Financing progress then supports a final investment decision. These milestones move proposed capacity toward construction and establish a clear pathway for diversifying nickel supply.

Lifezone Metals advanced the Kabanga Nickel Project into large-scale procurement, releasing approximately US$854 million of contracts to market while targeting a final investment decision in the first quarter of 2027. Pre-construction work is supported by US$21.7 million drawn from the Taurus facility and a US$25 million equity raise, while multiple strategic equity offers and indications of liquidity from development finance institutions and export credit agencies provide additional financing pathways.

8% Battery Price Decline Compresses Producer Margins & Tightens Financing

Average battery prices fell 8% in 2025 as manufacturing became more efficient and competition increased. Shifts toward lower-cost chemistries and cheaper mineral inputs reinforced the decline. Lower pack prices support deployment but compress margins from raw materials through cathodes and cells. Many cathode active material producers continued adding capacity despite operating losses, prolonging margin pressure. This pressure favors projects that remain profitable at lower prices and secure contracted revenue before construction. Controlling capital costs and meeting development milestones further improve access to financing.

Offtake Floors & Prepayments Strengthen Lithium Project Financing

Lower battery prices transmit pressure upstream, making lithium project financing more selective. Project economics must remain viable under conservative spodumene-price assumptions, and a lower initial capital requirement reduces the funding burden.

Lithium Ionic targets average production of 177,000 tonnes of spodumene concentrate annually over 18.5 years. Five-year offtakes covering approximately 170,000 tonnes annually, supported by market-linked pricing and a US$20 million prepayment facility, provide commercial validation and financing progress.

Blake Hylands, Chief Executive Officer of Lithium Ionic, explains why project timing matters for lithium supply:

“There aren’t many projects that are staged to push forward, but it’s really important to keep the pace and become a producer when this material is needed. There aren’t that many projects coming online to supply it.”

Battery Growth Expands Demand While Project Execution Determines New Supply

EV battery deployment grew almost 30% to 1.2 TWh in 2025, but China still controlled more than 80% of manufacturing capacity and produced more than 80% of global battery output. China’s lower production costs and control of essential components mean alternative suppliers must compete on cost and reliability rather than jurisdiction alone. Projects convert demand growth into saleable material only after securing permits and financing. They must also demonstrate consistent recovery and qualify products with customers.

Annual EV battery deployment above the 1.2 TWh 2025 base would confirm continued volume growth. Electric-truck and emerging-market deployment will show whether demand is broadening beyond passenger cars and China. The global LFP share and the nickel-containing share outside China will show how additional deployment affects lithium intensity and nickel demand. The spread between battery-pack prices and lithium or nickel input costs will reveal whether raw-material inflation is compressing margins or raising consumer prices. A decline in China’s share of battery output and component manufacturing would confirm that announced capacity elsewhere is reaching commercial operation.

The Investment Thesis for Battery Metals

Electric vehicle battery deployment reached 1.2 terawatt-hours in 2025, giving lithium and nickel demand a measurable installed-volume base rather than relying only on long-term adoption forecasts.

Lithium participates across lithium iron phosphate and nickel-containing batteries, giving low-cost lithium projects exposure to battery growth even when manufacturers alter cathode chemistry.

Nearly 80% of batteries deployed outside China used nickel-containing chemistries, preserving a regional market for nickel projects capable of satisfying non-China customer requirements.

Jurisdictions with established infrastructure, predictable permitting, and access to low-carbon power can reduce schedule or operating risk.

Binding offtakes, price floors, advanced engineering, and disciplined capital requirements improve financing visibility by reducing revenue, cost, or schedule uncertainty.

Large-scale procurement and funded pre-construction work move non-China nickel projects beyond planning, improving visibility toward final investment decisions and construction.

EV battery deployment increased almost 30% in 2025, expanding lithium demand across leading chemistries and preserving a large nickel market outside China for projects that pair competitive costs with contracted sales and proven processing. With battery manufacturing concentrated in China, alternative suppliers have a defined commercial opportunity if they meet customer requirements for product quality and reliable delivery.

TL;DR

EV battery deployment reached 1.2 TWh in 2025, almost 30% above 2024, widening lithium demand across LFP and nickel-containing chemistries. LFP exceeded 55% of global deployment, yet nearly 80% of batteries installed outside China still used nickel-containing chemistries. China retained more than 80% of manufacturing capacity and a major cost advantage, so diversified supply must compete on economics as well as jurisdiction. An 8% decline in average battery prices increased margin pressure across the supply chain, placing greater weight on competitive costs and binding offtakes. Engineering and procurement progress then show which projects are moving toward financing, construction, and production.

text:
The Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA) has announced up to $49 million in funding to support Hysata to establish a commercial-scale electrolyser manufacturing line at Port Kembla in New South Wales.

The $98 million project will establish a 50 MW per annum manufacturing line for Hysata’s Australian-developed capillary-fed electrolyser technology, with the facility designed to scale to 200 MW per annum through 24-hour operations as demand grows.

Developed from research at the University of Wollongong, Hysata’s technology is designed to produce renewable hydrogen more efficiently, helping lower costs and supporting the decarbonisation of hard-to-abate industries such as steelmaking, chemicals, shipping and heavy transport.

The project includes the deployment of early commercial megawatt-scale electrolyser systems, helping demonstrate the technology in real-world applications and support future commercial growth.

ARENA CEO Darren Miller said building Australia’s capability to manufacture renewable energy technologies locally would be critical to capturing more value from the energy transition.

“Australia has world-class clean energy innovators, and Hysata is a great example of home-grown technology with the potential to compete globally,” Mr Miller said.

“This project will help move Australian innovation from the lab into large-scale manufacturing, creating skilled jobs while strengthening Australia’s capability to produce critical clean energy technologies locally.”

“By supporting advanced manufacturing of electrolysers here in Australia, we’re helping build the industries that can underpin a future renewable hydrogen sector and create long-term economic opportunities.”

The project is expected to create around 40 new skilled jobs across manufacturing, engineering and technical roles in the Illawarra region. Hysata will also work with the University of Wollongong and TAFE NSW Illawarra to deliver training, internships and skills development pathways to help grow the local workforce needed to support the clean energy transition.

A key feature of the project is the planned local manufacture of core electrolyser components, including membranes, anodes and cathodes, supporting Australia’s sovereign manufacturing capability and clean energy supply chains.

This project is being funded under the Future Made in Australia (FMA) Innovation Fund. For more information visit ARENA’s website.
