text:
SHELBY COUNTY, Ala. —

The Environmental Protection Agency is proposing to approve Alabama's coal ash regulations, which it previously rejected two years ago for being "significantly less protective of people and waterways than federal standards require."

In Shelby County, the Coosa River serves as a popular destination for fishing, boating, and outdoor activities. However, near its banks in Columbiana stands Alabama Power's Gaston Coal and Gas Plant, which uses water from the river for its operations before treating and releasing it back.

On the same property lies a massive pile of coal ash—25 million cubic yards, equivalent to 12 Bryant-Denny Stadiums. Coal ash, a byproduct of burning coal for electricity, is currently being dumped into unlined, water-filled pits known as coal ash ponds.

"They're in the process of capping in place, which essentially means they're dewatering the pond and then they're covering it with astroturf," said Justinn Overton, executive director of Coosa Riverkeeper. "So, before too long, these coal ash ponds are going to look like grassy knolls instead of what they actually are, which is an externality of the cost of doing business for Alabama Power and leaving that ash on our river."

Overton has monitored the Coosa River for years and expressed concerns about the toxic heavy metals and radioactive elements coal ash can contain.

"These contaminants, whether we're talking about molybdenum or any of these heavy metals, they are moving throughout the area surrounding this coal ash pond," Overton said.

Currently, there are two approved methods for closing coal ash impoundments: capping them in place with an engineered cover - like astroturf - or excavating and transporting the ash to another location. Alabama Power has opted for the first method.

"One of the things that we are advocating for is for Alabama Power to move their coal ash to upland lined landfills, so they are not leaving our waterways vulnerable to groundwater pollution, as well as if there were a catastrophic event that would impact one of our greatest resources for tourism, but also drinking water," Overton said.

Longtime Coosa River resident and former Wilsonville Mayor Lee McCarty shared his concerns about the impact of coal ash on the river and surrounding wildlife.

"They tell us, 'We're going to dirty your river, and there ain't nothing you can do about it,'" McCarty said.

"I haven't eaten fish out of this river in 30 years," he added, expressing fears about contaminants affecting groundwater and wildlife.

"It's destroying this river. And it's destroying the health long term of the people who live here and their descendants and the wildlife and the plants. If I went to your garden and I poured toxic materials in your garden and you ate stuff you grew in your garden, you'd charge me with murder. What's the difference?"

Overton said groundwater monitoring data from Alabama Power shows violations connected to the coal ash pond.

"We don't need a catastrophic event to impact water quality because it's happening right now," Overton said. "Alabama Power's own groundwater monitoring shows violations of the permits that they have."

In 2018, the Alabama Department of Environmental Management (ADEM) fined Alabama Power $250,000 for groundwater violations.

Alabama Power confirmed the fine in a statement.

"The fine issued in 2018 was related to groundwater quality and an administrative order from ADEM. Since that time, there have been no additional violations or fines at the facility. The facility has been working through the closure of the impoundment for several years and will continue the closure process in accordance with federal and state regulatory requirements."

Overton emphasized the need for enforcement of regulations. State agencies are not required to test inland lakes and streams, which means problems can often go undetected.

"It's one thing to have a regulation, but what we need is enforcement of those regulations because the public is the loser in this scenario, while industry is able to get away with violating permit limitations with no real repercussions," Overton said.

Alabama Power has stated its support for the EPA's proposed approval of the permit program, saying the proposal provides the foundation for a protective and enforceable permit program.

Overton, however, expressed concerns about potential rollbacks in regulations.

"That's why these federal guidelines are so important because they create sort of an even playing field for what is legal and illegal," Overton said. "That is why the permit for ADEM was actually denied by the EPA two years ago. And that's why today it's so important that people speak out, because the permit that has now been approved by EPA is the same permitting program. So what has changed?"

McCarty urged people to consider the impact of coal ash on their health and environment.

"Would you be concerned if I poured toxins in your garden? I mean, this is a duh question. Of course they should be concerned. Mercury. Molybdenum. Radon. The list goes on. I don't want that in my body. I'm assuming nobody else does," he said.

On Monday, the EPA announced it is repealing rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas, an action the agency said would remove more than $300 billion in costs for the industry and help “unleash” American energy. EPA officials said the change would allow utilities to make the best decisions for their ratepayers rather than be forced to close aging or inefficient plants.

The rule, which is expected to face immediate legal challenges, also could prevent future administrations from regulating greenhouse gas emissions from power plants.

As for Alabama's request, the EPA said their decision Monday will not impact their consideration of Alabama's coal ash permitting program. The agency added there is a statutory 180-day consideration period. Alabama Power has stated it will continue to comply with all applicable federal and state environmental laws and regulations and follow any final court or agency decisions.

text:
The Trump administration has cut or frozen up to $177 billion in federal grants since the president took office for his second term, according to a tracking tool released Wednesday by a pro-democracy nonprofit and a group of researchers and scientists.

The cuts affected all 50 states and the District of Columbia, with health, nutrition, the environment and disaster relief making up the largest share of cuts, the States United Democracy Center and Grant Witness organization found.

Among the grants that were eliminated, frozen or delayed were ones related to maternal health in Michigan, education research in Mississippi and assistance to minority farmers in Iowa, the researchers found. California, Texas, New York, Illinois and North Carolina saw the highest amounts of interrupted grant money. The tracking tool is called Lost Funds.

“By bringing thousands of funding disruptions from the Trump administration together in a publicly accessible, verified database, Lost Funds puts the magnitude of their impact on full display,” Scott Delaney, co-founder of Grant Witness, said in a statement.

The $177 billion finding represents nearly 10% of federal discretionary spending, the groups said.

The tracker’s organizers said the disrupted grants were beyond the kind of cuts that typically happen when administrations change.

“Lost Funds shows the extraordinary scale and real human impact of these disruptions, and how states are once again on the front lines protecting their residents,” said Kelly Rader, States United Democracy Center’s research director.

In some cases, courts have ruled against the administration’s grant funding cuts.

The new tool, which is being made available for public use, relies on data from USASpending.gov, an open data source of federal spending information, according to the groups’ methodology. They said the tracker would be updated regularly as the administration takes new action and lawsuits move through the courts.

States United bills itself as a nonpartisan group dedicated to the rule of law and free, fair, secure elections. It was cofounded by Norm Eisen, an attorney who has been involved in prominent lawsuits against the Trump administration, including over the Kennedy Center. Eisen left the States United center in 2024.

Grant Witness is a group of scientists, researchers and attorneys who document how funding is changing under President Donald Trump’s administration.

A message seeking comment on the analysis was sent to the White House.

description:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE Contact: edeanne@nrdc.org, mediarelations@apha.org Environmental and public health groups sued to stop the Environmental Protection Agency’s repeal of critical standards for power plant carbon pollution.
“The Clean Air Act and Supreme Court precedent demand that the EPA address climate pollution from the largest industrial source in the nation.

text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Contact: edeanne@nrdc.org, mediarelations@apha.org

Environmental and public health groups sued to stop the Environmental Protection Agency’s repeal of critical standards for power plant carbon pollution. NRDC (Natural Resources Defense Council), American Lung Association, American Public Health Association, Clean Air Council, and Clean Wisconsin (represented by Clean Air Task Force), and the Environmental Defense Fund filed the action at the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit today.

Following are quotes from groups involved in the litigation:

“Repealing these standards without a replacement is an abdication of EPA’s legal responsibility to protect public health and the environment,” said Meredith Hankins, federal climate legal director at NRDC. “The Clean Air Act and Supreme Court precedent demand that the EPA address climate pollution from the largest industrial source in the nation. The EPA’s legal reasoning is fatally flawed, so we are going to court.”

“Clean air is a basic human right. Power plant pollution threatens the health of millions of Americans and fuels climate change, worsening extreme heat, poor air quality and other serious health risks,” said Georges C. Benjamin, MD, CEO of the American Public Health Association. “Weakening these life-saving standards would strip away vital protections for all, and especially for children, pregnant people and communities already overburdened by pollution. EPA must maintain strong clean air and climate standards so every community can live a healthy life.”

“Emissions from power plants drive climate change, and climate change is a health emergency,” said Harold Wimmer, president and CEO of the American Lung Association. “Measures that clean up power plant emissions also clean up other lung-harming pollutants at the same time. EPA has the authority and the responsibility to protect people’s health from air pollution.”

“This unlawful rollback will have devastating consequences if allowed to stand,” said Brett Korte, Senior Staff Attorney at Clean Wisconsin. “Here in Wisconsin, we’re experiencing warmer winters with less snow and ice cover, more exceedingly hot days in summer, and more frequent extreme weather events, like flooding and tornadoes, due to climate change. On top of that, Wisconsin has the ninth-highest death rate from particulate matter pollution from fossil fuel combustion. EPA abandoning its responsibility to regulate carbon pollution would only make these problems worse.”

“EPA is senselessly discarding readily attainable carbon standards for power plants mere weeks after the UN showed the world on a trajectory to exceed the heating limit needed to avoid severe levels of economic, ecological, and social disruption,” said Lawrence Hafetz, Legal Director of Pennsylvania-based Clean Air Council. “By rolling back these critical protections, millions of Americans will get sicker, face more extreme weather, and pay more for energy and electricity, with vulnerable communities suffering the most. EPA is supposed to protect people and the environment, not rewrite the rules to benefit polluters.”

“This unlawful rule seeks to remove our national limits on climate pollution from power plants at a time when more Americans than ever are suffering from the dangerous heat and more powerful storms caused by that pollution and are facing the ensuing skyrocketing insurance bills and health costs,” said Vickie Patton, General Counsel for Environmental Defense Fund. “Increased power plant pollution resulting from this rule will cause thousands of premature deaths and billions of dollars in additional health costs. We are taking action in the court of law to ensure EPA carries out its responsibilities under our nation’s clean air laws to protect the American people from this harmful pollution and to address the health risks and financial costs for people across the country.”

Background:

The 2024 standards the EPA finalized its repeal of today were estimated to deliver a net $370 billion in climate and health benefits – with benefits a stunning 20 times that of the costs to industry. A recent NRDC analysis found that this administration’s policies will destroy $700 billion in new power sector investments over the next decade and cut by half the power sector carbon reductions likely before its policies took effect.

The Clean Air Act obligates EPA to issue standards to reduce emissions from sources such as power plants that significantly contribute to dangerous air pollution. The EPA’s action follows a new United Nations report warning that the world is set to exceed a key climate threshold and so countries need to take more intensive actions to cut carbon pollution while also intensifying efforts to adapt to climate-fueled heat, storms and fires.

The carbon standards for power plants were finalized in April of 2024 and would require carbon pollution reductions from existing coal and new gas-fired power plants. Fossil-fuel power plants are responsible for about a quarter of the nation’s carbon emissions. Those standards were based on pollution controls that could be accomplished at an individual power plant, making them consistent with the Supreme Court’s decision in West Virginia v. EPA.

The legal filing is available here.

###

NRDC (Natural Resources Defense Council) is an international nonprofit environmental organization with more than 3 million members and online activists. Established in 1970, NRDC uses science, policy, law and people power to confront the climate crisis, protect public health and safeguard nature. NRDC has offices in New York City, Washington, D.C., Los Angeles, San Francisco, Chicago, Beijing and Delhi (an office of NRDC India Pvt. Ltd).

Clean Air Task Force (CATF) is a global nonprofit organization working to safeguard against the worst impacts of climate change by catalyzing the rapid development and deployment of low-carbon energy and other climate-protecting technologies. text:
The Trump administration has repealed an executive order that sought to coordinate the efforts of federal, state and local governments to protect and restore the Chesapeake Bay.

President Trump issued an executive order Wednesday to repeal a previous executive order that was established under the Obama administration back on May 12, 2009.

The original measure, known as Executive Order 13508, was designed to improve protection and restoration efforts for the Chesapeake Bay, the largest estuary in the United States.

According to a statement announcing the repeal, Executive Order 13508 "instituted a broad mandate for states and municipalities to contribute to improving the environmental health of the Chesapeake Bay, without providing clarity on how to implement that order's requirements."

In some instances, "this lack of clarity has led to harmful economic impacts on affected Americans," the statement added.

One example cited by the Trump administration is that the original order resulted in many localities having to implement stormwater management fees, commonly referred to as "rain taxes."

These fees sometimes reached hundreds of dollars in annual financial burdens imposed on residents and small businesses, even though nothing in the order required or explicitly justified such measures, the administration said, "with little to no measurable benefits to Chesapeake Bay or to those residents."

Administration says other programs have improved Chesapeake

Since Executive Order 13508 was signed, numerous other federal, state and local government initiatives and programs have resulted in significant improvements in the Chesapeake Bay, the administration noted.

Examples cited of this progress involved multiple jurisdictions of the Chesapeake Bay watershed, which includes New York, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Virginia, the District of Columbia, Delaware and West Virginia. These areas have collectively met 100% of their goal for sediment reduction, 90% of their goal for phosphorus reduction, and 57% of their goal for nitrogen reduction, according to Wednesday's statement.

These results are improving Chesapeake Bay health and have resulted "in thousands of acres of restored reefs and remain consistent with commitments made in the 2025 revised Chesapeake Bay Watershed Agreement," the administration said.

It was also noted that in 2026, scientists from the College of William & Mary, the Virginia Institute of Marine Science, FlowWest and the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science reported that the Chesapeake Bay's annual dead zone was projected to be among the smallest since 1985, or about 31% below the long-term average.

"Given this significant progress, and the need to provide clarity on how to continue improving the environmental health of the Chesapeake Bay, it is appropriate to revoke Executive Order 13508, which relevant jurisdictions have erroneously relied on to impose rain taxes, and to implement new actions and best practices that promote the economic health and wellbeing of the communities the Chesapeake Bay serves," the statement said.

Chesapeake Bay Foundation disappointed in new order

In response to the latest executive order, the Chesapeake Bay Foundation said the move "is jeopardizing decades of Bay restoration progress."

"For more than 40 years, the federal government has worked in partnership with the states across the watershed to reduce pollution to the Chesapeake Bay. That partnership was strengthened in 2009 when EO 13508 established a new framework for federal leadership, coordination, and accountability. Water does not respect state or political boundaries. What happens upstream affects people downstream," the foundation added.

The statement noted that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) recently recorded significant progress toward reducing pollution and restoring the Chesapeake Bay, however the new executive order "dismantles a key part of the federal-state framework that helped drive that progress."

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore also issued a statement condemning the move, as did Annapolis Mayor Jared Littmann.

"Trump's decision to slash federal support for the Chesapeake Bay is yet another attack against Maryland — this time on our farmers, fishers, and millions of people who rely on the watershed to filter their drinking water. The Bay is our jewel moving Maryland's economy forward, and we will protect it at all costs," Moore said on social media.

"Today we learned that environmental policies put in place 15 years ago to protect the Chesapeake Bay were revoked by the Trump Administration. The environmental health of the Chesapeake Bay, and local tributaries that feed the Bay, is not open for debate; it is not a policy preference that can be dialed back by Executive Order," said Littmann. "For Annapolis, protecting our waterways is a core duty to our residents, the local economy, and the future that we hand to the next generation."

title: The Iran war is driving clean energy development. It's not enough to help the planet, yet
description:
So far, more than 30 governments have enacted policies to move away from fossil fuels or improve energy efficiency.
Yet at the same time, global emissions of greenhouse gases increased slightly and investments in clean energy fell compared to the same period last year.
The Associated Press talked to a dozen experts who said that while the Iran war appears to be helping the adoption of clean energy, the world is still heavily dependent on fossil fuels.

“The Trump administration has been really focused on fossil fuels, but since they started this conflict, you have to ask the question, is this good for fossil fuels?
text:
Countries are embracing clean power and taking steps to use less energy because of the war against Iran, but it is not yet enough to help address climate change.

When the U.S. and Israel launched the war in February, some backers of renewables opined it could drive a green transition as oil and gas prices spiked. So far, more than 30 governments have enacted policies to move away from fossil fuels or improve energy efficiency. Yet at the same time, global emissions of greenhouse gases increased slightly and investments in clean energy fell compared to the same period last year.

The Associated Press talked to a dozen experts who said that while the Iran war appears to be helping the adoption of clean energy, the world is still heavily dependent on fossil fuels. They said it will take more time for new policies to show results.

“Governments are currently doing a dance between acknowledging the importance of clean power while continuing to support fossil fuel expansion,” war studies lecturer Pauline Heinrichs at King’s College London wrote in an email. “We are seeing an old and a new world interact in contradiction with each other.”

There has been a surge in solar installations in the United Kingdom. The government is also considering expanding natural gas production. In Asia, where there’s massive demand for solar power and electric vehicles, Indonesia is replacing some diesel power plants with solar, while also doubling down on coal for heavy industries.

Clean investment lost momentum globally, but the story differs importantly by region

Global investment in wind and solar deployment fell in the first half of 2026 compared to the same period last year, after several years of growth, according to Rhodium Group’s Clean Investment Monitor. China accounted for most of the global decline. In the U.S., Europe and India, where economies are more exposed to gas and oil prices, solar investment grew and wind investment held stable or grew, said Hannah Pitt, a director at Rhodium.

In February, Stanford University climate scientist Rob Jackson said it was “just wishful thinking” that the new war would boost support for homegrown renewables over imported fossil fuels — unless it turned out to be a sustained conflict.

Six months later, Jackson said he didn’t anticipate oil prices hurdling past $90 or $100 a barrel for so long. If dozens of countries are promoting electric vehicle incentives, charging infrastructure and electrification in general, that can help in the fight against climate change, added Jackson. But only if those actions are sustained.

“We need that action over years, to decades, to make a dent in the climate problem,” Jackson said Monday.

Climate pollution increased marginally

Thirty-three governments adopted policies to switch from fossil fuels to electricity or improve energy efficiency in response to the Middle East conflict, as of Sept. 9, according to the International Energy Agency. This includes supporting EV adoption, promoting renewable energy, replacing gas boilers with electric heat pumps and retrofitting homes and businesses to use less energy. The Netherlands, Spain and the U.K. are doing everything on that list.

China is working to make heavy industry more energy efficient and pushing to electrify heavy vehicles. India and Indonesia are shifting to electric stoves to replace imported liquefied petroleum gas as a cooking fuel. Laos suspended gas and diesel car imports through 2026 to boost EVs.

These efforts haven't moved the needle yet. Incentivizing EV purchases or encouraging energy efficiency take time and scale, according to researchers for the Climate TRACE database of emissions.

At the same time, many governments are cutting fuel taxes. That provides immediate relief to consumers but disincentivizes switching to EVs. And, the war itself will spike emissions.

Global greenhouse gas emissions increased 0.2% in the first half of 2026, compared with the first half of 2025, according to Climate TRACE. While emissions from road transportation increased, Climate TRACE found that power sector emissions declined, despite concern that disruptions in oil and gas markets would push countries to use more coal for electricity. Shipping emissions also declined, likely due to the Strait of Hormuz closure.

Countries that import fossil fuels are footing higher bills

Those bills would have been even steeper, though, if not for the clean power added since 2020.

Fossil fuel importers have paid prices that are $330 billion higher compared to prewar market expectations, making it the largest sustained price shock since the 1990 Gulf War, according to research by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. The European Union, China and India paid the most.

Countries that invested in clean energy after past energy crises saved an estimated $36 billion in avoided fossil fuel imports in the first five months of the conflict, the research found. China and Japan saved the most, followed by Spain, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Brazil and India.

Governments are trying to insulate themselves from geopolitical volatility and fuel price instability, said Caspian Conran, lead economist at the global consultancy firm Baringa. China knows it can rely on coal and the U.S. won’t run out of domestic natural gas, he said. Europe's politicians feel the most urgency to adopt new energy policies because their fossil fuel production is limited, said Conran, who is based in London.

“We simply don’t have a choice,” he said.

Too soon to say whether the war will be a net gain for renewables or fossil fuels

At this point, the signal would be small and there is a lot of other variation in the system, according to Michael Oppenheimer, a Princeton climate and international affairs professor.

“One thing is clear, however. When the trouble began, lots of people said there would be a rush to other, readily-available fossil fuel sources to replace Gulf oil and compensate for the price run-up, which would presumably bury any gain in carbon-free energy,” he wrote in an email. “Instead, at this point, it looks like events could turn out to be a net winner for renewables.”

Brookings Institution scholar Samantha Gross said the war is changing how people think about transitioning away from fossil fuels — that it’s not just for the climate, it’s an energy security strategy.

“That widens the appeal,” Gross said. “It brings in not just people concerned about the green side, but people concerned about hard security.”

President Donald Trump is shifting the U.S. away from renewables. The war underscores the risks of his relentless focus on fossil fuels.

“The Trump administration has been really focused on fossil fuels, but since they started this conflict, you have to ask the question, is this good for fossil fuels? And in short, I really think not,” Gross said. “Because the high prices and the uncertainty brought about by this war are helping to push other countries away from fossil fuels.”

BEIJING, Sept 17 (Reuters) – Chinese electric vehicle maker Xpeng plans to offer its technology to foreign automakers beyond partner Volkswagen as it seeks new revenue streams, according to two people familiar with the matter.

Xpeng has been in contact with some potential partners that have expressed interest in ​its technology, one of the sources said.

The company plans to offer its electrical and electronic ‌architecture, cockpit systems, Turing AI chips, and advanced-driver assistance software to other firms, the source said. Potential partners could also include foreign software developers and automobile suppliers.

The EV maker, which is expanding into robotaxis, humanoid robots and flying cars, also plans to broaden its technology licensing and customisation business to cover robotaxi, robotics and other physical AI applications, the second source said. ‌Its ​offering would also include the operational deployment of Xpeng’s robotaxis.

Reuters is reporting ⁠the plans for the first time.

The ⁠sources did not identify the automakers or other potential partners.

HIGHER-MARGIN SERVICES

The expanded offerings come as Chinese EV makers are reshaping vehicle design and technology worldwide.

Xpeng established a strategic commercialisation team about six months ago to explore new technology partnerships and other commercial possibilities, building on the experience gained through its ​alliance with Volkswagen, the sources said.

Xpeng’s partnership with Volkswagen began in July 2023 when the German automaker bought a 4.99% stake in the Chinese EV maker for about $700 million. The alliance covers EV platforms, ⁠software and electronic architecture.

The first jointly developed model, the ID.UNYX ⁠08 electric SUV, incorporates Xpeng’s cockpit systems, smart-driving technology and Turing AI chips.

The ​model entered mass production in March 2026, just 24 months after the collaboration started.

The partnership has emerged as a ​meaningful new source of revenue for Xpeng, particularly through technology services, although the company ‌remained loss-making in the first and second quarters of the current financial year.

While vehicle sales revenue was little changed in the second quarter and vehicle margin narrowed to 12.1% from 14.3%, revenue from services and other businesses almost doubled, lifting the segment’s margin to 75.1% from 53.6% a year earlier.

On a post-earnings call in late ⁠August, Xpeng’s management said the increase was driven mainly by technology research and development services provided under the Volkswagen partnership, as well as higher revenue from components and accessories sales.

The higher-margin services business could become increasingly ⁠important as Xpeng expands into physical ‌AI. CEO He Xiaopeng has said humanoid robots could eventually generate significantly higher ⁠margins than vehicles.

Xpeng’s general-purpose humanoid robot, IRON, walked off production lines earlier ​this month ‌as the company moves towards mass production by year-end. Xpeng plans to begin ​commercial deliveries ⁠in China and overseas markets in 2027.

The company has also accelerated its international expansion, with cumulative overseas sales surpassing 100,000 vehicles since entering Norway in 2020.

The G9L SUV, unveiled in Beijing on Thursday, is due to make its international debut at the Paris Motor Show next month and will become the fourth model to be built at Magna’s plant in Austria, after the G6, G9 and P7+.

text:
With gasoline prices climbing in Michigan, some drivers are looking at electric vehicles as a way to lower the cost of getting around.

AAA reported Michigan’s average price for regular gasoline at about $4.75 per gallon Thursday.

At the same time, the number of electric vehicles registered in Michigan continues to grow.

The U.S. Department of Energy reported about 112,600 registered electric vehicles in Michigan in 2025. That remains a small portion of the state’s vehicle fleet, which included more than 7 million gasoline-powered vehicles.

So, is charging cheaper than gas?

The answer depends on where an EV is charged.

Local: Men acquitted in Gretchen Whitmer kidnapping plot sue FBI, Michigan leaders

The U.S. Department of Energy estimates that, using a typical residential electricity rate, it costs about $2.46 in electricity to drive 100 miles in an electric vehicle.

Charging at home can therefore be significantly less expensive than buying gasoline for the same distance.

Public charging can be more expensive, particularly when using fast chargers. The cost varies depending on the charging network, location and type of charger.

Paul Pancella, a physics professor at Western Michigan University and president of the Kalamazoo Electric Vehicle Association, said the difference is especially noticeable for people who regularly charge at home.

“If you charge at home at typical residential rates, the equivalent, what you’re paying for fuel is about a third or less of what you are paying for gasoline now,” Pancella said.

Local EV owners said their own experiences have made the difference noticeable.

Chris Lawrence said he drives about 20,000 miles each year and estimates he saves about $2,500 annually on fuel compared with driving a gasoline-powered vehicle.

Kevin Collins, who has owned his vehicle for about five years, said he has also noticed lower maintenance costs.

“All I’ve had to do is rotate my tires,” Collins said. “That’s about the only maintenance I’ve done on the vehicle.”

Electric vehicles do not require traditional oil changes, and regenerative braking can reduce wear on brake components.

Michigan’s EV growth has also been accompanied by an expansion of charging infrastructure.

Local: Hundreds compete in 'premier' ice skating competition in Kalamazoo

Michigan EGLE reported that the number of registered EVs increased from about 20,000 in 2022 to more than 85,000 by June 2025.

Pancella said drivers have more charging options than they did several years ago.

“The charging infrastructure on the road is much better now than it was a few years ago,” he said.

For people considering an EV, home charging can be an important part of the financial calculation.

Some Michigan utilities also offer programs or incentives related to EV charging equipment, although eligibility and available incentives vary.

The federal tax credit that previously helped reduce the purchase price of qualifying electric vehicles is no longer available for new purchases, making the upfront price of the vehicle another factor for buyers to consider.

For Michigan drivers, the decision therefore goes beyond comparing the price displayed at a gas pump with the cost of electricity.

How often a driver travels, whether they can charge at home, the cost of public charging and the vehicle’s purchase price can all affect the overall cost of owning an EV.

text:
PHNOM PENH – Moving to clean energy is creating career opportunities for young people but employers and educators say graduates still lack the practical, technical and soft skills needed for the workforce.

Speaking at a Clean Energy Week 2026 Summit discussion on Sept. 16 at the Automotive Center of Excellence-Cambodia in Phnom Penh, government officials, teachers, companies and students discussed how schools and employers can work together to prepare young people for jobs in renewable energy, energy efficiency and electric vehicles.

Kaing Sokkheng, head of business operations at ONiON Mobility, said the company finds it easier to recruit mechanical workers than candidates with the electronics skills required in electric vehicle production.

“Electric vehicle assembly is not only about electrical systems. It also involves software and digital technologies,” Sokkheng said.

Although thousands of technical graduates enter Cambodia’s workforce each year, Sokkheng said many do not yet have the practical skills needed to contribute immediately.

Employers increasingly need workers who can apply their knowledge in ways that save time and costs while improving convenience for users.

She also highlighted language proficiency as an important skill for students, saying it allows them to communicate, conduct research and compete with workers across the region and internationally.

Alongside technical skills in mechanics, electronics and software, Sokkheng said employers value communication, problem-solving, leadership, teamwork and the ability to listen to others.

Chan Sarin, vice dean of the Department of Industrial and Mechanical Engineering at the Institute of Technology of Cambodia, identified limited hands-on training as another major challenge.

He said universities face constraints in teaching time, equipment and other resources, leaving students with fewer opportunities to gain practical experience.

Employers, meanwhile, often seek candidates who can begin working with limited additional training, creating what Sarin described as a cycle in which students need experience to secure jobs but need internships to gain that experience.

He said students also need to learn how to prepare reports and communicate their work according to professional standards, rather than relying only on technical or numerical knowledge.

Sarin said ITC is updating its curriculums across associate, bachelor’s, engineering and TVET programs to keep pace with technological changes and labor-market needs, drawing on education models from Singapore, Europe and Japan.

Students Find More Challenges to Enter Industry

For students, however, finding a pathway into the industry remains a challenge.

Molchann Sakhana, an 18-year-old electrical and electronics student at the National Technical Training Institute, found the discussion helpful in assisting her to understand the range of careers available in clean energy and the skills she needs to improve.

She is seeking an internship but said opportunities are limited. She also identified English and computer skills as areas where she needs further development.

“Even if the internship is unpaid, I am willing to do the work because I want to gain experience and learn through practical application,” she said.

Un Kompheak, a 22-year-old electrical engineering student at the same institute, said Cambodia’s expansion of electric vehicles, solar power and energy efficiency has increased his interest in pursuing a career in the sector.

“If I work hard to develop my skills in the energy sector now, I believe finding a job in the future won’t be difficult,” he said, adding that both the government and private sector are working to expand the industry.

Cambodia is targeting a 70 percent share of renewable sources in its energy mix by 2030. Under its National Policy on EV Development 2030, Cambodia has set a target of 720,000 electric vehicles by the same year.

As clean-energy transition accelerates, it is expected that the demand will increase for workers across renewable energy, energy efficiency and electric vehicles. EnergyLab assessments estimate more than 11,000 solar-sector jobs could be available each year by 2040.

This includes positions in manufacturing, construction and installation, and operations and maintenance. Roles include solar technicians and installers, electrical engineers, project developers and energy management specialists.

Chennai, September 17, 2026: Jubilant FoodWorks Limited, India’s leading foodservice company, has announced the launch of Popeyes®’ newest restaurant in Navalur, Chennai, taking the brand’s presence in the city to 12 restaurants. The launch marks a significant milestone for Popeyes® as Navalur becomes the brand’s first green store in India, under its “Popeyes Planet First” initiative.

The Navalur restaurant is designed with sustainability at its core and is targeting IGBC Gold certification, while retaining Popeyes®’ distinctive Louisiana-inspired restaurant experience.

The Navalur restaurant integrates sustainability-led measures across energy, water and resource management, with the store designed to target IGBC Gold certification while retaining Popeyes®’ distinctive Louisiana-inspired restaurant experience. The outlet features 17 solar panels with a total capacity of 9.95 kWp, expected to contribute approximately 8.8% of the restaurant’s annual energy consumption. An integrated energy monitoring system further enables the restaurant to track and optimise energy use across key operations, including air-conditioning, pumps and kitchen equipment.

Water efficiency is another key focus of the restaurant. Low-flow plumbing fixtures are designed to reduce water consumption by over 40%, while rejected water from air-conditioning units and RO purifiers is collected and reused for non-potable applications, including flushing and scrubber systems. The sustainability measures also extend to the design of the restaurant, with more than 95% of regularly occupied spaces featuring indoor plants, complemented by measures such as daylighting and ventilation to support a more comfortable indoor environment. Dedicated signage and digital displays also highlight the store’s green features and performance for guests.

The Navalur launch also reflects Jubilant FoodWorks Limited’s broader focus on renewable energy and resource-efficient operations. In FY26, 52.7% of the energy requirements at JFL’s commissaries came from renewable sources, while 67% of its delivery fleet comprised electric vehicles, supporting lower-emission last-mile operations. The company has also implemented rooftop rainwater harvesting at its commissaries, with 37% of water harvested through this initiative.

Speaking about the launch, Vibhor Gupta, EVP and Chief Business Officer, Popeyes®, Jubilant FoodWorks Limited, said, “As Popeyes® continues to expand its presence in India, we are also evolving the way we design and operate our restaurants. The Navalur restaurant reflects this approach, bringing together the distinctive Popeyes® experience with practical measures focused on energy efficiency, water reuse and responsible resource use. As we grow, our focus is on creating restaurants that are efficient in how they operate and thoughtful in how they use resources, while continuing to deliver the experience our guests and teams expect from Popeyes®.”

The launch brings Popeyes®’ signature Louisiana-inspired flavours and distinctive restaurant experience to Navalur, one of Chennai’s fast-growing neighbourhoods, while marking a new step in the evolution of the brand’s restaurant format in India.

About Jubilant FoodWorks Limited:

Jubilant FoodWorks Limited (JFL Group/Group), incorporated in 1995, ranks among the leading emerging markets’ food-tech companies. Its Group network comprises 3700+ stores across six markets – India, Turkey, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Azerbaijan and Georgia. The Group has a strong Portfolio of Brands in emerging markets with franchise rights for three global brands – Domino’s, Popeyes and Dunkin’ – and two own-brands, Hong’s Kitchen, an Indo-Chinese QSR brand in India, and a CAFÉ brand – COFFY in Turkey.

text:
Environmental and public health-focused organizations are suing the Trump administration over its move to wipe out most climate regulations on coal and gas power plants.

The Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), American Lung Association, American Public Health Association, Clean Air Council, Clean Wisconsin and the Environmental Defense Fund filed the suit on Thursday.

The move comes just days after the administration finalized its move to gut the nation’s climate rules for coal and gas plants, eliminating the vast majority of rules that the Biden administration said would prevent 1.38 billion metric tons of carbon emissions through 2047, the equivalent of taking 328 million gas-powered cars off the road for a year.

That’s because existing coal and new gas plants will no longer have to prevent 90 percent of their carbon dioxide emissions from entering the atmosphere.

As the electric sector makes up a quarter of the U.S.’s total planet-heating emissions, that move could be one of the Trump administration’s most consequential climate rollbacks.

The administration estimated that it could save $310 billion.

The groups that sued Thursday said the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has a legal responsibility to limit planet-warming emissions, and that not doing so would have significant health consequences.

“Repealing these standards without a replacement is an abdication of EPA’s legal responsibility to protect public health and the environment,” said Meredith Hankins, federal climate legal director at NRDC, in a written statement. “The Clean Air Act and Supreme Court precedent demand that the EPA address climate pollution from the largest industrial source in the nation. The EPA’s legal reasoning is fatally flawed, so we are going to court.”

“Emissions from power plants drive climate change, and climate change is a health emergency,” said Harold Wimmer, president and CEO of the American Lung Association. “Measures that clean up power plant emissions also clean up other lung-harming pollutants at the same time. EPA has the authority and the responsibility to protect people’s health from air pollution.”

The EPA declined The Hill’s request for comment on the lawsuit. When it put forward the rule, the agency said that its move was a money saver.

“For over 15 years, the Obama and Biden administrations implemented a war on coal to destroy reliable and affordable energy. The Trump Administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on,” said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin.

title: Maryland officials grapple with 'bizarre' Trump executive order on Chesapeake Bay
description:
Maryland’s entire congressional delegation — including lone Republican Rep. Andy Harris (R-1st) — released a statement Thursday opposing Trump’s executive order.
Make no mistake: the Chesapeake Bay is a national treasure.
Maryland officials are in a “wait-and-see” mode, he said, wondering precisely how Trump’s executive order could affect the federal government’s role in the decades-long effort to clean up the Chesapeake.
“You can’t take away state sovereignty,” said Mueller, a former vice president for litigation at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation.
This is absolutely not a time to step back,” Chesapeake Bay Foundation President and CEO Hilary Harp Falk said Thursday.
text:
Just months after federal officials joined Chesapeake Bay states in December to renew their pledge to restore the nation’s largest estuary, President Donald Trump on Wednesday rescinded an Obama-era executive order that called for federal leadership in the effort.

Trump’s executive order also railed against stormwater management fees, which he labeled “rain taxes” — a refrain from Republican Larry Hogan’s successful 2014 campaign for governor — arguing that they “impose hundreds of dollars in annual financial burdens on residents and small businesses,” with “little to no measurable benefits to the Chesapeake Bay.”

Some jurisdictions in the bay region, including some Maryland counties, collect fees from property owners to fund projects like rain gardens, tree plantings and permeable pavement installations that slow down runoff.

Maryland’s entire congressional delegation — including lone Republican Rep. Andy Harris (R-1st) — released a statement Thursday opposing Trump’s executive order.

“The 2009 Executive Order that the Trump administration just revoked provided vital federal resources that support state-led efforts to improve the health and productivity of the Chesapeake Bay and its surrounding area,” read the joint statement. “This decision is shortsighted and harmful to our communities. Make no mistake: the Chesapeake Bay is a national treasure. And we will continue to fight for it.”

Maryland Natural Resources Secretary Josh Kurtz said the timing of the order “is a little bit bizarre,” after December’s meeting.

“We just saw strong support from all of the partners involved to continuing the work that we’ve been doing,” Kurtz said.

Maryland officials are in a “wait-and-see” mode, he said, wondering precisely how Trump’s executive order could affect the federal government’s role in the decades-long effort to clean up the Chesapeake. Could some federal agencies step back from the restoration effort, rescinding personnel or funding?

“This now is going to require us to have individual conversations with each one of those agencies, get a sense for how they’re interpreting the [executive order], and then how they’re going to be turning that into their own policies,” Kurtz said.

Trump’s order also calls on federal agencies to “encourage the repeal or rescission of stormwater management fees imposed by States or localities.” But the power to levy fees — and consider rescinding them — rests with state and local governments, said environmental attorney Jon Mueller, who manages the University of Maryland’s Environmental Law Clinic.

“You can’t take away state sovereignty,” said Mueller, a former vice president for litigation at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation. “The Clean Water Act recognizes state sovereignty — and the fact that states can do more than the federal government as far as pollution goes.”

Maryland Department of the Environment spokesperson Aimena Lipscomb said in a statement that, because Maryland’s stormwater programs are established under state law and the federal Clean Water Act, Trump’s rescission of the 2009 executive order “will not alter our goals — nor will it derail our momentum, having already completed nearly 50,000 acres of local stormwater restoration.”

Rep. Rob Bresnahan Jr. (R-Pa.), who joined Trump during the executive order signing, said in a news release that he believes Obama’s 2009 executive order “created” the “rain taxes.” He praised Trump for “listening to the people of Northeastern Pennsylvania.”

Maryland first required certain jurisdictions to collect stormwater remediation fees in 2012, a move that became a political flashpoint in the 2014 gubernatorial campaign when Hogan decried the “rain tax” on his way to a stunning defeat of then-Lt. Gov. Anthony Brown (D) in deep-blue Maryland.

In 2015, Maryland removed the requirement that certain jurisdictions collect the fees, instead requiring that they submit periodic plans for how they will handle, and pay for, stormwater improvements. The goal is to reduce harmful flows of nitrogen, phosphorus and sediment that can cause oxygen-poor “dead zones” in the bay, harming underwater wildlife.

In fiscal 2024, seven Maryland counties were still levying the stormwater fees, out of the 10 largest counties in the state that were once required to do so, according to a state report. Two others were using tax revenue, and one — Baltimore County — repealed it altogether.

Most of the counties decided to keep the fees because they recognized the projects’ benefits, said Kristin Reilly, director of the Choose Clean Water Coalition, which represents 325 environmental organizations in the bay area, including riverkeepers, land trusts and park advocates.

“They help improve flooding issues, they help beautify communities, they address potential health challenges related to dirty water, and they are put toward fixing our water infrastructure — which is failing,” Reilly said.

Stormwater pollution is considered the fastest-growing category of pollution affecting the bay watershed, compared to categories such as agricultural pollution and discharges from sewage treatment plants and industrial facilities.

Bay states have struggled to curtail diffuse sources of pollution, including stormwater runoff, and they failed to reach a 2025 goal for reducing nitrogen, phosphorus and sediment by specific amounts.

New pollution goals, by way of a new computer model, are in the works. In the meantime, the bay states and the Trump administration signed a new bay agreement last year with a host of other goals for wildlife, coastal habitat restoration and more.

“The Bay states and federal partners just signed a new watershed agreement committing to bay restoration goals. There are a host of new challenges the bay is facing, from climate change to population growth and development. This is absolutely not a time to step back,” Chesapeake Bay Foundation President and CEO Hilary Harp Falk said Thursday.

She said the foundation, a leading nonprofit advocating for the bay, is “most concerned about the loss of federal leadership, accountability and cross-agency coordination that were flagships of the original executive order.”

Reilly said Trump’s executive order was another example of the administration’s “actions not reflecting” its approving words about the bay cleanup effort.

“Repeatedly, the administration has proposed the termination of critical federal funding for the Chesapeake Bay region and now this Executive Order aims to strip away the right of local governments to make decisions based on the needs of their community,” Reilly wrote in a statement.

But Mueller argued there are reasons for optimism.

The president did not signal an attempt to rescind the TMDL, or Total Maximum Daily Load — the legally binding “pollution diet” that the Environmental Protection Agency established in 2010.

In fact, the president “doubles down” on the bay restoration effort, Mueller argues. In the order, Trump calls on his federal agencies to focus their resources on “more direct, on-the-ground projects, in areas of highest need, that would result in the most impactful water quality improvements.”

“In the past there have been a lot of best-management practices — both in agriculture and in urban, suburban settings — that look good on paper and they got credits for them, but … are not as effective as they could be,” Mueller said.

But Kurtz pushed back against what he called the “implication” in Trump’s order that cost-effectiveness isn’t a priority.

“That’s just patently inaccurate here in Maryland,” Kurtz said. “Cost-effectiveness is really central to what we do, because we know that the cheaper the projects are, the more projects we can do.”

Even if the exact long-term impacts of Trump’s executive order for Maryland remain unclear, Kurtz said that the order has a negative impact in the short-term.

“Any confusion is only going to slow us down, and I think we’ve all recognized that we need to be going faster,” Kurtz said.

The four projects can supply energy or reduce demand when the electricity system needs it most, bolstering reliability during periods of peak demand, such as on hot summer days.

The Minns Labor Government is delivering new firming capacity to keep the lights on and put downward pressure on prices as ageing coal-fired power stations retire.

Delivered by AGL, Akaysha Energy, Iberdrola Australia and Enel X, the projects represent more than $1.8 billion of investment in NSW:

The projects have also delivered economic benefits for regional and metropolitan communities, supporting more than 1,500 jobs during construction while further strengthening NSW’s position as a destination for clean energy investment.

Tender Round 2 was delivered under the Roadmap, with additional support from the Commonwealth Government, to bring forward private investment in the firming infrastructure NSW needs to maintain reliability as coal-fired power stations retire.

Minister for Energy Penny Sharpe said:

“The completion of these batteries and the virtual power plant is an important milestone for NSW.

“Together, these projects can provide enough firming capacity to meet the peak electricity demand of around 400,000 homes, helping keep the lights on during the hot summer to come.

“These projects alone represent more than $1.8 billion of investment in NSW and have supported more than 1,500 jobs.”

Iberdrola Australia CEO Paul Simshauser AM said:

“We were excited to have Minister Sharpe officially open our 65 MW Smithfield BESS, which is now powering the equivalent of 20,000 homes in Western Sydney and importantly releasing energy during evening peaks which reduces costs to consumers.

“We’re proud to have delivered this project ahead of schedule, providing local jobs, using local businesses and equipment during construction.”

Akaysha Energy CEO Nick Carter said:

“The completion of these projects demonstrates how government policy and private investment can work together to accelerate the energy transition while maintaining reliability.

“As the developer and operator of the Orana BESS, one of the largest batteries in NSW, we're proud to have delivered this on time and help support NSW's energy security for years to come and provide critical capacity when the grid needs it most.”

AGL Chief Operations and Construction Officer Matthew Currie said:

“The Liddell Battery is one of Australia’s largest grid-scale batteries. It’s helping to support NSW’s transition to a renewable energy future.

“The 500-megawatt (MW) battery reached full commercial operations this month and is storing and dispatching energy to power homes and businesses.

“The battery is the first major development at the former Liddell Power Station site and is an important step in AGL’s plans to transform Liddell as part of our future Hunter Energy Hub.”

An Enel X spokesperson said:

“The work completed through this program demonstrates the important role of flexible demand in building a cleaner, more reliable electricity system.

“Enel X is proud to have delivered 95 MW of flexible demand capacity, with participating customers already helping the NSW grid during the December 2025 heat event and periods of peak demand.

“We look forward to continuing to strengthen NSW’s electricity system through future Roadmap initiatives, including delivery of an additional 32 MW under the latest Firming tender.”

text:
Winter Park could collect tens of thousands of dollars in federal tax credits for electric buses and charging infrastructure it already owns, even as recent changes to federal law have eliminated similar incentives for future purchases.

Winter Park Town Council voted Tuesday to hire TransTax Advisors to apply for clean energy federal tax credits.

Winter Park could receive up to $80,000 in credits from its two electric buses, and up to 30% of the cost of its two existing electric vehicle charging cabinets, according to TransTax’s Project Overview and Timeline and Transit Manager Charles McCarthy.

Any revenue earned from the tax credits would go toward the town’s transit fund, and could be used to offset future capital, maintenance, or operating costs, Town Manager Jon Peacock wrote in an email to Sky-Hi News. The transit and trails fund is also supported by a 2% sales tax, according to a draft of the town’s financial statement presented to the council Tuesday.

The IRS’s Elective Pay Program, or the Direct Pay Program, provides tax credits to local governments through the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, according to National League of Cities.

According to Assistant Town Manager Alisha Janes, municipalities do not typically have access to federal tax credits, but the Elective Pay Program provides an exception.

However, the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act changed several federal clean energy tax credits, one of which was the Qualified Commercial Clean Vehicle Credit. Thei credit provided up to $40,000 for electric vehicle purchases over 14,000 pounds, such as Winter Park’s two electric buses.

The One Big Beautiful Bill also moved the credit’s termination date from December 2032 to September 2025. Winter Park can no longer receive the credit for future EV bus purchases.

The law also moved up the termination date for a credit that provided up to 30% of the cost of EV charging stations, from December 2032 to June 2026. Winter Park can no longer receive tax credit for future EV charging installations.

But the termination dates do not mean Winter Park is ineligible for all federal tax benefits. Because the town purchased the two electric buses and installed the electric chargers before those dates, it still qualifies for the federal dollars, according to TransTax President Brett Duvall.

Under the contract, TransTax would receive 25% of gross savings related to credits from clean energy purchases made before the contract and 20% of revenue from future clean energy purchases.

Janes told Sky-Hi News that the town plans to install solar panels in Winter Park. Those installations could still be eligible for federal tax credits, as long as the projects are completed before December 2027, according to Duvall.

But changes to the tax credit program do not deter the town from purchasing electric buses and chargers — limited availability of zero-emission vehicle funding from the Federal Transit Administration does, according to McCarthy.

Because the federal government is moving away from funding clean energy programs, Winter Park could be more incentivized to purchase hybrid vehicles in the future, Janes said. Hybrid vehicles can be purchased or partially funded through federal grants, such as the Federal Transit Administration’s Low or No Emission Grant Program .

Potential risks associated with implementing clean energy in Winter Park could also impact future clean energy decisions, Janes said. The batteries that power electric buses can be susceptible to altitude changes and cold weather, she added.

Last week, the Shapiro Administration opened the 50th NEVI-funded EV charging station at Sheetz on Linglestown Road in Harrisburg and 38 more stations are in various stages of planning and construction.

text:
The state of Pennsylvania announced Thursday that it will direct $32 million in federal investments to build electric vehicle (EV) chargers in the eastern region of Pennsylvania as part of the Community Charging phase of the federal National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) program.

Applications will be accepted until March 12, 2027.

Through the Community Charging funding rounds, the state is directing over $100 million in federal funding to build public EV charging stations in Pennsylvania communities, in addition to the $58 million already invested in the state’s Alternative Fuel Corridors (AFCs) and Corridor Connections.

Last week, the Shapiro Administration opened the 50th NEVI-funded EV charging station at Sheetz on Linglestown Road in Harrisburg and 38 more stations are in various stages of planning and construction.

“With this investment, the Shapiro Administration has opened EV charger funding for every Pennsylvania community,” said PennDOT Secretary Mike Carroll, speaking at the announcement in Bethlehem. “Charger accessibility is the most critical element of EV adoption. We’re excited to be on the forefront of providing that for PA travelers.”

Since Pennsylvania’s first NEVI station opened in December 2023, NEVI-funded charging stations in Pennsylvania have supported over 146,000 charging sessions, over 17.3 million estimated miles driven, and reduced CO2 emissions by more than 3,700 metric tons.

“We spent a lot of time in workshops, listening sessions and through a survey asking people where they want to see charging stations,” said Lehigh Valley Planning Commission Executive Director Becky Bradley. “What we heard is that convenience and accessibility really matter. People want charging where they’re already going — where they shop, work and recreate. Building community charging into the major investments the Commonwealth continues to make along the highway network achieves everyone’s goals, supporting air quality improvements and our growing economy.”

text:
Buying a new car in the United States is getting harder on the wallet — unless you're shopping electric.

August pricing figures show the market moved in two directions. Typical new vehicles cost more than they did a year ago, while the average EV sold for less, narrowing a hurdle that has long kept many buyers from battery-powered models.

Here's what to know

According to the Kelley Blue Book report, as InsideEVs highlighted, the average transaction price for a new EV was $54,813 in August, down 2.7% from a year earlier and 1.2% from July. Over the same period, the average new vehicle sold for $50,089, up 1.9% year over year.

So, EVs still carried a premium in August — $4,724 above the marketwide average for new vehicles.

Manufacturers did not need to spend more on deals to get there. In August, EV incentives — including cash rebates, cheap leases, and special financing — equaled 12% of transaction prices, down from 14.6% a year earlier. Using the average sale price, that amounts to about $6,600 per vehicle.

Even after that pullback, electric vehicle incentives are still roughly twice what buyers usually find in the overall new-car market.

More background

Among major segments, compact cars posted a 2.9% annual price increase, while subcompact SUVs were up 2.2%.

Midsize SUVs moved past compact SUVs to become the top-selling segment, and that tilt helped lift the market's average transaction price.

Tesla was a big contributor to the decline in EV averages. Its August average transaction price came in at $52,616, and because it still makes up such a large portion of EV sales, its price moves have an oversize impact.

At the same time, stronger demand for used EVs suggests many shoppers are more willing to go electric when the upfront cost is low enough.

What can be done?

As the gap narrows, it makes sense to compare gas and electric models directly. Transaction prices, rebates, financing offers, and expected fuel and maintenance costs can vary widely.

Some brands are still offering aggressive deals. InsideEVs reported that Lucid is giving $10,000 off 2026 Gravity SUVs from inventory and adding 0% financing.

Pre-owned electric models can offer many of the same benefits — including low fueling and maintenance costs — at lower entry prices.

Electric vehicles remain expensive, but they are moving closer to the average price of a new vehicle.

Where can I learn more?

Falling EV transaction prices are only one part of the affordability picture. These stories look at how cheap new models, used-car incentives, and owner loyalty are changing what shoppers can expect from the electric market.

• In the U.K., BYD's ultra-cheap Dolphin EV shows how fast affordability is moving.

• U.S. used EV sales jumped 10.1% in July as lower prices did what tax credits couldn't.

• Across the market, EV owners' next cars are often electric.

At the gathering, Lee Zeldin, administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, announced the latest chapter in the battle over authority in America’s energy policy—a rollback of U.S. carbon emission rules.
Additionally, Zeldin announced a proposal to rescind the remaining greenhouse gas emission standards for the power sector.
Zeldin and supporters of the plan say the decision is based on the agency’s interpretation of the Clean Air Act.
But the regulatory rollback highlights a long-running political dispute about greenhouse gas production, and experts predict the EPA plan will end up in court.
“Eleven years ago in Houston, I called the Obama EPA’s Clean Power Plan a lawless attempt to destabilize America’s energy system.
text:
On Monday, diplomats and energy leaders gathered in the sweltering Texas heat to kick off the three-day G20 energy summit in Houston. At the gathering, Lee Zeldin, administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, announced the latest chapter in the battle over authority in America’s energy policy—a rollback of U.S. carbon emission rules.

“We have an abundance of natural resources to deliver,” Zeldin told summit attendees on Monday. “Our policies must meet our abilities.”

The EPA’s plan marks an overturning of most of the standards established to cut back on carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere during the administrations of Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden. Additionally, Zeldin announced a proposal to rescind the remaining greenhouse gas emission standards for the power sector. “All of them,” Zeldin emphasized at the Monday summit.

Specifically, Trump’s EPA will repeal the standards for existing fossil-fuel steam generating unit emissions, along with the carbon capture and storage standards for coal units and for combustion turbines. Under the existing standards, coal generation units would be required to capture and store up to 90% of carbon emissions by 2032, among other rules. But Zeldin’s plan would eliminate those requirements.

Zeldin and supporters of the plan say the decision is based on the agency’s interpretation of the Clean Air Act. But the regulatory rollback highlights a long-running political dispute about greenhouse gas production, and experts predict the EPA plan will end up in court.

“I think we’re gonna see a significant legal battle over the reach of the Clean Air Act, which was defined some years ago by the Supreme Court to include greenhouse gas emission,” said Dan Esty, a professor of environmental law and policy at Yale Law School.

“Getting rid of this is one of the reasons the environmental leftists will go to court to try and challenge this proposed rule, once it’s finalized,” added Benjamin Zycher, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute who specializes in energy and environmental policy.

In 2007, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 5-4 that greenhouse gases fall within the Clean Air Act’s broad definition of “air pollutant” in Massachusetts v. EPA. That case began when 12 states, alongside various organizations and cities, called upon the EPA to regulate greenhouse gases—but the EPA responded that such involvement would be outside of its jurisdiction. Ultimately, the high court ruled that the agency did possess authority to regulate greenhouse gases, and the EPA later agreed to do so after noting that greenhouse gases had a reasonable connection to public health and welfare. The effect of the regulations were to force American energy companies to begin transitioning to power generation sources that produce cleaner emissions with fewer greenhouse gases.

Now, President Donald Trump’s EPA claims the agency has since exceeded that authority granted by the Clean Air Act to manipulate Americans’ energy choices. Some members of Congress agree.

“Eleven years ago in Houston, I called the Obama EPA’s Clean Power Plan a lawless attempt to destabilize America’s energy system. Today, back in Houston, Administrator Lee Zeldin repealed the Biden administration’s 2024 power-plant rule, its successor,” wrote U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, in a Monday post on X. “Congress never gave EPA the authority to remake America’s power grid. The Supreme Court confirmed that limit in West Virginia v. EPA.”

In the 2022 Supreme Court case Cruz referenced, the court majority argued that the EPA had misused a section of the Clean Air Act to regulate carbon dioxide emissions from existing coal- and natural-gas-fired power plants. Chief Justice John Roberts authored the opinion, writing, “Congress did not grant EPA in Section 111(d) of the Clean Air Act the authority to devise emissions caps based on the generation shifting approach the Agency took in the Clean Power Plan.”

Zeldin and supporters argue that the rollback of regulations on power plant emissions will save American families and businesses billions of dollars and preserve $370 million in “direct compliance costs”—the expenses companies incur to follow government regulations.

In a Monday statement, Jarrod Agen, the executive director of National Energy Dominance Council—an advisory body created by Trump in 2025—said, “Thanks to President Trump’s EPA, common sense has prevailed, and our U.S. energy sector can unleash more reliable baseload power without the crippling regulations that have hurt American ratepayers.”

But critics say that the long-term consequences of the decision will lead to secondary costs and a slowdown in the development of other sectors, like clean energy.

“Their decision to pull down these regulations will save some compliance costs, but it will increase public health burdens across the country and around the world,” said Esty. “It is almost certain that these regulatory changes will make it more difficult for those in the United States that are attempting to put clean energy projects into place, and the result over time will be that the U.S. is economically disadvantaged.”

Micah Green, a chemical engineering professor at Texas A&M and pastor at New Life Baptist Church in College Station, Texas, agreed about wanting America to be a leader in clean energy. He said that what the energy industry needs is predictability. When I phoned Green on Wednesday, he was at an Advanced Research Projects Agency–Energy meeting in Houston, an Energy Department event not far from the G20 summit where Zeldin made his Monday announcement.

“I’m with a bunch of industry people right now here at a Department of Energy conference. And what they are asking for all the time is like, ‘Can you please tell us something we can count on for the long term?’” said Green. “Because if they know what the rules are and what the economics are, then they can plan, then they can invest, then we can create new technologies.”

With legal battles likely to ensue, the future of the Trump administration’s proposal is uncertain. But critics like Green argue that cutting carbon emission and capture standards for power plants will affect future generations.

“From a conservative Christian point of view, the national debt just seems wrong because we know that we’re spending money and asking our grandchildren to pay for it,” said Green. “To me, climate change is the same thing.”

Green added that the lack of congressional involvement in greenhouse gas emission regulation has contributed to the unpredictable landscape for the electricity industry. He faults Congress for passing legislation that is unhelpfully vague when it comes to power plant emission standards.

“Congress has been very happy to let the executive branch decide for itself what these regulations mean,” he said. “And that’s part of the reason that we have such sweeping effective changes in laws every time a new administration takes over.”

Zycher said he also would like to see congressional involvement in greenhouse gas policy, but argued that the House and Senate are too deeply divided to pass such legislation.

“I think greenhouse gas policies are fundamentally misguided, and they really ought to be thrown out wholesale,” said Zycher. “I wish Congress would do it, but Congress can’t. So we wind up with this yo-yo effect where Republican administrations get rid of these rules, and Democratic administrations reinstate them.”

text:
By Julian Hast

Data centers in the United States will consume more natural gas than most countries within a decade, according to a new outlook from BloombergNEF.

Gas consumption to produce electricity for data centers is expected to grow by 15 billion cubic feet per day in the ten years to 2035, even accounting for many currently planned projects never being built, BloombergNEF said. That’s more gas than is currently consumed by all nations except China, Russia, Iran and the US itself, according to data from the US Energy Information Administration. It’s also more than double BloombergNEF’s previous forecast in December of 6.9 billion cubic feet per day.

The report is the latest illustration of how the future of artificial intelligence is intertwined with the burning of vast amounts of fossil fuels, tying Big Tech’s ambitions to those of the legacy oil and gas industry.

Read More: Data Center Gas Plants to Boost US Power Emissions by 20%

The abundance and low cost of producing natural gas in the US, combined with gas power plants’ ability to quickly ramp up and down as needed by 24/7 data centers, are a key part of why the fuel is expected to supply 69% of the power needed by new grid-connected facilities in BloombergNEF’s forecast.

The wave of new projects powering the AI boom makes the power sector the second-largest driver of US gas demand in the decade through 2035, just behind the demand growth of new liquefied natural gas export terminals entering service on the US Gulf Coast, according to the outlook. Power-sector gas consumption is expected to increase to 54 billion cubic feet per day by 2035, up by 18 billion cubic feet per day in 2025, while gas demand from LNG exports rises by 21 billion cubic feet per day.

Read More: Exxon Boosts 2030 LNG Sales Forecast on Strong Demand Growth

Of course, given the uncertainty of how the AI boom will play out over the next decade, the “error bars” undergirding BloombergNEF’s forecast for data center gas consumption are “fairly large — both to the upside and the downside, frankly,” said Henry Eaton, a gas market analyst at BloombergNEF and the lead author of the report. “Our power demand estimates are definitely not low, but they’re not the highest on the Street.”

The soaring, simultaneous gas needs of AI data centers and LNG export plants pose “a complex challenge for domestic gas producers,” which are currently projected to raise gas output by 35 billion cubic feet per day between 2025 and 2035 but will need to produce an additional 11 billion cubic feet per day to meet forecasted demand, according to the outlook.

BloombergNEF’s report adds to the growing bullish chorus around US natural gas because of the data center and LNG build-out, alongside fears that some of the highest-quality acreage in major US gas fields could become depleted as operators drill it more aggressively.

Citing those same factors, Wood Mackenzie in July declared “the decade of cheap Henry Hub gas is coming to an end,” referring to the pipeline trading hub in Louisiana that sets the US benchmark for natural gas. The analyst firm projected power-sector gas demand to rise by 17 billion cubic feet per day “by the mid-2030s,” nearly identical to BloombergNEF’s forecast of 18 billion cubic feet per day.

Wood Mackenzie’s outlook was followed by a viral interview with Chronometer Holdings LLC Founder Matthew Smith, who predicted that by the end of the decade, “you’re going to start to see a knife fight to secure natural gas.”

“The biggest losers of this will be US consumer,” Smith said in the video interview which garnered 1.6 million views on X and was hotly contested by some in the industry.

“I couldn’t disagree more with Matt’s view,” Ben Dell, managing partner of co-founder of investment firm Kimmeridge Energy Management Co., wrote in response to Smith’s dire outlook. While the US gas market will see “considerable demand growth” from LNG and data centers, ample undeveloped acreage within US gas fields help to explain how the gas industry “has consistently met the demand while lowering costs on an inflation adjusted basis.”
