title: The EPA Has Stopped Doing Its Job - Protect Our Winters
description:
For decades, it fulfilled that mandate through the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act, and the science-backed rules that gave both laws their legal grounding.
The backbone is gone Eliminating the Endangerment Finding The EPA overturned the Endangerment Finding, the legal foundation that authorized the agency to regulate greenhouse gas emissions under the Clean Air Act.
Without it, there is no clear federal obligation to address climate pollution from power plants, vehicles, or heavy industry.
The EPA weakened limits on mercury, arsenic, and other air toxics from coal plants.
POW’s sister organization, POW Action Fund, will be heading to Washington, D.C., later this month to hold lawmakers accountable and ask them to make sure the EPA upholds its responsibility to protect clean air, clean water, and a livable future.
text:
Photo by Donny O’Neill

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) was built on a straightforward promise: to protect human health and the environment. For decades, it fulfilled that mandate through the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act, and the science-backed rules that gave both laws their legal grounding. Over the past year, that promise has been broken methodically, rule by rule.

At Protect Our Winters, we represent the Outdoor State — the 181 million Americans who recreate outside and care deeply about clean air, a stable climate, and the future of our planet. Backed by a science alliance, professional athletes, creatives, and major outdoor brands, we advocate for the communities whose livelihoods, health, and way of life are directly threatened by climate change. What is happening at the EPA threatens everything we stand for.

The backbone is gone

Eliminating the Endangerment Finding

The EPA overturned the Endangerment Finding, the legal foundation that authorized the agency to regulate greenhouse gas emissions under the Clean Air Act. Without it, there is no clear federal obligation to address climate pollution from power plants, vehicles, or heavy industry.

It’s the equivalent of dropping into a wind-loaded slope after ignoring every red flag. These actions would topple nearly all federal climate protection, and it’s happening at a time when the world is dangerously close to surpassing the 1.5°C warming threshold. This is a line scientists say we cannot afford to cross.

What’s in the air and water

Weakened rules, more toxic pollution

Beyond climate, additional rollbacks have dismantled protections against pollution with immediate, measurable consequences. The EPA weakened limits on mercury, arsenic, and other air toxics from coal plants. It rolled back rules on wastewater discharge, narrowed the legal definition of protected waterways, and granted dozens of coal plants exemptions from the standards still in effect. The result is increased contamination of the air and water communities depend on, and stronger links to asthma, heart disease, and lasting ecosystem damage.

For those of us who live, work, and recreate outdoors, these risks are deeply personal. The $1.1 trillion outdoor recreation economy, which supports over 5 million jobs, depends on clean air, a healthy snowpack, and stable seasons. Today, outdoor athletes and communities are already contending with wildfire closures, disappearing snow, and unbreathable air. Vermont alone has lost 22% of its snow days in the last two decades. Cities like Denver, Salt Lake City, and L.A. are seeing more high-smog days, leading to canceled outdoor activities and economic losses for local businesses. Weakening pollution rules only accelerates these losses.

No rules without enforcement

Letting polluters off the hook

Rules without enforcement are suggestions. The EPA has dramatically reduced inspections, cut penalties, and expanded the use of “enforcement discretion,” a mechanism that allows polluters to avoid consequences entirely. When the agency tasked with holding polluters accountable gives them a pass, the burden falls on the communities.

Politics replaces evidence

Sidelining science

Independent scientific advisory boards have been weakened or eliminated. Climate science skeptics have been recruited into advisory roles. Researchers and policymakers have lost the tools and databases they relied on, including EJScreen, the key pollution-mapping tool used by environmental justice advocates. When science is sidelined, decisions are made by politics rather than evidence, and the public bears the risk.

We’re heading to DC

Taken together, these aren’t a series of isolated policy adjustments. They represent a systematic dismantling of the agency’s core function to protect human health and the environment. The EPA was never supposed to be a friend of industry; it was built to regulate it. Restoring that role will require public attention, political will, and a clear-eyed accounting of what has already been lost.

POW’s sister organization, POW Action Fund, will be heading to Washington, D.C., later this month to hold lawmakers accountable and ask them to make sure the EPA upholds its responsibility to protect clean air, clean water, and a livable future.

Running list of deregulatory actions

Rescinded the Endangerment Finding

Greenhouse gas rules for power plants rollback

Emissions from coal and gas plant rollback

Vehicle emissions standards rollback

Social Cost of Carbon use eliminated

Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS) rollback

Reduced limits on mercury, arsenic, lead, and other toxic pollutants from coal plants.

Granted exemptions for dozens of coal plants from pollution rules

Allowed older plants to bypass air quality standards

Rolled back cross-state air pollution (“Good Neighbor”) rule

Weakened ozone (smog) standards

Rolled back hazardous air pollutant rules

Rolled back ethylene oxide (EtO) emissions limits

Wastewater pollution limits for coal plants rollback

Repealed limits on toxic wastewater discharge

Narrowed definition of “Waters of the United States” (WOTUS)

Weakened Clean Water Act Section 401 authority

Extended compliance deadlines for water pollution rules

Expanded allowable wastewater discharge uses

Declared “energy emergency” to keep coal plants operating

Required continued operation of aging coal plants

Reduced permitting requirements under New Source Review (NSR)

Reduced inspections, monitoring, and enforcement actions

Expanded “enforcement discretion” and exemptions for industry

Dismantled emissions monitoring infrastructure

Massive EPA budget cuts (~50%+)

Dismantled scientific research arms

Limited use of scientific studies in policymaking

Recruited climate science skeptics into advisory roles

Limited use of climate and pollution data tools

Shut down EPA Office of Environmental Justice

Eliminated environmental justice grants and programs

Removed EJScreen (key pollution mapping tool)

Framed EPA mission around deregulation and industry support

Staff reductions and loss of institutional expertise

Stacked leadership with industry-affiliated personnel

title: GM is Finally Solving the Biggest Problem With its EVs - Autonocion.com
description:
The Detroit-based manufacturer committed to ditching both Android Auto and Apple Car Play a few years ago.
Is the loss of Android Auto and Apple Car Play a big deal?
GM isn’t the only automotive company to pull away from Apple Car Play and Android Auto.
Having reviewed several GM EVs, none of which had Apple Car Play or Android Auto, I can outline the problem first hand.
Even in GM vehicles that were clinging on to Car Play and Auto, the apps weren’t particularly well integrated.
text:
GM is fixing the worst thing about its vehicles. The Detroit-based manufacturer committed to ditching both Android Auto and Apple Car Play a few years ago. As a result, the infotainment options are completely missing in all of the company’s current electric vehicles, and pretty poorly supported in its ICE and hybrid models.

Now, GM seems to have pulled a bit of a U-Turn on the matter. An upcoming infotainment update is going to bring both Apple and Google’s systems back into the fold while improving GM’s native offering and adding new features for truck owners.

Is the loss of Android Auto and Apple Car Play a big deal?

GM isn’t the only automotive company to pull away from Apple Car Play and Android Auto. But it was the first (and so far only) of the big three to do so, and it pulled away pretty hard. This annoyed many customers and stripped their vehicles of a feature millions of people prefer using.

Having reviewed several GM EVs, none of which had Apple Car Play or Android Auto, I can outline the problem first hand. Both Apple Car Play and Android Auto are very good infotainment systems. They’re easy to use, well laid out, and integrate with your phone perfectly. It also means I can look up my destination and choose my music on my phone before I leave, then have Spotify start and my directions come up automatically when I get into the car.

To make matters worse GM’s own infotainment system, the one they were forcing you to use, was awful. And it didn’t work well with phones. Navigating menus to reply to texts or make phone calls was clunky. If you were using a music app on your phone, the only real way to choose a different song or artist was to open your phone and use the app. Which is not something you should be doing while driving.

The omission of Android Auto and Apple Car Play took the shine off what would otherwise have been outstanding electric vehicles. So yes, it was a bad move on GM’s part. But hopefully, it will soon be fixed.

What’s GM’s new plan for Android Auto and Apple Car Play?

According to GM, the new version of its infotainment system “integrates Android Auto and Apple CarPlay with our native system, giving customers the best of both worlds.” Basically, that means you’ll have the Android Auto or Apple Car Play display loaded alongside GM’s own system on the same screen.

In theory, it does actually offer the best of both worlds. You can use your phone-based system for things like maps, calls, and music while things like trailering or GM’s map system (if you prefer to use that) will be available right alongside it. This means you can use both without wading through a whole bunch of menus.

Hopefully the U-Turn means the feature will also be fully supported. Even in GM vehicles that were clinging on to Car Play and Auto, the apps weren’t particularly well integrated. There were bugs, sometimes a vehicle would not connect wirelessly. Going forward, it would be nice to see both Google and Apple’s systems work as smoothly as they do in something like a Ford.

The system is set to roll out in GM’s light-duty pickup trucks first. But the company describes it as “a single scalable foundation that can extend across electric, gas and diesel-powered vehicles” while also promising it will eventually roll out across the entire portfolio.

With that being said, it is worth noting that this seems to be aimed at vehicles with full-dash or half-dash length displays. So the Chevy Trax may get an infotainment update before it gets the software update.

What other features is GM promising?

As the update seems to initially be truck-based, there are a few truck centric updates coming along with it. These are a “hands-free trailering and adaptive display,” “Hitch view and terrain cameras,” and “Mobile trailer light checks.” All of which should enhance the towing and trailering experience, taking pressure off experienced haulers and making everything easier for those getting started.

Many of the other updates center on the aesthetic. Menus have been redesigned to look cleaner, customization has been increased, and cluster layouts change the driver’s display depending on the circumstances.

A new 3D visualization gives a little bit more insight into SuperCruise by showing drivers what the vehicle’s Level 2 Self Driving system is seeing. Super Cruise will also be easier to enable. As things stand, you have to set a couple of things up before you can activate self driving. Going forward, it will just take a single button press.

Finally, when taking a call the call timer will be confined to a corner instead of taking up the whole screen. According to GM, this will be less distracting, though it isn’t known if this will carry over into calls accepted or started through Android Auto or Apple Car Play. .

text:
US specialty chemicals company Cabot Corporation is putting $125 million into expanding advanced battery material production, with a $50 million Department of Energy grant supporting the push.

The company will produce conductive carbons and carbon nanostructures designed to improve the performance of next-generation batteries at facilities in Louisiana and Texas.

The investment combines the DOE grant with about $75 million from Cabot. The company plans to expand production at its existing facilities in Franklin, Louisiana, and Pampa, Texas, rather than build entirely new sites.

The projects are expected to be operational by the end of 2028 and are aimed at rising demand from energy storage, grid modernization, electrification and power-hungry AI infrastructure and data centers.

Carbon materials power batteries

Conductive additives are materials added to battery electrodes to help create pathways for electrical current. They can improve the conductivity of an electrode, allowing batteries to make more effective use of their active materials.

Cabot plans to expand production of its LITX advanced battery-grade conductive carbons at the Franklin facility. At Pampa, it will establish what it says will be the first commercial-scale production of carbon nanostructures, or CNS.

The CNS technology is part of Cabot’s ENERMAX product family and represents a more advanced class of conductive additives in the company’s portfolio.

The two materials are intended to serve different battery manufacturing requirements as energy storage systems become larger and battery designs evolve.

See All

“This investment represents an important step in our strategy to build a differentiated battery materials business that supports some of the most significant growth trends shaping the global economy,” said Sean Keohane, president and chief executive officer of Cabot Corporation. “Demand for advanced batteries continues to expand across energy storage, electrification, and emerging AI-related infrastructure. By leveraging our existing manufacturing assets, we can efficiently expand our battery materials platform, strengthen our position in the North American battery ecosystem, and support our customers’ growth with localized supply.”

The DOE funding originally supported a Cabot project in Michigan. The modified grant redirects that funding toward the two-site brownfield expansion in Louisiana and Texas.

Using existing manufacturing assets could allow Cabot to expand its domestic production capacity while making use of infrastructure already at the two locations.

Battery demand drives expansion

The timing of the investment reflects several industries placing greater demands on batteries and electricity infrastructure.

Energy storage systems are expanding alongside renewable power and grid upgrades. At the same time, data centers supporting AI workloads require increasing amounts of electricity, creating additional demand for power infrastructure and storage technologies.

Cabot says its conductive additives are designed to support these applications by improving battery performance.

The company has decades of experience producing specialty carbon materials and already supplies battery manufacturers around the world. Its portfolio includes conductive carbons, carbon nanotubes and carbon nanostructures.

The expansion will also strengthen domestic production of battery materials in the US. Cabot expects the projects to support manufacturing and construction jobs while creating additional capacity for customers operating in the North American battery supply chain.

“Cabot is a trusted partner and technology leader in conductive additives for the battery industry, delivering innovative solutions backed by a global manufacturing footprint and technical expertise,” said Keohane. “These investments reinforce our commitment to the North American battery market and position us to be a reliable, long-term supplier as our customers scale production.”

At Franklin, the expanded LITX production will target battery-grade conductive carbons. At Pampa, the new CNS facility will move Cabot’s carbon nanostructure technology into commercial-scale manufacturing.

Both projects are scheduled to become operational by the end of 2028, giving Cabot additional US capacity as demand for advanced battery materials grows.

description:

text:
Clean Wisconsin has joined environmental and public health groups suing to stop the Environmental Protection Agency’s repeal of critical standards for power plant carbon pollution. NRDC (Natural Resources Defense Council), American Lung Association, American Public Health Association, Clean Air Council, and Clean Wisconsin (represented by Clean Air Task Force), and the Environmental Defense Fund filed the action at the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit today.

“This unlawful rollback will have devastating consequences if allowed to stand,” said Brett Korte, Senior Staff Attorney at Clean Wisconsin. “Here in Wisconsin, we’re experiencing warmer winters with less snow and ice cover, more exceedingly hot days in summer, and more frequent extreme weather events, like flooding and tornadoes, due to climate change. On top of that, Wisconsin has the ninth-highest death rate from particulate matter pollution from fossil fuel combustion. EPA abandoning its responsibility to regulate carbon pollution would only make these problems worse.”

The 2024 standards the EPA finalized its repeal of today were estimated to deliver a net $370 billion in climate and health benefits – with benefits a stunning 20 times that of the costs to industry. A recent NRDC analysis found that this administration’s policies will destroy $700 billion in new power sector investments over the next decade and cut by half the power sector carbon reductions likely before its policies took effect.

The Clean Air Act obligates EPA to issue standards to reduce emissions from sources such as power plants that significantly contribute to dangerous air pollution. The EPA’s action follows a new United Nations report warning that the world is set to exceed a key climate threshold and so countries need to take more intensive actions to cut carbon pollution while also intensifying efforts to adapt to climate change-fueled heat, storms and fires.

The carbon standards for power plants were finalized in April of 2024 and would require carbon pollution reductions from existing coal and new gas-fired power plants. Fossil-fuel power plants are responsible for about a quarter of the nation’s carbon emissions. Those standards were based on pollution controls that could be accomplished at an individual power plant, making them consistent with the Supreme Court’s decision in West Virginia v. EPA.

text:
Experiential learning is a pillar of an Elon education, and understanding campus as a “living lab” allows students, faculty and staff to support sustainability on campus through hands-on work. The Elon community can participate in integrated lab lectures, inquiry-based introductory courses or sustainable research to better understand just how campus functions as a living lab.

First introduced in 1749 but popularized in 1990, the concept of a “living lab” incorporates real-world experiences and scientific experiments to generate new knowledge to advance sustainable initiatives. This model is typically seen in research, where projects take place in everyday environments as opposed to isolated scientific spaces such as a lab. Adopting the idea of a living lab integrates community participation, multidisciplinary work and real-world sustainable solutions that can later be scaled beyond the community level.

How can we interact with a “living lab?”

University campuses provide ideal sustainable living labs as they intrinsically function as a small town: combining centralized housing, dining, energy systems and transportation under one management system. On Elon’s campus in particular, waste management systems, energy regulation, green architecture, and behavioral change initiatives grounded in experiential learning provide an ideal environment to conduct sustainable research outside of a controlled environment.

Students, faculty and staff can support campus as a living lab by participating in workshops, taking interdisciplinary classes that emphasize sustainable behavior, providing feedback to campus partners on initiatives or participating in campus research or class projects related to sustainability.

Sustainable research: What is already being done?

Elon’s Sustainability Project Database highlights existing classes and undergraduate research projects that connect to sustainability. This database explores existing campus initiatives while also identifying gaps in sustainable research and curriculum on campus. Alongside this database, the Sustainable Faculty Scholars program supports faculty on campus who are interested in incorporating sustainable principles into their courses. Courses that incorporate sustainability-based curriculum while also supporting student and staff project interests have created a space within Elon’s living lab for constant campus development that follows community interest and priorities. Courses that cover sustainability-related topics can be seen throughout departments across campus, such as history, engineering, theatre and Elon’s core curriculum.

Sustainable research: What can be done?

The Sustainability Project Database is ever expanding, and students, faculty, and staff are encouraged to collaborate to continue developing this resource. Collaboration is primarily encouraged through proposing a project idea or research question. These proposals highlight what the Elon community would like to see as class projects or on-campus undergraduate research and provide space for these ideas to be explored in a formal academic setting. Existing proposals alongside new ideas can help inform curriculum development and proposal ideas while simultaneously highlighting contacts across campus who are interested in supporting specific sustainability initiatives.

Elon further supports sustainable research through a Sustainability Research Grant that applies to any and all majors. With an emphasis on sustainable development goals, research grants are awarded to students who contribute meaningfully to the knowledge base of sustainability as a broad discipline.

The Campus as a Living Lab program provides space for students, faculty and staff to advance sustainability initiatives on campus. All Elon community members are encouraged to contribute to potential project or research questions and collaborate across disciplines, schools, and departments to foster sustainable development. By modeling a living lab, Elon is advancing on-campus sustainability while developing a more comprehensive understanding of sustainable research and community engagement.

text:
Environmental and climate issues are playing a lesser role in Michigan’s 2026 election in a landscape of rising gas, health care, and housing prices.

The environment ranked far behind other issues in a September WDIV/Detroit News poll that asked Michigan voters to identify their top concern. Jobs and the economy, and cost of living, were identified as the top concern by 14.3% and 11.4% of respondents, respectively.

Environmental issues and preservation; and data centers were each selected by 1% of those surveyed as their top concern.

Michigan voters will choose their next governor, state Legislature, attorney general, secretary of state, a U.S. senator, and U.S. representatives Nov. 3, as well as ballot questions including the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics initiative.

The midterms intersect with environmental issues in countless ways, from the governor’s approach to data center development to the attorney general’s role in utility regulation, and the policies impact everything from the air voters breathe to the utility bills they pay.

Climate change poses an existential risk to humanity, and Michigan has a unique responsibility to protect water in the Great Lakes, Dave Dempsey, senior advisor for the nonprofit For Love of Water, told Planet Detroit.

Michigan politicians are at best treating the environment as a “boutique issue” rather than using the bully pulpit to advance action on these issues, he said.

‘The vocabulary and framing has changed’

Democrats have been timid about discussing climate following President Donald Trump’s election in 2024, perhaps sensing that political winds shifted, Jonathan Hanson, a political scientist and lecturer at the University of Michigan, told Planet Detroit.

Environment and climate may not be the top issues this year, but the topics are intertwined with discussions over improving energy affordability, creating greater corporate accountability, and regulating data centers, according to those who spoke with Planet Detroit.

“I wouldn’t say environmental issues are absent; I would say the vocabulary and framing has changed,” said Tim Minotas, legislative and political director at the Michigan Sierra Club.

Issues like data centers and energy policy have environmental ramifications, but are being framed in terms of corporate accountability and affordability, he said.

For example, Michigan Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson is pushing a green energy message framed in terms of economic development, while Democratic House candidate Will Lawrence is making data center opposition a centerpiece of his campaign with a corporate accountability message.

Republicans argue that Democratic renewable energy policies are raising prices. State Sen. Jim Runestad (R-White Lake), who chairs the Michigan Republican Party, told Michigan Public on Wednesday the “Green New Deal” has been “absolutely horrendous for what we need here in Michigan; we have the highest energy costs in the Midwest.”

While the 2019 federal Green New Deal resolution was not adopted by the U.S. House, Michigan passed a clean energy law in 2023 that looks to achieve 100% renewable energy generation by 2040.

Data centers, corporate accountability, environment are linked: Lawrence

Data center projects are encountering intense pushback in Michigan. Sixty-two percent of Michiganders oppose data center developments in the state, and 73% oppose federal tax breaks or policies to support the facilities, according to an August EPIC-MRA poll.

Democrat Will Lawrence, who is running to unseat U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) in the 7th Congressional District, is someone running on environmental issues in an nontraditional way, Minotas said.

This district, which encompasses Lansing and Brighton, has seen several proposals for hyperscale data centers over the last year.

Lawrence, a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, a progressive climate group, vocally opposes data centers. His messaging focuses on resisting tech industry interference in local decision making rather than potential environmental impacts.

Data centers‘ water and energy needs raise the prospect of impacts on utility ratepayers, water resources, state climate goals — and noise and air pollution from backup generators.

At a June 1 Lyon Township Board of Trustees meeting, Lawrence commented on a proposed data center, saying state and federal officials have either been silent on data centers or are actively helping projects move into Michigan communities.

“Local township officials are in a tough spot, having to stand up against the bullying coming from literally the richest people in the world,” he said.

Lawrence released a plan to slow AI development on Thursday that calls for pausing data center and advanced AI development, and passage of a national “AI Compact.”

This compact would create a jobs program funded by AI profits, bar the technology from key decision-making, block AI bailouts, and add environmental guardrails for data centers, among other priorities.

Lawrence backs a federal data center moratorium on data centers, a campaign spokesperson told Planet Detroit.

It’s impossible to have a conversation about corporate accountability without touching on the environment, Lawrence said in a statement to Planet Detroit. Data centers could jeopardize Michigan’s air and water, and add costs for residents, he said.

“We need corporate accountability in D.C. for Silicon Valley, so Pure Michigan comes first, not corporations,” he said.

Lawrence also criticized his opponent for accepting contributions from businesses associated with data center developments.

Google, Oracle, and Microsoft are among the individuals and businesses involved in data center developments that contributed to Barrett’s campaign, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings.

The Lawrence campaign said it does not accept donations from corporate political action committees, and FEC data shows no corporate PAC donations.

Neither Barrett’s campaign nor representatives for the companies responded to questions about the donations.

In an August interview with CBS News, Barrett touted legislation he introduced to bar federal officials from signing nondisclosure agreements related to data centers; and legislation prohibiting federal agencies from overriding local land use decisions for data centers, or leveraging federal funds to compel state and local governments to give up their authority.

Barrett cosponsored the Ratepayer Protection Act, which looks to compel tech companies to cover infrastructure costs associated with data center development. The House passed the legislation Wednesday.

Barrett previously voted for a version of the One Big Beautiful Bill that included a 10-year moratorium on any state-level regulation of artificial intelligence, and supported the SPEED Act, which would have diminished federal environmental reviews for data centers and other projects.

When CBS reporter Major Garrett asked about these votes, Barrett said he supports robust oversight over “anything,” including data centers, adding that the SPEED Act was a permitting reform bill intended for many different types of development.

U of M’s Hanson said Lawrence is likely to have more credibility on the data center issue because he’s been out in front of it for so long.

Resistance to data centers ties into concerns over growing economic inequality, and tech companies that have been able to influence politics and push data center projects against local objections, Hanson said.

Benson ties climate to jobs, while James promises to repeal climate law

Climate has emerged more explicitly as a campaign issue in the governor’s race.

GOP gubernatorial nominee John James, a U.S. representative from Shelby Township, said clean energy is costing Michiganders. The Democratic nominee, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, said economic and environmental issues go hand in hand.

“We can create good-paying jobs, lower costs and protect our Great Lakes by investing in clean energy, strengthening local control and making sure corporations play by the rules,” Benson spokesperson Rajan Srinivasan said in a statement.

Benson’s environmental priorities include leading the country in clean energy and lowering utility costs, protecting the Great Lakes and Michigan drinking water, implementing guardrails to hold utilities and corporations accountable and fighting for environmental justice, the campaign said.

Benson supports a data center moratorium and only allowing data center projects that create union jobs, protect natural resources, and lower residents’ energy costs, the campaign said.

Benson had earlier supported guardrails for data centers and said she would hold companies that violate those rules responsible “up to and including a moratorium,” Bridge Michigan reported in July.

The James campaign did not respond to requests for comment for this story.

In August, The Detroit News reported that James initially sidestepped questions about a moratorium, before the campaign clarified that he supports a moratorium until there’s a local control standard, and environmental and ratepayer protections are in place.

At a Wednesday Detroit Economic Club event, where the moderator noted James’ support for a moratorium, the candidate said that as a conservative, he opposes bans and mandates.

“I have always said that we need to have local control. We need to prevent pollution. We need to make sure our electricity bills don’t go up,” he said when asked about data centers.

Like Barrett, James voted for a version of the One Big Beautiful Bill that included the 10-year moratorium on state-level AI regulation.

On renewable energy, James has said he would repeal Michigan’s clean energy law and argues net-zero mandates undermine energy affordability and reliability.

The candidate told Bridge Michigan his energy strategy would include “natural gas, nuclear, hydro, renewables where they make economic sense, biofuels and emerging technologies.”

U of M’s Hanson said ongoing energy affordability concerns and rising gas prices following the Iran war could lead Democrats to push back on this type of Republican opposition.

He said it wouldn’t be difficult for candidates to argue wind and solar are the cheapest forms of energy generation, or make the case for electric vehicles.

“I feel like the politics of this are ripe for a shift because people are seeing $4.20 gas.”

text:
September 17, 2026

SEATTLE, WA (September 17, 2026) - U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has begun a second Time-Critical Removal Action (TCRA) at the J.H. Baxter Superfund Site in Eugene, Oregon to prevent potential hazardous substance releases from underground contamination at the site that was exposed during the first removal action.

EPA mobilized to the site for the TCRA on September 14, 2026, and the work is expected to last into Spring of 2027.

“The J.H. Baxter site is a priority for EPA, and we want to accelerate cleanup of the site where we can,” said EPA Region 10 Administrator Emma Pokon. “Removing or controlling these underground sources reduces risk now and allows the broader Superfund investigation and cleanup process to move forward at the same time.”

EPA conducted its first TCRA at the facility in the summer of 2024. While that removal work reduced major immediate threats aboveground, it also identified additional contamination underground. The removal of tanks and other structures during the removal action allowed EPA to safely sample beneath the former tank farm, retort areas, wood-treating drip pads, and drying shed.

Through the sampling at the end of the first removal action and additional sampling conducted in February 2026, EPA found additional sources of contamination in subsurface soils. The contaminants mainly consist of pentachlorophenol, petroleum-based carrier oils, creosote-derived constituents, and metals.

In addition to contamination found beneath many of the previous structures, EPA confirmed the former wood-treating drip pads themselves were contaminated and required removal.

EPA’s February 2026 sampling included additional surface and shallow subsurface soil sampling to evaluate the impact of contaminated soil at the site on stormwater. The results confirmed a present ongoing release of contamination from soil to stormwater, which requires the ongoing operation of the stormwater treatment system. Based on these results, EPA may implement targeted removal, capping, or stormwater diversion measures to address surface soil contamination to reduce reliance on active operation of the stormwater treatment system.

It is important to note that EPA temporarily lined, backfilled and covered the known sources of contamination at the end of the first removal action. There is no present threat to the community.

This removal action is consistent with EPA’s Superfund Solutions Initiative, which aims to accelerate cleanup at high-priority National Priority List sites by addressing known sources of contamination without unnecessary delay. J.H. Baxter demonstrates how EPA can use removal authority to reduce near-term risk while the Remedial Program advances an efficient and cost-effective long-term cleanup.

This removal action will not address all contamination at the site. The site was listed on the National Priorities List on July 3, 2025, and additional remedial actions will address remaining contamination after this second removal action.

Background

From 1943 to 2022, J.H. Baxter treated wood products at their facility in West Eugene, Oregon. J.H. Baxter stopped operations at the site in January 2022. In 2024, EPA began removing tanks and chemicals from the site and demolishing remaining structures. During that removal action, EPA removed more than 750,000 gallons of hazardous waste at the site, and decontaminated and removed more than 65 tanks, vessels, sumps, and related facility structures.

EPA added the site to its Superfund National Priorities List in July 2025 to address remaining environmental contamination.

It is important to distinguish between EPA’s Removal and Remedial programs. At this site, the Removal program is addressing known, accessible source material, near-term exposure, and migration concerns, while the Remedial program evaluates the broader site, groundwater, surface water and sediment, residential properties, and long-term cleanup alternatives.

title: Congress votes on misguided measures attacking California's long-guaranteed right to ...
description:
The Trump administration is continuing its attacks on California’s long-guaranteed right under the Clean Air Act to protect residents from harmful air pollution.
Last year, EPA Administrator Zeldin summarily reclassified three preemption waivers for California’s clean vehicle safeguards as “rules,” and claimed they were subject to the CRA.
Environmental Defense Fund and others filed an amicus brief in support of the California standards.
Over the last 15 years, clean car standards have reduced smog-forming air pollution in California alone by tens of thousands of tons – saving hundreds of lives.
More than a dozen other states have adopted California’s Advanced Clean Cars I standards, extending those benefits to millions of additional Americans.
text:
The Trump administration is continuing its attacks on California’s long-guaranteed right under the Clean Air Act to protect residents from harmful air pollution.

On Tuesday night, the House of Representatives voted to pass H.J. Res. 210 under the Congressional Review Act (CRA). The 216 to 211 vote sought to disapprove a federal waiver for California’s At-Berth rules, which set limits on toxic diesel pollution emitted by vessels docked at California ports. And last night, by a 214 to 208 vote, the House passed a second measure – H.J. Res. 213 – which sought to disapprove a waiver for California’s Commercial Harbor Craft protections that reduce emissions from vessels operating near the California coast. Removing these protections would expose port communities to more harmful pollution, more health harms, and higher costs.

The House and the Senate may also consider additional resolutions in the near future that seek to disapprove other waivers for vital California safeguards, including the Advanced Clean Cars I program.

Together, these resolutions are part of a larger effort to try to prevent California from protecting its residents and communities from health-harming pollution and rising costs. Especially at a time when millions of Americans are struggling to make ends meet, this harmful legislative action would impose higher fuel costs and higher health care costs on millions of people.

The House voted on these misguided measures this week despite arecent federal court order that found EPA likely acted unlawfully when it reclassified the waivers for the At-Berth and Commercial Harbor Craft regulations — and several other waivers — to be “rules” subject to the CRA, which they are not and historically have never been. The court directed EPA to immediately withdraw or correct its submission to Congress.

More on that, and some other information that may be useful, below:

The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia issued an injunction blocking the Trump EPA’s attempt to use the CRA to attack California’s safeguards

The Clean Air Act allows California to adopt its own more protective emission standards for vehicles and vessels. In most cases, EPA must approve preemption waivers for those safeguards. For more than 50 years, across both Republican and Democratic administrations, EPA has granted California more than 100 such waivers, helping ensure that the state can reduce dangerous air pollution and protect its citizens’ health.

Across that time, EPA has always considered these actions as “orders” and not “rules” – and thus not subject to the CRA.

The Senate Parliamentarian, the Government Accountability Office (the nonpartisan legislative agency historically responsible for determining which agency actions are subject to Congressional review) and the independent Congressional Research Service have all determined that the CRA does not apply to preemption waivers.

Last year, EPA Administrator Zeldin summarily reclassified three preemption waivers for California’s clean vehicle safeguards as “rules,” and claimed they were subject to the CRA. California and 10 other states are already suing in that matter. Environmental Defense Fund and others filed an amicus brief in support of the California standards.

This summer, Administrator Zeldin announced that the EPA was doubling down on that legally dubious approach, and sent a total of six more waivers for California clean air safeguards to Congress for CRA review.

California immediately challenged that unlawful action, and earlier this month, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbiagranted the state two preliminary injunctions in a lawsuit about the six additional waivers. The judge’s orders found EPA likely acted unlawfully when it reclassified the waivers and directed EPA to return the status quo that existed before EPA’s unlawful reclassifications. The court’s extraordinary relief reflects EPA’s flagrant abuse of its authority and provides another powerful reason that Congress should not act on the disapproval resolutions.

The Trump administration is attacking longstanding state safeguards that reduce harmful pollution, save money, and expand consumer choice

The Trump EPA has asked Congress to overturn several vital clean vehicle safeguards. These include the Advanced Clean Cars I standards, which cover vehicles for Model Years 2015 to 2025, and separate 2009 Greenhouse Gas Standards, which cover vehicles for Model Years 2009 to 2016.

These standards require manufacturers to produce cleaner cars and trucks that save their owners money at the gas pump and emit fewer pollutants that cause deadly smog and soot. Notably, the vehicles on the road today already meet the standards that Congress is trying to roll back — there is nothing to fix.

Over the last 15 years, clean car standards have reduced smog-forming air pollution in California alone by tens of thousands of tons – saving hundreds of lives. More than a dozen other states have adopted California’s Advanced Clean Cars I standards, extending those benefits to millions of additional Americans.

The safeguards also save consumers money. According to the National Consumer League, improvements in clean vehicle technology since 2002 save owners of 2024 cars, light trucks, and SUVs more than $9,000 in avoided gasoline expenses over the life of the vehicle, amounting to more than $650 in savings each year.

Those savings are even higher for certain drivers. For example, light trucks owners will save approximately $800 per year in Michigan and North Carolina, more than $930 per year in Nevada, and well over $1,100 per year in Alaska. Repealing clean vehicle standards will only increase costs for consumers.

Repealing clean vehicle waivers will not improve consumer choice: States with clean car standards have 10% more vehicle model options than states without California’s standards – and not just more electric models but more gasoline models too.

Safeguards for ships and other significant sources of pollution

Originally adopted in 2007, California's Ocean-Going Vessels At-Berth regulation reduces toxic air pollution at California ports and provides vital health benefits to the people living and working in and around California's busiest seaports by requiring vessels to connect to onshore power when at berth instead of idling dirty diesel engines.

First adopted in 2009, California’s Commercial Harbor Craft regulation protects the health of Californians living and working in port communities by reducing emissions from harbor craft like tugboats and ferries operated near the Californian coast.

Advancing these harmful resolutions would impose higher costs and more pollution and health harms in communities and ignore a federal court order enjoining EPA’s unlawful actions.

title: A 128-megawatt battery next to 470,000 solar panels outside an Air Force base in Georgia ...
description:
Georgia Power covered 650 acres with over 470,000 solar panels, good for 128 megawatts, and it’s the utility’s biggest self-built solar farm.
It’s rated at 128 megawatts and can feed stored power back into the grid for as long as four hours.
Georgia Power did it again in Lowndes County, where a 49.5-megawatt battery sits beside the solar farm next to Moody Air Force Base.
Georgia Power’s first battery, the 65-megawatt Mossy Branch site near Columbus, is a standalone unit that charges straight from the grid.
Georgia Power had it down for November when construction started, and on September 15 the company said it’s close to finished.
text:
Living at the end of a military runway is about as much fun as it sounds. You get jets over your roof at all hours, and the land right around a busy base tends to get bought up so no one builds homes under the flight path. Around Robins Air Force Base in central Georgia, a big chunk of that kept-clear land ended up doing something useful. Georgia Power covered 650 acres with over 470,000 solar panels, good for 128 megawatts, and it’s the utility’s biggest self-built solar farm.

Now there’s a battery sitting next to it.

Georgia Power announced on September 15 that the Robins Battery Facility is in commercial operation, after a ceremony with leaders from the base, state lawmakers and Macon-Bibb County Mayor Lester Miller. It’s rated at 128 megawatts and can feed stored power back into the grid for as long as four hours.

If you’re keeping score, that’s the same 128 megawatts as the solar farm. Georgia Power’s release even bundles them together as the “128 MW Robins Solar and Battery Facility.” That’s probably not a coincidence, and it has a lot to do with why the battery ended up there in the first place.

So why park a battery next to solar panels?

The boring answer is plumbing. When Georgia Power announced construction, it said sharing the solar site meant it didn’t have to build a new generator step-up substation, and it could avoid some of the costs and long lead times tied to hooking a new project up to the transmission network.

A step-up substation is basically the big transformer yard that takes a power plant’s output and cranks the voltage way up so it can travel down transmission lines. They’re slow and expensive to build. The solar farm next door already has its connection to the grid. So the battery plugs into infrastructure that’s already there. That’s a pretty sensible bit of recycling, frankly.

It isn’t a one-off either. Georgia Power did it again in Lowndes County, where a 49.5-megawatt battery sits beside the solar farm next to Moody Air Force Base.

What do 128 megawatts for four hours actually get you?

You’ll see two units thrown around with grid batteries, and they measure different things. Megawatts are how hard the battery can push at any one moment, kind of like horsepower. Megawatt-hours are how much energy it holds, which is closer to the size of your gas tank.

Georgia Power only gives the first number and the four hours. Solar Power World did the multiplication and came up with 512 megawatt-hours. Tesla lists its Powerwall 3 home battery at 13.5 kilowatt-hours, so Robins holds roughly as much as 38,000 of them. That’s a lot of boxes on a lot of garage walls.

Still, it’s not exactly a monster. Georgia Power’s McGrau Ford site in Cherokee County comes in at 530 megawatts across two phases, against 128 for Robins. Over in Australia, an 850-megawatt battery just ran full-power tests.

The job is simple enough. According to Georgia Power, the battery soaks up energy when customers aren’t using much and hands it back when demand climbs, and the example the company keeps reaching for is cold winter mornings.

That one might surprise you. You’d probably assume July air conditioning is the grid’s biggest headache in Georgia, and it’s certainly a big one. But on a freezing morning, a lot of heating tends to switch on around the same time, and solar panels aren’t doing much at that hour. If your house heats with electricity, you’re part of that spike.

So does the battery only charge from the panels next door?

I honestly can’t tell you. Georgia Power’s first battery, the 65-megawatt Mossy Branch site near Columbus, is a standalone unit that charges straight from the grid. For Robins, the company only talks about storing renewable energy and pairing the battery with solar, and it hasn’t said whether the batteries ever take power from anywhere else.

It also hasn’t said what chemistry is inside or who made the cells. That’s a bit of a shame, because not every grid battery is lithium these days. There’s one outside Brisbane running on liquid sodium at up to 645 degrees.

The battery was actually done in March

Georgia Power’s release doesn’t mention when construction wrapped up. Macon TV station 41NBC ran a story on the facility on September 10, with Georgia Power executives on camera, and reported that it was finished in March. According to the station, it’s up and running now.

Georgia Power’s target for commercial operation had been June. Rick Anderson, Georgia Power’s senior vice president and senior production officer, told the station the project came in “ahead of schedule,” while the written release settles for saying Burns & McDonnell delivered it on time. I’ll take either. Neither one gives the exact day the battery officially went into commercial operation.

Georgia Power is building a lot more of these

By Georgia Power’s count, its finished battery sites in Cherokee and Lowndes counties add up to 579.5 megawatts. Add Robins and, by my math, you’re at 707.5, or 772.5 if you count Mossy Branch too.

The Georgia Public Service Commission has approved nine more battery facilities on eight sites, worth more than 3,000 megawatts between them. The list includes power plant sites (Bowen, Hammond, McIntosh, Wansley and Yates), plus standalone sites in Hall and McDuffie counties. Georgia Power also has approval for two solar farms with batteries attached in Laurens and Mitchell counties, with 350 megawatts of generating capacity combined.

The utility says it picked those sites partly because they’re close to existing infrastructure and substations. That’s the Robins reasoning all over again.

The 57.5-megawatt battery at the old Plant Hammond site in Floyd County is the next one due. Georgia Power had it down for November when construction started, and on September 15 the company said it’s close to finished.

description:
Background: In September 2026, the Chesapeake Bay WATERS Act passed the House of Representatives.
The Chesapeake Bay WATERS Act was co-lead by Congresswoman Kiggans, Congressman Rob Wittman (VA-01), Congressman Bobby Scott (VA-03), and Congresswoman Sarah Elfreth (MD-02).
In 2009, President Obama issued Executive Order 13508, Chesapeake Bay Protection and Restoration, establishing a federal framework for coordinating Chesapeake Bay restoration efforts across federal agencies and watershed jurisdictions.
The new Executive Order does not repeal the Clean Water Act, Chesapeake Bay TMDL, or State and local water-quality requirements.
As of 2025 the Chesapeake Bay watershed jurisdictions had collectively achieved 100% of their sediment-reduction goal, 90% of their phosphorus-reduction goal, and 57% of their nitrogen-reduction goal.
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, Congresswoman Jen Kiggans (VA-02) released the following statement after President Trump signed an Executive Order regarding “Providing meaningful water quality improvements through collaboration and oversight of federal support,” which repeals Obama-era EO 13508 and directs six federal agencies, including the Environment Protection Agency (EPA) to take practical and effective action to support water quality improvements in the Chesapeake Bay Watershed.

Congresswoman Kiggans said, “As a member of the House Committee on Natural Resources and the representative of a coastal district, I understand the importance of protecting the environmental assets that define our communities, including the Chesapeake Bay Watershed. Yesterday’s Executive Order eliminates outdated, vague regulations that have allowed local officials to hinder economic development. Virginians need to know that with commonsense, responsible reforms, they don’t have to choose between environmental stewardship and economic prosperity. While I appreciate the administration shifting its focus to measurable solutions that build on decade-long cleanup efforts, I will be closely monitoring the next steps and working with EPA Administrator Zeldin to ensure any action taken is done with the economic and recreational opportunities the Bay provides and the complex Bay ecosystem in mind.”

“The Chesapeake Bay is a natural treasure and environmental lifeline for families, visitors, and native species to the Commonwealth of Virginia and Maryland, and it must be preserved for future generations,” Kiggans continued. “I look forward to continuing work with the Environmental Protection Agency, our state and local partners, and communities to direct resources where they can have the greatest impact, advance our nation’s economic goals while safeguarding the natural resources that are so important to Coastal Virginia,” she concluded.

Read the Executive Order here.

Background:

In September 2026, the Chesapeake Bay WATERS Act passed the House of Representatives. The bill reauthorizes key programs at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Chesapeake Bay Office (CBO) to advance the restoration of the Bay and support local businesses, schools and coastal resilience. The Chesapeake Bay WATERS Act was co-lead by Congresswoman Kiggans, Congressman Rob Wittman (VA-01), Congressman Bobby Scott (VA-03), and Congresswoman Sarah Elfreth (MD-02). Read about the bill here.

The Advancing Water Research and Collaboration (AWRC) Act passed the House with Congresswoman Kiggan’s support reauthorizing the national network of Water Resources Research Institutes (WRRIs) in each state that work to address state and regional water challenges. Read the press release here.

The Chesapeake Bay is the largest estuary in the United States and supports significant economic, recreational, environmental, and commercial activity throughout the watershed.

In 2009, President Obama issued Executive Order 13508, Chesapeake Bay Protection and Restoration, establishing a federal framework for coordinating Chesapeake Bay restoration efforts across federal agencies and watershed jurisdictions. The September 16, 2026 Executive Order revokes EO 13508 and establishes a new federal approach focused on measurable water-quality improvements and direct, on-the-ground projects.

The new Executive Order does not repeal the Clean Water Act, Chesapeake Bay TMDL, or State and local water-quality requirements. Rather, it changes federal executive-branch policy and directs agencies to prioritize resources toward projects that can demonstrate reductions in nitrogen, phosphorus, and sediment pollution.

As of 2025 the Chesapeake Bay watershed jurisdictions had collectively achieved 100% of their sediment-reduction goal, 90% of their phosphorus-reduction goal, and 57% of their nitrogen-reduction goal. The Administration cites this progress as part of its rationale for replacing the 2009 framework.

The Bay has also experienced recent ecological improvements. In 2026, researchers projected the Bay’s annual dead zone would be approximately 31% below the long-term average and among the smallest since monitoring began in 1985.

The order also addresses stormwater management fees, which some State and local governments use to finance stormwater infrastructure and pollution-control requirements. The new order directs EPA to assess their financial impact and encourage States and localities to repeal or rescind resident-funded stormwater fees.

title: Powering Resilience: How Indonesia is Building a More Secure Energy Future
description:

UNIDO is also supporting the Ministry of Industry in developing eco-industrial parks, promoting energy efficiency, renewable energy use, wastewater recycling and improved waste management.
Unlocking Finance for the Energy Transition Indonesia has ambitious energy goals, including adding almost 43 gigawatts of renewable energy capacity by 2034.
Building Resilient Communities in Remote Areas In some parts of Indonesia, communities remain far from the national electricity grid.
Empowering Women Through Clean Energy Women have a key role to play in Indonesia's energy transition.
text:
As countries grapple with energy price shocks, supply disruptions and the growing impact of climate change, energy security has become a pressing concern.

In Indonesia, United Nations agencies have worked alongside the Government to build a more reliable and resilient energy system which is also helping communities to adapt to a changing climate.

Modernising the Electricity Grid

A reliable electricity grid is the backbone of energy security. To prepare for growing demand and integrate more renewable energy, the United Nations Office for Project Services (UNOPS) is working with the state-owned electricity company PLN to identify more than two gigawatts of solar energy potential that could be connected to the grid.

Solar energy and a new control centre will strengthen grid stability, reduce outages and lessen dependence on fossil fuels.

Using Energy More Efficiently

One of the simplest ways to improve energy security is to reduce network losses.

Working with Government partners, UNOPS has supported energy efficiency audits and policy reforms. These efforts help households, businesses and industries to optimise electricity use, which in turn lowers demand across the grid, ensuring more stable and affordable supply.

Making Industry Less Energy Intensive

Indonesia's industrial sector is one of the country's largest energy consumers, making efficiency gains particularly important.

The United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) is helping some of Indonesia's most energy-intensive industries cut energy use while improving productivity.

In the fertiliser sector, resource-efficient and cleaner production measures supported by UNIDO have helped participating companies avoid an estimated 328,000 tonnes of carbon emissions annually while reducing operating costs.

UNIDO is also supporting the Ministry of Industry in developing eco-industrial parks, promoting energy efficiency, renewable energy use, wastewater recycling and improved waste management.

Unlocking Finance for the Energy Transition

Indonesia has ambitious energy goals, including adding almost 43 gigawatts of renewable energy capacity by 2034.

Achieving this target will require up to $188 billion in investment.

To attract capital for renewable energy projects, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) is working with the Government to develop innovative financing mechanisms, including blended finance approaches that combine public and private investment.

Supporting Workers Through the Transition

Building a secure energy future is not only about technology and infrastructure. It also depends on people.

The International Labour Organization (ILO) is helping regions across Indonesia prepare for the social and economic impacts of the energy transition. This includes identifying new employment opportunities, supporting skills development and protecting workers whose livelihoods may be affected by changes in the energy sector.

By planning ahead, these initiatives help ensure that the transition strengthens communities rather than leaving workers behind.

Bringing Cleaner Energy to Coastal Communities

For many fishing communities, of which there are several in the Indonesia archipelago, rising fuel costs can threaten livelihoods.

UNDP has helped more than 2,400 small-scale fishers adopt cleaner technologies, including solar-powered boat engines, environmentally friendly cooler boxes and improved cold-storage systems.

These innovations reduce fuel consumption, lower operating costs and make incomes less vulnerable to energy price fluctuations.

Fishers have also received training to operate and maintain the equipment, helping ensure long-term benefits.

Building Resilient Communities in Remote Areas

In some parts of Indonesia, communities remain far from the national electricity grid.

To address this challenge, UNDP supported the installation of 1.1 megawatts of solar mini-grid capacity across 22 remote villages, providing reliable electricity to more than 3,400 households and public facilities.

The systems have reduced energy costs by up to 40 per cent while lowering carbon emissions by an estimated 1,800 tonnes annually.

Local operators, nearly half of them women, have been trained to manage and maintain the systems, helping ensure reliable access to power over the long term.

At the same time, UNOPS has supported the Ministry of Environment's Climate Village initiative in South Sumatra, where around 285,000 residents have received training on renewable energy, low-emission technologies and circular economy practices.

Empowering Women Through Clean Energy

Women have a key role to play in Indonesia's energy transition.

UN Women and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) have supported more than 400 women entrepreneurs to gain access to green finance and adopt climate-smart technologies.

These include solar drying systems, biogas cooking solutions and solar-powered water pumps that can lower energy costs while supporting sustainable livelihoods.

By expanding economic opportunities and increasing access to clean energy technologies, these programmes help ensure that the benefits of the energy transition reach more people.

‘Groundbreaking Work’

“From grid modernisation to industrial efficiency, from securing funding to community-based solar systems, the UN is partnering with the Government to support its groundbreaking work in strengthening the country's energy security,” said Gita Sabharwal, United Nations Resident Coordinator in Indonesia.

“These initiatives reduce dependence on volatile global energy markets, boost supply reliability and ensure that communities, from major industrial centres to remote villages, are contributing to a resilient future.”

name: Clean Energy
title: Off-grid solar is powering Syria's reconstruction | Corporate Knights
description:
When communities build energy systems because formal systems collapsed, can public policy and finance build those improvised assets into a sustainable and equitable recovery?
Self-installed solar in Syria Before the armed conflict, Syria had around 9.5GW of installed generation capacity.
The scale of Syria’s off-grid solar economy remains uncertain because much of it is privately financed and unregistered.
Syria’s solar boom has created an unequal energy market shaped by access to foreign currency, remittances and upfront capital.
Without careful planning, decentralised solutions risk creating a two-tier energy system.
text:
In a remote farming village in Syria, 24 households pay just US$0.20 a month for round-the-clock power.

Villagers began rebuilding Khirais, Syria, in 2021. But after years of armed conflict, which left the area badly damaged, they faced an energy shortage, with electricity running just an hour a day. Refrigerated food spoiled, children could not study after dark and local producers could no longer rely on basic electrical equipment.

Then, a regional nonprofit stepped in to help. Today the village is powered 24/7 from panels bolted to their community centre. The system powers lighting, refrigeration and essential appliances, supporting a revival of the village’s agricultural economy.

But Khirais is not a feel-good outlier. It’s a small project with larger implications. It shows what locally organised solar can provide when public grids, state budgets and conventional energy finance fail: not merely electricity, but continuity of daily life, income and essential services.

Khirais’s experience raises questions about areas that are under reconstruction not just in Syria, but beyond. When communities build energy systems because formal systems collapsed, can public policy and finance build those improvised assets into a sustainable and equitable recovery?

Energy resilience in fragile conditions

More than 80% of the estimated 800 million people worldwide without electricity live in “fragile” and conflict-affected settings, according to the Council on State Fragility. These areas are likely to account for a significant share of future electricity-demand growth, but financing in these regions is scarce. In 2025, the Green Climate Fund approved only around US$500mn for fragile and conflict-affected states, out of a record $3.26bn in new project approvals – roughly 15%.

The Council on State Fragility argues that “fragile” areas need systems that are “resilient in the face of conflict and uncertainty” as well as affordable and environmentally sustainable. Distributed renewable energy systems are small, local sources of clean energy, such as rooftop solar panels, small wind turbines and mini-grids, that generate and distribute power close to the people and businesses using it. They can operate alongside the national grid or independently when the grid is unavailable. Such systems can “disperse risk”, reducing dependence on a small number of generation plants, fuel supply lines and transmission corridors.

If energy becomes unaffordable, people can take it in their own hands.

– Shafiqul Alam, analyst, Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis

This is not an argument against public grids. The International Energy Agency (IEA) says grids are “essential for bringing power to industry, citizens and services”, and are a key source of flexibility as power systems integrate renewables. “Microgrids and storage will complement, but not replace, grid development,” it adds.

That distinction matters in Syria: grid reconstruction will take years, while distributed solar, batteries and local networks can provide a bridge: keeping critical services such as water pumps and businesses running in the meantime.

Evidence from Myanmar reinforces this point. One study of a solar-and-battery system in Yangon found that decentralised solar photovoltaic (PV) and storage could provide “meaningful energy resilience in fragile-grid contexts.” The system supplied 47.1% of annual electricity demand, and solar PV plus storage covered around 77% of its highest-demand hours.

Self-installed solar in Syria

Before the armed conflict, Syria had around 9.5GW of installed generation capacity. By the end of 2023, available capacity was at about 1.6GW, leaving millions of people with less than two hours of public electricity each day.

Into that vacuum came self-installed solar. The scale of Syria’s off-grid solar economy remains uncertain because much of it is privately financed and unregistered. Industry estimates suggest nominal capacity rose from around 250MW in 2022 to more than 2GW in 2025. Some estimates indicate that roughly one-quarter of households use solar equipment to manage outages.

These figures must be taken with a grain of salt. Nominal panel capacity is not the same as actual power available to the public system. Yet the overall direction is clear: Syrian people have built a substantial amount of decentralised, renewable capacity not chiefly as an environmental choice, but because they had few alternatives.

“If energy becomes unaffordable, people can take it in their own hands,” Shafiqul Alam, lead analyst for Bangladesh energy at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA), told Green Central Banking.

One study found that a 1% increase in conflict intensity in Syria was associated with a 9.71% increase in renewable-energy production in the short term, mitigating the effects of the energy crisis in Syria.

This is not evidence that conflict creates a green transition. It is better read as an indication that grid damage and fuel scarcity strengthen demand for power generated closer to where it is consumed.

“Distributed systems can be built fast, very fast,” says Alam. Rebuilding grid connectivity, by contrast, “will take time, a lot of time.”

That timing gap makes decentralised solar strategically useful. Alone, it cannot power the economy at national scale, but it can support the activities from which recovery begins: irrigating farmland, maintaining communications, powering shops and enabling small-scale food processing and light manufacturing. Or in one case, powering electric vehicles used for medical aid at just a fraction of the price a conventional fuel vehicle would cost.

The risk of a two-tier system

Despite its lowered cost, not everyone in Syria has access. Syria’s solar boom has created an unequal energy market shaped by access to foreign currency, remittances and upfront capital.

The households best placed to buy panels were often those “being paid in wages priced to the dollar, primarily, because this stuff was all imported,” says Hayley Schuler-McCoin, senior research fellow at energy think tank Carboun Institute, whose work examines international finance, economic policy and geopolitics in the ecological transition in south west Asia and North Africa.

International NGOs and households with “strong remittance networks” were also better able to absorb the upfront cost. Those without either, she says, were “still largely … limited to diesel generators and fuel or going without.”

In the Syrian context, “thousand-dollar startup costs are huge,” and likely to be prohibitively expensive even when low-income communities pool their resources. Batteries, maintenance, replacement components and poor-quality equipment in an inadequately regulated market can add to the cost and risk.

Neighbourhood systems can help, but it should not be assumed households can sustain a monthly payment. Some people, Schuler-McCoin says, may prefer to purchase one hour of generator power when needed rather than commit to a subscription they may not be able to afford reliably.

Without careful planning, decentralised solutions risk creating a two-tier energy system. Families with dollars, remittances or suitable rooftops can buy a degree of resilience and reduce their exposure to diesel price volatility. Those without may remain dependent on expensive generators, rationed public supply or no dependable electricity at all.

The same risk applies to larger commercial and agricultural investments, Schuler-McCoin says. She stresses that if a factory or agricultural site develops solar with public or concessional finance, it should be “paired with” provisions for “the adjacent neighbourhoods.”

Without such power-sharing arrangements, “disparities are going to become even more stark.”

The lesson from Bangladesh

For Alam, these dynamics make the design of finance crucial. He points to Bangladesh’s Infrastructure Development Company Limited, which combined capital subsidies with delivery through local partner organisations, rather than relying only on conventional commercial lending.

While some central banks have implemented refinancing schemes to help increase financing for green projects such as solar, Alam cautions that these schemes have sometimes been poorly suited to serve small household systems. Commercial lenders must make the loan first and only then seek refinancing; “it’s a delay,” he says. The process can also exclude borrowers with insecure incomes, limited collateral and no formal credit history.

For these groups, “a capital subsidy, part of the cost” can make a system affordable. Credit guarantees, pre-financing and local lending intermediaries can also address a basic barrier: for small borrowers, “banks don’t know the credit profile.”

The lesson is not that Syria should copy Bangladesh’s model one-for-one. It’s that household finance must address local realities – affordability, repayment capacity and trusted delivery channels – to be accessible.

A complement to the grid

Above all, Schuler-McCoin argues that reconstruction finance must not fund decentralised solutions at the expense of the grid. “The very immediate issues are going to be getting investors to prioritise the grid and not just the supply of energy,” Hayley says. That means grant funding for transmission and distribution repair, substations, metering, technical standards, maintenance capacity and network flexibility – the less visible investments private capital often avoids.

The World Bank’s $146mn Syria Electricity Emergency Project, which supports repairs to two 400kV interconnectors and high-voltage substations near demand centres and seeks to build sectoral capacity, is an important step. But it will not be enough on its own to restore Syria’s grid.

Related stories

“If there is a net-metering provision,” Alam says, households and businesses with surplus generation “can send back part of it to the grid … they can also earn money.” If properly designed, that could create a more predictable revenue stream for larger household, farm and small-business systems, while reducing the amount of locally generated electricity wasted when it cannot be consumed on site.

Alam does not present this as an alternative, but a complement, to grid reconstruction. “Grid investment, modernisation and flexibility … need heavy investment,” he says. “But distributed systems will help you reduce the cost” in the meantime. By meeting some demand locally while network repairs proceed, distributed systems can reduce the immediate infrastructure burden.

But he cautions that any tariff, pricing structure or subsidy must follow detailed country-specific analysis of electricity prices, household demand, network capacity, generator use, rooftop potential, battery costs and utility finances.

“The first process is to do that analysis,” he says. “Many small systems can make a massive revolution. Now you imagine if there is public support, the multiplier effect could be huge.”

description:
