text:
NY-17: First in a series on the environmental stakes of one of the nation’s most fiercely contested congressional races.

The Hudson River bisects New York’s 17th Congressional District, with basalt bluffs lining its western bank 40 miles north of New York City.

The district, which includes Putnam and Rockland counties, as well as parts of Dutchess and Westchester, boasts acres of protected parkland. Its lakes and reservoirs feed the Croton Watershed, a significant source of New York City’s drinking water.

This fall, the 17th district is among the most closely watched House races in what many consider the most consequential midterm elections in American history. The Cook Political Report has the district as one of 18 House “Toss-Up” races, and rates it as one of only two with a Democratic lean. This makes it one of the Democrats’ best pickup opportunities, with Republicans holding a slim 218–213 majority in the House.

The race pits Republican incumbent Mike Lawler against Democrat Cait Conley, a veteran and national security expert. She won 49.5 percent of the vote in the June 23 primary, beating Rockland state legislator Beth Davidson, who took 31.8 percent.

With President Donald Trump’s net approval rating at minus-30 among New York voters, according to polling by The Economist, Democrats hope to win over moderate Republicans.

“I am willing to cross party lines and vote for Cait Conley,” said William Knox, a resident of Dutchess County who supported Lawler in both 2022 and 2024. “He has consistently voted along lines that support the president’s agenda, rather than voting in ways that would support us, his constituents.”

Should Democrats win both the House and Senate, the midterms could put Trump’s political future in jeopardy and determine whether the United States returns to the emissions-reduction path set by the Biden administration. As it stands, Climate Action Tracker rates U.S. climate action as “Critically Insufficient.”

As the campaign has worn on, both candidates have sought to cast the other in a partisan light: Conley has painted Lawler as a lapdog of Trump’s “Make America Great Again” agenda, while Lawler has labeled Conley a Democrat allied with New York’s “radical, far-left socialists.” The race has become a mudslinging contest, rife with half-truths, over the Hudson Valley’s pocketbook issues.

Conley has focused her campaign on affordability issues, tying higher gasoline and grocery prices to Lawler’s support for Trump’s war with Iran. Lawler, meanwhile, has blamed Albany Democrats and Gov. Kathy Hochul for soaring utility costs driven by the closure of Indian Point Energy Center, the district’s retired nuclear power plant, and New York’s climate law.

Data centers are another flashpoint. Rockland, where Lawler lives, has five. Lawler has seized on growing public unease over AI, spotlighting more than $328,000 in payments from two AI surveillance companies disclosed in Conley’s financial filings. He has turned a remark made in April, isolated from its context and since clarified by Conley, into a campaign cudgel; her comment, “we need data centers,” anchors a new campaign ad. Conley, in turn, has pointed to Lawler’s record, accusing him of helping turn Rockland into a data-center hub, highlighting campaign donations from Big Tech.

The campaigns have devoted considerable energy to undercutting each other’s claims, while poring over one another’s records.

Lawler won his second term in 2024, picking up 52.1 percent of the vote. He was one of only three Republicans to win a congressional district that Democrat Kamala Harris won in her unsuccessful run for the presidency.

Democrats will be buoyed in the tight race by a sizable voter registration advantage in the district. As of February 2026, there were 194,295 registered Democrats and 138,421 Republicans, widening the gap since the 2024 election.

Many environmentalists across the district are looking for change.

“I’m concerned with the direction in which things are going. And I’m not looking for perfection,” said Kate Schlott, who serves on the Ossining Environmental Advisory Council.

Many of NY-17’s environmental assets are already blighted or under threat:

In the village of Buchanan, in Westchester County, Indian Point is undergoing a $2.3 billion decommissioning project. During its more than 50 years of operation, the plant routinely discharged low levels of treated radioactive wastewater into the Hudson River. But plans to release roughly 45,000 gallons of radioactive wastewater during decommissioning, approved by a court but now under appeal, along with calls to reopen the plant, have made Indian Point a hot political issue ahead of the November elections.

PFAS, man-made “forever chemicals,” contaminate Rockland County’s drinking water, with the Trump administration moving to roll back limits on some PFAS.

A data center in Orangetown, in Rockland County, has plans for a tax-subsidised expansion. The town has passed its own data center moratorium, but it does not apply to the project, and concerns surrounding noise pollution, diesel backup generators and the potential for contaminating the adjacent Lake Tappan Reservoir have mobilized local residents.

In early 2025, Politico reported that $26 million in Biden-era clean energy and climate funding was cut from the district by the Trump administration, including a $19.7 million IBM project set to characterize, track and mitigate methane emissions.

Throughout Conley’s campaign, she has argued that the climate crisis is a national security threat, not simply an environmental issue, a position couched in her experience as director for counterterrorism on the National Security Council during the Biden administration.

Conley opposes cuts to federal residential solar tax credits, supports reinstating clean energy grant programs and has called for modernizing the electric grid. She has also advocated moving away from fossil fuels in favor of solar, geothermal and wind power, while calling for greater accountability from utility companies, promising to haul them into public hearings and subpoena their records.

Conley does not oppose data centers outright.

“My policy on data centers has been very clear. If they’re going to be built, they need to be a net positive for the communities, not extorting the communities that they’re being built in,” she said in an early September interview on CNN’s “State of the Union.”

Lawler, who appeared on the same CNN program, emphasized the importance of preserving local authority over data-center development. Asked about his vote for the House version of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which would have barred state and local governments from regulating AI systems, he pointed to the provision’s removal from the final bill and his record of preserving local zoning authority.

He argued that New York’s decision to shut down nuclear plants, ban natural-gas extraction and block pipeline construction is part of the reason New York is struggling to deal with the issue of data centers.

“It’s my opponent, Cait Conley, who is bought and paid for by AI and Big Tech,” he said.

Conley opposes reopening Indian Point, unlike Lawler, who recently brought Energy Secretary Chris Wright to the site. She argues that the plant’s closure reflected the safety standards and technological limitations of its era.

She has not taken a broadly anti-nuclear position. Her stance may reflect a shift in public opinion: about 60 percent of Americans now favor building nuclear power plants, up from 43 percent in 2020, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey. And companies like Meta, Microsoft and Amazon are turning to nuclear energy to power their data centers.

After two terms in Congress, Lawler has a more concrete environmental record for voters to consider.

The League of Conservation Voters, which tracks members of Congress’ voting records on environmental legislation, gave Lawler a 12 percent score for 2025. He voted in favor of the environment just four of 33 times, the group found. This marks a decline from his score of 18 percent in 2024 and 19 percent in 2023.

Still, among New York’s seven House Republicans, Lawler, former executive director of the New York State Republican Party, was tied with U.S. Rep. Nick LaLota for the highest 2025 score. He also ranked among the highest-scoring House Republicans nationally. He has supported clean air and water legislation, co-sponsoring the NJ-NY Watershed Protection Act in 2023, which would have established an annual $20 million fund to keep the Hudson River clean, and supporting New York’s Environmental Bond Act, which makes $4.2 billion available for environmental and community projects.

He has also secured $35.9 million in funding for 17 projects across the district, the majority supporting environmental infrastructure, including clean-water and wastewater projects, PFAS treatment, stormwater management and dam rehabilitation aimed at reducing the risk of pollution and flooding.

Lawler has been less supportive of green energy investments, arguing that New York’s climate policies place an undue burden on taxpayers. He was among a group of House Republicans who urged leaders to preserve clean-energy tax credits, warning that eliminating them could jeopardize investments and projects in their districts, but ultimately voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that rolled back many of those subsidies. He has called for the repeal of the state’s landmark Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act.

In op-eds, he pits “basic economics and science” or “commonsense” against “fad green energy policies” advanced by what he calls “far-left” ideologues.

“I am somehow anti-environment for wanting to expand natural gas and nuclear—nonsense,” Lawler wrote.

Lawler co-chairs the House’s Extreme Heat Caucus and the Appalachian National Scenic Trail Caucus, and belongs to the Climate Solutions Caucus, PFAS Task Force and Conservative Climate Caucus. The latter advocates for an energy strategy that emphasises the continued use of fossil fuels—which are damaging the climate, with disastrous effects for New York and the rest of the world—alongside emerging technologies.

Before entering Congress, Lawler was a registered lobbyist and executive director of New Yorkers for Affordable Energy, a natural-gas advocacy group whose backers included utilities and fossil-fuel interests. And, in this election cycle, Lawler has received campaign donations from a range of oil and gas interests, including $10,000 from Koch Inc.; $5,000 from California-based utility company Edison International; $4,500 from Williams Cos.; and $1,000 from Entergy, the former owner of Indian Point. He has also received personal contributions from industry executives and owners, including $8,300 from the owner of Sunshine Gasoline, a Florida-based oil retailer; $7,000 from the chairman of United Refining Co., based in Warren, Pennsylvania; and $9,500 from the president of Texas Crude Energy.

Conley is part of Unrig Washington, a program in which candidates reject corporate PAC money. While Conley’s campaign website lays out her approach to “Fighting Climate Change as a National Security Priority,” she has not made the issue a major focus of her campaign.

Neither the Conley nor Lawler campaign responded to requests for comment.

Conley and Lawler will face off in a televised debate on Sept. 28 at 8 p.m. Eastern on News 12, followed by another on Oct. 14 at 7 p.m. on PIX11. As the general election draws closer, many are hoping the debates will force the candidates to take clearer, more specific positions on the environmental issues facing the district.

text:
Outlines strategic integration of solar, batteries, and energy electronics

Emphasizes technological innovation alongside supply chain discipline

Expands solar applications into space, offshore, and fuel production

China is intensifying its approach to clean energy manufacturing, particularly focusing on solar, batteries, and energy electronics, as it gears up for the period outlined in a fresh five-year plan. A recent roadmap put out by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology along with the National Development and Reform Commission highlights energy electronics as a key driver for China's wider electronics industry. At the same time, the policy hints that future growth should become more organized, technologically advanced, and less prone to reckless competition or unchecked capacity expansion.

The plan integrates clean-technology manufacturing within a broader push for industrial upgrades. Instead of considering solar modules, batteries, storage solutions, and related equipment as isolated industries, the roadmap advocates for closer ties among photovoltaic generation, energy storage, end-use devices, and digital technologies. This reflects an effort to connect manufacturing capabilities with smarter control systems, more digitized operations, and broader applications across the energy landscape.

Covering the timeframe specified in the plan, sources like pv magazine and other summaries suggest that the roadmap doesn’t set strict targets for how much is to be produced or deployed. Instead, it emphasizes technological priorities and industrial directions for photovoltaic and battery sectors. That makes it more strategic than simply setting numeric goals; it stresses which technologies deserve more attention, how supply chains should develop, and how capacity growth ought to be managed.

This structure is especially significant for firms involved in sourcing raw materials, electronics manufacturing, logistics, and clean-energy equipment. It links upstream materials and component development with downstream systems, including solar power, energy storage, power conversion, and end-user appliances. Essentially, it describes an ecosystem where materials, manufacturing processes, software, control technologies, and energy applications are expected to evolve more closely together.

Moving Solar Toward Better Efficiency and New Materials

On the solar front, China’s government is holding onto its goal of improving high-efficiency crystalline silicon solar cells, while also pushing ahead with the development of perovskite tandem cells, which look like strong contenders for the next generation of photovoltaic modules. The roadmap places this technology alongside ongoing improvements in the established crystalline silicon supply chain, indicating that the solar strategy involves both incremental enhancements and innovation in newer cell architectures.

The policy also pinpoints several manufacturing priorities aimed at boosting solar output and performance. These include producing polysilicon with lower energy consumption, making wafer slices thinner and larger, better encapsulating modules for durability, and developing smarter photovoltaic systems. Each of these addresses a different aspect of the solar value chain.

Lower-energy polysilicon manufacturing relates to the energy demands of making one of the foundational materials for crystalline silicon solar cells. Thinner and larger wafers pertain to the physical design of solar cells and modules, focusing on how they are made. Improving encapsulation techniques ensures better protection and longevity, while smarter PV systems involve integrating physical hardware with advanced monitoring, control, and digital functions.

The roadmap also emphasizes the digitalization of inverters, controllers, and trackers, components vital for managing and optimizing photovoltaic systems. These elements help handle power conversion, system control, and orientation. By highlighting their digitalization, China seems to be emphasizing more integrated solar electronics rather than treating modules as standalone hardware.

Materials such as perovskite compounds, polyolefin elastomers, and high-purity quartz sand are specifically called out for broader development. This suggests that the policy isn’t just about finished modules but also the inputs and components needed for manufacturing, which is essential for supporting suppliers and industry players focused on developing those specialized materials.

Expanding Solar Applications Beyond the Usual

The policy isn’t just about traditional utility-scale or rooftop solar; it broadens the horizon towards space-based and offshore solar systems. Beijing also encourages business models that integrate solar energy with the production of hydrogen, ammonia, and methanol, according to summarized versions of the plan.

This linkage between solar generation and other energy and industrial processes aims to push solar power into roles beyond just powering the grid or buildings. Instead, it’s about using solar energy to make fuels and chemicals, thereby integrating PV into larger industrial systems. The references to hydrogen, ammonia, and methanol hint at a broader, more versatile energy ecosystem.

Including space-based and offshore solar suggests a forward-looking approach, considering newer settings for deployment beyond traditional land. Although specific targets are not detailed, these areas are recognized as promising and are part of China’s bigger clean energy strategy.

This approach aligns with China’s focus on combining renewable energy with storage and grid management technologies leading up to the 15th Five-Year Plan. Solar isn’t just being viewed as generation capacity but as part of a comprehensive system that includes storing, converting, and wisely using electricity, making energy electronics more crucial because the system’s overall performance hinges on more than just the solar modules.

Batteries and Storage: Same Tech-Driven Push

Batteries follow a similar plan. China aims to maintain its leadership in lithium-ion technology, while also promoting the industrialization of emerging battery types like solid-state, sodium-ion, and flow batteries. Fuel cells are also included among the priorities.

Two main directions stand out: high-energy-density solid-state batteries and low-cost, long-life sodium-ion batteries. The former aims for higher energy storage capacity, while the latter focuses on affordability and longer usage cycles. While the plan doesn’t specify exact production volumes or deployment goals, it makes clear these technologies are to be prioritized for further development.

The policy highlights key materials and components for batteries, solid electrolytes, silicon-carbon anodes, high-capacity cathodes, and composite current collectors, indicating a comprehensive focus from raw materials all the way to system integration.

Solid electrolytes are tied to solid-state battery systems, and the other materials support these promising designs. Alongside these, better power electronics, more efficient storage integration, tighter control systems, and improved thermal management are also called for, recognizing that storage performance depends heavily on how batteries are controlled, cooled, and integrated within the broader energy system.

This holistic systems approach links battery development directly with energy electronics and software, emphasizing supply chain, control, safety, and operational efficiency.

A Shift Toward Supply Discipline and Better Management

Perhaps the most notable change is a stronger push for supply discipline. While encouraging advanced tech, the policy underscores the need for coordinated capacity planning, early-warning mechanisms, and measures against what China terms “involution-style” competition, basically, destructive price wars and overbuilding.

The idea is to prevent disorderly expansion, which can drag down quality, raise excess capacity, and lead to unstable markets. The roadmap calls for better planning to align investments with market needs, warning systems to catch risks early, and rules against aggressively competing by undercutting prices rather than innovating.

This message resonates across solar, battery, and energy electronics, where complex ecosystems, sourcing, and logistics are involved. If capacity grows unchecked, it could cause issues for suppliers, manufacturers, and downstream markets. Therefore, the plan indicates future growth should be mindful of not just scale, but sustainability and quality.

It also emphasizes safer management of lithium-ion batteries, especially when it comes to recycling and dealing with retired batteries and modules. This lifecycle perspective links manufacturing, deployment, and the end-of-life process, even if specific steps or measures are not detailed here.

Building on previous guidance from 2023, which supported new solar cell technologies and warned against overcapacity, this new roadmap maintains those support areas but adds a renewed focus on coordination, safety, and industrial control, balancing support for innovative tech with necessary regulation.

Takeaways

- China’s roadmap treats solar, batteries, storage, energy electronics, and digital technologies as parts of a connected industrial ecosystem.

- Solar priorities include high-efficiency crystalline silicon cells, perovskite tandem cells, lower-energy polysilicon, improved encapsulation, and smarter PV systems.

- Battery priorities include lithium-ion technology, solid-state batteries, sodium-ion batteries, flow batteries, and fuel cells.

- The plan emphasizes sourcing, materials, power electronics, software, thermal management, safety, and system integration.

- Coordinated capacity planning and early-warning mechanisms are intended to limit destructive competition and unchecked expansion.

- The roadmap does not establish strict production or deployment targets, focusing instead on technology and industrial direction.

text:
America’s commercial buildings are generating substantial economic value in markets across the country, according to a new study from Building Owners and Managers Association (BOMA) International. The report finds that commercial building operations and maintenance generate nearly $610 billion in annual economic activity, support 3.9 million jobs, and contribute $344.4 billion to U.S. GDP.

“Commercial buildings are economic engines, supporting businesses, jobs and communities across the country,” said Kjersten Jaeb, BOMA Fellow, RPA®, LEED GA, Chair and Chief Elected Officer of BOMA International. “Every building relies on an extensive network of professionals, service providers and businesses to keep it running safely and efficiently, from building managers, contractors and suppliers to maintenance and repair companies, utilities, insurers and security providers. Technology is also transforming how we manage energy, water, security, access and overall building performance. This study shows just how significant that entire ecosystem is to the U.S. economy.”

Commercial Buildings In A Changing Real Estate Landscape

In addition to measuring the economic impact of operating and maintaining commercial buildings, the study examines construction trends across the office, retail and industrial sectors, providing a broader look at how the U.S. commercial real estate landscape is evolving.

One notable shift is the rapid growth of data center development. Federal construction statistics classify data centers as private office construction, meaning their rapid growth is increasingly shaping overall office construction figures. In 2025, data centers accounted for approximately $41.2 billion, or nearly 46%, of the more than $90 billion in private office construction nationally, compared with less than 5% a decade earlier. Traditional office construction excluding data centers totaled approximately $48.4 billion in 2025.

Industrial construction also remains at historically high levels. Warehouse and manufacturing construction totaled approximately $274.2 billion in 2025. While down 7.9% from the previous year, investment remained more than twice its 2020 level and represented the third-highest annual total on record. Retail construction totaled approximately $47.1 billion in 2025, with activity increasing during the first three months of 2026. In addition, the U.S. life sciences real estate market is normalizing following several years of rapid expansion.

Economic Impact Across The Country

The economic impact of building operations is not limited to the country’s largest commercial real estate markets. BOMA’s 79 markets span 38 states, with building operations supporting local jobs, businesses and economic activity in communities of varying sizes across the country.

“The economic impact of commercial real estate is not a one-time event,” said Mary Lue Peck, President and COO, of BOMA International. “Ongoing investments in the operation, maintenance and improvement of our buildings generate economic activity that supports businesses, jobs and wages across the country creating an impact that lasts well into the future.”

The study was conducted by the Business Research Division at the Leeds School of Business at the University of Colorado Boulder on behalf of BOMA International. The full report and state economic impact profiles are available here.

text:
The U.S. Department of Interior's Bureau of Land Management has leased nearly 3,000 acres of the Wayne National Forest to oil and gas companies. Critics warn the move could be damaging to the region, but industry officials say the project is needed to help the nation meet its energy needs.

The Bureau announced its plans to lease the land in July. Following a mandatory protest period, 40 parcels within the Wayne National Forest were sold in an online auction on Tuesday. The sales totaled over $11 million.

The highest bid was nearly $10,000 per acre on a parcel in Monroe County.

Nathan Johnson, attorney of land and water for the Ohio Environmental Council, said the scale of the projects could radically change the area.

“We are talking about pipelines. We are talking well pads,” Johnson said. “We're talking [about a] huge increase in truck traffic. We're talking about major increases in air pollution as well.”

A history of deforestation

This isn’t the first time the Wayne National Forest has seen industrial changes. In the 19th and 20th centuries, the logging, mining and farming industries all cleared large swaths of forest land in the region.

Ecologist Glen Matlack with Ohio University says the area still hasn’t fully recovered.

“It takes a while to accumulate a whole forest community, to put together the entire forest. A forest is not just the trees that grow in the forest,” Matlack said.

Matlack has found small patches of forest herbs growing in the national forest. The native plants grow underneath established tree canopies and are a nutrient resource for wildlife. Matlack says the infrequency of the herbs is indicative of past deforestation.

“You can still recognize the history of disturbance in a forest patch here by the poverty of forest species in it,” Matlack said.

Private land owners may profit

The Wayne National Forest is home to several endangered species like the Indiana Bat. Because they’re protected, federal agencies can’t take actions that would put them at further risk.

Mike Chadsey, director of external affairs for the Ohio Oil and Gas Association, says oil and gas companies generally prefer to work with private landowners who have already clear cut their fields, instead of taking down trees in the national forest. That way they don’t have to worry about violating federal laws that protect endangered species.

“The vast majority of these well pad locations, they are going to be on private property,” he said. “When you try to take down trees you can only have a small window to do that because of Indiana bats and various other species that reside in those trees.”

Some private properties in Monroe and Washington Counties are surrounded by national forest land. Chadsey says opening up the forest for oil and gas development allows those landowners to lease their mineral rights, many for the first time.

Chadsey says some forest land will likely still need to be cleared for pipelines — and there’s no guarantee the oil and gas companies won’t place well pads in the Wayne — but he says the impact should be minimal.

“We have to be mindful of truck traffic, we have to be mindful of pipelines. So here's all the things that are involved. We are aware of them. We don't think that's a negative impact to the forest,” Chadsey said.

Overall, he thinks the development will be positive for the entire state, as thousands of products can be made from crude oil and gas.

“To be able to use that as a feedstock for manufacturing is huge for Ohio and West Virginia, because these are states that make things,” Chadsey said.

Cause for concern

The Ohio Environmental Council doesn’t think oil and gas drilling is worth the risk to the land.

“That's a huge chunk of public land for context. I mean, that's larger than Cuyahoga Valley National Park,” Ohio Environmental Council Attorney Nathan Johnson said. “It is larger than the largest state park in Ohio. It's more than 30,000 football fields.”

The Ohio Environmental Council filed a lawsuit claiming the Bureau of Land Management is violating several environmental laws by leasing federal forest land, and filed an official protest ahead of the auction.

Johnson said the Council is likely to file another suit now that the auction has taken place. The Council also argues the Bureau’s environmental studies neglected to fully consider the wells’ impact on air quality.

Ecologist Glen Matlock says opening up the area is especially concerning considering trees are natural air filters. They also naturally produce moisture, which cools the air.

In a press release, the Bureau of Land Management stated this week’s auction is only the first step of the process. Companies leasing the land still have to submit a drilling permit application, which the Bureau has to approve.

text:
Local authorities and community energy groups across the UK are being handed new opportunities to develop their own renewable energy projects, following the launch of a £30 million funding programme from Great British Energy.

The investment marks the first tranche of a wider commitment of up to £1 billion announced earlier this year. The initiative is designed to support more than 1,000 community and locally led clean energy schemes, ranging from solar panels on public buildings to village-owned wind farms and hydroelectric projects.

The funding will enable communities and councils to take greater control of their energy future, with ownership of projects remaining in local hands. Ministers say this approach will ensure the financial benefits of renewable energy stay within communities, helping reduce energy costs for public services while generating income that can be reinvested locally.

The announcement comes after a summer marked by record temperatures and extreme weather events, which have intensified concerns about climate change and the need to accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels.

By supporting locally owned renewable energy generation, the government hopes to empower communities to cut emissions, strengthen energy resilience and play a more active role in tackling climate change.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said:

“I know many people are worried about climate change and feel like they’ve got no control over where their energy comes from, or how they can actually make a difference.

“Today we’re changing that by giving people power. Whether it’s solar panels on a local library or a community-owned wind farm, we’re letting people decide what clean energy projects they want and making sure they feel the benefits of the clean energy transition in their pockets too.”

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh highlighted the role communities can play in responding to climate change. She said:

“All of us felt deep concern for our climate during the record-breaking temperatures we experienced this summer.

“Ahead of New York Climate week, we are putting power in the hands of people and places, so more communities can take action.

“Everyone deserves a stake in our energy future and through these local power projects, communities can reap the full benefits of clean energy – reducing emissions, cutting bills and reinvesting profits to benefit local areas, instead of big energy companies.”

Alongside direct support for local renewable energy schemes, the government has confirmed it will publish further details this autumn on plans to offer community energy groups ownership stakes in larger renewable developments.

The proposal is intended to strengthen partnerships between local communities and energy developers, ensuring a greater share of clean energy revenues remains in the areas where projects are built.

If implemented, the model would mirror successful approaches already used in countries such as Germany and Denmark, where community ownership has become a key part of the renewable energy landscape.

The announcement also coincides with progress on existing Great British Energy programmes. More than 150 renewable energy projects serving public buildings across England’s Mayoral Combined Authorities have now been completed and switched on.

According to ministers, these installations could generate up to £50 million in energy bill savings, allowing public sector organisations to redirect funding into frontline services and local priorities.

As pressure grows on councils and public services to reduce costs while meeting net-zero targets, the latest funding offers an opportunity for communities to take a direct stake in the UK's clean energy transition while delivering tangible local benefits.

text:
On a Friday afternoon in May, three men sat chatting on folding chairs inside Lordstown’s local United Auto Workers hall. Normally, they’d be on their shift at the massive battery plant a few miles away. But they’d been out of work all year.

The factory — owned by General Motors and South Korea’s LG Energy Solution — announced last fall that work would stop in January because of slow electric-vehicle sales. Their joint venture, Ultium Cells, indefinitely let go about 480 employees, and told the remaining 850 factory workers they wouldn’t be needed for many months.

That announcement came a few weeks after U.S. President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans killed a $7,500 tax credit that was intended to jumpstart consumer demand for electric cars, sending U.S. EV sales tumbling. The layoffs were a sobering letdown after the burst of optimism when the factory opened four years ago, said Steve Baier, one of the workers passing time inside the union hall.

Dublin, Sept. 17, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- "United States Rechargeable Battery Market Size and Share - Growth Analysis Report and Forecast Trends (2026-2035)" has been added to ResearchAndMarkets.com's offering.

United States Rechargeable Battery Market Forecast to Reach USD 68.0 Billion by 2035

The United States rechargeable battery market was valued at USD 28.0 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach USD 68.0 billion by 2035, expanding at a compound annual growth rate of 11.7%. Market growth is being driven by rising electric vehicle adoption, record investment in domestic battery manufacturing, rapid deployment of grid-scale battery energy storage systems, and sustained demand from consumer electronics and industrial applications.

Lithium-ion batteries account for approximately 75% of the US rechargeable battery market by value. Nickel manganese cobalt, nickel cobalt aluminum, and lithium iron phosphate chemistries serve electric vehicles, stationary energy storage, portable electronics, and industrial systems. Lead-acid batteries retain an estimated 15% market share, primarily across automotive starting, uninterruptible power supply, and backup power applications, while nickel-metal hydride batteries continue to support hybrid vehicle demand.

Electric Vehicle Battery Demand Accelerates

Electric vehicles represent the largest end-use segment, accounting for approximately 45% of total US rechargeable battery market value. US electric vehicle sales reached approximately 2.1 million units in 2023, compared with about 300,000 units in 2020. This expansion has substantially increased demand for battery cells, modules, packs, materials, and related manufacturing infrastructure.

Federal incentives are supporting continued market development. Consumer tax credits of up to USD 7,500 for qualifying electric vehicles encourage adoption while reinforcing North American assembly and domestic battery-content requirements. Tesla, Ford, General Motors, Rivian, and other manufacturers are expanding US production capacity, strengthening demand for localized battery supply chains.

Lithium iron phosphate batteries are gaining market share because of their competitive cost, cycle life, and thermal performance. LFP represented approximately 35% of US electric vehicle battery deployments in 2024, up from about 20% in 2022. Adoption by Tesla, Ford, and General Motors is expected to support further growth across both electric vehicles and stationary storage.

IRA Incentives Reshape Domestic Battery Manufacturing

More than USD 130 billion in US battery gigafactory investments have been announced, supported by the Inflation Reduction Act and its Section 45X Advanced Manufacturing Production Credit. The program provides credits of USD 35 per kilowatt-hour for qualifying domestically manufactured battery cells and USD 10 per kilowatt-hour for qualifying battery modules.

Major projects include LG Energy Solution facilities in Michigan and Arizona, Samsung SDI manufacturing in Indiana, SK On operations in Georgia, Panasonic's Kansas gigafactory, and additional investments from AESC and other market participants. These projects are expanding domestic cell production, reducing reliance on imported batteries, and increasing supply-chain resilience for automotive and energy storage customers.

Grid-Scale Battery Energy Storage Leads Application Growth

Energy storage systems represent approximately 20% of the United States rechargeable battery market and are projected to be the fastest-growing application segment, with an estimated compound annual growth rate of approximately 25%. More than 35 GWh of new US battery energy storage capacity was deployed in 2024, compared with approximately 10 GWh in 2022.

Deployment is being supported by federal investment tax credits, renewable energy integration requirements, utility resource adequacy programs, and rising electricity demand. California, Texas, and Arizona remain leading markets for utility-scale installations. Tesla Megapack, Fluence, and CATL are among the prominent suppliers competing for US battery energy storage system projects.

Residential solar-plus-storage is also expanding, supported by the 30% residential clean energy credit and declining system costs. The segment is projected to grow at approximately 18% annually, particularly in states with high electricity prices, time-of-use rates, and resilience requirements.

Next-Generation Battery Commercialization Advances

Solid-state battery development continues to progress toward pilot production and potential commercial deployment after 2027. Toyota has committed significant investment to solid-state technology, while QuantumScape and Solid Power are advancing automotive validation programs with Volkswagen, BMW, and Ford. QuantumScape reported customer deliveries of lithium-metal battery cells for extended testing in 2024, including performance exceeding 1,000 charging cycles with less than 5% capacity degradation.

Panasonic also advanced US production of large-format cylindrical cells at its Kansas facility, while LG Energy Solution continued development of its Arizona gigafactory, which is targeting annual capacity of 36 GWh. These investments reflect growing competition in advanced cell formats, manufacturing efficiency, energy density, and domestic production eligibility.

Competitive Landscape

The US rechargeable battery market features strong participation from Panasonic Energy, LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI, and SK On. Panasonic maintains a significant position through its relationship with Tesla, while LG Energy Solution supplies General Motors, Honda, and Stellantis. Samsung SDI is expanding prismatic-cell production for automotive partners, and SK On is investing more than USD 11 billion in US manufacturing, including its BlueOval SK partnership with Ford.

US-based companies are also expanding their roles across battery energy storage, silicon-anode technology, and solid-state development. Tesla Energy, Enovix, QuantumScape, and Solid Power address specialized segments within the broader rechargeable battery ecosystem.

Key United States Rechargeable Battery Market Highlights

The market is projected to increase from USD 28.0 billion in 2025 to USD 68.0 billion by 2035.

Lithium-ion batteries account for approximately 75% of total market value.

Electric vehicles represent approximately 45% of market value and remain the largest end-use segment.

More than USD 130 billion in domestic battery manufacturing investments have been announced.

Grid-scale battery energy storage is projected to grow at approximately 25% annually.

LFP chemistry reached approximately 35% of US electric vehicle battery deployments in 2024.

Solid-state battery programs are advancing toward anticipated commercialization in 2027 and 2028.

Supported by electric vehicle production, renewable energy integration, federal manufacturing incentives, and next-generation battery technologies, the United States rechargeable battery market is positioned for sustained expansion through 2035. Domestic manufacturing growth and continued investment in battery innovation are expected to strengthen the country's role in the global energy storage supply chain.

text:

In Washington, D.C.

EPA repeals power plant carbon standards

What’s the story?

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) on Sept. 14 repealed most Biden-era carbon emissions standards for coal- and gas-fired power plants and proposed eliminating remaining federal greenhouse gas requirements for the power sector.

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced the actions during a meeting of G20 energy ministers in Houston. The Biden-era standards required certain coal-fired power plants and new natural gas plants to reduce their carbon dioxide emissions, including through carbon capture and storage technology. Carbon capture and storage involves capturing carbon dioxide before it enters the atmosphere and storing it underground.

The EPA said the proposed repeal of the remaining standards would save the power industry $370 million in compliance costs over 20 years. Zeldin said the changes would make it easier to build generating capacity as electricity demand increases. Zeldin said, "That means cutting red tape so we can build new power-generating infrastructure."

The agency also proposed rescinding remaining greenhouse gas requirements for power plants based on its position that the Clean Air Act does not authorize the EPA to regulate the power sector's greenhouse gas emissions. That proposal would affect the legal basis for future federal carbon regulations covering power plants.

Why does it matter?

The EPA's actions remove most federal carbon requirements from a sector that accounts for nearly one-quarter of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions and propose eliminating the remaining requirements. The Biden administration estimated its power plant standards would prevent one billion metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions through 2047 and produce $370 billion in net benefits.

The repeal reduces federal compliance requirements for power companies, but state emissions rules will remain in effect. National Mining Association President and CEO Rich Nolan said the repeal "corrects the egregious misuse of the Clean Air Act as a political tool to end American coal generation and implements the law as Congress intended."

Environmental groups opposed the changes and said they would increase greenhouse gas emissions and associated health and environmental costs. Center for Biological Diversity Climate Law Institute attorney Maggie Coulter said, "Denying the existence of a quarter of the country's climate pollution is utterly reckless. It will lead to more lost lives and suffering from intense heatwaves, drastic storms and destructive wildfires, just like those we've seen this summer."

What's the background?

The Biden administration adopted the power plant carbon standards in 2024. The Trump administration proposed repealing them in June 2025 as part of a broader reconsideration of federal regulations covering fossil-fuel power plants.

President Donald Trump (R) and the EPA separately rescinded the 2009 endangerment finding in February 2026. The finding had concluded that greenhouse gases threaten public health and welfare and provided the legal foundation for federal greenhouse gas regulations covering motor vehicles. The administration also repealed federal vehicle greenhouse gas standards tied to that finding.

A coalition of 25 state attorneys general and other state and local officials sued the EPA in March 2026 to challenge the rescission. The plaintiffs argue the EPA's action violates the Clean Air Act and conflicts with U.S. Supreme Court precedent. The case remains pending in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit.

The EPA based that February action on its interpretation that the Clean Air Act does not authorize the agency to regulate greenhouse gases based on global climate effects. The Sept. 14 power-sector proposal would further limit the agency's authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from power plants.

SEC asks court to enforce ISS subpoena

What’s the story?

The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filed a court action Sept. 4 seeking to compel Institutional Shareholder Services (ISS), a proxy advisory firm, to comply with an administrative subpoena for information about its voting recommendations and clients' proxy votes.

The SEC filed the action in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania. The agency said it began examining ISS, which is registered with the SEC as an investment adviser, in March 2026.

The SEC said registered investment advisers have a fiduciary duty under federal securities law to act in their clients' best interests. The agency is investigating, among other things, whether ISS's proxy voting advice is influenced by political or policy objectives in ways that could conflict with that duty. Proxy advisors provide institutional investors with research and recommendations on how to vote on matters such as director elections, executive compensation, and shareholder proposals.

According to the SEC's filing, ISS provided sample reports but declined to produce all of the client-level information the agency requested. The SEC opened an inquiry in July and issued an administrative subpoena on July 21. The agency is asking the court to order ISS to comply.

ISS objected in part on First Amendment grounds, arguing that disclosing confidential information about its clients' voting decisions could expose ISS and its clients to retaliation for protected speech. ISS also argued the requested client-level data is confidential and that disclosure could cause its clients competitive harm. According to the SEC's memorandum of law, ISS sent the agency a letter on Aug. 24, 2026 requesting confidential treatment for any documents it produced, and at one point proposed providing anonymized data instead. The SEC said anonymized data would not satisfy the subpoena.

An ISS representative said, "The SEC's current demand—that ISS disclose confidential and detailed information about how its clients have chosen to vote their or their clients' shares in corporate elections—raises serious First Amendment concerns. Complying would expose ISS and its clients to potential retaliation for their protected speech and voting decisions on matters of public importance."

The SEC rejected ISS's First Amendment objection in its filing, saying, "It is wholly appropriate for the SEC to look into whether ISS's investment advice to clients on proxy voting is driven by a particular political or policy aim to the detriment of its clients' interests."

The SEC said its investigation is continuing and that it has not concluded that ISS or any other person or entity violated federal securities laws.

Why does it matter?

The case centers on whether the SEC can enforce its subpoena for client-level voting information as part of its examination of ISS. The dispute also raises a First Amendment question over whether the agency's request improperly targets protected voting advice and decisions, as well as a separate question over the scope of confidentiality protections for proxy advisors' client data.

The federal dispute comes as ISS challenges state laws regulating proxy advice. On Sept. 4, ISS separately sued to block an Oklahoma law requiring additional financial analysis when proxy advisors recommend votes against company management. Federal judges have temporarily blocked related laws in Kansas, Indiana, and Texas while litigation continues.

What’s the background?

President Donald Trump (R) issued Executive Order 14366 in December 2025 targeting proxy advisory firms, including ISS and Glass Lewis. The order said the two firms control more than 90% of the proxy advisor market and criticized their support for some environmental, social, and governance (ESG) and diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) policies.

The order directed the SEC chairman to review federal rules and guidance governing proxy advisors and shareholder proposals and to consider requiring greater transparency about proxy advisors' recommendations, methodologies, and conflicts of interest. It also directed SEC staff to examine whether registered investment advisers' use of proxy advisors for recommendations involving ESG or DEI considerations is consistent with their fiduciary duties.

The order separately directed the Federal Trade Commission to examine potential antitrust and consumer-protection issues involving proxy advisors. It directed the Department of Labor to review proxy advisors' role in voting shares for retirement plans governed by the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA).

Around the world

EU truckmakers seek three-year emissions delay

What’s the story?

European truck manufacturers have asked the European Union for a three-year delay in its 2030 carbon dioxide emissions target for new heavy-duty vehicles, moving the first compliance deadline to 2033.

The European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) said limited charging infrastructure, slow grid connections, energy costs, and low demand for zero-emission trucks make the current deadline difficult to meet. Chief executives from seven European truck and bus manufacturers backed the request.

EU rules require manufacturers to reduce the average carbon dioxide emissions of new heavy-duty vehicles by 45% in 2030 compared with 2019 levels. The required reduction increases to 65% in 2035 and 90% in 2040. Manufacturers that miss the targets face financial penalties.

ACEA said zero-emission trucks account for 2.4% of new heavy-duty truck registrations in Europe. Karin Rådström, president and CEO of Daimler Truck and chair of ACEA’s Commercial Vehicle Board, said, “We are fully committed to sustainable transport – the investments have been made, and a wide range of CO2-free vehicles is available today. But making them commercially viable at scale also depends on the wider ecosystem that is clearly delayed and not yet developing fast enough.”

Why does it matter?

The request could affect the pace of the EU’s effort to reduce emissions from commercial transportation. Manufacturers say meeting the targets depends not only on producing zero-emission trucks but also on fleet operators having sufficient charging infrastructure and an economic incentive to buy them.

Truckmakers are asking policymakers to accelerate charging infrastructure and grid connections and to use revenue from emissions trading to support zero-emission vehicle adoption. A three-year delay could give manufacturers and fleet operators more time to make the transition while reducing manufacturers’ near-term exposure to penalties. Keeping the existing deadline would maintain the current timetable for reducing emissions from new heavy-duty vehicles.

EU lawmakers advance sustainable finance disclosure changes

What’s the story?

A European Parliament committee voted Sept. 10 to advance changes to the European Union’s Sustainable Finance Disclosures Regulation (SFDR) that would create three categories for investment products making sustainability-related claims and reduce some disclosure requirements.

The Economic and Monetary Affairs Committee approved its negotiating position for talks with the Council of the European Union by a 37-9 vote, with four abstentions. SFDR requires financial firms to disclose sustainability information about investment products to help investors evaluate and compare them. The proposed changes would establish three categories:

Sustainable: Products that contribute to ESG goals and meet high sustainability standards.

Transition: Products investing in companies or projects moving toward ESG goals.

ESG Basics: Products that incorporate ESG goals but do not meet the Sustainable or Transition criteria.

The proposal would also reduce some disclosure requirements. Only certain financial market participants would have to report their effects on the environment and society, professional investors would be exempt, and financial advice and portfolio management would fall outside the regulation’s scope.

Lead lawmaker Gerben-Jan Gerbrandy said, “The goal remains intact, but the means are far more effective for consumers and more efficient for businesses: more clarity on how sustainability can be claimed, and a lot less paperwork.”

Why does it matter?

If approved, the proposal would replace the existing framework with standardized categories intended to make sustainability-focused investment products easier for investors to compare and reduce the risk of greenwashing, or making misleading claims about an investment’s environmental characteristics.

The committee’s position also sets up negotiations between Parliament and the Council over how fossil fuel investments should be treated. EU member states adopted a negotiating position in June that would allow certain fossil fuel companies into the Transition category if they meet specified investment and emissions requirements. Parliament’s committee added the requirement that qualifying companies invest more in environmentally sustainable activities than in new fossil fuel projects.

The committee’s negotiating mandate is scheduled to be announced at the beginning of Parliament’s October I plenary session. Parliament and the Council of the European Union would then need to negotiate the final legislation before it can take effect.

On Wall Street and in the private sector

BlackRock to liquidate two European ESG funds

What’s the story?

BlackRock is liquidating two European sustainability-focused investment funds after both failed to attract enough investor assets to reach commercial scale, despite both funds outperforming their respective sector averages over the last three years.

The asset manager notified shareholders Aug. 24 that it would close its Luxembourg-domiciled Impact Bond Fund and European Sustainable Equity Fund. BlackRock launched the Impact Bond Fund in October 2022 to give investors exposure to an impact-focused fixed-income strategy. The fund held €84.7 million in assets at the end of July. For comparison, BlackRock managed €1.84 trillion in European fund assets as of June 2026, according to Morningstar.

BlackRock said, “After careful consideration, the directors… have concluded that the fund is unlikely to attract significant further subscriptions in the near future and believe that placing the fund into liquidation is in the best interests of shareholders.”

BlackRock launched the European Sustainable Equity Fund in June 2021. BlackRock cited a lack of client demand in deciding to close the fund, which held €8.25 million at the end of July.

Why does it matter?

The closures show that investment performance did not translate into sufficient investor demand for either sustainability-focused fund. The Impact Bond Fund returned 14.3% over three years, compared with an 11.1% average. The European Sustainable Equity Fund returned 36.6% over the same period, compared with a 15.8% sector average, and ranked in the top quartile of its category over three- and five-year periods.

Climate scientists said that across the Himalayas rising temperatures are causing glaciers to retreat and thawing permanently frozen ground that helps bind fractured mountain rock together.
That means climate change can alter not only weather hazards such as heat and heavy rain, but the stability of the mountains themselves — threatening communities concentrated in narrow river valleys below.
The analysis did not determine whether the collapse would have happened without climate change, caused mainly by the release of greenhouse gases when fuels like oil, gas and coal are burned.
text:
BENGALURU, India (AP) — Human-caused global warming thinned glaciers and thawed mountain permafrost, likely helping to destabilize the Himalayan slope that collapsed last month and unleashed catastrophic flooding across Nepal, according to a report released Thursday.

The report by the World Weather Attribution cautioned that climate change was not the sole cause of the Aug. 26 disaster. A large 2015 Nepal earthquake may have weakened the rock years before the collapse, their analysis found.

“This disaster was not an extreme weather event, but the fingerprints of climate change are still clear to see in long-term changes,” said Ben Clarke, a climate researcher at Imperial College London who worked on the analysis, in a press statement.

More than 1,300 people were killed and over 5,000 remain missing after a massive section of rock and overlying glacier collapsed near Nepal’s border with China. The resulting torrent of water, ice, boulders and sediment swept through communities along the Trishuli River corridor and caused billions of dollars in damage.

Climate scientists said that across the Himalayas rising temperatures are causing glaciers to retreat and thawing permanently frozen ground that helps bind fractured mountain rock together. That means climate change can alter not only weather hazards such as heat and heavy rain, but the stability of the mountains themselves — threatening communities concentrated in narrow river valleys below.

The analysis did not determine whether the collapse would have happened without climate change, caused mainly by the release of greenhouse gases when fuels like oil, gas and coal are burned. However, researchers concluded that warming intensified several processes that made the slope less stable over decades.

Global warming weakens high mountain slopes

The report found that one of the clearest changes directly linked to climate change was the rising elevation of the freezing threshold.

The report found that warming had pushed the altitude at which ground remains consistently frozen upward by roughly 100 meters (328 feet) per decade. This exposes rock at increasingly high elevations to longer periods above freezing, thawing permafrost and causing cracks within the ice, ultimately weakening the rock face under the ice.

Jakob Steiner, a geoscientist at the University of Graz who has worked in the Himalayan region since 2006 but is not an author of Thursday’s report, said monitoring instruments around 5,000 meters (16,404 feet) now show that some rock and ground no longer remain frozen throughout the year.

“This means that the ground that was sitting below ice for hundreds and thousands of years is now becoming exposed,” said Steiner.

The report found that glacier retreat was another destabilizing force.

Glaciers in the region have been losing mass for decades at a rate equivalent to more than half a meter (about 1.6 feet) of thinning each year, the report found. The Langtang Lirung glacier, located in the region where the disaster occurred last month, has retreated about half a kilometer (0.3 miles) since the 1990s, exposing rock once covered by ice.

The Himalayan region contains the largest volume of snow and ice outside the polar regions. More than 63,000 glaciers in the area feed at least 10 major Asian river systems and support the food, water, energy and livelihood security of billions of people. However, various studies have found that around 78% of the glacier area, located between 4,500 and 6,000 meters (14,763 to 19,685 feet) above sea level, is highly exposed to warming. United Nations reports have found that between 2000 and 2019, glaciers lost 267 billion tons of ice per year, roughly equivalent to the mass of 46,500 Great Pyramids of Giza.

As glaciers shrink, they can remove pressure that helped support adjoining rock walls, while producing additional meltwater.

The weeks before the Aug. 26 collapse were also unusually warm. July and August 2026 were the warmest such months recorded locally, according to the analysis.

“Other than the potential geological factors like earthquakes that are weakening the bedrock, all these other factors are made worse by human-induced climate change,” said Friederike Otto, climate scientist at Imperial College London and one of the report’s authors.

Disaster exposes limits of adaptation

The report said the catastrophe also demonstrates how some climate-related risks in the world’s highest mountains may exceed the protection that early warning systems and other adaptation measures can provide.

Nepal has developed disaster risk reduction plans and warning systems, but researchers said the size and speed of the collapse overwhelmed those defenses. Unlike a flood caused by rainfall, which can sometimes be forecast hours or days ahead, catastrophic slope failures in remote high mountains can occur suddenly and remain extremely difficult to predict.

Otto, the climate scientist, said that the mountain ecosystem and societies are more vulnerable to climate impacts than those living in the plains. “Small changes in temperatures affect the stability of the land itself,” she said.

Better high-altitude monitoring, earth observation and warning systems could reduce some risks, the report said. But researchers warned there are limits to adaptation in Himalayan valleys where settlements, roads, hydropower projects and other infrastructure are concentrated along rivers.

Since glaciers and permafrost respond to temperature changes over decades, some mountain destabilization caused by warming has already been set in motion, said the report.

“The most important thing to minimize the risk in this region is to rapidly stop using fossil fuels that lead to increasing global temperatures,” said Otto. “All these drivers that we’ve talked about, permafrost melting, glacial melting, etc., will just become worse. And that means that events like this become more frequent.”

text:
Google is backing the buildout of a novel green-steel mill in Sweden as the tech giant grapples with rising greenhouse gas emissions from its AI expansion.

On Thursday, the company said it is partnering with Stegra to help bring the Swedish firm’s flagship facility online. Unlike traditional coal-fueled mills, Stegra’s project will use green hydrogen — made from renewable electricity and water — to produce what it calls ​“near-zero emission” steel.

The agreement helps address some of the thorny challenges facing green steel companies and data center developers.

Metal-makers need wealthy, early customers like Google to help stoke investor interest in their novel manufacturing plants. Meanwhile, tech companies need cleaner construction materials to curb their growing environmental impact. Google recently reported an 18% rise in its annual emissions from 2024 to 2025, owing to its increased use of steel, concrete, computing hardware, and other materials for data centers.

The Alphabet subsidiary is not slated to buy any metal from Stegra’s multibillion-dollar plant, which is under construction in Boden, just south of the Arctic Circle.

Instead, Google will procure ​“environmental attribute certificates,” which allow the company to count emissions reductions associated with a ton of Stegra’s steel toward Google’s own sustainability targets. In exchange, Google helps tdefray the extra costs involved with hydrogen-based steelmaking. Stegra then sells its metal into the European market as a standard product — without labeling it as lower-carbon steel.

“By supporting early-stage technologies like Stegra’s green steel, we are helping to create a market for materials that are essential to reducing emissions,” a spokesperson for Google said by email.

Thursday’s agreement is the second of its kind for Stockholm-based Stegra, formerly H2 Green Steel. Last year, the firm struck a two-part deal to sell the certificates to Microsoft and also physical steel to Microsoft’s equipment suppliers for European data centers. Neither Microsoft nor Google provided details about the financial value of their arrangements with Stegra.

The Swedish facility is one of a handful of projects advancing globally that aim to dramatically reduce emissions from iron and steel production, which accounts for roughly 9% of human-caused carbon dioxide emissions every year. The vast majority of that pollution comes from using coal in giant, dirty ironmaking furnaces.

Stegra says its operation will slash carbon emissions from steelmaking by up to 95%, compared with traditional methods. The facility taps the abundant hydropower and wind resources in northern Sweden to produce hydrogen gas — fuel that’s used to convert iron ore into iron. That iron is then transformed into steel using electric arc furnaces, also powered by renewables.

Under the new deal, Google will receive certificates from a portion — up to 91,000 metric tons — of the steel made in Stegra’s first year of production. It’s not clear exactly when operations will start. Stegra, which has weathered a series of financial woes over the last year, said its project timeline is still under review.

The facility is expected to produce 2.5 million metric tons of steel in its first phase, before ramping up to make 5 million metric tons at full tilt.

“Our procurement is directly contributing to Stegra achieving project financing for the second phase expansion of their production facility,” the Google spokesperson said.

Environmental attribute certificates can play a crucial role in helping build out the world’s next generation of iron and steel facilities, experts say. Efforts to develop hydrogen-based steelmaking and other cutting-edge technologies have in recent years faced significant hurdles to scaling up, owing to their high costs and technical complexities — as well as the difficulty of competing with cheaper coal-based steel products.

The instruments are ​“a great mechanism to overcome different market barriers in industries where we need to see increased investment,” said Claire Dougherty, an industrial decarbonization program manager at RMI. The clean-energy think tank has spearheaded much of the industry’s emerging work around low-carbon iron and steel certificates.

“A hydrogen [steel] facility can cost billions of dollars, and that can be very difficult to get funding for, particularly without a guarantee that someone’s going to buy your decarbonized product at a premium,” she said. At the same time, the companies that are most willing to pay a premium — like data center developers — aren’t typically in the business of buying steel, or their operations aren’t close enough to green steel mills to justify sourcing the metal directly.

Certificates ​“can help to expand the demand pool and help those suppliers achieve bankable offtake,” Dougherty said.

Proponents are hoping to grow this model beyond pilot agreements like Google’s by creating a formal market, known as a ​“book and claim” system, for buying and selling iron and steel certificates.

Earlier this month, Stegra and the cleantech startups Electra and Charm Industrial, along with the nonprofit Roundtable on Sustainable Biomaterials, said they were working toward that goal by developing shared standards and metrics for how emissions reductions are counted, and for ensuring environmental claims are independently verified and traceable. The initiative builds on a comprehensive framework that RMI is set to unveil next week that lays out rules for operating a credible book-and-claim system for iron and steel.

“We view this as a really important next step, in terms of scaling the [certificate] market for low-carbon iron and steel producers,” said Maressa Brennan, Electra’s senior director of regulatory policy and markets.

Colorado-based Electra is developing a novel approach to ironmaking that avoids the need for a scorching furnace. Instead, the company produces iron with electrochemical devices, which are powered by renewables and can run at the same temperature as a fresh cup of coffee.

Last year, the startup announced a deal to provide environmental attribute certificates to Meta. Electra is set to start operations later this year at a demonstration plant in Jefferson County, Colorado, which will initially produce up to 500 metric tons of high-purity iron per year. The company is also assessing a few global sites for its first commercial facility, which could come online in the early 2030s, Brennan said.

“Our agreement with Meta was an early example to indicate that there’s a market interest in … these types of technologies,” she said. ​“The work we’re doing now [with the registry] is to more formally establish a marketplace that helps these approaches scale.”

title: NDA secrecy for major projects hovers over Louisiana's congressional elections
description:
By signing the NDA, Letlow might have had access to information about Meta’s business operations and finances not available to the public.
As the underdog in the Senate race, Davis is trying to make Letlow’s Meta NDA into a campaign issue and brought it up during a speaking engagement at LSU this week.
Of the five major candidates, two said they signed NDAs as elected officials in order to receive information about economic development projects.
“The only legislators who have not signed NDAs are people who weren’t asked,” Cathey said.
State Sen. Rick Edmonds, R-Baton Rouge, said he has signed one NDA with the Louisiana Economic Development agency.
text:
Jamie Davis believes there’s one specific reason Congresswoman Julia Letlow hasn’t agreed to appear in person with him for debates or any other events during their U.S. Senate race.

Letlow, the Republican candidate, doesn’t want to answer questions about the nondisclosure agreement she signed with a Meta company about Richland Parish’s $50 billion dollar data center project, he said.

“Any other questions I want to ask about Meta, she won’t be able to answer because she might break her NDA,” said Davis, the Democratic candidate.

Letlow not only signed the NDA but also began buying stock Meta and Nvidia, a company that makes computer equipment for data centers, in the months that followed, according to reporting from Gulf States Newsroom. The congresswoman didn’t disclose the stock purchases publicly until more than a year after the federal deadline to do so.

By signing the NDA, Letlow might have had access to information about Meta’s business operations and finances not available to the public.

Letlow’s campaign spokesperson did not respond to multiple requests this week for comment about the NDA. But in August, her congressional staff told Gulf States Newsroom she was unaware the Meta and Nvidia trades were happening on her behalf at the time.

As Louisiana undergoes an industrial megaproject boom, the extent to which public officials are trading away public transparency for economic investment through NDAs has become controversial.

Dozens of local and state elected officials signed NDAs related to economic development projects such as the SpaceX complex in Vermilion Parish, the Hyundai steel plant in Ascension Parish and data centers in other parts of the state.

More than 100 employees in Gov. Jeff Landry’s office also signed blanket NDAs prohibiting them from talking about what they learn working for the governor.

Landry and his administration have said the NDAs are necessary to attract global brands. But the agreements raise questions about whether government officials are free to share information about the projects’ impacts on resources such as water and the electrical grid.

LSU political science professor Robert Hogan said backlash over NDAs is part of a broader “general distrust that people have of government” right now.

“I do believe this could be a very effective issue at sowing seeds of doubt in the minds of voters about people who signed these,” Hogan said in an interview this week.

As the underdog in the Senate race, Davis is trying to make Letlow’s Meta NDA into a campaign issue and brought it up during a speaking engagement at LSU this week.

Davis said he never signed an NDA when he was an elected member of the Tensas Parish Police Jury and wouldn’t sign one if he was elected to the Senate.

NDAs could creep into competitive US House races

In addition to the Senate race, the NDA issue could come up in the U.S. House races, including open races for the 5th and 6th congressional districts, where many of the closely guarded industrial projects will take shape.

Four state legislators and the chair of the Board of Regents, which oversees state higher education, are among the nine candidates running to replace Letlow in the 5th District.

Of the five major candidates, two said they signed NDAs as elected officials in order to receive information about economic development projects.

State Sen. Stewart Cathey, R-Monroe, confirmed he signed an NDA to learn basic details about the Meta data center coming to Richland Parish from state Economic Development Secretary Susan Bourgeois before the project was publicly announced.

Even after he signed the agreement, Cathey said Bourgeois would only tell him it was a data center project and not the name of the company behind the site. He’s not sure if he would sign an NDA again if elected to Congress.

“The only legislators who have not signed NDAs are people who weren’t asked,” Cathey said.

State Rep. Gabe Firment, R-Pollock, said he signed an NDA required to attend a meeting about a data center under construction in Rapides Parish, but the information shared at the meeting didn’t turn out to be particularly confidential.

“I would not sign one again,” Firment said. “A lot of people I represent and I may represent in the future are not comfortable with that.”

State Rep. Mike Echols, R-Monroe is one of the three 5th District contenders who has not signed an NDA as an elected official. He said he also wouldn’t sign one as a member of Congress.

“I want to be as transparent as possible. I don’t see value for me,” Echols said.

State Rep. Pat Moore of Monroe, the Democratic Party-endorsed candidate, said she has not signed an NDA as a legislator and could not recall signing one while a member on the Ouachita Parish Policy Jury.

Misti Cordell, a Republican from West Monroe who leads the Board of Regents, said she hadn’t signed an NDA while in her current public position.

But Moore and Cordell wouldn’t rule out signing NDAs if elected to Congress.

Cordell said she would make sure any agreement she signed didn’t require her to shield information about what might hurt the public.

Moore said she wouldn’t personally benefit from any information she received through an NDA.

“If there was confidential information that I could not disclose, I would not do anything to profit off of it,” Moore said.

Two legislators are also among the 10 candidates running to replace U.S. Rep. Cleo Fields, D-Baton Rouge, in the 6th District. Fields decided against running again after state lawmakers redrew the district’s lines to make it harder for a Democrat to win.

State Sen. Rick Edmonds, R-Baton Rouge, said he has signed one NDA with the Louisiana Economic Development agency. He said he couldn’t say whether he would sign any if elected to Congress because he doesn’t know entirely what the position would entail yet.

State Sen. Blake Miguez, R-New Iberia, did not return phone calls seeking comment on his policy regarding NDAs. It’s not clear whether he has signed one as an elected official.

Two Democrats in the race, Pat Forbes and Lindsay Garcia, have not held elected positions previously and said they would not sign NDAs if elected to Congress.

“I don’t think NDAs have any place in government,” said Forbes, who led disaster relief efforts as the head of the state Office of Community Development for several years.

“There is a distinct irony in you serving the interest of the public while keeping the public in the dark,” said Garcia, a community organizer and former teacher who graduated from Southern University Law Center last year.
