title: Building an equitable clean energy workforce - Community College Daily
description:
Combining workforce training with contractor support offers a more effective and equitable model for clean energy workforce development than traditional approaches that address these functions separately.
Recognizing the growing labor shortage in the clean energy sector, Illinois enacted the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act (CEJA) to establish a statewide framework to expand the clean energy workforce and broaden economic participation.
Under this framework, the College of DuPage (COD) was selected to lead two regional initiatives to strengthen the energy workforce and business capacity in the clean energy economy.
The Clean Jobs Workforce Network Training initiative prepares a diverse pipeline of workers for clean energy careers through free training, employment readiness services and wraparound support.
The Clean Energy Contractor Incubator builds upon COD’s Innovation DuPage platform to support the launch and growth of small energy firms that contribute to Illinois’ clean energy economy.
text:
The transition to a clean energy economy has emerged as a major driver of employment growth in the United States.

In 2023, clean energy employment expanded at more than twice the rate of the overall U.S. labor market, with the sector employing more than 3.4 million workers nationwide, according to the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE). While this growth has accelerated demand for skilled labor across multiple segments of the energy economy, meeting that demand requires more than technological innovation or regulatory mandates. It requires coordinated workforce and economic development strategies that expand opportunities while addressing persistent inequities in access to capital, training and industry networks. Combining workforce training with contractor support offers a more effective and equitable model for clean energy workforce development than traditional approaches that address these functions separately.

Recognizing the growing labor shortage in the clean energy sector, Illinois enacted the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act (CEJA) to establish a statewide framework to expand the clean energy workforce and broaden economic participation. Under this framework, the College of DuPage (COD) was selected to lead two regional initiatives to strengthen the energy workforce and business capacity in the clean energy economy.

The Clean Jobs Workforce Network Training initiative prepares a diverse pipeline of workers for clean energy careers through free training, employment readiness services and wraparound support. The Clean Energy Contractor Incubator builds upon COD’s Innovation DuPage platform to support the launch and growth of small energy firms that contribute to Illinois’ clean energy economy.

This article is featured in the latest issue of AACC’s Community College Journal.

Participation in the CEJA represents an important milestone for COD, positioning the college as a regional convener rather than solely a training provider. This approach also reflects a broader understanding that economic development advances when community colleges collaborate with municipalities, workforce agencies, peer institutions, community organizations and industry partners.

By integrating technician training with contractor incubation, the college extends its role beyond traditional workforce preparation to support entrepreneurship, regional coordination and inclusive economic growth. Together, these initiatives function as a regional hub for clean energy technician training and contractor development across Kendall, Kane, DuPage, and parts of Cook County in the Chicago–Naperville–Elgin Metropolitan Statistical Area. Collaborating with six collar county community colleges further aligns regional labor markets with growing demand for the sustainable energy sector.

Boosting the regional ecosystem

The Workforce Network Training Hub and the Clean Energy Contractor Incubator were launched as part of the COD’s longstanding institutional commitment to regional partnership and entrepreneurship.

For more than four decades, the college has supported small business development through its Small Business Development Center, International Trade Center and Apex Accelerator. The establishment of Innovation DuPage expanded these efforts through incubation, advising and industry engagement. Complementary initiatives introduce youth to clean energy career pathways through the Youth Academy and connect underemployed adults to workforce opportunities through adult education programs.

Building on this foundation, the Workforce Network Hub and Contractor Incubator integrate business incubation, technical assistance, workforce alignment and entrepreneurial support within a coordinated regional system. Partnerships with peer community colleges, workforce boards, municipalities, chambers of commerce and community-based organizations broaden recruitment capacity and strengthen alignment between the training pipeline and employer demand. This networked structure enables the college to extend resources beyond its district and to support workforce and contractor development across the Chicago-Naperville-Elgin Metropolitan Statistical Area.

The CEJA initiatives also address inequities through intentional program design and targeted participation strategies. Program priorities focus on environmental justice communities and residents of historically disinvested areas who face compounding barriers, including language access challenges and prior involvement with the justice system.

These initiatives operate within the broader statewide framework established by the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act, which links workforce training, pre-apprenticeship pathways, energy transition navigators and contractor incubators across Illinois. Shared curricula, coordinated referrals and aligned apprenticeship pathways allow participating institutions to function as interconnected nodes within a statewide system.

Impact assessment

Early outcomes demonstrate the scope and potential impact of the regional model. During the pilot phase, the Contractor Incubator supported 39 energy contractors whose firms collectively reported more than $27.8 million in annual revenue and supported nearly 300 workers across full-time, part-time, and independent roles. These firms secured more than $4.8 million in grants and loans, strengthening their readiness for capital investment and expanding their ability to compete in the clean energy market. Participating companies represented a range of sectors, including solar installation, electric vehicle technology, sustainable construction, energy efficiency and decarbonization consulting.

The Workforce Network Hub trained 79 students through energy bridge programs. Fifteen students completed solar training, seven completed energy audit training, and two earned HVAC certification. Students completing the energy audit certificate applied their training by conducting audits of college facilities as part of a learning laboratory. These assessments identified potential annual energy savings exceeding $300,000. The college plans to expand this model to additional campus buildings using student interns and has extended the approach to other community colleges and public facilities, creating opportunities for additional cost savings.

Participants across both initiatives benefited from individualized advising, cohort learning and engagement with industry experts. The curriculum emphasized financial readiness, wage compliance, project management, workforce utilization and access to capital. Early outcomes indicate increased contractor engagement in solar installations, energy-efficiency retrofits, electric-vehicle infrastructure and sustainable construction services.

Program projections indicate continued growth. Enrollment in the Workforce Network Hub is expected to increase substantially, while Contractor Incubator participation is projected to expand to as many as 200 firms by fiscal year 2029, with more than 100 cohort graduates. These targets reflect a deliberate effort to develop a scalable contractor ecosystem that can strengthen regional labor markets over time.

Despite these early successes, challenges remain, including the need for sustained funding, coordination across multiple institutions, and continued support for participants navigating complex regulatory and market environments.

Implications and the path forward

Outcomes from the CEJA initiatives illuminate how community colleges can navigate the intersection of workforce development and economic transformation. As states expand investments in renewable energy infrastructure, institutions face the dual challenge of expanding labor supply while ensuring equitable access to emerging opportunities. Programs that intentionally serve both workers and contractors illustrate how workforce development functions most effectively as a comprehensive economic strategy integrating credential attainment with entrepreneurship, business capacity, and regional coordination.

The experience at COD highlights the capacity of community colleges to function as system-level actors within this landscape. When colleges align workforce training with contractor development and collaborate across public, private and community sectors, they create regional ecosystems capable of sustaining employment growth.

More broadly, the clean energy transition reframes the role of community colleges in economic development. The CEJA model demonstrates how policy, education, and industry engagement can be integrated to advance inclusive growth rather than isolated programmatic outcomes. Sustained collaboration, intentional equity-centered design, and long-term institutional partnerships will remain essential to ensuring that the clean energy economy develops in ways that reflect and invest in the communities it is intended to serve.

name: North Carolina Environment
title: Many Richmond County residents are already sick. An Amazon data center could make it worse.
description:
Shaun Ingram keeps his black aviator sunglasses on as he sits inside a local community center.
To get the data center off the ground, Duke Energy will operate temporary, “bridge-power” generators for one year until the facility is fully connected to the grid.
But for local organizer Ingram, who has family buried along the Pee Dee River, these actions don’t compare to the toll the data center is taking.
Environmental groups could appeal the air permits in court.
The data center is expected to start some operations early next year.
text:
Shaun Ingram keeps his black aviator sunglasses on as he sits inside a local community center. Metal chairs form a rough circle in the center of this large room where the Richmond County Coalition for Justice and Black Empowerment meets every Thursday.

“ The Coalition came together based off Black land, the disenfranchisement of Black people in our community, (and) people not recognizing our indigenous status,” said Ingram, 42, a Richmond County native.

The Coalition has also been a vital source of information for community members to learn about Amazon’s $10 billion data center that’s under construction a few miles away from this meeting place.

The facility will need approximately 1 gigawatt of energy. That’s more power than the Sharron Harris nuclear plant in Wake County produces in one year.

To get the data center off the ground, Duke Energy will operate temporary, “bridge-power” generators for one year until the facility is fully connected to the grid.

State officials recently approved that air permit, along with a separate permit for Amazon to use emergency backup generators during power outages.

Combined, the permits give approval to 645 generators. Ingram said these operations are expected to increase air pollution in a community that’s already riddled with sickness.

“What happens when the air pollution is so bad where people can’t breathe and they die?” said Ingram. “Just last week, six or seven people died. Every day there’s a funeral.”

Community profile: Existing industry and illness

Reports from local and state health officials show this rural county near the South Carolina border has a higher rate of adults with heart disease than the national average. This community is also one of the top five counties in North Carolina with the highest rates of lung cancer.

When Ingram returned home after 20 years in the Navy, he soon developed a consistent cough and phlegm in his chest. He asked his doctor about it.

“We’re both retired Navy. His response to me was, ‘Well Shaun can’t you just leave? You can travel to wherever you want in the world,’” said Ingram. “But people don’t understand that my family is here. This is my home and my ancestral lands.”

Ingram and his family have indigenous roots in this area, stretching back for hundreds of years. He believes the degradation of his community is destroying people’s health.

“There are people who are carrying around asthma pumps,” said Ingram. “They’re carrying around oxygen tanks. They’re going to dialysis three or four times a week.”

These conditions are not a coincidence, contends Caroline Cress, an attorney for the Southern Environmental Law Center.

She points to existing industry in the area, including a wood pellet plant, a solid waste facility, and two natural gas plants. Last year these four facilities alone emitted almost 250 tons of fine particulate matter, or tiny soot particles that can get deep in the lungs and bloodstream.

“(Particulate matter) not only (has) respiratory effects like exacerbating asthma … they also have cardiovascular effects, and it's associated with premature death,” said Cress.

Similar to Ingram, Cress expressed frustration and disappointment at the air permitting process.

She argues it should’ve been one air permit instead of two.

“If they were permitted properly as a single major stationary source, they would be subject to a lot more stringent requirements under the Clean Air Act,” Cress said. “For example, they would have had to do a year of pre-construction air quality monitoring in the area to figure out basically what the existing pollution levels are. That's really important here because there's no air quality monitor for thirty miles. So there's no way to tell how bad the air is right now.”

North Carolina State University professor Jennifer Richmond-Bryant writes in a recent analysis how air emissions from data center operations may raise the risk of respiratory, cardiovascular and neurological health effects for residents.

“(The generators are) operating as a combined stressor,” said Richmond-Bryant. “So if you are living in that community, you're not gonna feel like, ‘Oh, now I'm feeling Amazon's particulate matter. Now I'm feeling Duke's particulate matter.’ It's all going to be combined.”

State environmental officials responded to this criticism in a press release announcing the approved air permits for Amazon and Duke.

“While both air quality permits relate to Amazon’s data center, the two permitted activities are not under the control of the same company and the two permits serve different purposes on different time horizons,” read the statement. “Amazon controls the emergency backup engines and Duke Energy controls the temporary bridge power engines before Amazon’s connection to the grid. Under normal operation, Duke Energy’s bridge power and Amazon’s backup engines will not operate concurrently.”

The press release goes on to say issuing these “permits follows Richmond County’s approval of a county incentive package to Amazon for building the data center near Hamlet.”

This project was first announced last June, with Governor Josh Stein in attendance. As Inside Climate News reports, Richmond County officials secretly worked with Amazon for months, meaning there was no real public input on the deal.

Amazon hosts open house

Amazon recently hosted an open house at Richmond Community College for local residents to ask questions about the data center’s sound pollution, environmental impact, and water and energy usage. The company reassured meeting attendees they're committed to building and operating data centers responsibly.

Spokesperson Roger Wehner said Amazon’s generators will only be used for emergencies and routine testing.

“Our generators will only use less than 10 hours for each one, just for testing,” said Wehner. “The same way … a hospital (or) a nursing home… has standby generation and everybody tests it."

Wehner adds Amazon wants to be a helpful community partner.

“We've been good corporate citizens with a 20-year track record,” said Wehner. “Our contributions around tax revenues, workforce development, educational investments, and philanthropic investments are bar raising.”

Amazon is committing $1.5 million to a local fire department to help buy new fire trucks and build a new fire station. The company is also partnering with the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation to restore 20-thousand acres of longleaf pine forests in the Pee Dee River Basin.

But for local organizer Ingram, who has family buried along the Pee Dee River, these actions don’t compare to the toll the data center is taking.

“It's another example of companies exploiting the community,” said Ingram.

Environmental groups could appeal the air permits in court. The data center is expected to start some operations early next year.

description:
by Jack Evans, Asheville Watchdog The owner of Woodfin’s Silver-Line Plastics will fund the next phase of a yearslong cleanup that began when floodwaters swept its inventory into the French Broad River during Tropical Storm Helene.
“It’s been a long road, and we weren’t sure we would ever get to this point,” Greg Parlier, a MountainTrue spokesperson, said Wednesday.

An IPEX-commissioned survey of the river will help cleanup crews target the most severe areas of debris, according to the news release.

text:
by Jack Evans, Asheville Watchdog

The owner of Woodfin’s Silver-Line Plastics will fund the next phase of a yearslong cleanup that began when floodwaters swept its inventory into the French Broad River during Tropical Storm Helene.

IPEX, the multinational corporation that bought the plant — one of Woodfin’s largest employers — from the local Silver family in 2019, agreed to give $500,000 to MountainTrue, the regional environmental nonprofit that has handled much of the cleanup, the two organizations said in a joint news release Wednesday.

“It’s been a long road, and we weren’t sure we would ever get to this point,” Greg Parlier, a MountainTrue spokesperson, said Wednesday. “At some point it wasn’t even really about getting money to help fund the cleanup, it was just about getting participation from a corporate neighbor. To get funding to help fund some teams into next year is kind of a cherry on top.”

IPEX has spent more than $100 million to rebuild the riverside facility, according to the release. But in the nearly two years since Helene, it has frequently come under fire for long periods of silence on Helene recovery, its lack of funding for public cleanup efforts and its continued practice of storing inventory outdoors. Last month, it publicly committed to shoring up those storage practices.

Funded largely by a state contract, MountainTrue has pulled more than 6 million pounds of debris from rivers and streams around western North Carolina, including hundreds of thousands of pounds of Silver-Line pipe from the stretch of the French Broad between Woodfin and Tennessee’s Douglas Lake.

But cleanup leaders have said the state funding, set to run through the end of 2026, wouldn’t be enough to finish the job. The $500,000 from IPEX will allow the work to continue into 2027. An IPEX-commissioned survey of the river will help cleanup crews target the most severe areas of debris, according to the news release.

The news release also affirms IPEX’s commitment, which MountainTrue leaders described to Asheville Watchdog last month, to commissioning an engineering study on the Silver-Line property and working with Woodfin and MountainTrue to make the facility more resilient.

MountainTrue earlier this year began a public pressure campaign centered on the storage practices.

“This is a win not only for MountainTrue, but the whole French Broad River community,” said Gray Jernigan, MountainTrue deputy director and general counsel. “Our supporters stepped up to speak on behalf of the river, and it led to real, tangible results.”

But it remains unclear, Parlier said, what finally brought IPEX to the table.

“Ultimately we were pleasantly surprised when they called,” he said. “It’s been really important to them to try to ensure us that they’re not simply dropping off a check and saying, ‘Good luck.’”

Asheville Watchdog welcomes thoughtful reader comments on this story, which has been republished on our Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube pages. Please submit your comments there.

title: EPA, Army Corps Takes a Further Step to Redefine WOTUS - NAM
description:
The administration has made another move to redefine “waters of the United States” (POLITICO Pro, subscription).
The proposal builds on one the EPA and Army Corps laid out in November 2025 and is narrower in scope than the one the Supreme Court called for in its NAM-backed 2023 decision in Sackett v. EPA.
That ruling found that the EPA only had jurisdiction over wetlands with “continuous surface connection” to navigable waters.
Defining key terms: “The latest proposal focuses on several key terms used to determine federal jurisdiction, including ‘relatively permanent’ waters and wetlands with a ‘continuous surface connection’ to other jurisdictional waters” (Texas Farm Bureau).
NAM Vice President of Domestic Policy Chris Phalen told POLITICO that the new proposal “looks to be a really positive step forward.” POLITICO Pro, subscription).
text:
The administration has made another move to redefine “waters of the United States” (POLITICO Pro, subscription).

What’s going on: In “a major leap forward for energy companies, farmers, housing developers and other industries,” the Environmental Protection Agency and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers on Sept. 4 released a supplemental proposal responding to comments submitted by the NAM that could further right-size the scope of what qualifies as a WOTUS and what projects need federal permits.

The U.S. Army is awarding up to $2.2 billion to five nuclear energy developers to build and operate microreactors at military installations in four states (POLITICO Pro, subscription).

What’s going on: “The Army expects more than 20 nuclear microreactors to be built in connection to the awards as part of its Janus Program, launched last year to support nuclear power generation at domestic military locations.”

The microreactors, which generate up to 20 megawatts of power and “can be deployed in bunches” (Axios), will be owned and operated by the contractors, and the Army aims to take delivery of all five in the next five years.

The nuclear companies, which include BWXT Advanced Technologies and Westinghouse Government Services, will receive the funding via a “milestone-based payment model,” according to an Army news release.

The reactors will be built at military installations in North Carolina, Texas, Kentucky and Georgia.

Part of a larger plan: The administration has made nuclear power a cornerstone of its energy agenda.

In May 2025, President Trump signed an executive order calling for the Defense Department to begin construction of 10 large nuclear reactors by 2030.

Big demand: The funding announcement comes as the U.S. is seeing explosive growth in power demand, which is expected to rise further with the construction of more data centers.

“To meet that demand, the Trump administration is pushing for an American nuclear energy renaissance that would also see the deployment and commercialization of small modular reactors, microreactors and other advanced reactor technologies.”

Who’s doing what: BWXT was chosen to build a microreactor for Fort Campbell in Kentucky, while Westinghouse was chosen to build one for Fort Drum in New York.

BWXT, which said it expects to break ground in Kentucky in 2028 and start reactor operations in the early 2030s, “said in a news release that it will be developing a 20-megawatt electric version of its BANR microreactor.”

The three other military sites slated to get microreactors are Fort Bragg in North Carolina, Fort Hood in Texas and Fort Benning in Georgia.

Navy, too: The Navy will install its first advanced nuclear micro modular reactor at Naval Weapons Station Crane by September 2028, according to a recent announcement.

title: New and used EV sales jump as prices fall - CBT News
description:
According to the latest Cox Automotive EV Market Monitor report, both new and used EV sales increased in August, showing a maturing market.
Additionally, more off-lease returns gave used EV buyers more options, while EV supply and prices are getting closer to those of gas-powered vehicles.
New EV sales edge up as Tesla slips U.S. new EV sales reached about 78,895 units in August, up 2.5% from July.
Off-lease returns drive used EV sales Used EV sales increased by 25.9% from July to 44,350 units, and were up 14.7% compared to last year.
Tesla models made up nearly 30% of used EV sales, while Nissan, Cadillac and Kia posted the biggest used sales gains by brand.
text:
On the Dash:

New EV inventory ended August two days above gas-powered vehicles, the closest spread this year.

Used EV sales jumped 25.9% from July as off-lease returns expanded supply.

The new EV price premium over gas-powered vehicles shrank to $4,847 as cheaper models gained share.

According to the latest Cox Automotive EV Market Monitor report, both new and used EV sales increased in August, showing a maturing market. The report notes that new EV sales grew across more brands, even as Tesla’s market share declined. Additionally, more off-lease returns gave used EV buyers more options, while EV supply and prices are getting closer to those of gas-powered vehicles.

New EV inventory ended August just two days above gas-powered vehicle levels, which is the closest the two have been all year. Used EV supply went a step further, matching gas-powered vehicles for the first time in 2026.

Sign up for CBT News’ daily newsletter and get the latest industry stories delivered straight to your inbox.

New EV sales edge up as Tesla slips

U.S. new EV sales reached about 78,895 units in August, up 2.5% from July. Sales fell 46.9% from a year ago, when buyers rushed to use expiring tax credits. EVs made up 5.7% of all new-vehicle sales.

While Tesla still sold more than half of all new EVs, its sales dipped 3.8% from July. Its market share fell to 51.7%. Gains at other brands more than made up the difference. Toyota also led growth, with EV sales up 34.9% to 4,964 units. Chevrolet, Cadillac and Kia also posted double-digit gains. New EV days’ supply dropped to 78 days, down 9.6% from July.

Off-lease returns drive used EV sales

Used EV sales increased by 25.9% from July to 44,350 units, and were up 14.7% compared to last year. Cox notes that the availability of more off-lease EVs is providing shoppers with greater options. Cox Automotive Chief Economist Jeremy Robb projected EVs would make up about 12% of 2026 off-lease volume, up from about 5% in 2025.

It’s important to note that used EV days’ supply fell to 42 days, even with gas-powered vehicles. Tesla models made up nearly 30% of used EV sales, while Nissan, Cadillac and Kia posted the biggest used sales gains by brand.

EV prices keep falling

In August, the average new EV price was $54,754, a 1.3% decline from July. The price difference between EVs and gas-powered cars narrowed to $4,847. The decrease was largely influenced by lower-cost models like the Toyota bZ and Chevrolet Bolt. Incentives also averaged about $6,594 per new EV, down 19.9% from a year ago. Used EV listing prices averaged $37,441, down 1% from July but up 8.2% from last year.

As last year’s tax credit surge fades, Cox says the next test is whether these gains can last. Pricing, incentives and demand for more used EVs are the trends to watch, according to the report.

text:
Elevated Materials, a developer and manufacturer of ultra-thin lithium films for next-generation batteries, has been selected by the US Department of Energy for $50 million in federal funding to help develop a new advanced battery materials facility.

The proposed $100 million plant will be built in the United States and is expected to have an annual manufacturing capacity of approximately 3.5 GW.

Elevated Materials announced the project from Santa Clara, California, although it did not disclose the facility’s planned location or construction timeline.

The expansion is intended to take the company’s ultra-thin lithium-metal films and prelithiated materials to gigawatt-hour-scale production.

These materials could support batteries with greater energy density and faster charging while expanding domestic manufacturing capacity and reducing dependence on overseas supply chains.

Scaling ultra-thin lithium films

Elevated Materials manufactures its ELi ultra-thin lithium-metal films using proprietary roll-to-roll vacuum deposition platforms. The company describes ELi as the industry’s highest-quality ultra-thin lithium-metal film.

The films are designed to support next-generation anode architectures across electric vehicles, consumer electronics, defense, aviation and grid-scale energy-storage applications.

According to the company, demand has been particularly strong for lithium-metal anodes, where its material can improve battery performance and safety.

More from Energy

See All

Over the past year, Elevated Materials said it had recorded its highest output of ultra-thin lithium-metal films. It shipped more than 250,000 meters of material to over 30 customers worldwide during that period.

The planned facility is expected to accelerate the company’s effort to commercialize a domestic supply of lithium-metal films and prelithiated materials at a much larger scale.

Strengthening US battery production

Elevated Materials was one of seven companies selected to receive funding through the Department of Energy’s Battery Materials Processing and Battery Manufacturing Grants program.

The selected projects are set to share a combined $500 million in federal funding.

The company’s $50 million selection will support half of the proposed facility’s estimated $100 million development cost.

The project also aligns with the department’s effort to expand battery manufacturing within the United States and secure domestic access to critical materials.

“The United States has made advanced battery manufacturing a national priority, and securing a domestic supply of critical materials that significantly increases energy density is central to that effort,” said Jim Cushing, CEO of Elevated Materials.

From California research to gigawatt scale

Elevated Materials developed its lithium-film technology in California with support from Department of Energy research and development programs.

The latest funding would help move the technology beyond its current production level and toward substantially larger commercial volumes.

“We developed this technology in California with support from DOE R&D programs and are proud to have been selected by the Department of Energy to now ramp it up to gigawatt scale,” Cushing said.

Elevated Materials is part of the TPG Rise Climate portfolio and was carved out of Applied Materials.

The company is now focused on scaling its battery materials to support US competitiveness and the electrification of industries ranging from transportation and electronics to defense and energy storage.

title: Both Democrats and Republicans Are Increasingly Worried About AI's Environmental Impact
description:
As data centers break ground in communities across the country, Americans are growing more concerned about the environmental impacts.
More Democrats, Republicans, and Independents said they are “extremely or very” worried about the environmental impacts compared to last year—with 65% of Democrats, 42% of Republicans, and 49% of Independents reporting their concern this year.
Democrats seem to be the most concerned by the environmental impacts of data center growth.
By contrast, about half of Independents and 4 in 10 Republicans are highly concerned about the environmental impact of AI.
(Some research has shown that, while data center construction can yield a number of temporary jobs, facilities tend to employ fewer permanent employees.)
text:
As data centers break ground in communities across the country, Americans are growing more concerned about the environmental impacts. That’s according to a new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago, which found that about half (53%) of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about AI’s environmental impacts. The number is up from 41% last year.

The concern is shared across all party affiliations. More Democrats, Republicans, and Independents said they are “extremely or very” worried about the environmental impacts compared to last year—with 65% of Democrats, 42% of Republicans, and 49% of Independents reporting their concern this year.

There are currently 1,287 data centers in operation in the U.S., with more than 2,000 planned projects, according to Clearview, a market intelligence company tracking U.S. power infrastructure and data center development. Virginia and Texas currently have the most data centers in operation, but many new developments are planned in rural areas in the South and Midwest. The growth is driven by the rise in hyperscale data centers, which are larger, more powerful, and often used to train and run large-scale AI models.

Despite the boom, Americans seem to be increasingly supportive of measures to regulate growth. About 6 in 10 Americans said they would support limiting the number of new data centers that can be built—including most Democrats and Republicans—the survey found.

Democrats seem to be the most concerned by the environmental impacts of data center growth. About two-thirds say they are “extremely” or “very” concerned about how AI will affect the environment, the poll found, compared to about half in 2025. By contrast, about half of Independents and 4 in 10 Republicans are highly concerned about the environmental impact of AI.

Republicans, on the other hand, are more likely to see the benefits of data centers. Yet about 3 in 10 Republicans still believe the centers are “not very” or “not at all” beneficial for improved infrastructure and job creation.

A majority (60%) of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the impact of data centers on electricity prices or the water supply in the communities where they are built, according to the new poll.

The concerns are not unfounded. A U.N. report published in June estimated that the water used by AI is expected to greatly expand in the coming years—equaling the needs of 1.3 billion people by 2030 and threatening natural resources for billions around the world. In the U.S. alone, data centers could account for 11.8% of electricity consumption by 2030, according to a 2024 report from the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory Report.

The poll found that Americans are more worried about the environmental impact of AI than other industries with a substantial environmental footprint like the meat industry or air travel. About two-thirds of U.S. adults are in favor of requiring data centers to use clean energy sources, like wind or solar, to supply their electricity needs. Roughly 8 in 10 Democrats support this, along with 56% of Republicans.

The Trump Administration—which has been undoing climate rules that could help spur clean energy—has strongly supported data center expansion, urging communities to "let Data Reign” in a social media post on Monday. "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” he wrote. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign."

Americans seem to be less certain. Roughly a quarter of U.S. adults surveyed said data centers are “extremely” or “very” beneficial when it comes to technological advancement, and only about 2 in 10 say the same about job creation. Many U.S. adults say data centers are “somewhat” beneficial or aren’t sure, while about one quarter say they’re “not very” or “not at all” beneficial for technological advancement, and around a third don’t see any benefit for job creation. (Some research has shown that, while data center construction can yield a number of temporary jobs, facilities tend to employ fewer permanent employees.)

The survey results come as a growing number of cities and states have been placing moratoriums on data center growth until the impacts are better understood. As of September 2026, 313 moratoriums have been enacted, affecting 44 states and more than 200 cities, counties, and localities, according to the Urban Institute.

This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief

Clean energy developers can sell their federal tax credits to companies that need them to reduce their tax bills, but developers are now generating credits faster than companies are buying them. That imbalance is giving buyers more bargaining power and putting pressure on sellers to compete for deals, Renewable Credit Management’s third quarter 2026 market report finds.

Production tax credits are holding up, with solar and wind credits fetching 92 to 94.5 cents per $1 of credit. Buyers favor these credits over investment tax credits in part because they are easier to evaluate and carry less risk, according to RCM.

Investment-based tax credits for solar, battery storage and biogas, calculated as a percentage of eligible project costs, are selling for 90 to 93 cents per $1, while technology-neutral ITCs are facing more price pressure as buyers weigh uncertainty over new federal rules. RCM reports those credits are currently selling for 88 to 91 cents per $1.

Dive Insight

The market for buying and selling investment tax credits is becoming a more important part of corporate tax planning as more companies look to use credits generated by clean energy projects to reduce their federal tax bills.

About one in four Fortune 1000 companies now participate as a buyer, according to Crux, a financial services company that facilitates deals. Financial services firms account for 45% of market volume, while energy and utility companies account for 34%.

Public filings rarely identify both the corporate buyer and type of tax credit, but Opal Fuels, the Nasdaq-listed renewable natural gas company, disclosed that Athene, a retirement solutions provider, bought ITCs tied to two of its projects. Athene bought an undisclosed portion of $17.4 million in credits from a Florida project last year; in March 2026, Athene and its reinsurance affiliate bought $22.9 million in credits from its subsidiary Land2Gas LLC, providing the seller $21.6 million in proceeds.

The market has shifted from the buyer-constrained conditions of 2023-24 to a supply-rich environment, according to RCM, with residential clean energy financing platforms increasingly selling credits to raise working capital.

Sunnova, formerly listed on the New York Stock Exchange, was among the early residential solar finance companies to monetize transferable credits, reporting $207.4 million in ITC sales in 2023 and about $645.5 million in 2024. Residential solar alone was expected to generate roughly $6 billion in investment tax credits in 2025, according to Reunion Infrastructure. Final, audited figures for last year are still being officially tabulated.

Ethanol is expected to become the largest source of transferable clean fuel credits, adding to a broader influx from advanced manufacturing projects and putting pressure on prices at the low end of the market, where credits are currently clearing at 87 to 92 cents per $1.

Timothy Doran, a director at RCM, said a “limited pool of buying capacity,” partly reflecting changes to bonus depreciation and Section 174 expensing under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, is also weighing on the market.

The growing supply is giving buyers more choice, making them more selective about projects and transactions that carry additional compliance risk. Buyers are also seeking protection against having to repay the value of a tax credit if the IRS later determines it does not qualify, RCM finds.

Developers increasingly are being asked to secure bank-backed indemnities rather than rely solely on commercial insurance, while some buyers are delaying transactions until they have greater clarity about whether credits from projects with potential foreign entity of concern, or FEOC, issues will qualify.

“ITC sellers are very anxiously awaiting regulations and additional guidance so that their credits can be insured, and the buyers can feel more comfortable purchasing,” Doran said. Pricing pressure is likely to continue for ITCs subject to FEOC requirements even after additional guidance is issued.

text:
WASHINGTON (September 16, 2026) – The American Chemistry Council (ACC) issued the following statement today on the Fifth Circuit’s decision regarding methylene chloride:

“America’s chemical manufacturers welcome the Court’s decision, which reinforces that TSCA decisions must be grounded in science, evidence, and real-world conditions. We appreciate the current EPA's efforts to bring greater transparency, stakeholder engagement, and regulatory certainty to TSCA implementation, and this ruling provides an important foundation for that work.

“For years, ACC has maintained that TSCA requires EPA to evaluate and manage risk based on individual conditions of use and the best available science, including consideration of existing workplace protections and real-world exposure information. The Court agreed, rejecting EPA’s improper ‘whole chemical’ approach and affirming that risk determinations must consider individual conditions of use, including proven workplace protections such as personal protective equipment. The Court highlighted the need for EPA’s risk management approach to consider current OSHA standards and exposure limits as well as the economic consequences of restrictions. The ruling makes clear that TSCA is designed to manage unreasonable risk through targeted, evidence-based regulation and is not a zero-risk statute.

"Importantly, this decision addresses policy interpretations adopted during the previous Administration's implementation of TSCA, giving EPA and stakeholders important clarity for future TSCA reviews. It emphasizes that chemical evaluations must be based on the statute, sound science, and practical risk-management principles. ACC looks forward to continuing to work with EPA and other stakeholders to support a science-based approach that protects workers and communities, promotes innovation, and strengthens American competitiveness.”

title: NDA secrecy for major projects hovers over Louisiana's congressional elections

As the underdog in the Senate race, Davis is trying to make Letlow’s Meta NDA into a campaign issue and brought it up during a speaking engagement at LSU this week.

text:
Jamie Davis believes there’s one specific reason Congresswoman Julia Letlow hasn’t agreed to appear in person with him for debates or any other events during their U.S. Senate race.

Letlow, the Republican candidate, doesn’t want to answer questions about the nondisclosure agreement she signed with a Meta company about Richland Parish’s $50 billion dollar data center project, he said.

“Any other questions I want to ask about Meta, she won’t be able to answer because she might break her NDA,” said Davis, the Democratic candidate.

Letlow not only signed the NDA but also began buying stock Meta and Nvidia, a company that makes computer equipment for data centers, in the months that followed, according to reporting from Gulf States Newsroom. The congresswoman didn’t disclose the stock purchases publicly until more than a year after the federal deadline to do so.

By signing the NDA, Letlow might have had access to information about Meta’s business operations and finances not available to the public.

Letlow’s campaign spokesperson did not respond to multiple requests this week for comment about the NDA. But in August, her congressional staff told Gulf States Newsroom she was unaware the Meta and Nvidia trades were happening on her behalf at the time.

As Louisiana undergoes an industrial megaproject boom, the extent to which public officials are trading away public transparency for economic investment through NDAs has become controversial.

Dozens of local and state elected officials signed NDAs related to economic development projects such as the SpaceX complex in Vermilion Parish, the Hyundai steel plant in Ascension Parish and data centers in other parts of the state.

More than 100 employees in Gov. Jeff Landry’s office also signed blanket NDAs prohibiting them from talking about what they learn working for the governor.

Landry and his administration have said the NDAs are necessary to attract global brands. But the agreements raise questions about whether government officials are free to share information about the projects’ impacts on resources such as water and the electrical grid.

LSU political science professor Robert Hogan said backlash over NDAs is part of a broader “general distrust that people have of government” right now.

“I do believe this could be a very effective issue at sowing seeds of doubt in the minds of voters about people who signed these,” Hogan said in an interview this week.

As the underdog in the Senate race, Davis is trying to make Letlow’s Meta NDA into a campaign issue and brought it up during a speaking engagement at LSU this week.

Davis said he never signed an NDA when he was an elected member of the Tensas Parish Police Jury and wouldn’t sign one if he was elected to the Senate.

NDAs could creep into competitive US House races

In addition to the Senate race, the NDA issue could come up in the U.S. House races, including open races for the 5th and 6th congressional districts, where many of the closely guarded industrial projects will take shape.

Four state legislators and the chair of the Board of Regents, which oversees state higher education, are among the nine candidates running to replace Letlow in the 5th District.

Of the five major candidates, two said they signed NDAs as elected officials in order to receive information about economic development projects.

State Sen. Stewart Cathey, R-Monroe, confirmed he signed an NDA to learn basic details about the Meta data center coming to Richland Parish from state Economic Development Secretary Susan Bourgeois before the project was publicly announced.

Even after he signed the agreement, Cathey said Bourgeois would only tell him it was a data center project and not the name of the company behind the site. He’s not sure if he would sign an NDA again if elected to Congress.

“The only legislators who have not signed NDAs are people who weren’t asked,” Cathey said.

State Rep. Gabe Firment, R-Pollock, said he signed an NDA required to attend a meeting about a data center under construction in Rapides Parish, but the information shared at the meeting didn’t turn out to be particularly confidential.

“I would not sign one again,” Firment said. “A lot of people I represent and I may represent in the future are not comfortable with that.”

State Rep. Mike Echols, R-Monroe is one of the three 5th District contenders who has not signed an NDA as an elected official. He said he also wouldn’t sign one as a member of Congress.

“I want to be as transparent as possible. I don’t see value for me,” Echols said.

State Rep. Pat Moore of Monroe, the Democratic Party-endorsed candidate, said she has not signed an NDA as a legislator and could not recall signing one while a member on the Ouachita Parish Policy Jury.

Misti Cordell, a Republican from West Monroe who leads the Board of Regents, said she hadn’t signed an NDA while in her current public position.

But Moore and Cordell wouldn’t rule out signing NDAs if elected to Congress.

Cordell said she would make sure any agreement she signed didn’t require her to shield information about what might hurt the public.

Moore said she wouldn’t personally benefit from any information she received through an NDA.

“If there was confidential information that I could not disclose, I would not do anything to profit off of it,” Moore said.

Two legislators are also among the 10 candidates running to replace U.S. Rep. Cleo Fields, D-Baton Rouge, in the 6th District. Fields decided against running again after state lawmakers redrew the district’s lines to make it harder for a Democrat to win.

State Sen. Rick Edmonds, R-Baton Rouge, said he has signed one NDA with the Louisiana Economic Development agency. He said he couldn’t say whether he would sign any if elected to Congress because he doesn’t know entirely what the position would entail yet.

State Sen. Blake Miguez, R-New Iberia, did not return phone calls seeking comment on his policy regarding NDAs. It’s not clear whether he has signed one as an elected official.

PITTSBURGH — Duquesne Light Company (DLC) hosted the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) today at its Woods Run campus on the North Side to showcase the utility’s ongoing commitment to deploying new technologies that can increase capacity and resiliency on the regional electric grid. At a press conference, both organizations celebrated the progress that has been made and reiterated the need for more transformative projects that will ensure affordable, resilient and reliable power for generations to come.

In 2023, DLC received a $19.7 million grant from the DOE to invest in grid modernization projects over the next five years in Allegheny and Beaver counties. Paired with a matching amount from DLC, the funds are part of the Grid Resilience and Innovation Partnerships (GRIP) Program, which seeks to enhance grid flexibility and improve the power system’s resilience against increasingly extreme weather and climate change.

“Unleashing American energy dominance requires a grid that can deliver affordable, reliable and secure power,” said Assistant Secretary for the DOE’s Office of Electricity Katie Jereza. “Together with Duquesne Light Company, we’re putting public-private partnerships into action to unlock more capacity from existing infrastructure we have. For western Pennsylvania, that means a stronger foundation to power homes, businesses and economic growth.”

Since receiving the GRIP grant, DLC has further implemented new technologies on the grid, including dynamic line rating sensors on seven of its transmission lines. Developed by LineVision, the sensors provide enhanced visibility across the transmission system and provide real-time capacity insights. DLC expanded its partnership with LineVision in 2025 after previous deployments dating back to 2021 showed a potential 25% increase in transmission line capacity, which can help unlock more clean energy sources; enable the grid to accept new sources of energy generation; and build a cleaner energy future for the Pittsburgh region.

DLC is also partnering with Itron to deploy tens of thousands of smart meters across its service territory beginning this October. These devices, which are installed on customer metering points, use real-time data to identify anomalies, support faster interconnection times and build a foundation for future advanced grid applications.

“DLC greatly values our partnership with the DOE and consistently works to ensure that federal dollars are being spent efficiently and ultimately in the best interests of our customers,” said Director of Advanced Grid Solutions and Strategic Planning Josh Gould. “As our industry rapidly changes, we remain committed to leveraging this opportunity to uncover additional technologies that will allow us to bring even more value and better service to our communities.”

About the Office of Electricity

The Office of Electricity (OE) leads DOE efforts to stabilize, optimize and expand the U.S. electricity system. Through cutting-edge research, system-level analysis and strong public-private partnerships, OE drives the technological advancements needed to secure the grid, power national prosperity and deliver affordable, reliable and secure energy to American homes, businesses and communities.

Last Friday, current and former Longhorns gathered with industry leaders in the Zlotnik Family Ballroom for the Kay Bailey Hutchison Energy Center’s annual Energy Symposium. The all-day event brought together experts from across the industry to discuss the most pressing issues in energy, including the future of traditional and emerging sectors, accelerating energy demand, artificial intelligence, and the race for energy security.

The program began with an introduction by the center’s founding member, former Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison, who discussed the speakers and presentations tackling the forces reshaping global energy systems. Jack Balagia, the center’s executive director, kicked off the morning by moderating a talk with Michael Wirth, chairman and CEO of Chevron, on the global energy company’s future related to supply chains and growth, and balancing long-term investment with geopolitical risk.

The second presentation brought together UT Executive Vice President and Provost William Inboden and author Daniel Yergin, vice chairman of S&P Global. The pair discussed the past, present and future of energy production, energy industry and geopolitics, as well as Yergin’s collection of books and experience as a policy adviser on the U.S. Secretary of Energy Advisory Board. His book “The Prize: The Epic Quest for Oil, Money, and Power” won the 1992 Pulitzer Prize in general nonfiction.

“I sometimes say, there’s two kinds of people in the world,” Inboden said. “Those who have read “The Prize” and those who need to read “The Prize.”

Yergin and Inboden continued with discussion of U.S. energy independence, the future of oil and gas, and new energy growth, including nuclear, hydrogen and batteries. They closed their talk with optimism about the future of energy and current innovation, which excited current Longhorns in the room hopeful to go into the energy sector.

Other panels throughout the day included industry leaders such as Gloria Moncrief, president and CEO, Montex Drilling Company; Pablo Vegas, president and CEO, ERCOT; and Bill Nelson, a former NASA administrator and U.S. senator. University leaders at the panels included Dean Bradley R. Staats of the McCombs School of Business; Dean Bobby Chesney of the UT School of Law; and Marek Locmelis, professor at the Jackson School of Geosciences.

Sessions and panels throughout the afternoon showcased expert voices on energy infrastructure growth, high-stakes decision-making, and advice to future Longhorns about going into the field. Many presenters had spent years on the Forty Acres themselves, showing that the present and future of energy and the University are distinctly intertwined.

The day concluded with a joint event with the Clements Center for National Security and Strauss Center for International Security and Law, marking the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. Hutchison and Inboden led a conversation on energy security and the evolving nature of global threats after participants shared stories of their experiences on the day of the attacks.

text:
As the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial Meeting concludes on Wednesday in Downtown Houston, international diplomats and federal energy officials are focusing their closing message squarely on consumer wallets: driving down costs at the pump and easing power bills for working families.

Hosted in the "Energy Capital of the World," the three-day summit brought delegates from the world’s 20 largest economies to discuss global supply bottlenecks, grid stability, and energy security. But while international trade and deals dominated closed-door sessions, host delegates continually pointed back to the everyday impact on local communities.

G20 summit addresses local impacts

Focus on Consumer Costs:

U.S. Under Secretary of Energy Kyle Haustveit emphasized that the administration's top priority remains leveraging domestic production to lower consumer costs.

"President Trump and the entire administration are focused on driving prices down. We start with natural gas, and natural gas is the lowest price in the world thanks to the shale revolution. When it comes to refined products for gasoline and diesel, we're focused on increasing supply, increasing production of the raw product and increasing the refining capacity to make sure we can drive those prices down low for hardworking Americans," Haustveit said.

Haustveit teased that additional international commercial and governmental deals focused on expanded energy trade are set to be finalized before the summit concludes.

Texas as the Model:

U.S. representatives praised Texas as a practical example of balancing conventional energy with grid innovation.

Advocating for a region-by-region approach, officials pointed to Texas' rapid adoption of solar power and utility-scale battery storage as a pragmatic approach to keeping power reliable and affordable.

"We're focused on pragmatism: what's reliable, affordable, secure and the answer to that is different depending on where you are in the country," Haustveit noted. "Texas has incorporated a lot of solar into their system and a lot of batteries. If you can do that in a region and make sure the total cost to the consumer and hardworking American is a net benefit, then we are supporting math, science, and the best decision to provide the reliable, affordable, secure energy that Americans deserve."

Repeal of carbon limits

Major announcement:

At the Houston summit, Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin, formally announced the total repeal of federal carbon pollution standards for power plants.

The action repeals the 2024 limits requiring new natural gas and existing coal-fired plants to capture carbon emissions.

The administration argues the rollback will save power companies over $300 billion, ultimately lowering household electricity costs.

However, the announcement has received pushback from environmental scientists and climate advocates, who warn we will see an increase in carbon dioxide emissions.

With the summit ending, local officials and consumers will be watching to see how the agreements finalized in Houston translate into tangible price relief at Texas gas pumps and on monthly electricity bills in the months ahead.

title: A Defanged EPA Offers Few Protections for the American People - Atmos Earth
description:
Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin on Monday announced the repeal of most of the Biden administration’s greenhouse gas requirements for coal and gas power plants—and proposed to eliminate what remains.
Power plants are the second-largest source of CO2 emissions in the country.
There’s no question that the EPA hindering its own ability to regulate power plants under the Clean Air Act will save the fossil fuel industry money.
Without the rule, power plant operators will no longer have to make investments required to meet emissions standards, including in carbon capture and storage technology.
Other rollbacks we’ve seen from the EPA in the past year include revoking the foundational scientific finding for regulating greenhouse gas emissions from vehicles, which led to the elimination of federal greenhouse gas emissions standards for cars and trucks.
text:
Standing on stage before a group of world leaders earlier this week, the head of the United States agency responsible for clean air, good health, and a flourishing environment announced the federal government would weaken a rule that does just that.

Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin on Monday announced the repeal of most of the Biden administration’s greenhouse gas requirements for coal and gas power plants—and proposed to eliminate what remains. Power plants are the second-largest source of CO2 emissions in the country.

He said the reason for the policy change, first proposed last year, was economics:

“Americans will see a decrease in electricity prices, but this is just the beginning. We are working to go even further so that American energy can be fully unleashed. Realizing the full potential of American energy means more jobs, lower prices, and a more prosperous America.”

Zeldin delivered the remarks during the EPA’s first-ever G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial, a three-day event held in “The Energy Capital of the World”: Houston, Texas.

The EPA characterized the event as an opportunity to bring together ministers from some of the world’s wealthiest countries and business leaders to provide “businesses the certainty they need to invest and build.”

In attendance were the CEO of U.S. energy company Entergy, along with Chevron’s executive vice president of Oil, Products & Gas. A delegation from Venezuela was a surprise guest. The country is not a member of the G20, but the U.S. announced earlier this month that the two struck a deal to increase American control over oil production in the South American country.

The event comes a week before international leaders are slated to meet in New York City for the General Debate of the United Nations General Assembly. When President Donald Trump attended the event last year, he called climate change “the greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world.”

The G20 event and EPA’s announcement set the stage for the messaging we can all expect to hear from the White House next week.

But they also sent another message. Buried in the agency’s platitudes about saving money is further evidence that the agency has not just shifted its priorities, but arguably abdicated its role as environmental protector.

Zeldin promised that “the United States is proving that we can protect human health and the environment while growing our economy and getting important projects built,” but he never explained how it’s able to do both with this change.

There’s no question that the EPA hindering its own ability to regulate power plants under the Clean Air Act will save the fossil fuel industry money. Without the rule, power plant operators will no longer have to make investments required to meet emissions standards, including in carbon capture and storage technology. It could also keep some coal-fired power plants open longer—an effort the government has been actively supporting through controversial orders that forced plants to remain open despite plans to retire.

Here’s what we also know:

Electricity generation is responsible for a quarter of all U.S. greenhouse gas emissions; and

The EPA itself calculated that repealing the rule would result in 123 million metric tons of additional carbon emissions in the next decade.

So what about the human and ecological toll?

The EPA was established in 1970 during the Nixon administration to mitigate worsening air and water pollution. Industry has pushed back on its regulations since its inception. But politicians on both sides of the aisle—including a Republican president—recognized the need for the federal government to step in when human and environmental health was at stake.

Whether climate change is part of the EPA’s mandate is a more complicated debate. Obama’s capstone Clean Power Plan, which aimed to set the first national limits on carbon dioxide emissions from power plants, was blocked by the Supreme Court in 2016 and formally replaced by the EPA when Trump took office the following year. Former President Joe Biden set his own power plant rule focused on greenhouse gases—and it’s those standards the Trump administration is now dismantling.

Republicans and industry execs have long argued it’s not within the purview of the EPA to regulate greenhouse gases for the purpose of addressing climate change. The Trump EPA is now making that argument explicitly, contending that the Clean Air Act does not authorize the agency to regulate power plant emissions in response to global climate change concerns.

But carbon emissions are also a health concern. Fossil fuel combustion produces pollutants that contribute to ground-level ozone and health issues like asthma. Carbon dioxide also drives rising atmospheric temperatures, which contribute to extreme heat and can exacerbate conditions associated with drought, wildfires, and flooding.

The truth is, science shows it’s impossible to fully decouple the health consequences of burning fossil fuels from their impact on the planet—the two are intrinsically interconnected.

But that doesn’t mean the Trump administration isn’t trying. Other rollbacks we’ve seen from the EPA in the past year include revoking the foundational scientific finding for regulating greenhouse gas emissions from vehicles, which led to the elimination of federal greenhouse gas emissions standards for cars and trucks.

The EPA’s perspective on what—or whom—it aims to protect seems clear in its representatives’ own words and actions.

Zeldin on Monday promised that the power plant rule reversal would save Americans and the power sector up to $310 billion. But the EPA also offered another interpretation of the changes.

According to an analysis by EPA staff in 2024, Biden’s power plant rule, if left in place, would have delivered $370 billion in net benefits. In 2035 alone, the agency estimated that the air-quality improvements delivered via regulations would prevent 1,200 premature deaths and 360,000 cases of asthma symptoms.

But some of those numbers can no longer be considered by the EPA, because Trump earlier this year eliminated yet another measurement—a way to calculate the dollar benefit of saving lives.

For decades, the agency used the “value of a statistical life,” currently estimated at $11.7 million, to help quantify the benefits of regulations that prevent premature deaths. Now, that value is effectively $0 in the agency’s regulatory cost-benefit calculations.

As the EPA makes industry benefits from regulatory rollbacks abundantly clear, each policy change makes it increasingly difficult to show just how much the public stands to lose from the same actions.

It is said its to be done in order to ensure affordable and reliable energy supplies.

The repeal, which was backed by Trump, is the largest power sector deregulatory action in U.S. history, says the EPA. Now, Trump wants to repeal all remaining greenhouse gas emissions standards for power plants.

Under the Clean Air Act, Carbon Pollution Standards enforced limits on carbon emissions based on the EPA's evaluation. The limits reduced millions of metric tons of harmful air pollutants that are known to endanger public health.

How polluted is Louisiana? How many metric tons of carbon emissions are released into air

In Louisiana, close to 150 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalents are emitted from facilities across a number of sectors, according to the EPA. Emissions in Louisiana are likely much higher than this number, as the EPA's report does not include agricultural sectors and facilities with emissions below 25,000 metric tons.

Louisiana is among the most polluted states in the U.S., but around 66% of Louisiana's greenhouse gas emissions were produced from facilities in one specific area.

How much more polluted is Cancer Alley than the rest of the state?

"Cancer Alley" refers to an 85-mile stretch of communities along the banks of the Mississippi River between New Orleans and Baton Rouge where residents live in close proximity to approximately 200 fossil fuel and petrochemical operations, according to Human Rights Watch.

Residents of this area have been detrimentally impacted by the surrounding fossil fuel and petrochemical production plants, as the area has the highest risk of cancer from industrial air pollution. Residents also face elevated risks and rates of respiratory ailments, as well as maternal, reproductive and newborn health harms, according to John Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

As for the environment, power plant byproducts and emissions seep into communities' air, water and soil.

Governor spent months advocating against the Trump Administration to reverse Trump directive requiring coal plants to stay open past their useful life, which was expected to raise energy costs for Wisconsin working families

MADISON — Gov. Tony Evers today, during National Clean Energy Week, celebrated the recent U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit ruling that President Donald J. Trump and the Trump Administration overstepped its emergency powers when it forced coal plants to stay online past their scheduled retirement date. Gov. Evers spent months urging President Trump and the Trump Administration to reverse course on its decision to invoke Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act to force the extension of operations of expensive coal power plants in the Midwest region. The effort by Trump to keep the coal plants online past their useful life is part of the Trump Administration’s larger efforts to revive coal plants throughout the nation and walk back clean energy regulation, further raising energy costs for Wisconsinites and hindering the state’s efforts to promote clean energy resilience.

“There is no such thing as ‘clean coal,’ and the Trump Administration’s efforts to keep aging coal plants online would only further increase energy bills for Wisconsinites while undermining our efforts to build a more sustainable, reliable, and resilient clean energy future for our state,” said Gov. Evers. “I’ve spent months urging the Trump Administration to reverse course on this shortsighted and wrongheaded decision. While it’s disappointing that the Trump Administration refused to do the right thing without a court making them, this is an important fight for our clean energy efforts and our work to leave our kids and grandkids a better future than the one we inherited. Here in Wisconsin, we know that promoting a clean energy economy and bringing down energy costs are not mutually exclusive goals, and we will continue our efforts to protect the well-being and interests of our communities and safeguard the health of our environment.”

Gov. Evers earlier this year, in letters to the Trump Administration in April and July, respectively, accused the Trump Administration of unjustifiably invoking Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act to revive or extend the life of old, expensive coal power plants, including the J.H. Campbell Power Plant in Michigan and the R.M. Schahfer and F.B. Culley generating stations in Indiana. The three coal power plants run on the same regional electric grid that Wisconsin is part of, spreading the increasing costs across states in the region. An analysis outlined in July shows that the Trump Administration’s decision to force several coal plants to stay online is estimated to cost Americans between $3.1 billion and $5.9 billion over the next few years, including an estimated $117 million in increased costs to ratepayers in Wisconsin alone.

Prior to the Trump Administration’s ongoing efforts to revive coal plants throughout the nation, these coal power plants had gone through extensive business analysis and energy reliability planning, which concluded the plants were no longer economically viable and their closures would have no impact on the electricity supply and grid. All three coal power plants were scheduled to retire due to the plants reaching the end of their useful lives, until the U.S.DOE issued the abrupt orders forcing them to remain open, resulting in dramatically increased costs to operate. In fact, the owner of the F.B. Culley generating station described this power plant as “an inefficient and increasingly unreliable asset” in a letter asking the U.S. DOE to stop forcing them to keep this plant online. Since the initial extension orders, the U.S.DOE has ordered multiple extensions for the coal power plants, racking up additional costs to utility ratepayers.

Gov. Evers has consistently advanced a clean energy economy in Wisconsin and focused on reducing out-of-pocket costs for families. In his first year in office, Gov. Evers joined the U.S. Climate Alliance, of which he was the first Midwest governor to serve on the executive board and as co-chair. The governor, along with his fellow U.S. Climate Alliance governors, is committed to collectively achieving the goals of the 2015 Paris Agreement to combat climate change and has established an ambitious goal of ensuring 100 percent carbon-free electricity consumption in Wisconsin by 2050.

In addition to joining the Alliance in 2019, in his first year in office, Gov. Evers signed Executive Order #38 to create the OSCE, charging the office with developing the Wisconsin Clean Energy Plan to promote the development and use of clean and renewable energy across the state, advance innovative sustainability solutions that improve the state’s economy and environment, and diversify the resources used to meet the state’s energy needs. In accordance with Gov. Evers’ Executive Order #38, the state’s first-ever Clean Energy Plan was released in 2022, providing a roadmap for the state to lower energy bills and prices at the pump for Wisconsin families, promote energy independence by reducing reliance on out-of-state energy sources, create an estimated more than 40,000 jobs by 2030, and invest in job training and apprenticeship programs in innovative industries and technologies. Last month, OSCE released the 2026 Clean Energy Plan Progress Report, outlining the strides the state is making to meet its clean energy goals.

Additionally, in his most recent state budget, Gov. Evers successfully eliminated the sales tax on household utility bills, which is expected to save Wisconsin households $178 million over the biennium. The Evers Administration has also led the nation in the rollout of the state’s Home Energy Rebate programs, which assist homeowners in making energy efficiency and electrification upgrades to lower energy bills. Since launching the programs in 2024, $17 million in rebates have been paid to Wisconsin households to install popular energy-efficient measures, including air sealing, insulation, heat pumps for cooling and heating, and electric panels and wiring. Gov. Evers has also proposed increasing funding for Focus on Energy, the state’s energy efficiency program, to further help Wisconsin homeowners reduce their energy use and lower energy bills.

text:
WASHINGTON D.C. — The Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Coalition for Community Solar Access (CCSA) today announced that the two organizations will combine following approval from each organization’s Boards of Directors. Effective in early October, CCSA will integrate its team, resources, and policy work within SEIA.

The two organizations both have successful individual histories of driving growth for segments of the industry. SEIA is the largest national trade association for the solar and storage industry and has a longstanding track record, with its founding in 1974, of spurring growth across the industry, including utility-scale, commercial, and residential segments. CCSA has operated as the national trade association for community solar and storage developers, businesses, and nonprofits, and has driven the rapid acceleration of the market over the last decade.

“By bringing CCSA into SEIA, we’re creating a stronger, more unified voice for the solar and storage industry,” said SEIA CEO Tim Pawlenty. “Together, we’ll build on CCSA’s success and become a more powerful advocate for every segment of the industry.”

Combined, the two organizations now form the only national trade association representing every segment of the solar and storage industry, with an expanded network and enhanced capabilities to shape market and policy priorities at both the state and federal levels.

The organization will represent companies across utility-scale, residential, commercial, and community segments. Together, the organizations form a single, powerful voice for solar and storage, driving and realizing continued growth and representing the full expansion of these resources across the country.

“A little more than a decade ago, CCSA was formed to create greater access to solar for all Americans. Today, as distributed community power has become one of the most credible solutions to affordability and grid reliability, so has the need for greater scale, resources, and expertise to meet the moment,” said Jeff Cramer, departing CEO of CCSA. “I am deeply proud of the work we have done, the team we built, and the industry we helped shape, and equally excited to see it evolve inside SEIA.”

Solar and storage continue to expand their roles in the U.S. energy system. Together, these technologies represent over 70% of new capacity added to the grid so far in 2026, and the energy storage market saw its largest quarter on record in Q2. The U.S. also continues to set solar and storage manufacturing records.

Learn more about SEIA’s policy advocacy work.

###

Media Contact: Rachel Skaar, SEIA’s Director of Communications, rskaar@seia.org (406-461-9694)

About SEIA®:

The Solar Energy Industries Association® (SEIA) is leading the transformation to a clean energy economy. SEIA works with its 1,200 member companies and other strategic partners to fight for policies that create jobs in every community and shape fair market rules that promote competition and the growth of reliable, low-cost solar power. Founded in 1974, SEIA is the national trade association for the solar and solar + storage industries, building a comprehensive vision for the Solar+ Decade through research, education and advocacy. Visit SEIA online at www.seia.org and follow @SEIA on Twitter, LinkedIn, and Instagram.

About CCSA:

CCSA is the national trade association advancing competitive distributed power solutions, including community solar, mid-scale solar, and distributed storage, as the fastest, most affordable path to meeting America’s growing energy needs. Alongside our members, more than 100 developers, businesses, and nonprofits, we champion policies that unlock private investment, accelerate deployment of locally sited energy resources, ensure open and competitive procurement, and position distributed power plants as central to a modern, resilient, and affordable grid.

text:
