text:
The Trump administration threw another lifeline to coal generation Monday.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency will abandon Biden-era rules that force coal-burning power plants to capture most of their CO2 emissions or shut down.

The agency is also expected to argue it lacks the legal authority to regulate carbon dioxide.

In a statement, EPA administrator Lee Zeldin said the agency's action would promote reliability and affordability.

"Americans will see a decrease in electricity prices, but this is just the beginning," he said. "We are working to go even further so that American energy can be fully unleashed. Realizing the full potential of American energy means more jobs, lower prices, and a more prosperous America."

CO2 is a greenhouse gas that's making the planet hotter.

Under the Biden administration, coal plants would have been required, in the next several years, to capture 90% of their carbon emissions. The industry said the cost would have been prohibitive and the technology not feasible. The only choice was to retire the coal fleet, it said.

Environmental groups, including the Sierra Club, have been making that their goal.

Elisa Owen, senior energy organizer for the Sierra Club in Kentucky, says the EPA move rewards more expensive forms of electricity.

"The current administration has made clear that it prefers burning fossil fuels," she said. "It's not good for anyone except the fossil fuel industry."

In its latest Short Term Energy Outlook, Trump's U.S. Department of Energy forecasts an 8% decline in nationwide coal generation this year, and another 6% drop next year.

Nationwide, solar surpassed coal in electricity generation for the first time in May. Solar is the fastest growing form of generation on the U.S. grid, and that's expected to continue.

Kentucky's Republican leaders have supported the Trump administration's rollback of regulations they say have hurt the state's coal industry.

A spokeswoman for Attorney General Russell Coleman declined to comment Monday.

In February, Coleman appeared in Louisville with federal and state officials to announce the rollback of another Biden rule limiting mercury and other toxic materials in power plant emissions.

WEKU also asked the Kentucky Coal Association for comment on the rule change.

The Trump administration has enacted other policies favorable to coal in recent years. Those include declaring an energy emergency that forced older coal plants to remain on the grid rather than retire.

A federal district judge in the District of Columbia last week dealt an initial blow to that policy.

Echoing many critics of fossil fuels, Owen said the Trump policy on CO2 won't make coal plants more competitive.

"The economics are the economics," Owen said, "and those aren't changing regardless of how you choose to regulate what we call greenhouse gases, those that make the effect of warming, global warming, worse."

According to the Sierra Club, three of the power plants that emit the most carbon dioxide nationwide are in the region.

They include the Tennessee Valley Authority's Cumberland plant in West Tennessee, Kentucky Utilities' Ghent plant in Northern Kentucky and Mon Power's Harrison plant in West Virginia.

The Ghent and Harrison plants emitted more than 10 million tons of CO2 in 2025, while the Cumberland plant emitted more than 9 million.

Other big emitters include East Kentucky Power's Spurlock plant and Appalachian Power's Amos plant, in Kentucky and West Virginia, respectively. Both emitted more than 8 million tons of CO2 in 2025.

text:
The US Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation (CMEI) has launched the PROSPECT Planning Prize, a $16 million initiative to address the critical shortage of skilled professionals in mining and minerals. This prize, part of the broader $100 million Providing Opportunities for Specialized Education in Critical Technologies (PROSPECT) program, seeks to empower academic institutions to develop innovative training programs that will prepare the workforce needed to secure America’s energy future.

Addressing workforce shortages in critical minerals

The initiative comes at a pivotal moment as the US works to rebuild its domestic battery supply chain. New mines, processing facilities, manufacturing capacity, and recycling infrastructure are essential to achieving energy independence. However, these efforts require a new generation of engineers, scientists, technicians, and skilled professionals to sustain them.

The PROSPECT Planning Prize encourages academic institutions to design programs that target a diverse range of beneficiaries, including early-career professionals, educators, students in universities, community colleges, and high schools. By expanding access to training and experiential learning opportunities, the initiative helps grow and strengthen the future of the domestic critical minerals industry.

Closing skills gaps in US battery manufacturing

The DOE has launched other efforts, such as the Battery Workforce Initiative (BWI) in 2022, yet recruiting skilled labor remains challenging. One of the most urgent challenges the PROSPECT Planning Prize seeks to address is the skills gap in US manufacturing. “Mining and critical minerals professionals are essential to America’s success in manufacturing, AI, energy, and national security—but this country isn't producing enough of them,” said Assistant Secretary of Energy Audrey Robertson. “Through this prize competition, DOE will empower universities to pursue more ambitious strategies to attract and educate the workers we need for a robust critical mineral supply chain.”

Batteries, particularly lithium-ion batteries, are critical for electric vehicles (EVs) and renewable energy storage. However, the US domestic workforce lacks the specialized expertise required to support the full lifecycle of battery production—from mining raw materials to recycling used components.

The shortage of skilled professionals in battery manufacturing has slowed down the US’s ability to compete globally in this sector. By investing in workforce development, the DOE aims to close these gaps. “This prize is about more than just education—it’s about securing America’s future,” Robertson emphasized. “By building a skilled workforce, we’re not only strengthening our domestic supply chains but also ensuring that the US remains a global leader in energy innovation and manufacturing.”

$16 Million to transform US workforce development

The PROSPECT Planning Prize challenges US-based academic institutions to submit plans for programs to substantially increase the number of graduates and credentialed professionals in mining and supply chain fields by 2028. Up to 16 institutions will receive $1 million each to implement their plans, focusing on creating pathways to job placement upon graduation or program completion.

Applications for the PROSPECT Planning Prize are now open, with a submission deadline of October 5, 2026. The winners will be announced on October 20. Interested institutions can find more information, including eligibility requirements and submission guidelines, on the PROSPECT Prize page.

By investing in education and workforce development, the DOE is laying the foundation for a resilient and sustainable future where America leads the way in critical minerals and energy innovation.

text:
Egypt – PM witnesses signing of contract to build plant for electric batteries CATL

Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly on Sunday, September 13, 2026, witnessed the signing of a contract to establish a plant producing various types of electric batteries within the frame of a partnership between Egyptian battery maker BME and China’s Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL), the world’s largest electric battery manufacturer.

The contract was signed by Chairman of BME Maged Wahib and Luo Director of international investment at CATL Luo Haining, in the presence of Minister of Industry Khaled Hashem, MBA/PMP – Sr. IT Project Manager Amin Karim Ghabbour and BME board member Lotfy Tadros.

BME was established by Egyptian transport manufacturer MCV and Auto D for Industry, Trade and Supplies.

The new plant aims to establish a specialized industrial base for battery systems in Egypt, initially producing batteries for heavy commercial vehicles, with plans to expand into passenger-car batteries and energy-storage solutions.

The project is intended to serve the growing transport and energy sectors and support manufacturing and exports.

The plant’s first phase will have an annual production capacity of 1 gigawatt-hour, with initial investments exceeding 2 billion Egyptian pounds (dlrs 39 million). The second phase will raise capacity to 5 gigawatt-hours annually and include production of passenger-car batteries as well as batteries for storing solar and wind energy.

The project targets a local component ratio of 40% and is expected to supply both domestic and international markets, while creating jobs and developing technical skills for Egypt’s workforce.

The partnership combines Egyptian manufacturing and engineering capabilities with CATL’s battery technology, production equipment and technical support. The plant will supply locally manufactured battery systems to vehicle manufacturers in Egypt, reducing reliance on imports and associated shipping and logistics costs.

Speaking at the signing ceremony, Madbouly welcomed the agreement with CATL, saying the company was one of the leading global players in the battery industry and had extensive expertise and capabilities.

He said the government expected work on the project to begin quickly and that it would take the necessary steps to support the development and localization of battery manufacturing in Egypt.

The minister of Industry said the plant represented an important step towards developing Egypt’s domestic battery manufacturing capacity as the global shift towards electric vehicles and energy-storage solutions accelerates.

Hashem said automotive component industries were a cornerstone of Egypt’s national program to develop the automotive industry and were key to attracting global carmakers.

He also said the agreement with the world’s largest electric battery manufacturer demonstrated the ability of Egypt’s industrial sector to meet international manufacturing requirements and produce competitive, high-quality products.

Project manager Amin Karim Ghabbour said the agreement was part of government efforts to deepen local manufacturing, localize modern industries and technologies and strengthen Egypt’s capabilities in producing automotive components, especially for electric vehicles and battery systems.

He said the partnership with CATL would combine advanced global battery technology with Egyptian industrial and engineering capabilities, supporting technology and knowledge transfer and the development of a local supply chain.

Ghabbour further added that BME aimed not only to produce battery systems for heavy commercial vehicles, but also to establish the foundations for an integrated battery industry that could eventually expand into passenger-car batteries and energy-storage solutions.

The expansion, he said, would create new opportunities for investment, manufacturing and exports and support Egypt’s efforts to become a regional hub for emerging industries.

text:
DJIBOUTI CITY, September 13, 2026 – The World Bank Group today released a Country Private Sector Diagnostic (CPSD) for Djibouti, identifying reforms that could unlock at least US$600 million in private investment and create around 12,000 jobs over five years in off-grid solar energy, data centers, and tourism. The report outlines targeted policy actions that would enable such investment.

Positioned at the intersection of some of the world's busiest shipping lanes and serving as the primary maritime gateway for Ethiopia, Djibouti has seen GDP growth average 5.3 percent annually from 2016 to 2024 and has attracted substantial foreign direct investment in port infrastructure. Yet high electricity tariffs, limited access to finance, skills gaps, and restrictions on competition in key sectors have constrained private sector expansion. With unemployment remaining high, the CPSD identifies opportunities to create jobs in strategic sectors.

Solar Energy: Up to $390 Million and more than 8,500 Jobs

Private investors have deployed approximately 10 megawatts of off-grid solar capacity in Djibouti since 2022, with additional projects in preparation. Commercial electricity tariffs at 25 US cents per kilowatt-hour – against an Africa regional average of 14 cents – are the largest single cost factor for businesses operating in the country. The CPSD identifies targeted regulatory reforms, including raising self-generation limits, clarifying power purchase arrangements, strengthening sector regulation, and expanding skills development to attract private investment. Together, this could attract up to $390 million in investment and create more than 8,500 jobs over five years.

Data Centers: Up to $240 Million and 1,300 Jobs

Eight operational submarine cables run through Djibouti, connecting Asia, Europe, and Africa. Current data center capacity is nearing full utilization. The CPSD identifies reforms to the regulatory framework, energy provisioning, and market access that would unlock private investment in the sector, with potential for between $160 million and $240 million in investment and between 700 and 1,300 new jobs.

Tourism: Up to $180 Million and 2,600 Jobs

Djibouti's tourism assets include Lake Assal (the lowest point on land in Africa), the limestone chimneys of Lake Abbe, marine ecotourism such as whale shark sightings, and a cultural heritage recognized when Djibouti City became the first African metropolis named World Capital of Culture and Tourism by the European Council on Tourism and Trade. The CPSD identifies licensing, data, and skills reforms that would convert investor interest into committed capital, with potential for between $66 million and $180 million in investment and 2,600 jobs.

title: 2028 Volvo XC60 AWD First Look: Doubling Down on Plug-In Power - MotorTrend
description:
With the updated 2028 XC60, Volvo indicates how it sees hybrids as pivotal to its emissions-free aims.
ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW Around back, the taillights also gain black enclosures with slim inlaid red LEDs.
The 2028 XC60 looks familiar in profile, especially with the 18- or 19-inch wheels that roll over from last year.
ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW Inside Adaptations Like outside, changes in the cabin are subtle.
Yet with hybrid mode available, a full battery charge and fuel tank give the XC60 T8 up to 590 miles of total driving range.
text:
Did Volvo get ahead of itself with its electrification commitments? Not long ago, it set 2030 as the year it would have a fully electric lineup. Its combustion powertrains—including hybrids—would be phased out along the way.

But the market conditions Volvo predicted haven’t transpired. It’s had to backtrack on its EV targets and adapt its product strategy. It will build new EVs, but through this turmoil, hybrids have remained a steady theme. With the updated 2028 XC60, Volvo indicates how it sees hybrids as pivotal to its emissions-free aims.

ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW

Biggest Update Yet

Ten years is a long production run for any car, but the XC60 isn’t giving way to a new generation yet. This version went on sale for 2018 and has received gradual updates over the years, most recently for 2026. These efforts made it Volvo’s bestseller. Now, a more thorough refresh for 2028 extends its lifespan further.

ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW

Looks Similar but Better

Ten years is also long enough for any car to look stale, but the XC60 has stood the test of time. This year’s updates revive its contemporary appearance. Fundamentally, it’s the same SUV, retaining its basic structure and many body panels. Still, this is an attractive design evolution.

Everything ahead of the front doors is new, with the fascia more obviously updated than the fenders and hood stampings. A slimmer grille sits in a bumper with more modern, edgy graphics. Most prominent are the headlights, which get revised, trademark “Thor’s Hammer” accents that appear to float inside new, black-backed lenses. Functionally, the headlights gain Matrix LED projectors that adapt to avoid dazzling oncoming drivers.

ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW

Around back, the taillights also gain black enclosures with slim inlaid red LEDs. Designers told us the goal was to look “drawn with a pen of light” onto the surface. The tailgate panel is slightly changed, as well, while the bumper is reworked for cohesion with the front. No emissions-spewing tailpipes are visible, as has been Volvo’s practice for years.

The 2028 XC60 looks familiar in profile, especially with the 18- or 19-inch wheels that roll over from last year. However, new 20- and 21-inch wheel designs become available, while new Heather Bronze paint balances being trendy and timeless.

ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW

Inside Adaptations

Like outside, changes in the cabin are subtle. Much of the dashboard is revised. Textile trim panels have reshaped wood decor below, bisected by an ambient light strip, and the treatment continues on the front and rear door panels, which gain illuminated wood trim near the release handles. Rather than the previous gloss black and chrome, the air vent surrounds are now matte black with a slim gloss-black insert. Light brown Cardamom Nappa leather remains available and can now be paired with ventilated front seats.

In its 2026 update, the XC60 gained a 11.2-inch infotainment touchscreen with Google Gemini AI voice assistant functionality. That remains for 2028 but is relocated by a few millimeters for better visibility. No functionality is added to the 12.3-inch driver info display, keeping it low-feature compared to other automakers’ equivalents.

Safety Tech Enhancements

A car can never be safe enough for Volvo, and the automaker continues its tireless pursuit in the 2028 XC60 update. New ultrasonic and radar sensors embedded in the front bumper enhance collision avoidance, especially with crossing traffic. The vehicle can also detect passing cars and cyclists and warn the driver before they open the door.

Semi-automated lane change functionality is added to the available Pilot Assist driver assist suite. Additional exterior cameras enable a movable 3D view for the 360-degree camera.

ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW

PHEV Pump-Up

As before, the 2028 XC60’s base engine is the B5 2.0-liter turbocharged I-4, which sends 247 hp and 266 lb-ft of torque through an eight-speed automatic transmission to standard AWD.

The highlight change is the available T8 plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrain. It continues to use a 2.0-liter turbocharged I-4 engine to drive the front wheels and an electric motor to power the rear wheels. Although system output remains at 455 hp, that’s now accomplished with a less powerful engine and slightly stronger motor.

Most notable is the high-voltage battery. At 41.2 kWh (37.9 usable), the new pack has more than double the previous capacity. That gives the updated T8 more than double the previous all-electric range: up to 78 miles, versus 35 miles before.

ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW

Rather than a long, boxy shape running through the center tunnel, the new pack is flat-mounted under the floor, like in full EVs. This required structural reengineering but, impressively, does not affect ground clearance or passenger measurements. In fact, the hump between the rear seats becomes smaller. Curb weight increases by about 200 pounds, however.

Although Level 3 DC fast charging is not available, Level 2 home charging capacity increases from 3.6 to 7.2 kW. So even with the significantly larger battery, total charge time is only slightly longer.

All this is intended to give XC60 drivers a more EV-like experience. Needing to plug in becomes less frequent. The stronger rear motor is meant to make the XC60 T8 feel more electric; full one-pedal driving remains part of its capabilities. Yet with hybrid mode available, a full battery charge and fuel tank give the XC60 T8 up to 590 miles of total driving range.

Twice as Nice?

Had things played out as Volvo anticipated, this refresh might have never happened. Perhaps, at its dignified age, the XC60 would’ve been retired and replaced by the recently revealed EX60 as Volvo continued its all-electric transition.

Instead, Volvo has had to adapt. EVs haven’t taken over as anticipated, and Volvo isn’t the only automaker adjusting to today’s conditions. Updating the XC60 for 2028 could be seen as a backup plan. Nevertheless, it makes a nice SUV nicer and increases its capabilities in ways that support today’s drivers and Volvo’s long-term plans. B5 models will be built in Charleston, South Carolina, and T8 models in Torslanda, Sweden.

text:
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin announced the rollback of Biden-era greenhouse gas standards for power plants at a press conference in Houston during a G20 energy conference on Monday.

"The unlawful Biden administration's 2024 greenhouse gas requirements for power plants were a direct attempt to shift away from essential and affordable energy," he said. "It was this belief that in the name of protecting the environment that we should suffocate out of existence entire sectors of our energy economy. President Trump has made it clear that those days are done."

The standards issued under President Joe Biden limited the amount of greenhouse gases that natural gas- and coal-fired power plants could emit.

Zeldin said the changes would save "$310 billion for American families" and argued the Biden administration exceeded its authority in imposing the requirements.

"Today's announcement isn't just about restoring the American economy," he said. "It's also about restoring the rule of law."

The elimination of the standards could have sweeping impacts for Texas, which lead the country in carbon emissions from power plants in 2025.

According to EPA data, Texas power plants emitted more than 193 million metric tons of carbon dioxide in 2025, leading the 49 states who reported the data. Carbon dioxide emissions information for Alaska was not included in the EPA dataset.

Rice University civil and environmental engineering professor Daniel Cohan said while the rollback is focused on greenhouse gases linked to climate change — like carbon dioxide — other pollutants are released alongside those emissions, like ozone, smog and particulate pollution. With Texas leading in carbon dioxide emissions from power plants, the state is likely to see an outsized impact, he added.

"For Texas, this means that we're likely to be breathing far more pollution coming out of our power plants for years to come, and we're affected more than any other state," he said.

Meanwhile, Texas environmental groups also slammed the EPA's decision.

Air Alliance Houston Executive Director Jennifer Hadayia said in a statement that the EPA's decision would "negatively impact public health and the climate for generations to come."

title: Samsar Upcycles Electric Vehicle Battery From 1000th Nissan Leaf - EIN Presswire
description:
With this milestone Samsar has proven to be the solution – new energy storage from old cars.
It’s affordable, sustainable, and built here, in the USA.” Samsar Resources remanufactures battery packs from Nissan Leaf sedans at its factory outside of Houston, Texas.
Nissan Leaf batteries are the perfect fit for this model thanks to their air-cooled pack architecture and well-understood lifetime performance.
On the contrary, Nissan Leaf batteries that have left their original vehicles have enormous value.
The Samsar team needed three years to remanufacture our first 1,000 battery packs.
text:
The Samsar team with outboard remanufactured EV batteries that have been tested and certified for reuse

Samsar technicians celebrate remanufacturing their 1,000th Nissan Leaf pack, seen here just prior to disassembly.

The Team at the Samsar Factory in Sugarland, Texas

Samsar has returned over 25 MWh of battery capacity to the field instead of the recycler.

It was a lot of sweat, tears, and late nights. But we got it done and I am so proud of what our team has achieved here in Sugarland. Hitting one-thousand. This is big.”

— CEO Dr. Guillermo Garcia, Phd

SUGARLAND, TX, UNITED STATES, September 15, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Samsar Resources, a start-up turned industry leader in the re-manufacturing of electric vehicle batteries, is proud to celebrate the transformation of 1,000 Nissan Leaf electric vehicle batteries into new forms of energy storage.

Founded by Steve Hellman, a venture capitalist and founder of Mobility Impact Partners, Samsar was created to capture the full value of lithium batteries by designing batteries made to be remanufactured at the end of their first service life, and by remanufacturing high value lithium batteries like those found in electric vehicles.

For Guillermo Garcia, founding CEO, hitting this milestone was a hard earned moment: “When I joined the team in 2022 we didn’t know if this was going to work. We had this amazing opportunity with Nissan to do something will all the thousands of batteries that were coming out of old Nissan Leafs each year. But every process we developed, every step in building a factory for re-manufacturing EV batteries was new. There was no playbook. It was a lot of sweat, tears, and late nights. But we got it done and I am so proud of what our team has achieved here in Sugarland. Hitting one-thousand. This is big.”

Named after the concept of *samsara*, the cycle of life, death, and rebirth, Samsar designs batteries for a circular economy. Batteries designed to last and designed to be easy to service and repair. Champions of the concept of Design for Remanufacturing (DfRem), by hitting this milestone Samsar has demonstrated that remanufacturing lithium batteries like the Nissan Leaf can be a profitable alternative to recycling or the landfill, while building a more robust US lithium battery supply chain and conserving precious rare earth minerals.

For Kent O’Hara, former President of Nissan Energy, and new Samsar board member, this moment validates a long standing personal mission: “At Nissan I saw how hungry the world was for energy and knew that in a few years there was going to be millions of EV batteries that would be headed for recycling. I knew there must be a way to match the need for power with the growing supply. With this milestone Samsar has proven to be the solution – new energy storage from old cars. It’s affordable, sustainable, and built here, in the USA.”

Samsar Resources remanufactures battery packs from Nissan Leaf sedans at its factory outside of Houston, Texas. Samsar’s cost-conscious approach captures 90% of the value of each pack by downsizing to modules and performing cell-level quality control. Nissan Leaf batteries are the perfect fit for this model thanks to their air-cooled pack architecture and well-understood lifetime performance.

This milestone represents a moment of exponential growth for the company. In 2022 only 20 Nissan packs were re-manufactured. By 2025 over 300 packs a year were being disassembled, tested, and rebuilt, Today, half way through 2026 we proudly announce that we have remanufactured 1,000 Nissan Leaf packs (and counting.)

Battery remanufacturing is the practice of disassembling packs, performing quality control on internal components, and refurbishing as needed. EV batteries are replaced when they reach a threshold of remaining capacity (typically in the range of 80% - 90%).

Industry refers to this threshold as “end-of-life” but that moniker can be deceiving. What it means, really, is that this specific battery is no longer useful for this specific context. It doesn’t mean the battery doesn’t have value.

On the contrary, Nissan Leaf batteries that have left their original vehicles have enormous value. In fact, they are coveted among remanufacturing companies for their air-cooled pack architecture and well-understood lifetime performance. That remaining capacity can be used fruitfully for industries like security, marine, or energy storage at work sites. Samsar uses industry-leading remanufacturing methods to capture that value and sell on to the right customer, at the right price.

Leading the team for this milestone is Carlos Contreras, Operations Manager at Samsar’s Sugarland factory. Carlos is a Manufacturing leader with over 18 years of experience managing operational excellence, quality systems, and EHS compliance across production environments.

Certified as a Lean Six Sigma Green Belt (LSSGB) and Operational Excellence (OpEx-L), he specializes in establishing sustainable systems, optimizing throughput, and building cross-functional teams in high-growth operations.

Carlos has managed manufacturing operations across multiple industrial sectors. Most recently, as a Manufacturing Engineer in piping solutions, he designed technical systems and streamlined production workflows. Previously, he spent nearly four years as a Senior Production Supervisor in fencing manufacturing, directing 65 employees across three departments to meet safety and quality compliance targets. His earlier background includes frontline management, where he managed plant organization, inventory control, and employee training.

The Samsar team needed three years to remanufacture our first 1,000 battery packs. Now that we’ve grown our team and matured our processes, we expect to hit the 2,000 pack milestone sometime in 2027.

You can follow our journey to remanufacturing at scale, and everything else we’re working on, by joining our email list today. Thanks for being part of the adventure!

The new $10 million Sun and Solar Program will help integrate solar energy into agricultural operations, supporting clean energy while ensuring we can continue to feed families across New York and beyond.
This new program builds on the over $7 million awarded by NYSERDA in November 2025 to projects that co-locate solar and agricultural operations in New York State.
The 2025 State Energy Plan anticipates that ground mounted solar projects could play an important role in addressing New York’s long-term energy needs.
NYSERDA also supports New York State’s farmers in managing their energy use through no-cost technical assistance through the Agriculture Energy Audit Program.
text:
Multi-Year Initiative Supports Continued Research and Engagement with Farmers to Realize Benefits from Co-Located Solar Energy and Working Farmland

The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) today announced the launch of a new $10 million Sun and Soil Program to help interested farmers and agricultural communities benefit from the integration of solar energy in ways that sustain active farmland, known as agrivoltaics. This multi-year initiative, first introduced in Governor Hochul’s 2026 State of the State, provides funding for planning and implementing innovative agrivoltaic projects while supporting applied research and problem-solving efforts to address market barriers and expand economic opportunities for farmers.

NYSERDA President and CEO Doreen M. Harris said, “Under Governor Hochul’s leadership, NYSERDA is proud to support expanding opportunities to advance the dual goals of preserving agricultural operations and advancing clean energy projects. We look forward to receiving forward thinking, innovative proposals through this new program, and working with farmers, agricultural communities and solar companies on workable and responsible solutions.”

Agriculture is a critically important sector of New York's economy, with over 33,000 farms across approximately 20 percent of the state's land area, or close to 7 million acres. Through ongoing community engagement, including a request for information issued earlier this year to help inform the program, farmers have expressed interest in the potential for solar energy to provide an additional revenue stream. Additionally, the New York State Farmland Protection Working Group, overseen by New York State Department of Agriculture and Markets (AGM), also recommended that New York study co-utilizing land for renewable energy generation and agricultural production with the potential to play an important role in meeting the State’s future energy and agricultural development needs.

State Agriculture Commissioner Richard A. Ball said, “We are optimistic about the opportunities that the Sun and Soil Program may present to our farmers, putting into practice a system that will allow a farm business and solar to co-locate without compromising actively farmed land. We look forward to seeing these innovative projects and accompanying research across the State take shape, understanding that the goal of the program is to balance the State’s renewable energy agenda alongside our efforts to protect farmland, particularly our prime soils.”

NYSERDA’s competitive Sun and Soil Program , administered by the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) and developed in partnership with AGM, seeks proposals from interested farmers, or solar developers and organizations, for planning and implementing both agrivoltaic projects for on-farm powering and those that deliver a portion or the entirety of solar production to the electrical grid, as well as solar and battery storage for on-farm energy projects. Projects for retrofitting previously constructed solar energy projects for agrivoltaics with or without on-farm powering are also eligible. NYSERDA will also accept proposals that utilize new or adapted agrivoltaic technologies, equipment, or agricultural practices, feature novel configurations or retrofits, bring agrivoltaics to areas where it has not yet been applied, or provide market solutions, guidance, and training.

NYSERDA is accepting proposals through the first and second rounds of the program under four categories:

Solar and Agriculture Integration – On the Ground Projects

Addressing Barriers and Challenges – Creating Opportunities

Building Capacity and Support for Farmers and Communities

Increasing Access to Opportunities within the Integration of Solar Energy and Agriculture

NYSERDA anticipates awarding multiple projects within each category. Awards are expected to be up to $200,000 for planning proposals and up to $350,000 for implementation proposals. Cost-sharing is encouraged but not required.

Proposals for the first round of funding will be accepted until December 10, 2026, by 3:00 p.m. ET.

Proposals for the second round of funding will be accepted until April 20, 2027, by 3:00 p.m. ET.

Additional information including a complete list of all eligibility rules, evaluation criteria, and future application due dates can be found in the solicitation summary on NYSERDA’s website . Additional rounds of funding are expected to be made available in the future.

Senate Energy and Telecommunications Chair Kevin Parker said, “New York is proving that we do not have to choose between protecting our farmland and building a clean energy future, we can do both. The Sun and Soil Program puts farmers at the center of our clean energy transition, creating new economic opportunities while keeping productive farmland in use. While Washington remains mired in gridlock and uncertainty, New York is moving forward investing in our farmers, our communities, and a stronger energy future. This is the kind of innovative leadership that gets results, and New York is showing the country how it’s done.”

Senate Agriculture Chair Michelle Hinchey said, “Agrivoltaics gives us hope as we confront serious challenges for the future of our food supply and energy system. Building on our work to support agrivoltaics research, the Sun and Soil program will help farmers co-produce food and clean energy on the same land, helping to keep our family farms in business and protect farmland, while diversifying the grid to lower costs for ratepayers. We encourage farm businesses to submit their proposals and thank Governor Hochul and NYSERDA for recognizing and encouraging this opportunity.”

Assembly Agriculture Chair Dona Lupardo said, “It is important that we protect New York’s valuable prime farmland, while at the same time providing interested farmers with an additional revenue stream. The Sun and Soil Program is designed to achieve that balance with a well-thought-out approach to preserving farmland while meeting our energy goals. I’d like to thank the Governor, Ag & Markets, and all my colleagues for supporting this innovative approach to addressing the opportunities and challenges involved with agrivoltaics.”

Senate Environmental Conservation Chair Peter Harckham said, “At a time when New Yorkers are facing high energy costs and the price of fossil fuels continues to rise, it is more important than ever that we pursue low cost, renewable solar energy. Agrivoltaics offer an innovative solution that addresses two challenges at once: supporting our vital agricultural industry while expanding the supply of affordable, clean energy to meet our growing needs. I commend Governor Hochul and NYSERDA for this timely investment in clean energy and New York farmers.”

Assembly Environmental Conservation Chair Deborah Glick said, “As we see climate change increasingly impact farming across the globe, New York’s farms will become even more important to the health and well-being of New Yorkers. The new $10 million Sun and Solar Program will help integrate solar energy into agricultural operations, supporting clean energy while ensuring we can continue to feed families across New York and beyond. I applaud Governor Hochul, NYSERDA President and CEO Doreen Harris, and Agriculture and Markets Commissioner Richard Ball for advancing this important program, which will have a lasting positive impact on our farms, our environment, and our future.”

Information and lessons learned from the awarded projects will be shared to help others benefit from the integration of solar energy with active agriculture and understand the opportunities and market potential for scaling agrivoltaics in New York State. This new program builds on the over $7 million awarded by NYSERDA in November 2025 to projects that co-locate solar and agricultural operations in New York State.

Additionally, NYSERDA convenes the New York State Agricultural Technical Working Group (A-TWG), an independent advisory body comprised of farmers and farming stakeholders, solar developers, state agencies and non-governmental organizations, to advise and steer efforts in advancing solar energy development in a responsible way that supports New York State's agricultural operations, lands, farmers and communities.

The 2025 State Energy Plan anticipates that ground mounted solar projects could play an important role in addressing New York’s long-term energy needs. Agriculture is a vital component of New York’s economy, but many farmers within the State face very narrow profit margins, high levels of risk, and limited access to capital for investments to adjust to changing market conditions. Solar energy can provide reliable on-farm power when paired with battery storage that can be used to offset electricity purchases or be available for backup power during outages.

NYSERDA also conducts policy and analysis-oriented environmental research to provide pertinent information on the impacts and opportunities of clean energy choices and arising energy options. NYSERDA also supports New York State’s farmers in managing their energy use through no-cost technical assistance through the Agriculture Energy Audit Program.

Funding for this initiative is provided through the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative.

New York State's Climate Agenda

New York State's climate agenda calls for an affordable and just transition to a clean energy economy that creates family-sustaining jobs, promotes economic growth through green investments, and directs a minimum of 40 percent of the benefits to disadvantaged communities. New York is advancing a suite of efforts to achieve an emissions-free economy, including in the energy, buildings, transportation, and waste sectors. The State is also working to disburse the historic $2 billion Sustainable Future Program, which will deliver targeted funding to lower emissions, reduce household energy costs, and spur green job growth.

NYSERDA

Since 1975, NYSERDA has been working to advance New York’s energy system and economy. As a public benefit corporation, NYSERDA has served as an objective source for information and technical expertise to drive innovation and investment. NYSERDA professionals have worked to protect the environment and help New Yorkers increase energy efficiency, save money, and reduce reliance on fossil fuels. To learn more about NYSERDA’s programs and funding opportunities, visit nyserda.ny.gov.

Echion Technologies and Energy Tech Solution (ETS) have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to develop battery technology based on Echion’s industry-leading XNO niobium-based anode material

Developed for mass industrial applications such as mining, rail, maritime and data centres, XNO outperforms mainstream lithium-ion batteries in performance and durability.

ETS has joined the Echion partner network as the first total battery solution provider, covering production line design, cell assembly equipment, and Korea-based cell design R&D for XNO.

ETA develops battery manufacturing equipment for startups and gigafactories worldwide, providing personnel support, product strategy, and hardware sales. ETS also acts as a contract cell manufacturer for next-generation battery startups from Asia, Europe, and North America. Echion and ETS provide a complete solution for cell OEMs wanting to diversify into XNO.

Y.H. Kim, ETS CEO, said, “Echion has demonstrated incredible performance capabilities in our custom-designed cells. As battery technology saturates every aspect of the global energy system, this long-lasting and high-performance chemistry will find its place serving the most demanding users.”

Under this MoU, Echion will use ETS as a vetted contract manufacturing partner for demonstration cell provision and product design iteration. For customers interested in XNO cells, ETS will assign a portion of capacity at its battery hub in Chungju to customise cells to cylindrical, pouch, and prismatic form factors. Interested parties can rely on ETS for full turnkey cell design and manufacturing.

Jean de La Verpilliere, Echion CEO, said, “Energy Tech Solution offer a comprehensive range of battery solution services and manufacturing expertise, and have shown themselves to be adept at bridging process engineering and scientific R&D. We’re confident that XNO batteries manufactured by the experts at ETS, on their well-trusted equipment, will give those customers seeking to produce their own XNO batteries the charging speed and cycle life they need to run their businesses.”

Niobium-based batteries, including those powered by XNO, are considered a higher-performing alternative to titanium-oxide, or LTO, batteries, in the premium category of fast-charging batteries with excellent cycle stability and high-rate charging capability, targeting up to 50,000 cycles and charge rates up to 10C.

title: Building Colombia's Nature Economy Could Create Hundreds of Thousands of New Jobs
authors: Héctor Miguel Donado, Carolina Useche, Diego Gómez, Celine Novenario
description:
As the world shifts toward a more resilient, low-carbon economy, Colombia has a significant opportunity to create hundreds of thousands of new jobs in emerging industries such as green infrastructure, clean transport and the circular economy.
An estimated 4.7 million workers, roughly 22.6% of the current workforce, are in occupations that will be directly affected by the climate transition.
Policies are needed to focus on workforce development, skills upgrading and new economic opportunities that will help drive Colombia’s long-term competitiveness.
Integrating employment and skills into climate finance is key to maximizing the economic and social returns of climate investment.
Colombia’s Moment to Build a New Economy Colombia’s opportunity for a new economy — rooted in nature, driven by innovation and designed for inclusion — is a practical, achievable agenda.
text:
As the world shifts toward a more resilient, low-carbon economy, Colombia has a significant opportunity to create hundreds of thousands of new jobs in emerging industries such as green infrastructure, clean transport and the circular economy.

Globally, this transition is expected to generate approximately 375 million jobs. Around 280 million jobs will be linked to adaptation, with 195 million of those adaptation jobs linked to nature-based solutions and regenerative agriculture.

As the second-most biodiverse country in the world, Colombia’s ecosystems represent enormous untapped economic potential across even more emerging industries, such as ecotourism, bioeconomy and sustainable exports. Nature tourism and agribusiness alone could create 775,000 jobs by 2035, with many of these jobs concentrated in Córdoba, Atlántico, Nariño, Caldas, Magdalena and Bolívar, expanding economic opportunities in regions whose vast natural landscapes and agricultural potential make them well-positioned for these industries. Colombia's agricultural capacity, strategic natural ecosystems and regional diversity also position it as a potential leader in nature-based economic development across Latin America.

Colombia’s government has already identified more than $32 billion in green investment opportunities spanning renewable energy, ecosystem protection and sustainable agriculture — sectors where the country already holds a competitive advantage.

The Central Challenge: Making Growth Inclusive

But turning this potential into reality requires confronting challenges in Colombia’s labor market. For many Colombians, the opportunity to find secure, well-paid and protected employment still depends on their gender, age and where they live, with women, young people and rural communities often facing the greatest barriers.

In June 2026, for instance, around 55% of workers were employed informally, working without formal contracts or access to benefits such as social security, paid leave or legal protections. Female labor force participation was about 54%, compared to 76% for men, a gap driven largely by the unequal distribution of unpaid care work. Youth unemployment is around 15%, almost double the national average.

An estimated 4.7 million workers, roughly 22.6% of the current workforce, are in occupations that will be directly affected by the climate transition. These include new and emerging roles, such as solar photovoltaic installers and environmental economists; existing occupations requiring new skills, such as electrical engineering technicians, construction inspectors, and bus and truck mechanics; and occupations likely to experience increased demand, including electrical powerline installers and repairers, chemical engineers, forest and conservation technicians, electricians and bus drivers.

Alongside new opportunities, the adoption of low-carbon technologies and growing demand for lower-emission goods may displace some workers. New jobs will not necessarily emerge in the same regions, require the same skills or offer comparable pay. Without deliberate management, workers facing these changes and people already excluded from secure employment may struggle to access new opportunities.

None of this will change on its own. Policies are needed to focus on workforce development, skills upgrading and new economic opportunities that will help drive Colombia’s long-term competitiveness.

The country has already taken several steps: 100% of universities and technical education institutions are expected to offer programs aligned with the needs of a carbon-neutral economy by 2030, and green jobs should represent 45% of total employment by 2050, according to Colombia’s Long-Term Climate Strategy (E2050).

The next four years, which coincide exactly with Colombia's nationally determined contribution (NDC) commitments and the incoming 2026-2030 National Development Plan, represent a strategic opportunity to translate its climate commitments into concrete programs, targets, institutional responsibilities and financing. Colombia’s large working-age population also gives the country an advantage — but that window will not remain open indefinitely.

Policy Levers for Sustainable and Inclusive Growth

A new WRI study sets out three priority areas Colombia will need to focus on to move its economy in this low-carbon, resilient and competitive direction:

Reconversión laboral, mejora de competencias y empleos verdes con enfoque de equidad: recomendaciones para el Plan Nacional de Desarrollo 2026-2030 de Colombia.

Download

1) Governance and Political Intent

Colombia has already made progress in embedding just transition principles into its national climate commitments, including the NDC and its Long-Term Climate Strategy. These principles support workers and communities affected by the shift away from high-emitting industries and enable them to benefit from opportunities created by a low-carbon economy. Likewise, the Ministry of Labor has moved this forward by creating a workforce strategy. The task now is to put them into action.

The National Development Plan must translate these commitments and strategies into concrete programs, such as regional economic diversification initiatives that provide business development and market access for sustainable agriculture, nature tourism, ecosystem restoration and bioeconomy business, transition support for workers and communities affected by declining industries, like reskilling and upskilling training programs, and measures to ensure that new investment creates formal jobs.

These measures could include agreements between project developers and local authorities that set explicit targets for local hiring and formal job creation in the regions where projects are developed. Delivering these programs will require clear institutional owners, timelines and funding sources, ideally, by aligning labor, education, investment and climate policy.

These areas are often planned and implemented separately, leading to disconnected initiatives, preventing policies and investments from working toward the same goal. National targets must be matched by local transition agreements: tailored plans that bring together governments, trade unions, businesses and communities, aligned with broader local and regional development strategies.

2) Training Innovation

A low-carbon, climate-resilient economy is not built by policy alone; it is built by people, by their hands and skills. Reskilling and upskilling workers will be needed faster than traditional education allows. To meet this demand, short, modular, flexible and stackable training programs can help workers to more quickly update their technical skills. This is particularly important in Colombia, where many in its informal workforce lack paid time off or employer-supported training and cannot afford to step away from their jobs while they retrain.

At the same time, recognizing the skills people already have will be essential. The National Learning Service (SENA), which already certifies skills acquired through practice, has already reached more than 260,000 Colombian workers in 2025. Expanding this model and complementing it with clear occupational certifications would help informal workers to convert practical experience into recognized credentials and access better-quality formal employment.

None of this will be inclusive by default. Women face barriers that training programs rarely account for: a disproportionate share of unpaid childcare, eldercare and household tasks, leaving less time for training; limited rural connectivity, which restricts access to online and in-person courses; and exclusion from technical training, which narrows their pathways into emerging green jobs. Programs must therefore be designed around these lived realities, not just formally open to them.

3) Financing and Incentives

Financing the transition requires a different way of thinking about costs. Reskilling and workforce development should be treated not as recurrent expenditure but as an investment in people.

Public spending can also serve as direct leverage: Large infrastructure, energy and transport contracts financed with public resources should require local hiring, skills certification and training to turn projects into workforce development.

Incentives matter most for the smallest firms. Micro, small and medium-sized businesses generate around 80% of national employment, yet they have the least capacity to absorb the cost of retraining staff or adopting low-carbon technologies. A combination of fiscal and financial incentives, access to credit and technical assistance — paired with gradual steps toward formalization — can help businesses retrain workers and adopt low-carbon technologies while improving employment quality.

Finally, international climate finance should go in the same direction. This is particularly relevant in Colombia, where international support for protecting globally important ecosystems such as the Amazon could also help Indigenous Peoples and local communities develop skills and access green jobs in restoration, sustainable forest management, nature tourism and bioeconomy enterprises.

International cooperation and development bank lending should explicitly direct a share of climate funding toward a green and equitable labor transition — including reskilling, social protection and the expansion of training institutions like SENA. By building local skills and employment opportunities, these investments can make conservation and sustainable resource use viable sources of employment and income, reducing reliance on activities that degrade ecosystems. Integrating employment and skills into climate finance is key to maximizing the economic and social returns of climate investment.

Colombia’s Moment to Build a New Economy

Colombia’s opportunity for a new economy — rooted in nature, driven by innovation and designed for inclusion — is a practical, achievable agenda. The building blocks are in place: extraordinary biodiversity, a young workforce, proven agricultural capacity and growing investor interest in nature-based economic development.

Now is the time for Colombia to simultaneously address the climate crisis and expand its economy for its people. With the right policies, this transition can improve the lives of millions of workers. Realizing this opportunity will require deliberate action across workforce development, local planning and climate investment.

description:

By advancing Canadian clean fuels initiatives, we are committing to lowering emissions and investing in our low carbon future.
Today, the Honourable Ruby Sahota, Secretary of State for Combatting Crime, on behalf of the Honourable Tim Hodgson, Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, announced $4 million in funding under Natural Resources Canada’s Energy Innovation Program Clean Fuels Call for Proposals for two projects in the Greater Toronto Area that will strengthen Canada’s clean fuels sector.

Together, these investments will accelerate Canada’s path to net-zero, advancing domestic innovation, building a competitive clean technology sector and strengthening Canada’s position as a global leader in clean fuels.
text:
September 15, 2026 Mississauga, Ontario Natural Resources Canada

As Canada works to build a stronger, more resilient economy, investments in clean fuels and emerging energy technologies are helping turn Canadian innovation into economic growth, strengthen energy security and create new opportunities for workers and businesses across the country. By advancing Canadian clean fuels initiatives, we are committing to lowering emissions and investing in our low carbon future.

Today, the Honourable Ruby Sahota, Secretary of State for Combatting Crime, on behalf of the Honourable Tim Hodgson, Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, announced $4 million in funding under Natural Resources Canada’s Energy Innovation Program Clean Fuels Call for Proposals for two projects in the Greater Toronto Area that will strengthen Canada’s clean fuels sector.

The funding will support research and development projects led by Next Hydrogen and CERT Systems Inc.

Next Hydrogen will receive $2 million for its project, Fabrication and Integration of New High-Performance Electrodes for Next Hydrogen’s Advanced 3rd Generation Water Electrolyser Module, to develop a scalable fabrication process and improve the efficiency, performance and cost of electrolyzer modules. This will support the wider adoption of clean hydrogen energy by advancing technologies for low-carbon hydrogen production, which, when powered by low-carbon energy such as wind, solar, nuclear and hydro, the company estimates can achieve emissions reductions of up to 95 percent compared with conventional hydrogen production through unabated steam methane reforming.

CERT Systems will receive $2 million for its project, Direct Air-to-Ethylene Conversion for Sustainable Aviation Fuels, to advance a process that converts captured carbon dioxide into ethylene, a chemical building block to sustainable aviation fuel. This process could result in an estimated 93.8% reduction in lifecycle emissions when compared with conventional jet fuel.

Together, these investments will accelerate Canada’s path to net-zero, advancing domestic innovation, building a competitive clean technology sector and strengthening Canada’s position as a global leader in clean fuels.

title: Hitachi Energy brings largest U.S. investment to date to Mississippi - Magnolia Tribune
description:
Governor Tate Reeves and the Mississippi Development Authority announced Tuesday that Hitachi Energy is investing $528 million to expand its operations in Copiah County.
The announced expansion project is Hitachi Energy’s largest investment to date in the U.S., officials said.
“Hitachi Energy could’ve made its largest investment in America anywhere in the country – but the company chose Mississippi,” the governor said.
Hitachi Energy was incorporated in June 2021, but its founding dates back over a century from predecessor companies ABB and its parent company, Hitachi Ltd. Hitachi Energy is now a global leader in electrification that manufactures transformers and other equipment to help power homes, businesses and communities.
Andreas Schierenbeck, CEO, Hitachi Energy, said demand for electricity is growing rapidly, and the grid must grow with it.
text:
The $528 million expansion project in Copiah County will increase the company’s production capacity and expand the range of small power transformers manufactured domestically, while creating over 650 jobs.

Governor Tate Reeves and the Mississippi Development Authority announced Tuesday that Hitachi Energy is investing $528 million to expand its operations in Copiah County.

The governor made the announcement from the G20 energy summit in Houston, Texas, alongside Energy Secretary Chris Wright, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin and other federal energy leaders.

The announced expansion project is Hitachi Energy’s largest investment to date in the U.S., officials said.

Calling it “a massive win for Mississippi and the United States,” Reeves said the company plans to create 654 jobs in its expanded Mississippi transformer manufacturing factory.

“Hitachi Energy could’ve made its largest investment in America anywhere in the country – but the company chose Mississippi,” the governor said. “Mississippi’s momentum is growing stronger every day, and it is our people who are building the future of American energy infrastructure.”

Reeves added that Mississippi is proud to play a leading role in powering America’s future.

Hitachi Energy was incorporated in June 2021, but its founding dates back over a century from predecessor companies ABB and its parent company, Hitachi Ltd. Hitachi Energy is now a global leader in electrification that manufactures transformers and other equipment to help power homes, businesses and communities.

The company’s current facility in Copiah County produces small power transformers and employs 475 people.

Andreas Schierenbeck, CEO, Hitachi Energy, said demand for electricity is growing rapidly, and the grid must grow with it.

“This investment in Mississippi, our largest ever in the U.S., reflects our long-term commitment to American manufacturing and building the grid infrastructure that will help power America’s growth for decades to come,” Schierenbeck said. “We are pleased to work with the Trump administration and Governor Reeves to support investment in American manufacturing at a pivotal time for U.S. energy security.”

MDA said the expansion project will significantly increase Hitachi Energy’s production capacity and expand the range of small power transformers manufactured domestically, helping meet growing demand across North America while strengthening the domestic supply chain for critical energy infrastructure.

The project includes the purchase of a 45-acre site at the Copiah County Industrial Park in Gallman, the construction of a new facility, new manufacturing equipment and infrastructure improvements. Construction is expected to begin later this year, with transformer production scheduled to start in 2029.

The company is taking advantage of the Mississippi Flexible Tax Incentive, or MFLEX, program, and MDA is also assisting with site development and infrastructure improvements. Copiah County is assisting with the project, as well.

“Reliable energy infrastructure has become one of the most important factors in economic growth, and that starts with the ability to manufacture the equipment that keeps the grid running,” said Mississippi Development Authority Executive Director Bill Cork. “At $528 million, Hitachi Energy’s expansion is a massive addition to the investment taking place in Mississippi and puts Copiah County at the center of an industry that is increasingly critical to economic development.”

title: Southwest Louisiana carbon project faces growing pushback
description:
Jeff Landry’s October 2025 moratorium on new carbon sequestration applications, carbon capture projects continue to move forward in southwest Louisiana under exemptions included in his order, The Current reports.
GCS has already filed a Class VI permit application for Project Goose Lake, which is one of two of the company’s carbon sequestration projects exempt from the moratorium and placed on Landry’s priority list.
Residents were particularly concerned about the Chicot Aquifer, which provides drinking water for 15 parishes stretching from Southwest Louisiana to Acadiana, with opponents warning that carbon sequestration could threaten the region’s drinking-water supply.
GCS defended the project, saying its founders already privately own the land and that the site’s geology is well suited for carbon sequestration.
The Louisiana Department of Conservation & Energy is considering the Goose Lake permit and is also preparing a final decision on GCS’s separate Project Minerva in Cameron Parish.
text:
Despite Gov. Jeff Landry’s October 2025 moratorium on new carbon sequestration applications, carbon capture projects continue to move forward in southwest Louisiana under exemptions included in his order, The Current reports.

Gulf Coast Sequestration, or GCS, is seeking a coastal use permit for Project Goose Lake, which would involve construction of one drinking-water monitoring well and two Class V carbon capture and sequestration testing wells near the Intracoastal Canal and Sabine National Wildlife Refuge on the Cameron-Calcasieu parish line, followed by an injection well.

GCS has already filed a Class VI permit application for Project Goose Lake, which is one of two of the company’s carbon sequestration projects exempt from the moratorium and placed on Landry’s priority list.

The proposal has drawn opposition from Calcasieu Parish residents, who spoke out at a recent public hearing primarily over potential environmental impacts rather than land rights. Residents were particularly concerned about the Chicot Aquifer, which provides drinking water for 15 parishes stretching from Southwest Louisiana to Acadiana, with opponents warning that carbon sequestration could threaten the region’s drinking-water supply.

GCS defended the project, saying its founders already privately own the land and that the site’s geology is well suited for carbon sequestration. The company said it believes the project would be a responsible and beneficial use of coastal resources. The Louisiana Department of Conservation & Energy is considering the Goose Lake permit and is also preparing a final decision on GCS’s separate Project Minerva in Cameron Parish.

text:
It’s no secret that European (and US and Japanese) automakers and truckmakers have fallen far behind their Chinese competitors, even as they continue to lobby against emissions regulations and other measures designed to force them to catch up. Now Transport & Environment has put some numbers to the ongoing market shift.

The EU heavy truck market, which amounts to around 245,000 vehicles annually, is dominated by a small group of legacy truckmakers: Daimler Truck, Traton, IVECO, DAF and Volvo Group. Zero-emission trucks accounted for 5.6% of sales in the EU countries in 2025, double the figure from a year earlier (over 15% in Norway, Sweden and the Netherlands).

T&E predicts that new entrants could capture a big part of the market quickly by offering comparable quality at lower prices—and Chinese truckmakers have announced plans to do just that. Based on stated goals, they hope to grab up to a quarter of the heavy e-truck market by 2030.

European truckmakers aren’t standing still—they’re steadily improving their electric trucks—but T&E’s research finds that Chinese EVs perform as well as European trucks on key metrics, including driving range, charging time, maximum payload and energy efficiency—and deliver a total cost of ownership that can be as much as 12% lower. This can be a game-changer in the haulage sector, where profit margins can be between 1.5-2%, according to T&E.

The Chinese aren’t the only wolves at the Europeans’ door. Tesla has announced plans to bring its Semi to Europe, and it’s been logging major sales at much lower prices than its US competitors can offer.

“Competitive Chinese and US truck models are already in the European market, and many more are poised to enter soon,” said Stef Cornelis, Director of Freight and Fleets at T&E. “This is a critical moment for Europe’s trucking industry, which should learn from what has happened to the car industry. Weakening the pace of electrification now would present an opportunity for US and Chinese competitors to gain a significant share of the market, in Europe and the rest of the world.”

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressman Bob Latta (OH-05), Chairman of the Subcommittee on Energy, delivered the following opening statement at today’s hearing to discuss America’s nuclear fuel policy in support of American energy dominance.

Subcommittee Chairman Latta’s opening statement as prepared for delivery:

“Today the Energy Subcommittee will examine the Department of Energy’s work to develop what are called Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses.

“These campuses represent a new and fresh effort by DOE and the Administration to [quote] ‘transform the nuclear fuel cycle.’

“The program intends to support the nation’s nuclear policy ambitions as well as to begin to address the federal government’s statutory responsibility for disposal of nuclear waste.

“This involves taking spent fuel from reactors around the nation to a state that volunteers to host the campus, where the fuel can be stored, recycled, and related waste disposed.

“When it comes to increasing reprocessing, my view is: it is about time. Our policy should be to use our technological abilities to take fuller advantage of the remaining usefulness of spent fuel—and this, in turn, reduces the waste that must be placed in a permanent repository.

“Maximizing the remaining energy and other useful isotopes from spent fuel presents an attractive financial incentive for taking a more wholistic look at the full fuel cycle.

“This explains why six states so far are stepping up to negotiate how to develop, in partnership with DOE, lifecycle innovation campuses.

“And, as we will hear this morning, it may well offer a workable path for updating our nuclear waste policy.

“But of course, there is a long way to go to develop durable state agreements—and durability is key.

“The idea of consolidating spent fuel from sites under a federal program with voluntary host states is not a new one.

“Congress authorized a nuclear waste negotiator to set up something like that in the early 1990s. For various reasons, that did not work out—as have other efforts with respect to attracting durable state support.

“What must be done differently this time around?

“There are also commercial and economic realities when it comes to our fuel cycle that factor into what may eventually develop.

“This hearing will help us identify what Congress must do to enable continued work on these campuses, given their potential.

“Our focus should be on policies that complement existing law—and the designated federal disposal site at Yucca Mountain—and protect the interests of ratepayers and taxpayers under that law. This means not rushing to restart fees on nuclear power generation or irresponsibly raiding the nuclear waste fund.

“We should not forget that our bi-partisan legislative work in 2018 provided substantial changes to the law that would have incentivized completion of the Yucca license, enhanced host state benefits, and accelerated the type of program envisioned in the current proposal.

“Those reforms passed the House by a vote of 340-72. Unfortunately, politics obstructed the potential for the reforms.

“Perhaps with tremendous new support of nuclear in recent years means we’re in a different place today.

“We will take testimony from two panels.

“On the first panel, we will hear from the Department of Energy. Assistant Secretary of Energy Ted Garrish, who heads the Office of Nuclear Energy and can explain the program, state interactions, and what Congress may do to help enable its progress forward.

“Our second panel will provide perspective from key stakeholders.

“We will hear from Stacy Paradis, an Illinois public utility commissioner speaking on behalf of NARUC. Electric ratepayers, under the law, are responsible for paying for the ultimate disposal of nuclear waste and she can speak to the importance of protecting ratepayer funding and the nuclear waste fund.

“Maria Korsnick will provide the perspective of the Nuclear Energy Institute on the fuel cycle, and on the policies surrounding storage and disposition of spent nuclear fuel.

“Jared des Rosiers (day-roe-sher), will speak on behalf of the Decommissioned Plants Coalition, which represents closed nuclear plants that continue to store spent fuel.

“And, finally, Greg White, also a former state utility commissioner, will provide the perspective of the Nuclear Waste Strategy Coalition, which represents a range of stakeholders that seek to get our nuclear waste policy back on track.

“We welcome the witnesses and I yield back the balance of my time.”

text:
Reports early yesterday speculated that the Trump administration would roll back carbon pollution standards for fossil fuel-fired power plants…and it turns out that where there’s smoke, there’s fire. With the G20 energy summit in Houston as a backdrop, the EPA announced the controversial moves later in the day, saying the changes will save the energy industry more than $300 billion and “unleash” American energy.

What’s changing:

Essentially, all Obama and Biden-era climate-protection measures that required gas plants to burn cleaner fuels and coal plants to capture most of their emissions by 2039 will be eliminated. These changes will take effect shortly after the agency officially publishes them.

In a separate rule proposed yesterday, the EPA will also argue that greenhouse gases do not endanger human health or the environment. This could prevent future administrations from reinstituting the restrictions.

The science: If the US power sector were a country, it would be the world’s sixth-largest greenhouse gas emitter, according to an NYU analysis of 2022 emissions data. The regulations being wiped away could prevent ~30,000 deaths, according to Associated Press research. Even a partial unraveling, per the AP, would lead to more smog, mercury, and lead in the air (though some restrictions on mercury and other contaminants will remain in place even if all the climate rules go).

With great power…

…comes great (or at least more) AI data centers. Coal plants said that capturing and storing carbon underground, as required by the EPA’s old regulations, was so cost-prohibitive that they had to close. Since 2010, 330 coal plants have retired and another 60 have announced plans to shut down by 2031, according to the Sierra Club.

Making it cheaper to use fossil fuels coincides with the push from the tech sector to build more data centers that have been straining grids and driving up energy prices for consumers.

title: How States Are Deciding Whether Data Centers Lower Your Power Bill or Raise It
description:
