title: The Long Game on Energy Affordability - Center for American Progress
description:
Why energy efficiency matters The case for energy efficiency is well documented.
Maryland’s experience underscores why states should avoid financing energy efficiency programs in ways that enrich utilities and put efficiency programs at risk.
Energy efficiency should not be simply another line item on a utility bill; it should be viewed as preventive care for the energy system.
Rather than scaling back energy efficiency investments funded through utility rates, lawmakers expanded them as part of a broader affordability package.
The most durable affordability strategy pairs immediate bill relief with continued investment in the resources that lower energy costs over time.
text:
As the war in Iran drives up energy prices1 and as heat waves blanket much of the country,2 Americans’ electricity bills are rising.3 Energy efficiency improvements are some of the most cost-effective tools available to help make homes more comfortable and lower household energy costs.4 But while these improvements save households money over time,5 their upfront costs make them an easy target for policymakers seeking to lower consumers’ energy bills in the short term. In many states, utilities finance these investments through energy efficiency programs, reducing household energy use while making it easier to plan for and meet growing electricity demand without overbuilding new generation and grid infrastructure. When states fund these programs by tacking higher utility charges onto consumers’ bills, policymakers facing pressure to deliver immediate bill relief may target them for cuts—especially if the savings are not immediately apparent.

Therein lies an affordability trap: The public’s demand for immediate relief can entice policymakers to reduce or eliminate investments that keep energy bills lower over time in order to find savings today. Fortunately, states such as Rhode Island and Massachusetts, along with Washington, D.C., have recently rejected or reversed proposals to scale back energy efficiency investments, recognizing that short-term cuts to cost-effective investments can come at the expense of long-term affordability. In medicine, preventive care is cheaper than emergency treatment. Energy efficiency works in much the same way: States can skip the checkup, but they should not be surprised if the treatment ends up costing more down the road.

Why energy efficiency matters

The case for energy efficiency is well documented. States use different methodologies to measure benefits, but across the country, well-designed energy efficiency investments have consistently delivered customer savings that exceed their costs. For decades, many states and utilities have treated efficiency as a resource because the cheapest unit of electricity is often the one that never has to be generated. Recent analysis by the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy (ACEEE) found that energy efficiency could avoid roughly 70 gigawatts of unnecessary electricity demand in the United States by 2040, which would complement the construction of new generation and grid infrastructure needed to serve an otherwise growing electricity sector.6 States ranging from Massachusetts, California, New York, Vermont, and Virginia to Utah, Arkansas, and Tennessee have invested in energy efficiency as part of their long-term energy planning, demonstrating its appeal across the political and geographic spectrum.7

Short-term savings, long-term costs

The design of energy efficiency policy is essential to its durable success. For example, from 2008 to 2024, Maryland’s flagship energy efficiency program, EmPOWER, helped households and businesses reduce energy use,8 with installed measures expected to generate more than $15.8 billion in lifetime savings.9 Since EmPOWER’s inception, however, the Maryland Public Service Commission permitted utilities to spread the cost of the program over five years—and charge interest on costs that had not yet been collected from customers. Over time, those unpaid costs piled up, leaving customers paying for both current programs and past expenditures plus interest. By 2024, the legislature cracked down on this misuse of ratepayer funds, but the damage was already done, with some utility charges for EmPOWER at $15 to $20 per month.10

Faced with rising electricity costs and the structural challenges of EmPOWER’s financing model, Maryland enacted the Utility RELIEF Act,11 legislation that reflects the difficult trade-offs states face as they work to lower energy costs. Signed into law by Gov. Wes Moore (D) in May 2026 amid growing concerns over rising utility bills, the legislation included several positive reforms,12 including the more than $200 million for local clean energy development, storage, and targeted bill relief highlighted in CAP’s “State Climate Action in 2026” report,13 as well as continued investments in energy efficiency for low- and moderate-income households and data center regulation.14

At the same time, the law temporarily scaled back EmPOWER’s energy efficiency requirements and expected spending between 2027 and 2029. ACEEE estimated that an earlier version of the Utility RELIEF Act, which would have lowered EmPOWER’s annual energy savings target from 2.5 percent to 1.5 percent, could increase electricity costs for Maryland customers by $592 million.15 The final law ultimately adopted a smaller reduction, lowering the target to 1.75 percent. Based on 2024 program performance, the Maryland Public Service Commission estimated that EmPOWER’s residential programs deliver approximately $1.84 in benefits for every $1 invested.16 But only the cost of the program appears on customer bills, and nowhere does the bill list utility profits. Maryland’s experience underscores why states should avoid financing energy efficiency programs in ways that enrich utilities and put efficiency programs at risk.

Energy efficiency should not be simply another line item on a utility bill; it should be viewed as preventive care for the energy system.

Other states have faced similar pressures, even for efficiency programs not bogged down by Maryland utilities’ financing model. Like Maryland, Washington, D.C., Rhode Island, and Massachusetts have financed energy efficiency programs through utility bill charges. All three ultimately rejected or reversed proposals to scale back energy efficiency investments, recognizing that any short-term savings could come at the expense of higher long-term costs.

In its fiscal year 2027 budget proposal for Washington, D.C., Mayor Muriel Bowser’s (D) administration proposed redirecting a substantial share of Sustainable Energy Trust Fund (SETF) dollars away from energy efficiency investments.17 According to the D.C. Policy Center, the proposal would have redirected roughly 70 percent of SETF funding away from clean energy and energy efficiency investments and toward covering the district government’s energy costs.18 Funded through the SETF, these programs help residents and businesses reduce energy use through weatherization, efficient appliances, and building upgrades. Since 2011, roughly $360 million has been invested through these efforts, generating an estimated $2.2 billion in gross lifetime energy bill savings for district residents and businesses, or about $6 in gross savings for every $1 invested.19 Recognizing those benefits, in June 2026, the D.C. Council moved to restore portions of the Sustainable Energy Trust Fund.20

Rhode Island almost walked into a similar trap. Last year, the Rhode Island Public Utilities Commission approved Rhode Island Energy’s proposal to reduce the state’s electric energy efficiency budget from roughly $82 million in 2025 to $62.9 million in 2026.21 The Acadia Center estimated that the nearly $20 million reduction could have eliminated more than $46.1 million in benefits for Rhode Islanders, including lower long-term energy bill savings and more than 400 fewer clean energy jobs.22 The cuts in Gov. Dan McKee’s (D) FY 2027 budget proposal were even more severe,23 proposing to cap Rhode Island’s energy efficiency program at $75 million annually—down from the previously approved $95 million—as part of a broader affordability package that also included related energy efficiency reforms.24 This proposal came despite Rhode Island’s efficiency programs having historically delivered about $3 in benefits for every dollar invested.25 In June, the state legislature rejected the governor’s efforts and preserved the state’s energy efficiency funding and the savings it will deliver.

Massachusetts lawmakers also entered the debate. Earlier this year, the Massachusetts House of Representatives approved legislation that would reduce roughly $1 billion in Mass Save spending as part of a broader affordability package,26 though Senate leaders rejected the proposed cuts in June. Mass Save reports that its programs have generated approximately $31 billion in benefits for Massachusetts residents and businesses,27 including more than $3.6 billion in benefits in 2025 alone,28 and estimates that every dollar invested returns $2.76 in customer benefits.29

The same dynamic extends beyond traditional utility energy efficiency programs. In 2023, participating Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI) states30 invested roughly $852 million in proceeds toward energy efficiency, clean energy, bill credits, and other consumer benefit programs.31 RGGI estimates those investments will generate approximately $2.7 billion in lifetime energy bill savings over the lives of the funded projects, including roughly $1.9 billion from energy efficiency measures. Yet the program has faced participating states’ periodic legislative and political efforts to withdraw.32

An easier road

Rather than sacrificing savings from efficiency investments for the sake of immediate savings, states should pair long-term investments with policies that simultaneously protect ratepayers in the short term. Promising avenues include innovative financing for energy efficiency programs, including making artificial intelligence (AI) data centers pay their fair share33 and cover the costs of efficiency and grid upgrades.34

In April, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) signed H.B. 2, which expands access to weatherization and efficient electric heat pumps for low-income households.35 The state also invested $25 million in state funding for weatherization and energy efficiency programs to help lower household energy bills.36 According to ACEEE, combining heat pumps with weatherization improvements could reduce heating costs for participating families by as much as $1,400 per winter.37

Illinois took another effective approach. Rather than scaling back energy efficiency investments funded through utility rates, lawmakers expanded them as part of a broader affordability package. Earlier this year, Gov. JB Pritzker (D) signed the Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act,38 which expands energy efficiency programs, modernizes the grid, and includes other measures aimed at reducing utility bills and long-term system costs. The law substantially increases utility-funded energy efficiency investments, including nearly $192 million annually for income-qualified households.39 Those investments are recovered through regulated utility rates. The governor’s office estimates the law will save Illinois consumers $13.4 billion over the next two decades.40 After reviewing analysis prepared by the Illinois Power Agency, the Clean Grid Alliance concluded that the law is expected to save consumers roughly $13 for every $1 invested.41

New Jersey is also taking a forward-looking approach.42 Following Maryland’s lead, Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) signed legislation requiring large data centers to pay their fair share of grid infrastructure costs, while also encouraging investments in distributed energy resources, including energy efficiency, that help lower system costs.43

Additionally, states have other options to improve affordability without cutting energy efficiency. Similar to the approach long used in California,44 states can adopt a “loading order” that requires utilities to pursue all cost-effective energy efficiency before investing in more expensive generation and grid infrastructure. States can also expand innovative financing models such as Pay As You Save (PAYS®),45 which Missouri has implemented46 and Virginia is now exploring,47 and follow Maryland’s and New Jersey’s lead by ensuring that large new electricity users, including AI data centers, pay their fair share of grid costs. As Rewiring America has argued,48 states should treat buildings as energy infrastructure by investing in energy efficiency, electrification, and other distributed energy resources that can help meet growing electricity demand while lowering customer bills and overall system costs.49 As outlined in CAP’s recent electricity affordability report, policymakers should also accelerate low-cost clean energy deployment, modernize and expand the electricity grid, and provide targeted support to help stabilize residential electricity bills.50

See also

A Plan for American Electricity Affordability

ReportMay 18, 2026

A Plan for American Electricity Affordability

Trevor Higgins, Shannon Baker-Branstetter, Michael Negron, 2 More Lucero Marquez, Kendra Hughes

Conclusion

Energy efficiency should not be simply another line item on a utility bill; it should be viewed as preventive care for the energy system. Policymakers should be cautious about sacrificing long-term affordability for short-term bill relief, and efficiency programs must be designed with sustained savings in mind. States do not have to choose between near-term affordability and long-term savings. The most durable affordability strategy pairs immediate bill relief with continued investment in the resources that lower energy costs over time.

Meanwhile, the price of Brent crude, the global oil benchmark set out of Europe, briefly surpassed $109 per barrel before coming back down to $106 by the time the market closed Monday. West Texas Intermediate, out of the U.S., hit about $102, while Murban crude from the United Arab Emirates shot up 10% to $131 per barrel. The latest surge came after Saudi Arabia halted shipments via its East-West Pipeline, the main conduit through which the kingdom has exported oil since the Strait of Hormuz’s closure stopped tankers from leaving the Persian Gulf.

2. Fuel surcharges for shipping grain by rail more than doubled in the past year

The average fuel surcharge for grain shipments on U.S. railways more than doubled over the past year, in the latest sign of how soaring energy prices will spur inflation of food costs. The surcharge skyrocketed 153% to 48 cents per rail car-mile by the second week of September, according to a Reuters analysis of U.S. Department of Agriculture data. The surcharges accounted for 11% of the total rail transportation costs for shipping corn and soybeans, compared to 5% a year ago. Railroads collected about $3 billion in fuel surcharges in the second quarter of this year, covering 90% of diesel costs. The situation highlights why now is “the worst time for diesel to get expensive,” my colleague Matthew Zeitlin wrote last month, since harvest season is around the corner and most farming equipment runs on the fuel.

3. Democrats have a new climate policy agenda

House Democrats are out with their first new climate agenda since the Green New Deal’s glory days of 2020. This time, however, it’s more of what the top Democrat behind the proposal called “a workable plan for long term economic and job growth” than an emissions-cutting blitz. My colleague Emily Pontecorvo has a detailed breakdown of what’s in it, but here are the five big takeaways:

Wind and solar tax credits probably aren’t coming back.

Congress is poised to get wonkier on energy markets and transmission.

Future policies will be difficult to “Trump-proof.”

Data centers are in the middle of everything.

Instead of calling it “climate change,” they’re talking around issues of “risk” and “adaptation.”

“We’re not introducing a bill after this,” Representative Kathy Castor, the Florida Democrat who oversaw the project to draft the agenda, told Emily. “We’re providing it to policymakers in Washington for them to build the bipartisan support you need to get something across the finish line. The Trump administration is going to be there for two more years. What can we get done now that would have bipartisan support?”

Sign up to receive Heatmap AM in your inbox every morning:

4. The U.S. data center boom needs $110 billion for 45 gigawatts of new power generation

The U.S. needs $110 billion to build 45 gigawatts of new power generation through 2030 to meet the surging demand from data centers, according to a Moody’s Ratings analysis. More than 30 gigawatts of that supply is slated to come from natural gas-fired plants, with solar and storage making up much of the rest and nuclear restarts accounting for less than 5%, Bloomberg reported. That all sounds like a lot. But consider that the U.S. started this year on track to add 86 gigawatts of new generation, much of which it from solar and storage, according to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration. In other words, we deployed nearly twice as much new generation in the past year as we would need for data centers through the end of this decade.

The nation’s largest operator of nuclear and geothermal power plants, Constellation Energy, certainly sees gas as the likelier near-term source of power generation in New England. On Monday, Utility Dive reported that the utility giant plans to buy the 609-megawatt Rhode Island State Energy Center from Shell Energy for $715 million. It’s easy to see why gas looks like a safe bet. Three Massachusetts utilities are now suing Hydro-Quebec, the state-owned utility in Canada’s French-speaking province, over a shortfall in deliveries during particularly hot days this summer — while Hydro-Quebec is, in turn, suing for payments it says the American power companies owe, according to Canary Media. That electricity drama is unfolding as New Englanders prepare to “pay through the nose to stay warm this winter” as the price of heating fuel soars, Matthew wrote last week.

5. U.S. takes a 10% stake in company behind Alaskan mining project

Where the road will go. Bonnie Jo Mount/The Washington Post via Getty Images

Almost exactly a year ago, Trump issued an executive order approving the long-stalled federal project to build a road through the Alaskan wilderness to support production of minerals from the remote Ambler Mining District. Now the U.S. government is taking a 10% stake in Trilogy Metals, the 50% co-owner of a joint venture with the Australian miner South32 focused on extracting copper, zinc, and other metals from the site. As part of the deal, the company said in a press release, the Department of Defense “committed to work in good faith to help facilitate financing required for construction of the proposed 211-mile, industrial-use-only Ambler Road.”

The Pentagon also inked a $450 million deal with The Elmet Group, an integrated miner and processor, with $150 million earmarked for Toronto-based Blue Moon Metals’ tungsten mine in Nevada, Mining.com reported.

THE KICKER

There’s still an open debate about how much of the nuclear supply chain Saudi Arabia would be allowed to control under the kingdom’s coveted deal with the Trump administration. Whether the Saudis should enrich — or, even more worrying from a nonproliferation standpoint, recycle — nuclear fuel will generate heated discussion in the years to come. But it looks increasingly likely that the oil-rich nation will mine at least some of its own uranium. “Exploration and geological studies at the Jabal Sayid project in Madinah have revealed estimated resources of around 110 million tonnes of ore with high concentrations of rare earth minerals, especially the heavy elements, alongside promising concentrations of uranium,” Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, the kingdom’s energy minister, told Arab News.

Kathy Castor, a representative from Florida who led the project, told me that instead of a platform, I should think of the project as “a workable plan for long term economic and job growth.”

“We’re not introducing a bill after this,” she said. “We’re providing it to policymakers in Washington for them to build the bipartisan support you need to get something across the finish line. The Trump administration is going to be there for two more years. What can we get done now that would have bipartisan support?”

Nevertheless, this is still the most sweeping environment and energy policy document Democrats have published since 2020, when the House Select Committee on the Climate Crisis — which Castor also chaired — published a nearly 550-page plan to “solve the climate crisis.” Much of that work became a part of the 2021 bipartisan infrastructure law and the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act. Of course, significant chunks of those laws, including tax credits for wind and solar projects, were later dismantled by the Trump administration in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

The Climate Crisis Committee disbanded in 2023, but the Thriving Economy Project is, in some ways, a continuation of its work. The document itself is the product of an independent nonprofit, which Democrats from the Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition enlisted to probe experts, local leaders, companies, and advocates around the country for ideas about what Congress should do to create jobs, lower energy costs, foster innovation, and shore up communities. The nonprofit, known as the Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition Institute, convened working groups, roundtables, and listening sessions. It also issued a public Request for Information that generated more than 1,300 policy recommendations from around 150 responders, including businesses and trade associations, local governments, nonprofits, and universities, the report said, and assembled a “20-person steering committee of ideologically diverse experts” to challenge its own assumptions.

The resulting report asserts that it is “not a consensus document, nor was it ever intended to be. It is a menu of ideas that have been challenged, refined, and improved by people approaching the same problems from very different perspectives.”

Perhaps that’s why the document reads a little bit like throwing spaghetti at the wall. There’s plenty in it that could conceivably be bipartisan, but there’s also a lot that stands no chance of passing under Trump, even if Democrats take the House and Senate in November’s midterm elections. In that light, it’s both a menu for the next two years and a window into how Democrats are generally thinking about climate policy in the post-IRA era. Here are five of my takeaways after going through it.

1. Some of the IRA is worth reviving … but not the wind and solar tax credits.

The authors do not spill any digital ink lamenting Trump’s dismantling of the IRA. They do, however, propose restoring a bunch of what’s been lost and building on the lessons learned from the brief time the policies were in effect.

For example, the report suggests reinstating federal tax credits for home energy efficiency improvements and residential clean energy systems such as rooftop solar, but recommends offering the credits as a point-of-sale rebate rather than a return claimed on the buyer’s taxes. That would be similar to the way electric vehicle buyers could transfer their tax credit to the dealer to get the discount on their purchase immediately. The goal, according to the report, is to “minimize the upfront costs and administrative frictions for consumer-facing incentives.”

Speaking of the electric vehicle tax credit, bringing it back is also on the menu, justified as a demand pull to support domestic supply chains and as a complement to the manufacturing tax credits, which largely survived the IRA purge (more on that below). Interestingly, a separate section of the report proposes a perhaps more politically palatable consumer rebate for new vehicles based on fuel efficiency rather than a strict EV-only subsidy, framing the idea as an option to address “unaffordable gasoline.”

There is a meaty section on extending and expanding the manufacturing tax credits, which, as you may remember, will no longer apply to wind turbine components after 2027, thanks to Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The report suggests cancelling that early termination. It also proposes extending the subsidy to a long list of additional advanced energy technologies, including power transformers, industrial heat pumps, and long duration energy storage components. Additionally, there are several sections on improving federal support for early-stage technologies, helping them get through the “valley of death” to commercial deployment — a major theme in both the bipartisan infrastructure law and IRA.

Notably absent is any discussion of reinstating the tax credits for wind and solar generation. When I asked Castor about that, she said “a lot of that ground had been plowed already,” referring to the contentious battle over the credits during the OBBBA negotiations. “In this Congress, that’s not going to happen. This effort is driven by solving problems ASAP where we think there can be bipartisan support going forward.”

2. Congress could get more wonky about energy markets and transmission

The report intentionally stays away from one of the most significant ways Congress could speed up solutions to address rising energy demand: permitting reform. A disclaimer at the top notes that since Congress was actively debating legislation on that issue while the report was being written, the authors chose not to tackle it directly.

It does, however, spend plenty of time working around the edges on ways to clear up clogged interconnection queues and fix bottlenecks to getting more transmission online. For one, it suggests more funding for the Department of Energy’s Transmission Facilitation Program, which allows the agency to temporarily serve as an anchor customer for new transmission lines. Creating a 30% investment tax credit for transmission lines is another idea in the report.

A lot of the recommendations revolve around improving grid planning and integrating grid-enhancing technologies, advanced conductors, and energy storage into the process. The report suggests establishing a national transmission conductor standard, for example, setting a minimum efficiency level for the wires strung along transmission lines to reduce waste.

Beyond transmission, there are a slew of ideas for reforming energy markets to better support demand response and virtual power plants. Congress could create federal guidance for how grid operators and state regulators assess the value of energy storage to the grid, and direct the DOE to provide more technical assistance to operators on incorporating flexible resources that can shift load, relieve congestion, and integrate more renewables into the grid.

3. Trump-proof future policies will be difficult

One of the biggest challenges Democrats will have to contend with is writing policy that can endure past a change in party control. Trump has found myriad ways to block projects approved by the previous administration and withhold congressionally mandated funding. The courts are still deciding whether his administration’s methods are actually legal. Nonetheless, the report reflects an interest in creating more certainty for federal grantees and restoring trust in the federal government as a funding partner.

For one, it explicitly recommends that Congress restore awards that were legally obligated under IRA programs such as the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, the Environmental and Climate Justice Block Grants, the Community Change Grants, and the Neighborhood Access and Equity Grants that the Trump administration has attempted to terminate — though it stops short of specifying how.

In the future, though, it recommends that federal funding be funneled through “trusted third-party fiscal intermediaries to allow for nimbler program management and structural insulation from political shifts.” Congress should also more narrowly define the circumstances under which an award can be terminated, it says, offering the suggested language: “funds awarded under [identified programs] may not be rescinded, reprogrammed, or deferred except by law.”

In cases where an administration does rescind or terminate funding, it recommends that Congress put in law that any legal challenge to the termination belongs in the U.S. District Courts. The Department of Justice is attempting to argue that the disputes over Trump’s grant terminations constitute breach of contract claims, and therefore belong in the court of federal claims. If the cases end up there, however, the grantees will only be able to sue for damages — they won’t be eligible to get their grants reinstated. A provision explicitly placing these cases in the district court would ensure awardees have a path to actually contributing to congressionally-mandated goals.

While these provisions are promising, however, it’s hard to imagine that Trump would sign off on them.

4. Data center electricity demand is a central organizing problem for policymakers.

One of the most obvious differences between the world we live in now and the world lawmakers occupied in 2020 is that the race for artificial intelligence is in full swing, driving a surge in electricity demand the country has not seen in decades. Data centers have become the locus of a number of intersecting issues — permitting obstacles for energy infrastructure, rising electricity costs, local opposition to anything getting built at all, fear of AI, and concerns about cybersecurity.

The Thriving Economy Project treats data centers as a central organizing problem across several of its chapters. It offers policies to address environmental concerns such as requiring data centers to use closed-loop cooling systems to reduce water use. It proposes unifying the piecemeal approach states are taking to meet data center electricity demand under a federal standard that would require large loads to pay the full cost of connecting to the grid.

There’s a whole section on the challenges of meeting data centers’ power needs that contains more than two dozen policy ideas. A few that stand out include mandatory energy and water use disclosure requirements, a federal Energy Star-equivalent for AI tools, and the creation of a “U.S. Electron Accelerator.” That last idea is one of the most interesting proposals I came across. Data centers would pay into a fund for every kilowatt-hour of their demand not met with clean electrons generated at the same time and in the same location. The funds would then be available to help data centers cover the premium for procuring round-the-clock clean electricity from nuclear and geothermal plants.

Similarly, the report suggests requiring data centers to pay into a fund to support the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program and the Weatherization Assistance Program, two perennially underfunded federal programs that help Americans who are struggling to pay their energy bills.

It also raises the concern that data centers powered by behind-the-meter natural gas plants will drive up the price of natural gas for other customers, thereby increasing home heating and residential electricity bills. The report suggests several ideas to reduce natural gas price volatility, including taxing oil and gas companies to create a “strategic energy affordability reserve.” If the president declares an “energy affordability emergency,” it says, the funds can be released to states to help residents pay their bills. Additionally, Congress could create an “energy price safety valve” to temporarily ban exports of key fuels when prices spike.

5. Risk and adaption are the new watchwords

A lot of the Thriving Economy Project reads like a manual for playing defense in an increasingly dangerous world. It is consumed with addressing risk — the risk of cybersecurity attacks on our electric grid, water systems, and airports, and of global supply shocks that throttle domestic energy prices and supply chains. While discussion of “climate change” as a problem to tackle is notably absent from the report, a rhetorical shift I wrote more about here, adapting to the realities of a warming planet is one of its main preoccupations.

It suggests establishing a federal climate relocation program, for example, and setting federal climate-adapted transportation standards, such as elevation in flood zones and transit facility shading. There’s a recommendation to build a “national climate-health early warning system” to alert people about extreme heat, wildfire smoke, vector-borne diseases, and harmful algal blooms. Along those lines, it suggests that severe wildfire smoke events qualify for federal disaster assistance. At the same time, federal disaster assistance is too fragmented across various agencies, it says, and the government could establish a single, mobile-friendly app “as the front door to all federal individual disaster aid.”

It recommends creating an independent National Disaster Safety Board, an independent watchdog to investigate deaths and damages after a disaster and issue recommendations for how governments at all levels can prevent these losses the next time. Congress could also establish a national climate risk disclosure standard for the real estate industry, giving homebuyers access to more consistent, transparent data about property risks.

These are just a few of many dozens of proposals to improve federal leadership on this especially local, disjointed issue.

BorgWarner is set to showcase its latest portfolio of electrification, propulsion and thermal management technologies for commercial vehicles at IAA Transportation 2026, as the automotive supplier targets greater efficiency, performance and sustainability across battery-electric and combustion-powered applications.

The company is exhibiting its technologies at Booth C65 in Hall 12 at the trade show in Hanover, Germany, which is being held from September 14 to 20.

Advt

Next-generation LFP battery pack

A key highlight of BorgWarner’s display is its LFP next-generation Compact Pack, which the company is showcasing for the first time at a European trade show.

The battery pack features a redesigned architecture aimed at optimising weight, footprint and cost. BorgWarner said the new design also delivers improved performance, higher energy efficiency and an extended operational lifetime.

“Commercial vehicle manufacturers must balance increasingly complex requirements, from emissions reduction and energy efficiency to performance, durability and cost,” said Dr. Paul Farrell, Executive Vice President and Chief Strategy Officer, BorgWarner Inc.

Supporting multiple propulsion pathways

Beyond battery technology, BorgWarner is displaying solutions spanning multiple propulsion platforms, reflecting its strategy of supporting propulsion diversity in commercial vehicles.

The portfolio on display includes advanced battery systems, integrated eDrive solutions, power electronics and thermal management technologies for a range of commercial vehicle applications.

The company said its approach is focused on helping manufacturers improve vehicle efficiency and performance while reducing emissions, rather than relying on a single propulsion technology.

title: Save energy and money with efficient home upgrades – City of Mississauga
description:

text:
Fall is almost here. Now is a good time to prepare your home for cooler weather and explore ways to lower your energy bills. Small changes can help you stay comfortable and save energy without turning up the heat. They will also help to make Mississauga a more climate-friendly city.

In 2024, residential buildings across Mississauga produced roughly 15 per cent of the city’s greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Homeowners can help reduce emissions by making their homes more energy efficient.

Understand your home’s energy use

If you need help getting started, sign up for a home energy coaching session. For example, the Centre for Community Energy Transformation (CCET), a non-profit organization serving Mississauga, Brampton and Caledon, provides a coaching session for free. An energy coach can help you understand your options and create a plan. Toronto and Region Conservation Authority (TRCA) also offers a free one-on-one consultation through its Climate Ready Homes Program, where residents will receive resources to help them save energy and water, reduce waste, create sustainable gardens and improve the comfort of their homes.

In addition to these free coaching services, homeowners can also get a more detailed home energy assessment to see where their home is losing energy. This is a paid service offered by independent energy auditors. After the assessment is complete, the auditor will provide the homeowner with a personalized report that identifies upgrades that could help save money and energy.

Upgrade your home

Home upgrades, also called retrofits, can help your home use less energy, lower utility bills and reduce GHG emissions.

One example is a heat pump. A heat pump warms your home in winter and cools it in summer using less energy than other traditional systems.

Other energy-saving upgrades include:

Sealing cracks and gaps around windows and doors to stop warm or cool air from escaping.

Installing a smart thermostat that can adjust temperature automatically.

Adding attic insulation to keep heat inside during winter and outside during summer.

Installing solar panels and battery storage to produce clean energy at home.

Replacing old appliances with ENERGY STAR® models that use less energy.

Connect with the City’s Climate Change team

Have questions about climate action, energy efficiency or home retrofit programs?

Meet the City’s Climate Change team at a free Energy Savings Workshop hosted by TRCA, in collaboration with the City of Mississauga, and delivered by Kambo Energy’s Empower Me on Tuesday, September 22, from 6:30 to 8 p.m. at the Malton Community Centre.

Workshop participants will learn:

How to reduce energy use at home.

Which home upgrades can save money on your utility bills.

What financial support programs are available.

Sessions will be offered in English and Punjabi. The event is free, family-friendly and open to everyone. Snacks and door prizes will be available. Registration is recommended, but walk-ins are welcome.

Free services and rebate programs

These programs can help you with your energy-saving upgrades:

Home Renovation Savings Program: Rebates for eligible energy-efficiency upgrades.

Energy Affordability Program: Free home energy upgrades for eligible low-income households.

Peak Perks Program: Participants agree that their thermostats can be automatically adjusted when energy use is at its highest. Participants receive a $75 gift card for enrolling and a $20 gift card for each year they stay enrolled in the program.

Home Solar Accelerator Service: Free advice for homeowners interested in installing solar in their homes.

Home Energy Coach Service: Free guidance from CCET on planning home energy upgrades.

Peel Climate Ready Homes: Free one-on-one consultations and resources to help residents save energy and water, reduce waste, create sustainable gardens and improve the comfort of their homes. Free practical incentives are available to program participants to support their home upgrades.

Climate Change Action Plan update

The City is updating its Climate Change Action Plan with stronger goals to reduce GHG emissions. The City is investing in actions such as zero-emission vehicles and electric vehicle charging stations and energy-efficient buildings.

Learn more about the City’s Climate Change Action Plan at: https://www.mississauga.ca/publication/climate-change-action-plan/.

description:
US EV charging market size 2026 The North American EV market size varies across different analyses, but all projections indicate substantial growth between now and 2035.
This includes both the North America EV charging market and the general North America EV market.
The North America EV charging market is expected to reach US$52.21 billion by 2034 with a CAGR of 31.8%.
PwC analysts suggest the EV charging market in North America could grow from 4 million charging points today to 35 million charging points by 2030.
Tesla Tesla leads the ultra-fast charging market in North America, with 38,000 supercharger ports located across 3,000 supercharger stations across North America.
text:
The North American EV charging market is currently experiencing significant growth. Whilst it's not the largest EV market globally, the region is following a worldwide trend of increased market valuations and infrastructure development.

According to Fortune Business Insights, the global EV market was valued at US$927.69 billion in 2025, with predictions suggesting this year (2026) will increase that value to US$1,023.81 billion. The industry is anticipated to reach US$2,190.37 billion by 2034, representing a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 9.97%.

Within the broader EV industry, Precedence Research predicts the global EV charging infrastructure market will reach US$492.59 billion by 2035, with a CAGR of 26.32% from 2026 to 2035. The market was valued at US$47.61 billion in 2025, with expectations that this year will reach US$59.94 billion.

The growth of the global charging industry has been driven by fast chargers, which contributed to an 89.6% market share in 2025. The commercial sector also generated a 90.4% market share in 2025 of global charging infrastructure, with the Combined Charging System (CCS) market capturing 40.72% of the global market in 2025. The Asia-Pacific region dominates the market with over 50% of the global share, but the North American market is growing at a significant rate.

US EV charging market size 2026

The North American EV market size varies across different analyses, but all projections indicate substantial growth between now and 2035. This includes both the North America EV charging market and the general North America EV market. Many analysts are predicting a 20%+ CAGR through the early 2030s, demonstrating considerable potential in the region. Whilst much of this growth is concentrated in the US, both the Canadian and Mexican markets are also showing promising signs, with Mexico demonstrating the highest potential growth rate based on current industry positioning.

Fortune Business Insights estimates the global EV charging infrastructure market in 2025 was US$45.78 billion, expected to grow to US$55.97 billion by the end of 2026, and reach US$279.34 billion by 2034 with a CAGR of 22.3%.

In 2025, the US market was estimated at US$5.35 billion, accounting for only 9.6% of the global market. By comparison, the Asia Pacific region captured 65.51% of the global market during the same period. Over the next eight years, Fortune Business Insights predicts the commercial vehicles sector will expand most significantly with a CAGR of 24.7%, whilst the residential sector follows closely with an anticipated CAGR of 19.6%.

Grand View Horizon predicts the EV charging market in North America will reach US$41,792.9 million by 2033, with a CAGR of 25.6% between 2026–2033—with Mexico demonstrating the highest CAGR of all North American nations. Grand View Horizon also stated that the North American EV charging market in 2025 was valued at US$6,710.1 million and is expected to reach US$8,454.4 million by the end of 2026. The analysts noted the fastest growing charger market in 2025 was the fast charger segment, with a revenue share of 81.56%.

According to Market Data Forecast, the North America EV charging market size was valued at US$4.35 billion with an estimated US$5.73 billion market size by the end of this year. The North America EV charging market is expected to reach US$52.21 billion by 2034 with a CAGR of 31.8%. The US held the highest market share within North America at 74.2%. Within this analysis, Market Data Forecast stated that fast chargers held the largest market share with 65.6%, but the fastest growing segment is residential and workplace Level 2 chargers with a CAGR of 30.8%.

This mirrors the fact that the largest installation sector in 2025 was the commercial sector with a market share of 55.2%, but the residential sector has the highest growth projection with a CAGR of 35.3% due to increased home charging needs driven by greater EV ownership—the US Department of Energy estimates that 80% of EV charging currently occurs at home, hence the anticipated growth of the residential market.

PwC analysts suggest the EV charging market in North America could grow from 4 million charging points today to 35 million charging points by 2030. It's estimated there will be 27 million EVs on US roads by 2030 and 92 million EVs by 2040. PwC has also estimated that the electric vehicle supply equipment (EVSE) market could grow from US$7 billion to US$100 billion by 2040, with a CAGR of 15%.

Chargepoint operators (CPOs) are expected to capture 65% of the market by 2040, whereas the market share held by hardware providers is expected to drop from the current 46% to 35% in 2030 and 20% by 2040. However, bidirectional charging, spearheaded by increased interest in vehicle-to-grid (V2G) operation, could drive US$20 billion in revenue for hardware providers.

Next MSC stated the North America EV charging market size is expected to reach US$10.4 billion by 2030, with a CAGR of 20.93%. The analysis also showed that the US accounts for 82.7% of the EV charging market in North America.

Yahoo Finance and Research and Markets estimate the North America EV market size will grow from US$95.05 billion in 2025 to an anticipated value of US$102.66 billion in 2026 and US$150.92 billion by 2031. This represents a CAGR of 8.01% between 2026-2031, driven by lower battery costs, improved EV range, government incentives, and increased interest in domestic battery production (for example, in the battery belt region of the US). Passenger cars capture 77.13% of the North American EV market, but light commercial vehicles (LCVs) are expected to be the fastest growing EV category in the coming years with a CAGR of 9.02%.

US federal policy changes in 2025-2026

As of 2026, the US$7,500 federal EV tax credits for new EV purchases and the US$4,000 credit for used EVs has ended for vehicles acquired after 30th September 2025. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act was signed on 4th July 2025 and signalled the end of the EV tax credits in 2026. This includes 30D new EV credits, 25E used EV credits, and 45W credits for commercial EVs.

The 30C home and commercial EV charger installation tax credits that covered up to US$1,000 per charging port for equipment and installation costs for qualifying EV purchases also ended on 30th June 2026. Despite the reduction in EV tax credits in 2026, numerous state-level incentives remain available for EV owners.

The other major programme undergoing changes is the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) programme. In 2025, NEVI funding was frozen by the Trump Administration, pausing a US$5 billion EV charging initiative. However, it has since been unblocked by the Federal courts, meaning funding is now available again through the NEVI programme. The NEVI programme maintains its original goals and core mission to deploy 500,000 chargers by 2030.

The NEVI programme is distributing US$885 million in 2026, and 42 states have currently signed up for the programme. The NEVI programme provides funding to states (that sign up to participate) for deploying EV charging infrastructure, with up to 80% of project costs available to those looking to install new EV chargers. As of April 2026, there were approximately 550 NEVI-funded fast charging points in operation across 19 states.

2026 has also seen other key changes to the NEVI programme alongside the release of funds. States are no longer bound by the '50-mile spacing rule' for new chargers to be eligible for the programme. This rule stated that sites needed to be within maximum 50-mile intervals. Now, if states can justify that a specific transport corridor is 'fully built out', available NEVI funds can be redirected to roads, secondary highways, and medium- and heavy-duty charging hubs that would have traditionally fallen outside this scope. The new rules provide states with greater flexibility regarding where they can install much-needed charging stations.

To be eligible for the 80% cost coverage, installation projects need to meet a strict set of criteria at both the federal and state level. This includes:

Auto loan interest deduction

Outside of changes to EV tax credits and the NEVI programme, the other new federal initiative is the Auto Loan Interest Deduction. This is part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act where all new EV buyers can receive a federal tax deduction of up to US$10,000 per year on qualifying new vehicle loans between 2025–2028.

To be eligible for the tax deduction, the EV needs to be new and have its final assembly in the US, the EV needs to be for personal use (commercial and fleet EVs don't qualify), and the vehicle loan must be both a secured loan and be signed after 31st December 2024. There are no limits to the number of vehicles that can qualify.

Biggest state-level EV incentives in 2026

With federal incentives diminishing in 2026, state-level policy and EV incentives provided by individual states have become significantly more important for new EV owners—as this is where most savings are being found. However, not all states offer incentives, and the level of support varies considerably across states, with some providing modest incentives, whilst others—such as California, Colorado, New York, and Massachusetts—provide larger independent programmes. Each state EV incentive in 2026 has different availability and funding requirements, so prospective EV buyers need to continually check the incentives available as they change over time.

As of July 2026, there have been several changes this year to different state EV incentives. This includes Oklahoma and Vermont ending their EV tax credit programmes, Rhode Island increasing their standard EV rebate from US$1,500 to US$3,000, and Wyoming reducing EV fees.

Colorado offers state EV tax credits called the 'Colorado electric car tax credit'. This remains active in 2026, but the credit is lower than in previous years. Someone purchasing a new EV with an MSRP between US$35,000–US$80,000 can receive a US$750 credit. EVs with a retail price under US$35,000 can receive a credit up to US$3,250.

Additionally, income-qualified drivers using Vehicle Exchange Colorado can also receive US$9,000 towards a new EV or US$6,000 towards a used EV. This rebate can be combined with the tax credits provided both requirements are met.

However, this year's amount is lower than last year, where the base credit amount was US$3,500, and the additional credit was still US$2,500. This meant that last year's credits were worth up to US$6,000 instead of US$3,250. Next year onwards could see higher amounts again, with the base credit rising to US$2,000 in 2027 and dropping to US$1,000 in 2028, with the additional credit remaining the same. This means there will be up to US$4,500 available in 2027 and US$3,500 in 2028.

In Massachusetts, the Massachusetts Offers Rebates for Electric Vehicles programme (MOR-EV) provides assistance for the purchase of new and used EVs. The total MSRP of the vehicle cannot exceed US$55,000 if new, or US$40,000 if used, and the rebate offers between US$3,500–US$6,000. The base rebate is US$3,500, but eligible applicants (income-qualifying assistance programme) can obtain an extra US$1,500 through the MOR-EV+ programme, and an extra US$1,000 for trading in an old ICE vehicle. As of August 2026, rule changes have been proposed that will be put to the public in September, but will look to change the vehicle price caps, truck rebates, and MOR-EV+ eligibility.

For EV drivers who drive for a ride-sharing company, such as Uber, Lyft, or a taxi company, there are other, more beneficial, rebates available. The Ride Clean Mass programme currently offers financial incentives of up to US$14,000 for a new rideshare EV, US$6,500 for a used rideshare EV, US$17,500 for a new taxi EV, and US$12,500 for a used taxi EV. These incentives can be paired with other state incentives provided all requirements are met.

California has numerous different state EV incentives in 2026. It is the state with the most extensive incentive programmes, some of which are very situation-specific. However, provided the different requirements are met, all of California's EV incentives can be combined for higher savings. As of August 2026, the Replace Your Ride California incentive has been paused but many others remain available.

One of the biggest developments in 2026 is the MyFirstEV programme. This was launched on 7 August 2026 and allows any Californians obtaining their first EV to be eligible for US$3,500 off a qualifying new EV or US$1,750 off a qualifying used EV. As of the end of August, Chevrolet, Ford, Hyundai, Kia, Lucid, and Rivian are all advertising manufacturer-specific MyFirstEV offers. Tesla did participate for a short time, but the funding for it ran out within a few days. It's expected that Honda and Subaru will join the programme in September, followed by Mitsubishi in November, and Toyota, Lexus, Nissan, and Volvo at a later date.

California also has the Clean Cars 4 All Programme, which provides income-qualified residents with up to US$12,000 for a vehicle, plus up to US$2,000 for charging infrastructure. Both new and used EVs are eligible, as are PHEVs and zero-emission motorcycles. Those who buy battery EVs, or PHEVs, can qualify for both the vehicle and charger assistance. Eligibility for the programme is income-based against the median income of the area, owning an old vehicle that doesn't meet emission standards, and residency within a participating district.

There are also rebates available for people who are customers of specific utility companies. Those residing in Los Angeles can also obtain a rebate for home EV chargers providing they are served by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power (LADWP). LADWP offers up to US$1,000 for most customers, with up to US$1,500 for income-eligible households towards the purchase and installation of a level 2 home charger with either an SAE J1772 or J3400 connector. An extra US$250 rebate is available for the installation of an EV time-of-use (TOU) metre. A TOU EV rate energy discount is also available for those who charge during off-peak hours.

Another specific rebate is the Pacific Gas & Electric Company (PG&E) EV rebate which provides a US$1,000 standard rebate, or US$4,000 income-qualified rebate, towards buying a used EV or PHEV for its customers. The only caveat is that the customer needs to be an electric customer, not a gas-only customer. PG&E also offers a separate residential EV charging programme that will reimburse up to 50% of one approved equipment or will provide income-qualified assistance up to US$2,000 for an eligible charger project. This increases to US$5,000 when electrical-panel work is required.

Southern California Edison (SCE) runs a similar scheme to PG&E for its customers, who can also qualify for a US$1,000 standard rebate, or US$4,000 income-qualified rebate, when buying a used EV or PHEV. SCE also offers up to US$4,200 for home panel, circuit, and outlet work, but not for buying the charger itself.

Other state EV incentives in 2026

Whilst the above states offer the major incentives, a number of rebates, credits, and exemptions are available in many other states around the US. This includes:

Connecticut: US$500-US$5,000 rebates are available for EVs and PHEVs with an MSRP of US$50,000. US$1,000 is given to EVs and US$500 to PHEVs, but an additional US$1,500-US$4,000 is available for low-income applicants depending on the type of EV—US$1,500 for new PHEVs, US$2,500 for used PHEVs, US$3,000 for new EVs, and US$4,000 for used EVs.

Delaware: US$1,000-US$2,500 rebate available for new or used EVs, including up to US$2,500 for EVs below US$40,000, and US$1,500 for EVs below US$50,000.

Illinois: US$2,000-US$4,000 rebate for new and used EV purchases. EV purchases below US$80,000 can qualify for a US$2,000 rebate, whilst low-income applications can qualify for an additional US$2,000.

Maine: US$3,000-US$8,000 rebate for new or used EVs. EVs below US$55,000 can qualify for a US$6,000 rebate, whilst a used EV below US$40,000 may be eligible for a US$3,000 rebate. Low-income applicants can qualify for additional help taking the rebates to US$8,000 and US$4,000, respectively. However, these figures include a US$1,000 rebate that will expire 30th September 2026.

Maryland: EVs and PHEVs can qualify for a US$3,000 credit against the 6.5% vehicle tax in Maryland. However, whilst this incentive programme still exists, there are currently no more funds available so it is not accepting new applications currently.

New Jersey: US$1,500-US$4,000 rebate for EV purchases. EV purchases below US$55,000 can qualify for a US$1,500 rebate, and applicants with a modified adjusted gross income of US$75,000 or less, or those in some public assistance programmes can qualify for up to a US$4,000 rebate.

New Mexico: US$2,000-US$3,000 credit available for the purchase of EVs and PHEVs below US$55,000. New EVs can qualify for US$3,000, new PHEVs and used EVs can qualify for a US$2,500 credit and used EVs US$2,000 credit.

New York: US$500-US$2,000 rebate available for EVs and PHEVs. EVs and PHEVs with 200+ range and MSRP of less than US$42,000 can qualify for US$2,000, vehicles with range between 40-200 miles can qualify for US$1,000, and vehicles with less than 40 miles range or MSRPs above US$42,000 can qualify for a US$500 rebate.

Oregon: US$1,500-US$7,500 rebate for EVs and PHEVs. EVs and PHEVs below US$50,000 and battery capacity below 10 kWh can qualify for a US$1,500 rebate, whilst vehicles above 10 kWh capacity can qualify for US$2,500. Low-income applicants can receive up to US$5,000 for a used vehicle and US$7,500 for a new vehicle. However, whilst this incentive programme still exists, there are currently no more funds available, so it is not accepting new applications currently.

Pennsylvania: US$1,500-US$4,000 rebate for EVs and PHEVs. EVs above US$45,000 can qualify for a US$3,000 rebate, whilst PHEVs can qualify for a US$1,500 rebate. Low-income applicants can qualify for an extra US$1,000.

Rhode Island: US$1,750-US$4,500 rebate for EVs and PHEVs. New EVs with an MSRP of up to US$75,000 can qualify for a US$3,000 rebate, used EVs with a price up to US$55,000 can qualify for US$2,500. New PHEVs can qualify for US$2,000 whilst used PHEVs can qualify for a US$1,750 rebate. Low-income applicants can receive an additional US$1,500.

Texas: New EVs and PHEVs can qualify for a US$2,500 rebate. However, whilst this incentive programme still exists, there are currently no more funds available, so it is not accepting new applications currently.

Utah: US$4,000-US$10,000 grant. Utah's Electric Vehicle Replacement Assistance Programme provides grants to low-income applicants who want to replace their ICE vehicle that is either 8+ years old or has failed an emissions test in the last 30 days with a new or used EV. To be eligible, the EV needs to cost up to US$48,125. US$4,000 is available for applicants with an income 401% to 500% of the federal poverty level. US$7,000 is available for applicants with an income 301% to 400% of the federal poverty level. US$10,000 is available for applicants with an income 300% or less of the federal poverty level.

Virginia: New or used EVs up to US$25,000 can qualify for a US$2,500 rebate. Low-income families can receive an extra US$2,000. However, whilst this incentive programme still exists, there are currently no more funds available, so it is not accepting new applications currently.

Until recently, Canada had a federal EV sales mandate that required 20% of new passenger vehicle sales to be zero-emission by 2026 and 100% by 2035, but it has since been paused. Canada's EV sales mandate pause has not been due to the inability to meet targets but is instead related to local geopolitics pushing up the cost of EVs for the average consumer.

The EV Availability Standard (EVAS) policy was introduced when Justin Trudeau was Prime Minister but has now been paused whilst Prime Minister Mark Carney finds ways to make EVs more affordable. The affordability of EVs for the average Canadian has decreased recently due to the US increasing tariffs on both steel and aluminium and on auto parts and vehicles. These tariffs are pushing vehicle prices up, so the Canada EV mandate has been paused for 2026 to see how things will evolve.

To try and still promote EV sales, the current Canadian administration is encouraging automakers to produce more zero-emission vehicles for EV models between 2027–2032. The Canadian government has also introduced a new scheme to make EVs more affordable for Canadians, that could lead to 75% of new sales being EVs instead of 100% by 2035.

The US$2.3 billion programme provides incentives of up to US$5,000 for EVs and US$2,500 for PHEVs to try and stem the cost somewhat. These rebate values are only available for 2026 and will reduce after 2026 until 2030. The PHEVs must be under US$50,000 to be eligible and made by countries that Canada has free trade agreements with, so excludes Chinese-made vehicles. No price cap will apply to Canadian-made vehicles. With the new incentives, the government aims to achieve up to 75% of new EV sales by 2035, and 90% by 2040.

Mexico's growing role in the North American EV market

Whilst it's currently a smaller market, Mexico's EV market growth is projected to have the highest CAGR in the coming years, so it represents a significant opportunity for EV makers and EV charging companies to take advantage of an emerging market. Mexico's EV charging infrastructure is also emerging in line with the industry and has not yet been as well-established as other countries, such as the US. However, major cities like Mexico City, Monterrey, and Guadalajara are becoming early adopters of EVs and new EV infrastructure.

Federal support in Mexico is still relatively limited, but local initiatives and private investments are currently driving EV growth. The Mexican Energy Regulation Commission has stated that targets have been set for 1 million EVs on the road by 2030. However, for this to become a reality, there will need to be significant investment into new EV charging infrastructure to support the growing number of EVs. Whilst incentives for consumers have not been promoted as much at a government level, the Mexican government has been investing in infrastructure upgrades to support the growth of the EV charging station market.

Mexico EV market growth projections

Next MSC has stated that the Mexico EV market growth could reach a CAGR of 23.54%, making it the highest growth market in North America. According to Next MSC, this is being driven by trade agreements, export-oriented industrial expansion and increased urbanisation, as well as an increase in environmental sustainability awareness. Partnerships with private companies and import duty reductions are also playing their part.

Markets and Markets has stated that Mexico's EV market was valued at US$6,948.4 million in 2025 and is predicted to reach US$10,453.6 million by 2030, and it's expected that Mexico will capture a significant share of North American EV production and sales by 2030.

Mexico Business News has stated that sales of EVs and hybrids (both mild and PHEV) have increased by over 44% year-on-year into the first half of 2026, reaching over 95,000 units sold compared to just 65,000 units in the same period last year. Over 170 electrified models are currently available in Mexico, including 110 full EVs and 60 PHEVs and extended-range electric vehicles (EREVs). Many of the brands sold in Mexico come from Asian markets including Chinese brands and Japanese brands, and within the first five months of 2026, just over 77,000 units had been sold, and the breakdown was around 54,000 mild hybrids, 12,000 PHEVs, and 11,500 full EVs, showing that the market is still more dominated by hybrids than full EVs.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) states that 75% of Latin America EV sales come from Mexico and Brazil. According to the IEA, electric car sales in Mexico tripled in 2025, with imports from China representing 85% of all electric car sales (up from 60% in 2024). Because of the Chinese imports, the price competitiveness of battery EVs and PHEVs increased massively against ICE vehicles and was a key market growth driver—with 80% of all battery EV and 90% of PHEV sales being Chinese-made models. In 2025, the Chinese EVs had a similar price point to ICE vehicles, with PHEVs being 10% cheaper than the average ICE car. BYD was by far the most popular automaker in 2025, capturing 70% of the market.

However, there could be a shift towards more domestic production in the coming years as new tariffs imposed this year (up to 50%) will hit the automobile industry from countries that do not have a free-trade agreement with Mexico, and this includes China. Despite the tariffs, as of July 2026, Reuters has reported that Chinese brands have still captured 17% of Mexico's new vehicle sales, with Chinese-brand vehicle sales rising above 137,000 units in the first half of this year. However, the effects of the tariffs are starting to be seen as there has been a 43% decline in import of Chinese vehicles in the first five months compared to last year.

Top EV charging networks in North America

According to the Department of Energy's Alternative Fuels Data Center (AFDC), the US now has over 250,000 public EV charging ports in operation today. There are many EV charging network operators in North America, with some of the major players being ChargePoint, Electrify America, EVgo, Tesla, and BP Pulse.

There are also many other companies contributing to the improvement and expansion of EV infrastructure. For example, XCharge and JOJO partnered this year to deploy a high-power EV charging network across Illinois, installing 800 kW ultra-fast chargers across nine locations. However, some companies, such as Shell, have scaled back, and Shell has since halted operations on its 2,000-charger Volta network, with some of it being sold off to JOLT.

However, 2025 continued to show a significant increase in the number of installed DC ultra-fast chargers across the US, with Tesla installing 45% of all charging points in Q3. The AFDC shows that the 250,000+ individual charging hookups are spread out across 80,000+ station locations. This includes over 180,000 level 2 chargers and 73,000 DC fast chargers. Around 50,000 new chargers were added in the last few months, meaning that there is considerable growth currently ongoing in the US and is being driven by various EV charging network operators.

EV charger installation is also growing in many locations, from commercial hubs to residential complexes, but the biggest growth shift has been seen within highway and freight corridors. The shift towards freight corridors is being driven by companies such as Pilot Flying J, with their fast-charging network in collaboration with EVgo and General Motors. This fast-charging network has now surpassed over 300 DC fast charging stations and over 1,300 fast charging stalls across 40 states. These fast-charging stations now cover many of the major freight routes and cover roughly 75% of the contiguous US.

ChargePoint

ChargePoint holds the largest market share in the US, with almost 82,000 charging ports across 46,500 charging station locations. ChargePoint holds the largest market share of level 2 infrastructure in the US, with over 76,000 charging connections. ChargePoint also recently announced expansion plans through two new charging infrastructure partnerships targeting the US market. These agreements will add an extra 200 public charging ports in the Southeast US and will deploy ultra-fast charging stations in 12 highway plazas in Pennsylvania and New York.

Electrify America

Electrify America has a smaller overall market share but Electrify America does have a high market share of individual DC ultra-fast chargers across North America. To date, Electrify America has over 5,600 individual DC fast chargers across 1,080 charging stations in North America. These figures include both Electrify America and Electrify Canada charging locations and includes over 1,100 chargers with 350 kW charging speeds.

These charging stations are located across 47 US states, Washington DC, and six Canadian provinces. The largest allocation of charging stations is in California, with over 360 charging stations, but Electrify America has also recently expanded into previously unserved regions, including North Dakota, Hawaii, South Dakota, and Wyoming. Most of the charging ports and charging stations are located in the US but Electrify Canada does operate 248 ultra-fast charging ports across 52 charging stations within the six Canadian provinces—but they are primarily concentrated in major transit corridors around Quebec, Alberta, Ontario, and British Columbia.

EVgo

EVgo currently operates over 5,280 public DC fast charging ports at more than 1,200 charging stations across 47 US states. This includes 3,990 EVgo branded chargers, and over 1,100 fleet-dedicated charging ports that have been built for third parties—including Pilot Flying J. Currently, over 40% of the US population lives within 10 miles of an EVgo charger, and alongside travel corridors, EVgo are also expanding their charging capabilities at major retail storefronts across the US.

Following a pilot programme in 2025, and the installation of 100 North American Charging Standard (NACS) connectors across 22 major metropolitan areas, EVgo are now introducing over 500 NACS with 500 kW charging speeds that are compatible with both Tesla and future NACS vehicles (estimates are that 80% of EVs will have NACS charging capabilities in North America by 2030).

Tesla

Tesla leads the ultra-fast charging market in North America, with 38,000 supercharger ports located across 3,000 supercharger stations across North America. Tesla's chargers also account for 50% of DC fast charging ports across North America and all use NACS connectors.

BP Pulse

BP Pulse is smaller than many of the other companies but still has over 90 charging stations spanning 19 states in the US. BP Pulse has also developed large-scale charging hub setups near LAX airport (48 charging bays) and Houston Hobby Airport (40 charging bays). BP Pulse chargers offer up to 400 kW charging speed and BP Pulse has just moved into Alabama for the first time, and has expanded their rollout of chargers in California, Oregon, Texas, and Washington.

What this means for EV infrastructure investment decisions

There is considerable potential in the North American market. From the vast networks being built and expanded upon in the US to the high expected CAGRs of Mexico, there is significant potential for EV charging infrastructure investment in 2026. Within this growth, there are still challenges to navigate, as the policy across the countries continues to change quickly, and fleet operators buying EVs and installing charging stations need to keep up with these continually changing policies. For many fleet operators, particularly in the US, federal incentives have become almost non-existent, so there is going to be a greater reliance on keeping up with state level incentives as these are where the biggest savings can be made on both EV procurement and charger installation.

There are now more vendors than ever operating in the North American market, which means that a range of chargers are available to meet different budgets and charging speed requirements depending on size and operational requirements of the fleet. Many EV charging companies are starting to focus on freight and fleet corridors, giving fleet operators more options for charging during working hours. With large public infrastructure developments, the need for private chargers may become less desirable, as many ultra-fast chargers can refill enough range during a break to ensure that the vehicle reaches the next scheduled break. Others may still want onsite chargers for overnight charging. With EV sales increasing in the US market, more options are becoming available to the public and fleet owners, and it’s expected that investments and charger installation are set to grow throughout North America in the next 10 years.

text:
Gov. Janet Mills says the Trump administration is putting Maine's environment at risk by relaxing the nation's emissions standards.

The Environmental Protection Agency is repealing rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas, an action the agency said would save industry more than $300 billion in costs and help “unleash” American energy.

The EPA also proposed a separate step to prevent future administrations from regulating climate pollution from power plants.

Elimination of the power plant rule, first proposed last year, represents a fundamental shift from efforts by Democratic Presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama to address climate change and clean up industrial pollution.

Also read: Environmental groups sue EPA over illegal repeal of climate regulations

EPA officials said the change would allow utilities to make the best decisions for their ratepayers rather than be forced to close aging or inefficient plants.

Mills is critical, saying the added emissions "endanger public health and contribute to the increasingly stronger storms that have washed out roads in the Oxford Hills, flooded towns like Madison and Skowhegan, and washed working waterfronts into the sea."

She continued, "The president calls climate change a 'hoax.' The real hoax is his promise to lower costs while he puts Maine taxpayers on the hook for future storm damage."

text:
Huge EV battery plant to have 'uplift' in builders

The number of construction workers at the site of Britain's biggest electric vehicle (EV) battery factory is expected to increase in the coming months.

Up to 2,900 workers are expected at the Agratas plant near Bridgwater, Somerset, this autumn as the company said the first building was nearly water-tight and internal fit-out could get under way.

Meanwhile, Tata Group and Agratas Chairman, Natarajan Chandrasekaran, has visited the site days after Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), also owned by Tata, announced it would cut 4,000 jobs - partly blamed on JLR's delayed transition to EVs.

The Somerset plant expects to start producing batteries in late-2027, initially for JLR vehicles.

A spokesperson for Agratas said: "The increase in the construction workforce reflects the changing nature of the work.

"As we move into this next phase, we will have a greater number of specialist trades working across the building to deliver the internal systems and infrastructure required for the facility.

"The site visit was an opportunity for our group chairman to see that progress first-hand as the project moves into this increasingly intensive phase of construction."

A recent update report to Somerset Council said there would be an "uplift" in workers from this autumn with 2,500 to 2,900 construction workers expected on site.

In June, a new construction company, TSL, was appointed to replace Sir Robert McAlpine.

Sir Robert McAlpine said it had "mutually agreed to part ways" with Agratas, having "successfully completed" the first phase of the battery manufacturing facility in Somerset.

text:
A new report from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) has found that the United States now has enough solar capacity to power more than 50 million homes across the country.

The new findings mean that solar energy is cumulatively capable of powering more than one-third of all households nationwide. Part of the U.S. Solar Market Insight report from SEIA and Wood Mackenzie, the findings show that the solar industry added 11.4 GWdc of new electricity generating capacity during this year’s second quarter, a 45 percent year-over-year increase, and a 43 percent increase over the first quarter of this year.

“Solar and storage have grown to a scale most Americans have yet to fully realize, and we simply can’t meet America’s growing energy needs without these technologies,” SEIA CEO Tim Pawlenty said.

Utility-scale solar grew 61 percent year-over-year with nearly 10 GWdc (9.6) installed. The quarter reflects developers moving quickly to bring projects online ahead of the July 2026 deadline for tax credit eligibility. Substantial solar projects will continue through the years ahead, the report said.

Together, solar and storage account for 70 percent of all new capacity added to the grid in the first half of 2026, the report found. The report’s forecasts show that the US solar market will nearly double over the next five years, demonstrating the industry’s ability to deliver large amounts of power to meet the country’s rising energy demand while strengthening grid reliability and managing costs.

“Robust project pipelines and the build out of safe-harbored capacity will sustain roughly 44 GWdc of annual capacity through 2031,” Caitlin Connelly, senior analyst at Wood Mackenzie, said. “However, permitting and the post-ITC transition remain significant headwinds.”
